122:
## 2. Commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta
## Commentary on the Talk of the King's Ministers

The words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" constitute the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. In this sutta, the following is the sequential commentary on the words. "Rājagahe" means in the city of that name. It is called "Rājagaha" because it was possessed and governed by such figures as King Mandhātu and the treasurer Mahāgovinda. Other teachers also provide different explanations for this term; however, what benefit is there in those? This is merely the name of that city. Furthermore, this city exists as a city during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch). At other times, it is deserted and remains as a forest area possessed by Yakkhas, serving as their dwelling place.

The word "viharati" (dwells), in a general sense, indicates being endowed with one of the modes of dwelling, such as balancing the postures (iriyāpatha), the divine dwellings (dibba-vihāra), the Brahma dwellings (brahma-vihāra), or the noble dwellings (ariya-vihāra). In this context, however, it indicates being engaged in one of the postures, namely standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. Therefore, whether the Blessed One is standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, He should be understood simply as "dwelling." This is because the Blessed One interrupts the fatigue of one posture with another posture, thereby maintaining the physical body (attabhāva) so that it does not collapse; for this reason, it is said "viharati."

The phrase "Jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane" (in Jīvaka Komārabhacca's mango grove) indicates the dwelling place situated near the village where the Blessed One resorts for alms. Therefore, in the passage "He was dwelling at Rājagaha, in Jīvaka Komārabhacca's mango grove," the meaning should be understood as: He was dwelling in the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca, which is near Rājagaha. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity.

In that context, he is called "Jīvaka" because he lives (jīvati). He is called "Komārabhacca" because he was raised by a prince (kumārena bhata). As the Blessed One has stated: "Friends, what is this surrounded by crows?" When asked, they replied, "Your Majesty, it is a child." "Friends, does he live?" When asked, they replied, "Your Majesty, he lives." "Friends, if that is so, take that child to our inner palace and give him to the nurses to be raised." Based on the word "he lives" (jīvati), they named the child "Jīvaka." Because he was caused to be raised by the prince, they named him "Komārabhacca." This is just a summary here. The detailed account has already appeared in the Jīvaka-vatthu of the Vinaya Mahāvagga Khandhaka. The analytical discussion (vinicchaya-kathā) of it is also stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary.
123:
On one occasion, this Jīvaka, having administered a purgative to the Blessed One's body which was suffering from an excess of humors (phlegm), and having offered a pair of cloths from the Siveyya country, became established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) at the conclusion of the discourse of appreciation for the cloths. Then he thought: "I should go to attend upon the Buddha two or three times a day. This Veḷuvana monastery is too far, but my mango grove park is much closer. What if I were to have a monastery built for the Blessed One here?"

In that mango grove, he prepared night quarters, day quarters, caves, huts, pavilions, and so forth. Having caused a Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi) suitable for the Blessed One to be built, he had the mango grove enclosed by a wall eighteen cubits high and the color of copper plates. Then, having served the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with robes and alms-food, he poured the water of donation and offered the monastery. With reference to that monastery, it is said: "in Jīvaka Komārabhacca's mango grove."

"Aḍ္ဎတေဠသေဟိ ဘိက္ခုသတေဟိ" (with twelve hundred and fifty monks) means with thirteen hundred monks less fifty. In the words such as "Rājā" (King), he is called a "Rājā" because he shines with his own sovereign prosperity and because he pleases (rañjeti) and prospers the great multitude through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). He is called "Māgadha" because he is the lord of the Magadha country. He is called "Ajātasattu" because soothsayers predicted that even before he was born, he would be the king's enemy (ajāta-sattu).

It is said that while he was in the womb, such a pregnancy craving (dohala) arose in the Queen: "O, that I might drink the blood from the King's right arm!" She thought, "A craving has arisen for a difficult thing; it is not possible to tell anyone," and being unable to speak of it, she became thin and pale. The King asked her: "Dear, your physical appearance is not its normal color; what is the reason?" "Do not ask, Great King," she said. But the King persisted in various ways, saying, "Dear, if you do not tell your desire to me, to whom will you tell it?" and thus made her speak. Having heard it, he said, "Foolish woman, why did you consider this a difficult matter?" He then summoned a physician, had his arm opened with a small golden blade, took the blood in a golden bowl, mixed it with water, and gave it to her to drink. When the soothsayers heard of this, they predicted: "This fetus will be the King's enemy; the King will be killed by him." When the Queen heard this, she thought, "The one born from my womb will kill the King," and wishing to induce an abortion, she went to the garden and had her belly massaged, but the fetus did not fall. She went again and again and had the same done. The King [asked] for what purpose...
124:
When the King repeatedly investigated why the Queen went to the garden so often, he learned the reason and said, "Queen, it is not yet clear whether there is a son or a daughter in your womb. If the people in this Jambudīpa come to know that you have treated the child born of your own womb in such a way, a great mass of demerit will be revealed. Do not do this." He then forbade her and provided guards. When the time came for her to give birth, she thought, "I will kill him." Even then, the guards took the child away from the mother. Later, when the prince reached adulthood, they showed him to the Queen. Upon seeing the prince, she felt a mother's love for him and, because of that intense love, was no longer able to kill him. Gradually, the King appointed his son to the position of Crown Prince (Uparāja).

At one time, Devadatta went into seclusion and thought, "The following of the Venerable Sāriputta is large; the following of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is large; the following of the Venerable Mahākassapa is also large. Thus, these elders are each leaders of their own groups. I, too, shall lead a group." He thought, "It is not possible to create a following without gain. Now, I will generate gain." Following the method mentioned in the Cūḷavagga Khandhaka, he inspired Prince Ajātasattu by performing a miracle. Knowing that Prince Ajātasattu, who came to serve him with five hundred chariots every evening and morning, was very trusting, he approached him one day and said, "Prince, in former times, humans were long-lived, but now they are short-lived. Therefore, Prince, kill your father and become King; I will kill the Blessed One and become the Buddha." Thus, he urged the prince to kill his father.

Prince Ajātasattu thought, "The Venerable Devadatta possesses great power; there is nothing unknown to this venerable one." He tied a small dagger to his thigh and, in broad daylight, being fearful, agitated, apprehensive, and terrified, he entered the inner palace and behaved in the unseemly manner already described. Then the ministers seized and interrogated him, and after consulting together, saying, "The prince should be killed, Devadatta should be killed, and all the monks should be killed," they decided to act according to the King's command and informed the King.

The King stripped the ministers who wanted to kill them of their ranks and placed the ministers who did not want to kill them in high positions. He then asked the prince, "Prince, why do you wish to kill me?" "Great King, I desire the kingship," he replied. The King then gave the kingship to Prince Ajātasattu.
125:
Prince Ajātasattu informed Devadatta, "My heart's desire has been fulfilled." Then Devadatta said to him, "You think you have accomplished your task like a man who puts a jackal inside a drum and beats it. In just a few days, your father will reflect on the insult you have committed and will become King again himself." "Venerable sir, if that is so, what should I do?" he asked. "Kill him by cutting off the root," Devadatta replied. "Venerable sir, is it not true that my father is not one to be killed with a weapon?" he asked. "Then kill him by cutting off his food," Devadatta said.

Ajātasattu had his father placed in a heating house (tāpana-geha). A heating house is a smoke-house built for the purpose of punishment. He said, "Do not allow anyone to see him except my mother." The Queen placed food in a small golden bowl, carried it in her waistband, and entered. The King ate that food and sustained himself. Ajātasattu asked, "How does my father sustain himself?" and upon hearing the news, he said, "Do not allow my mother to enter by carrying food in her waistband." From that day on, the Queen placed food in her hair knot and entered. Hearing of this, he said, "Do not allow her to enter with her hair tied in a knot." Then she placed food in golden slippers, sealed them, and entered wearing the slippers. The King sustained himself with that food. Again, he asked, "How does he sustain himself?" and hearing the news, he said, "Do not allow her to enter even wearing slippers." From that day on, the Queen bathed in scented water, smeared her body with the four sweets (catumadhura), put on her cloak, and entered. The King sustained himself by licking the Queen's body. Again, he asked and heard the news, and said, "From today, forbid my mother from entering." The Queen stood at the door and cried out, "Lord Bimbisāra, when this person was young, you did not allow him to be killed; you yourself raised your own enemy. Now, this is the last time I shall see you. From today, I shall not have the chance to see you. If I have any fault, please forgive me, my Lord." She wept and lamented, then turned back.

From that day on, the King had no food. The King sustained himself through the bliss of the Path and Fruit and by walking meditation. His physical body shone exceedingly bright. Ajātasattu asked, "Friends, how does my father sustain himself?" and hearing, "Great King, he sustains himself by walking meditation, and his body is exceedingly radiant," he thought, "Now I will destroy that King's walking meditation." He sent barbers, saying, "Slice my father's feet with a razor, smear them with salt and oil, and roast them over smokeless acacia embers." When the King saw them, he thought, "Surely my son must have been persuaded by someone; these people are my..."
126:
King Bimbisāra thought, "These barbers have come to tend to my beard." Those barbers approached, paid homage, and stood there. When asked, "Why have you come?" they reported the message (the order). When told, "Do as your king wishes," they said, "Sit, O King," and after paying homage to the king, they said, "Great King, we are carrying out the king's command; do not be angry with us. Such anger is not fitting for righteous kings (dhammarāja) like you."

Then, holding his ankles with their left hands and a razor with their right hands, they sliced the soles of his feet, smeared them with salted oil, and roasted them over glowing khadirā coals. It is said that in the past, King Bimbisāra had walked on the terrace of a cetiya wearing sandals, and had also stepped on a mat spread for sitting with unwashed feet; this suffering in his feet was the result of that unwholesome deed. Intense pain arose in the king. While repeatedly reflecting, "Wonderful is the Buddha! Wonderful is the Dhamma! Wonderful is the Saṅgha!" the king withered away like a flower cast upon a cetiya terrace and was reborn in the Cātumahārājika deva realm as a yakkha named Janavasabha, an attendant of King Vessavaṇa.

On that very day, a son was born to King Ajātasattu. Two letters arrived at the same moment: one to announce the birth of the son and the other to announce the death of the father. The ministers thought, "We will first announce the birth of the son," and they placed that letter in the king's hand. At that very moment, fatherly love arose in the king, shaking his entire body and reaching even to the marrow of his bones. At that instant, he realized the virtues of his own father, thinking, "When I was born, such love must have surely arisen in my father as well." He said, "Go, friends, and release my father."

"Why should he be released, O King?" they said, and placed the other letter (regarding the father's death) in his hand. Upon hearing that news, he wept and went to his mother, asking, "Mother, when I was born, did my father have love for me?" The mother said, "Foolish son, what are you saying? When you were young, a boil developed on your finger. At that time, when they could not stop your crying, they took you to your father who was sitting in the hall of judgment. Your father put your finger in his mouth. The boil burst right in his mouth. Then, out of love for you, your father swallowed that pus mixed with blood without spitting it out. Such was the nature of your father's love." He wept and lamented, and then performed the funeral rites for his father.

Devadatta also approached King Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, command men who will deprive the ascetic Gotama of life." He sent the men provided by King Ajātasattu, and he himself climbed Gijjhakūṭa Mountain to roll down a rock using a machine, and also had the elephant Nālāgiri released. Although he tried to kill the Blessed One by various means, he was unable to do so. His gains and honor declined, and when he requested the five practices and was refused, he thought he would win over the people with those five practices and committed a schism in the Saṅgha. When Sāriputta and Moggallāna departed taking their followers with them, he vomited hot blood from his mouth and for nine months...
127:
Devadatta also approached King Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, command men who will deprive the ascetic Gotama of life." Having sent the men provided by the king, he himself climbed Gijjhakūṭa Mountain and rolled down a rock with a machine, and also had the elephant Nālāgiri released. However, he was unable to kill the Blessed One by any means. As his gains and honor declined, he requested the five practices (vatthu), and not receiving them, he planned to win over the people with those five practices and committed a schism in the Saṅgha. When the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna departed taking their followers with them, he vomited hot blood from his mouth and lay on a sickbed for nine months. Filled with remorse, he asked, "Where does the Teacher dwell now?" When told, "In Jetavana," he said, "Carry me on a bed and show me to the Teacher." While being carried, because he had not performed any wholesome deed worthy of seeing the Blessed One, the earth split into two near the pond by Jetavana Monastery, and he was swallowed by the earth and established in the Great Hell (Mahāniraya). This is a brief summary here. The detailed account appears in the Khandhaka of the Vinaya. Since it is already mentioned in the Khandhaka, it is not fully repeated here. Thus, because the soothsayers pointed out even before his birth that he would be the king's enemy, he is called "Ajātasattu."

Regarding "Vedehiputta": This King Ajātasattu was the son of the daughter of the Kosala king, not the son of the Videha king. "Vedehī," however, is a designation for one who is wise. As it is said: "The householder Vedehikā," and "The Venerable Ānanda is a Vedeha-muni (a wise sage)." In this context, the etymological meaning is: "Veda" refers to knowledge, as it is that by which one knows. One who strives or exerts effort through that knowledge (veda) is "Vedehī." The son of that Vedehī is "Vedehiputta."

"Tadahu" means it happened on that day; it means on that day. "Uposatha" is so called because beings dwell (upavasanti) in observance on this day. "Dwell in observance" means they live endowed with virtue (sīla) or by fasting (anasana). To extract the meanings in this context: In passages such as "Come, friends, let us go to the Uposatha," Uposatha refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In passages such as "Visākhā, the Uposatha endowed with eight factors is thus observed," it refers to virtue (sīla). In passages such as "For the pure, it is always Phaggu; for the pure, it is always Uposatha," it refers to fasting (upavāsa). In passages such as "The Naga King named Uposatha," it refers to a proper name.
128: By definition, in sentences such as "Monks, on that Uposatha day, from a monastery where there are monks (one should not go to a monastery where there are no monks)," the day on which the Uposatha is observed is called "Uposatha." Here too, only that Uposatha day is intended. That Uposatha day is of three kinds: the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth. To exclude the other two days, it is called "the fifteenth day." Therefore, it is said, "Because they observe the Uposatha on this day, it is called Uposatha." "Komudiyā" means because there are white water lilies (kumuda). At that time, it is said that the white water lilies are in full bloom; because those lilies exist on this full moon day, it is called "Komudī." "Cātumāsiniyā" means "Cātumāsī" because it is the end of the four months (of the rainy season). Here, however, it is called "Cātumāsinī." It is called "Puṇṇā" because it is full due to the completion of the month, the completion of the season, and the completion of the year. "Mā" refers to the moon; because the moon is full on this day, it is called "Puṇṇamā." In this way, the meaning of the two words "Puṇṇāya Puṇṇamāya" should be understood. "Rājāmacca-parivuto" means that on a night illuminated by the rising radiance of the full moon, which is free from the four defilements, the king is surrounded by his ministers, as if the quarters were being washed by streams of milk flowing from silver pots, and as if strewn everywhere with pearl necklaces, jasmine garlands, fine cloth, and clusters of white water lilies falling from a silver celestial mansion. "Upari-pāsāda-vara-gato" means having reached the upper part of the noble palace. He sits on a golden throne with a raised white parasol, fit only for noble persons. Why is he sitting there? It is to dispel sleep. From the day this king made an effort (to kill) his father, as soon as he closes his eyes saying, "I will go to sleep," he wakes up crying out as if being pierced by a hundred spears. When asked, "What is this?" he says nothing. Therefore, sleep is unpleasant for him, and he sits there to dispel sleep. Alternatively, on that day, a festival had been proclaimed. The entire city was sprinkled and swept, strewn with white sand, and every house door was decorated with five-colored flowers, parched rice, and full water pots. All quarters were decorated with raised banners and flags, and adorned with rows of brightly lit lamps. The city was crowded with people enjoying the festival games in the main streets and alleys. It is said that he was also sitting there because it was a festival day. However, even after saying this, the conclusion is made: "For royalty, there is always a festival; in truth, this king sits there only to dispel sleep."
129:
"He uttered an inspired utterance" (udānaṃ udānesi) means he spoke words of joy. For example, when oil cannot be contained in a jar and overflows, that oil is called 'avaseka' (or āseka). When water cannot be contained in a tank and overflows, that water is called 'ogha' (a flood). Similarly, when words of joy cannot be contained in the heart, becoming excessive and unable to remain within, they come out; such speech is called 'Udāna.' It means he emitted such speech born of rapture (pīti).

"Dosinā" refers to a faultless night. It means a night free from the five obscurations: clouds, fog, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. Therefore, the five words beginning with "Ramaṇīyā" are words of praise for the night. It is called "Ramaṇīyā" (delightful) because it delights the minds of the people. It is called "Abhirūpā" (beautiful) because it has an extremely beautiful appearance, being illuminated by moonlight free from the aforementioned five faults. It is called "Dassanīyā" (lovely to behold) because it is fit to be looked at. It is called "Pāsādikā" (pleasing) because it gladdens the mind. It is called "Lakkhaññā" (auspicious/noteworthy) because it is fit to be a mark for the day, month, and so on.

"Kaṃ nu khvajja" should be broken down as "Kaṃ nu kho ajja" (Whom indeed today?). In the phrase "Samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā," he is called a "Samaṇa" because he has stilled evil, and a "Brāhmaṇa" because he has put away evil. "Yaṃ no payirupāsato" is a grammatical variation. It means: "If we were to attend upon such a Samaṇa or Brāhmaṇa by asking questions, and having heard the sweet Dhamma, our minds would become clear—how good that would be!" Thus, with all these words, the king made an indirect hint (obhāsa-nimitta). To whom did he make it? To Jīvaka. For what purpose? For the purpose of seeing the Blessed One. Is he unable to go to see the Blessed One on his own? Yes, he is unable. Why? Because of his great crime.

For that king had killed his own father, who was a noble disciple and a supporter of the Blessed One. Also, Devadatta, depending on that king, had done much harm to the Blessed One. Thus, because of this great crime, he did not dare to go on his own. Jīvaka, however, was a supporter of the Blessed One; the king made the indirect hint thinking, "I will see the Blessed One under the protection of Jīvaka." Does Jīvaka know, "This indirect hint is intended for me"? Yes, he knows. Then why did he remain silent? It was for the purpose of cutting off the distraction of speech.

In that assembly, many supporters of the six [heretical] teachers were gathered. Because they attended upon teachers who had no proper training, they themselves were untrained. When I [Jīvaka] make an effort to speak of the virtues of the Blessed One, they might stand up in between and speak of their own teachers'...
130:
If I were to begin speaking of the qualities of the Blessed One, these ministers would repeatedly stand up and speak of the qualities of their own teachers. In that case, the discourse on the qualities of my teacher, the Blessed One, would not reach its conclusion. Moreover, the King, having approached their teachers and realized their worthlessness, would become displeased with their praise and would question me. At that time, without any distraction, I will praise the qualities of the Blessed One and take the King to the presence of the Blessed One. Knowing this, I remained silent to prevent any interruption.

Those ministers also thought: "Today the King praises the night with five statements. Surely, he wishes to approach some recluse or brahmin, ask a question, and listen to the Dhamma. If he gains faith after hearing the Dhamma of a certain teacher, he will offer great honor to that teacher. If a minister's teacher becomes the King's teacher, it will be beneficial for that minister."

151-152. Having thought thus, they each began to praise their own teachers, thinking, "I will speak of the virtues of my own teacher-recluse and take the King there; I will go." Therefore, it is said: "When this was said, another royal minister..." and so on. In that passage, "Pūraṇa" is the name of that person who claimed to be a teacher. "Kassapa" is his clan name (gotta). It is said that he was born when a certain family was one slave short of a hundred (the ninety-ninth), so they named him "Pūraṇa" (the Filler). Because he was an auspicious slave (maṅgaladāsa), no one said "it is poorly done" to him, and even if he did not work, no one said "he did not do it." That Pūraṇa thought, "Why should I live here?" and fled. Then, thieves stripped him of his clothes.

That Pūraṇa, not even knowing how to cover himself with leaves or grass, entered a village naked, just as he was born. When people saw him, they approached him with cakes, rice, and so on, saying, "This recluse is an Arahant, one of few wishes; there is no one like him." Pūraṇa thought, "This benefit has arisen because I am not wearing a robe." From that day on, even when he obtained a robe, he did not wear it; he accepted that very nakedness as his monkhood. Five hundred other men also went forth under him. Referring to him, it is said: "Pūraṇa Kassapa."

He is called "Saṅghī" because he has a community (saṅgha) of monks. He is called "Gaṇī" because he has such a group (gaṇa). He is called "Gaṇācariya" because he is the teacher of that group by way of teaching conduct and training. "Ñāta" means he is well-known and famous. He reached fame as "one of few wishes and easily satisfied." He is called "Yasassī" because he has a following. "Titthakara" means one who establishes his own doctrine. "Sādhusammata" means one who is regarded as "this person is good, excellent, a virtuous man." "Bahujanassa" means regarded by the multitude of uninstructed, foolish worldlings. He is called "Rattaññū" because he knows many nights that have passed since his going forth. Since the beginning of his going forth...
131:
That Pūraṇa Kassapa, being easily satisfied, did not even wear clothes due to his fewness of wishes. Because he possessed such fame and following, he is called 'Yasassī' (famous). 'Titthakara' means a founder of a sect (one who creates his own doctrine). 'Sādhusammata' means one who is regarded as 'this person is good, excellent, a virtuous man.' 'Bahujanassa' refers to the multitude of uninstructed, foolish worldlings. He is called 'Rattaññū' (one of long standing) because he knows many nights have passed since his going forth. He is called 'Cirapabbajita' because it has been a long time since his going forth. This is said because the words of one who has recently gone forth are not reliable. 'Addhagata' means one who has traveled a long journey, implying he has outlived two or three reigns of kings. 'Vayoanuppatta' means one who has reached the final stage of life (old age). Both of these are said with reference to the fact that 'the words of a young person are not reliable.'

'He remained silent' (tuṇhī ahosi) is like a man who wants to eat a sweet, golden-colored ripe mango, but when it is brought and placed in his hand, he sees it is a poisonous fruit (kājara). The King, who wished to hear a sweet Dhamma discourse endowed with qualities such as jhāna and higher knowledge (abhiññā) and connected with the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), was displeased just by seeing Pūraṇa Kassapa earlier; now, hearing the praise of his qualities, he became even more displeased and remained silent. Although he was displeased, he thought: 'If I threaten this man, grab him by the neck, and have him thrown out, others will be afraid that "the King does this to whoever speaks," and no one else will say anything.' Thus, enduring those unpleasant words, he remained silent. Then another minister thought, 'I will speak of the qualities of my own teacher,' and began to speak. Therefore, it is said: 'Then indeed another...' and so on. All of this should be understood in the manner already described.

In this context, 'Makkhali' is his name. He received the second name 'Gosāla' because he was born in a cowshed. It is said that while he was walking on muddy ground carrying a pot of oil, his master said, 'Dear, do not slip (mā khali).' Due to negligence, he slipped and fell, and out of fear of his master, he began to run away. The master ran after him and caught the hem of his garment. He abandoned the cloth and fled naked (acelaka). The rest of the story is similar to that of Pūraṇa.

'Ajita' is his name. He is called 'Kesakambala' because he wears a blanket made of human hair. Combining these two names, he is called 'Ajita Kesakambala'.
132:
It is so stated. In that name (Ajita Kesakambala), 'Kesakambala' refers to a blanket made of human hair. There is no garment more loathsome than a blanket made of human hair. Thus, the Blessed One taught: 'Monks, of all woven garments, the hair-blanket is said to be the most loathsome. Monks, a hair-blanket is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly in color, foul-smelling, and harsh to the touch.' (A. Ni. 3.138).

'Pakudha' is his name, and 'Kaccāyana' is his clan (gotta). Combining the name and clan, he is called Pakudha Kaccāyana. He is one who habitually avoids cold water; even after defecating, he does not perform the act of washing with water. He only performs washing if he obtains hot water or sour gruel. If he happens to cross a river or water on the road, he thinks, 'My virtue is broken,' and after making a sand stupa and re-undertaking his virtue, he proceeds. Such a person holds an inglorious view.

'Sañjaya' is his name. Because he is the son of Belaṭṭha, he is called Belaṭṭhaputta.

'We have no defilements that bind, no defilements that obstruct; we are free from the bonds of defilements'—because of this doctrine he frequently asserts, he is named 'Nigaṇṭha' (the Bondless). Because he is the son of Nāṭa, he is called Nāṭaputta.

## Explanation of the Account of Jīvaka Komārabhacca

Regarding the words 'Atha kho rājā' (Then the King): It is said that when the King heard the words of those ministers, he thought, 'Whosoever's words I do not wish to hear, they alone speak. But he whose words I wish to hear, this Jīvaka remains silent like a Garuḍa king that has drunk dragon-fat. It is indeed a loss for me.' Then this thought occurred to the King: 'Jīvaka is the attendant of the peaceful Blessed One, the Buddha; he himself is peaceful. Therefore, like a monk endowed with proper conduct, he sits in silence. This Jīvaka will not speak unless I speak to him. Indeed, while an elephant is trampling, one must seize the elephant's foot itself.' Thinking thus, he began to converse with Jīvaka himself. Therefore, it is said, 'Atha kho rājā.' In that context, the question 'Why is he silent?' (Kiṃ tuṇhī) implies: 'These ministers do not have enough mouth to speak the praises of the monks they personally attend. Do you not have a monk you attend like them? Are you poor? Did my father not give you wealth and status? Or are you without faith?'
133:
Then this thought occurred to Jīvaka: 'This King wishes me to speak of the virtues of the monk I attend. Now is not the time for me to remain silent. Just as these ministers, while remaining seated after paying homage to the King, spoke of the virtues of the monks they attend, it is not proper for me to speak of the virtues of my Teacher in such a manner (while seated).' Thus, rising from his seat and facing the monastery where the Blessed One resided, he paid homage with the five-point prostration. Raising his joined palms, radiant with the meeting of his ten fingernails, to his head, he said: 'Great King, do not think of me thus: "This Jīvaka approaches just any monk." Indeed, Great King, at the descent of my Teacher into his mother's womb, at his birth from his mother's womb, at his Great Renunciation, at his Enlightenment, and at his turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten thousand world systems trembled. He performed such a Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya); he performed such a descent from the deva realm. Great King, I shall speak of the virtues of my Teacher; listen with a one-pointed mind.' Having said this, he spoke the words beginning with: 'Sire, that Blessed One is an Arahaṃ, a Sammāsambuddho...' 

In that text, 'Taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ' is the accusative case (upayogavacana) used in the sense of describing someone who has reached a certain state. It means 'of that Blessed One.' 'Kalyāṇo' means endowed with beautiful qualities, meaning 'excellent.' 'Kittisaddo' means fame itself, or the sound of praise. 'Abbhuggato' means having spread and risen, pervading the world including the devas. How has it spread? As follows: 'Thus indeed is that Blessed One an Arahaṃ, a Sammāsambuddho... [pe]... Bhagavā.'

The connection of the words in that text is: That Blessed One is an Arahaṃ for this reason, a Sammāsambuddho for this reason... [pe]... a Bhagavā for this reason. It means 'for this reason and for that reason.' Among those qualities, that Blessed One should first be known as 'Arahaṃ' for these reasons: because of being far from defilements, because of having destroyed the enemies (defilements), because of having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because of being worthy of requisites and the like, and because of the absence of doing evil even in secret. Having laid down the headings (mātikā) in this manner, all these terms have been explained in detail in the 'Explanation of the Recollection of the Buddha' (Buddhānussati-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga. Therefore, the detailed explanation should be taken from that work.

Jīvaka, having concluded the meaning of each term, said: 'Thus, Great King, my Teacher is an Arahaṃ; thus he is a Sammāsambuddho... [pe]... thus he is a Bhagavā.' Then he said: 'Sire, may you attend upon that Blessed One. Perhaps, while you are attending upon that Blessed One, your mind may become clear.' Here, in saying 'May you attend upon him,' the meaning is: 'Great King, even if a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand people like you were to ask, my Teacher, the Blessed One, has the power of knowledge to answer by capturing the minds of all. Approach him boldly.'
134:
Jīvaka said, "Great King, even if a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand people like you were to ask, my Teacher (the Blessed One) has the knowledge and the power of wisdom to understand the minds of all and answer them. Great King, approach him with confidence and ask."

Upon hearing the words praising the virtues of the Blessed One, the King’s entire body was continuously suffused with the fivefold joy (pīti). At that very moment, desiring to go, he thought, "At this time, as I go to the presence of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), no one else but Jīvaka will be able to prepare the vehicles quickly." Thus, he said, "Friend Jīvaka, if that is so, have the elephant vehicles prepared."

In that passage, 'tena hi' is a particle used in the sense of urging, meaning "Friend Jīvaka, go [and do it]." Regarding the use of 'hatthiyānāni' (elephant vehicles): although there were many types of vehicles such as horse-carriages and chariots, he thought that the elephant vehicle is the most noble, and one should approach the Noble One only with a noble vehicle. Furthermore, horse-carriages and chariots are noisy and can be heard from afar, whereas even those walking step-by-step beside an elephant vehicle do not hear any noise. He also thought that one should approach the Peaceful One (the Blessed One) only with peaceful vehicles. For these reasons, he said "elephant vehicles."

'Pañcamattāni hatthinikāsatāni' means five hundred female elephants. 'Kappāpetvā' means having them prepared and ready for riding. 'Ārohaṇīyaṃ' means suitable for riding, implying elephants covered with golden ornaments. Did Jīvaka do only what the King commanded, or did he do more? He did more than what was commanded. Why? Because of his wisdom. This thought occurred to Jīvaka: "The King says he will go at this time of night, and kings have many enemies. If any danger should occur on the way, people will blame me, saying, 'How does Jīvaka listen to my words? He takes the King out even at an improper time.' They might also blame the Blessed One, saying, 'The Ascetic Gotama, thinking only that his own discourse is proceeding, teaches the Dhamma without considering the time.' Therefore, I will act in such a way that no blame arises for me or for the Blessed One, and the King's protection is well-arranged."

Then, thinking, "There is no danger for men when they are with women; I will go comfortably surrounded by women," he had the five hundred female elephants prepared. He had five hundred women take the appearance of men and said, "Surround the King while holding swords and spears." Then he thought again, "For this King, in this existence..."
135:
"...this King has no strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits (magga-phala) in this life. The Buddhas only teach the Dhamma after seeing the supporting condition. Now, I will gather a great multitude. When they are thus assembled, the Teacher will preach the Dhamma based on the supporting condition of someone [in the crowd]. That discourse will be for the benefit of the great multitude." Thus Jīvaka sent orders to various places and had the drum beaten [to announce]: "Today the King goes to the presence of the Blessed One. Let everyone, according to their own wealth, take up the protection of the King."

Then the people thought, "It is said the King is going to see the Teacher. What kind of Dhamma teaching will it be? What is the use of our festival games? We will go to that very place where the Dhamma is taught." All of them took perfumes, flowers, and so on, and stood on the road awaiting the King's arrival. Jīvaka then informed the King, "Great King, your elephant vehicles are prepared. Now, whenever you think it is the right time [to depart, please do so]." In that context, "yassa dāni kālaṃ maññasi" is a polite idiomatic expression. The meaning is: "I have done what was commanded by you. Now, you know the time for going or not going; do as you please."

'Pacceka itthiyo' means individual women; it means one woman for each elephant. 'Ukkāsu dhāriyamānāsu' means while torches were being held. 'Mahacca rājānubhāvena' means with great royal majesty. There is also the Pali reading 'mahaccā', which means 'mahatiyā' (great); this is a change of gender. Royal majesty (rājiddhi) is called 'rājānubhāva'. What was his royal majesty? It was the glory of sovereignty over two great kingdoms spanning three hundred yojanas. Although King Ajātasattu had not made a prior appointment saying, "I will visit the Tathāgata on such and such a day," at that very moment of wanting to go, five hundred women took the appearance of men, donned turbans, slung swords over their shoulders, and came out holding goads with jewel-inlaid handles. It is in reference to these five hundred women that it is said, "having mounted the individual women."

Another sixteen thousand court ladies (nāṭakitthi) surrounded the King. Beyond them were hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, and other servants. Beyond them were the palace guards and trusted men. Beyond them were sixty thousand ministers in various splendid costumes. Beyond them, adorned with various ornaments...
136:
Ninety thousand sons of ministers, like young vijjādharas (knowledge-holders) carrying various weapons in their hands, followed in the procession. At the end of those ministers' sons, ten thousand brahmins, wearing garments worth a hundred [units] and placing garments worth five hundred [units] over one shoulder, well-bathed and anointed, and adorned with various ornaments such as golden garlands, went shouting cries of victory with their right hands raised. Following those brahmins were the five-fold musical instruments. Following those instruments were rows of archers. Following those archers were herds of elephants. Following the elephants were rows of horses, their necks touching. Following the horses were chariots, side by side. Following the chariots were soldiers, their arms brushing against each other. Following those soldiers were eighteen types of guilds (military divisions), shining with ornaments suitable for them.

In this way, just as an arrow shot from the outer edge of the crowd cannot reach the King, Jīvaka Komārabhacca arranged the King's retinue and walked not far from the King himself, thinking, "If any danger arises, I shall be the first to give my life for the King." As for the number of torches, there was no limit to the hundreds or thousands; referring to such royal majesty, it is said: "With great royal majesty, he went to Jīvaka Komārabhacca's mango grove."

Regarding the phrase "Ahu deva bhayaṃ" (There was indeed fear), there are four types of fear: fear due to mental terror (cittutrāsabhaya), fear due to knowledge (ñāṇabhaya), fear due to an object (ārammaṇabhaya), and fear due to moral dread (ottappabhaya). Among them, the fear described by the method starting with "fear and terror because of birth" is called cittutrāsabhaya. The fear mentioned in the passage, "Even those [deities], having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata, for the most part, fall into fear, urgency, and terror," is called ñāṇabhaya. The fear mentioned in the passage, "Surely this terrifying and hair-raising object is coming," is called ārammaṇabhaya.

The fear described as, "The wise praise one who fears wrongdoing; they do not praise the bold in that regard. The virtuous do no evil because they fear the consequences," is called ottappabhaya. Among these four, in this context, it means that cittutrāsabhaya (mental terror) occurred. "Ahu" means it happened. "Chambhitatta" means the state of being paralyzed with fear, referring to the trembling of the whole body. "Lomahaṃsa" means horripilation, the standing up of body hairs. This horripilation can also occur due to joy (pīti) when listening to the Dhamma and so on.
137:
In times of joy, horripilation occurs because of pīti. For those of a fearful nature, it also occurs because of fear when seeing a battlefield or a demon (pisāca), etc. Here, it should be understood as horripilation due to fear (bhayalomahaṃsa).

Why was he afraid? Some teachers say it was because of the darkness. It is said that in Rājagaha, there are thirty-two main gates and sixty-four small gates. Jīvaka's mango grove is situated between the city wall and Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa). The King went out through the eastern gate and entered the shadow of the mountain; there, the mountain peak obscured the moon, and it was dark due to the mountain's shadow and the trees' shadow. However, that reason is groundless. For at that time, there was no limit to the hundreds and thousands of torches.

But this King became afraid because of the silence, becoming suspicious of Jīvaka. Jīvaka had previously told the King while still in the palace: "Great King, the Blessed One desires little noise; one should approach in silence." Therefore, the King stopped the sound of the musical instruments. The instruments were merely held; they did not even speak loudly, moving only by hand signals. In the mango grove, not even the sound of someone sneezing could be heard. Kings, by nature, delight in sound. Because of that extreme silence, he felt uneasy and developed suspicion toward Jīvaka. He thought: "This Jīvaka told me, 'In my mango grove, there are twelve hundred and fifty monks.' Now, I do not hear even the sound of a sneeze; I think he spoke falsely. This Jīvaka has led me out of the city, placed his army in front, and intends to capture me and raise the parasol of kingship for himself. This man possesses the strength of five elephants. He is walking near me, and I do not have even a single man with a weapon by my side. Alas, ruin has come upon me!"

Though he was thus afraid, he could not maintain a pretense of being unafraid. He made his state of fear clear to Jīvaka. Therefore, it is said: "Then the King... (etc.) ... there was no sound." In that passage, "Samma" is a term for addressing a friend; it means "Friend Jīvaka, are you deceiving me?" "Na palambhesi" means "Do not mislead me by saying what is not there exists." "Nigghosa" is the sound of conversation. Jīvaka said, "Do not fear, Great King." Jīvaka thought, "This King does not yet know me as one who would not deprive another of life. If I do not reassure him, he might be ruined." Wishing to reassure him firmly, he said, "Do not fear, Great King," and addressed him with "Na taṃ devā," and so on.
138:
Thinking, "If I do not reassure him, he will be ruined," and keeping his mind firm with the desire to comfort him, [Jīvaka] said, "Do not be afraid, Great King," and spoke the words beginning with "Na taṃ devā." "Abhikkama" means to go forward or to enter. Because saying it only once might not be firm enough, he said it twice in haste. He said, "Great King, lamps are burning in this assembly hall; a band of robbers does not typically stay with lamps lit. Lamps are burning in this assembly hall. Great King, proceed by the sign of these lamps."

## Commentary on the Questioning of the Fruits of Recluseship

"Nāgassa bhūmi" refers to a place where one who is riding an elephant can go; this place is called the "ground for an elephant." "Nāgā paccorohitvā" means having dismounted from the elephant at the outer gatehouse of the monastery. As soon as he set foot on the ground, the power of the Blessed One pervaded the King's entire body. At that very moment, sweat broke out from his entire body, such that his robes seemed as if they should be wrung out. Remembering his own crime, great fear arose. Being unable to go directly into the presence of the Blessed One, the King held Jīvaka's hand and, as if strolling through the park, praised the monastery, saying, "Friend Jīvaka, you have built and offered this monastery well; this part is well-made." Thus, he gradually approached the door of the assembly hall; the meaning is that he arrived there.

Why did he ask, "Friend, where is the Blessed One?" Some teachers say, "He asked because he did not know." It is said that although this King had seen the Blessed One before when he came with his father as a youth, he had not come into the presence of the Blessed One since then, having associated with evil friends, murdered his father, sent archers, and released the elephant Dhanapāla. Thus, having committed great crimes, he asked because he did not recognize Him. That argument is groundless. For the Blessed One, adorned with the great and minor marks and illuminating the entire park with six-colored rays, sat in the midst of the assembly hall surrounded by the community of monks, like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. Who would not know Him? In truth, this King asked out of his royal pride. It is the nature of royal families to ask as if they do not know, even when they do. When Jīvaka heard those words, [he thought], "This King, while standing on the earth, asks 'Where is the earth?'; while looking up at the sky, asks 'Where are the moon and sun?'; while standing at the foot of Mount Sineru..."
139:
"...while standing at the foot of Mount Sineru, asks 'Where is Sineru?'; even so, while standing before the Blessed One, the One of Ten Powers, he asks 'Where is the Blessed One?'" Thinking, "Now I will show the Blessed One to this King," Jīvaka raised his joined palms in reverence towards where the Blessed One was and said, "That is He, Great King," and so on. "Purakkhato" (surrounded) means He was sitting in front of the community of monks who sat surrounding Him.

"Approached where the Blessed One was" means he went to the place where the Blessed One was and arrived in His presence. "Stood to one side" means he stood alone in a suitable place for himself, having paid homage to the Blessed One, without brushing against the Blessed One or the community of monks. "Silent, silent" means that wherever he looked, there was only silence. Among those monks, there was not even the sound of a single monk fidgeting with hands or feet, or even a sneeze. Not a single monk looked at the King, who stood before the Blessed One surrounded by his harem and adorned with all ornaments, nor at the King's retinue. All the monks sat looking only at the Blessed One.

The King, being inspired by their calm, repeatedly looked at the community of monks whose faculties were tranquil like a clear lake free from mud, and uttered an inspired utterance (udāna). In that inspired utterance, "by this [calm]" indicates that the community of monks is peaceful through the tranquility of virtue occurring in the doors of body, speech, and mind; [he wished to show], "If [my son Udayabhadda] were endowed with this tranquility of virtue, [it would be well]." He did not say this with the intention, "Oh, would that my son go forth and be as peaceful as these monks." Rather, this King, seeing the community of monks and being inspired, remembered his son. It is the nature of the world to remember beloved relatives and friends when obtaining something rare or seeing something wonderful. Thus, seeing the community of monks and remembering his son, he spoke in this way.

Furthermore, he spoke this way because he had suspicions about his son and desired his tranquility. It is said that he thought: "My son will ask me, 'My father is young. Where is my grandfather?' Hearing 'He was killed by your father,' he will think, 'I too will kill my father and rule the kingdom.'" Thus, having suspicions about his son and desiring his tranquility, he spoke in this way. Although he spoke thus, his son would indeed kill him. In that lineage, parricide continued for five generations. Ajātasattu killed Bimbisāra; Udaya [will kill Ajātasattu]...",
140:
Ajātasattu was killed by his son Udayabhadda. The son of that Udayabhadda, named Mahāmuṇḍika, killed Udayabhadda. The son of that Muṇḍika, named Anuruddha, killed Muṇḍika. The son of that Anuruddha, named Nāgadāsa, killed Anuruddha. As for that Nāgadāsa, the citizens became angry, saying, "These kings are destroyers of the lineage; what is the use of this royal family?" and they killed him.

Why did the Blessed One say, "Great King, you have come according to your affection"? Even before the King spoke, the Blessed One thought, "This king has come and stands silently; what is he thinking?" Then, knowing the King's mind, He thought, "This king, unable to converse with Me, is looking at the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and remembering his son. If I do not start the conversation, he will not be able to say anything. Therefore, I will engage in conversation with him." For this reason, following the King's words, He said, "Great King, you have come according to your affection." The meaning of those words is: Great King, just as rain falling on high ground flows to the low ground, even so, you have looked at the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and your mind has gone towards where your affection lies (towards your son).

Then the King had this thought: "Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha! There is no one who has offended the Blessed One as much as I have. I have killed the Blessed One's chief supporter (King Bimbisāra). Following the words of Devadatta, I sent archers. I released the elephant Nāḷāgiri. Because of me, Devadatta rolled a stone. Despite my having committed such great offenses, the Blessed One's speech is not discordant (He shows no anger) when calling me. Oh, the Blessed One is well-established in the quality of steadfastness (tādi-lakkhaṇa) through five factors. I shall not abandon such a Teacher to seek another elsewhere." Thus, filled with joy, he addressed the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, my son is dear to me," and so forth.

Regarding "paying homage to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with joined palms," it is said that the King had this thought: "If I pay homage to the Blessed One and then go here and there to pay homage to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, I would be turning my back to the Blessed One, and that would not be respectful. Just as one who pays homage to a king and then to the viceroy shows disrespect to the king." Therefore, after paying homage to the Blessed One, while standing in his original place, he paid homage to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with joined palms and sat down in a suitable place. "A certain place" means a certain opportunity (spot).
141:
Then the Blessed One, wishing to inspire effort in asking questions, said, "Great King, ask whatever you desire." The meaning of those words is: "If you desire, ask; there is no burden for Me in answering the question." Or else, He made the "Omniscient Invitation" (sabbaññu-pavāraṇā), which is not shared by Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, or Great Disciples, saying, "Great King, ask whatever you desire, and I shall answer everything for you." For those individuals such as Paccekabuddhas do not say, "Ask whatever you desire"; they only say, "We shall know after hearing."

But the Buddhas say, "Friend, ask whatever you desire" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.237), or "Great King, ask whatever you desire," or:
"Vāsava, ask Me any question that you wish in your mind;
I shall bring an end to each and every such question for you." (Dīgha Nikāya 2.356) Or:
"Therefore, monk, sit in your own seat and ask whatever you desire." Or:
"For Bāvarī or for yourself, for the sake of all doubts of all,
I have given the opportunity; ask whatever you wish in your mind." (Sutta Nipāta 1036) Or:
"Sabhiya, ask Me any question that you wish in your mind;
I shall bring an end to each and every such question for you." (Sutta Nipāta 517)
Thus, they make the Omniscient Invitation to various yakkhas, kings, devas, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers.

It is not surprising that the Blessed One, having reached the stage of Buddhahood, should make such an invitation. Even while He stood in the stage of a Bodhisatta with partial knowledge:
"Koṇḍañña, answer the questions;
The sages of good conduct entreat you.
Koṇḍañña, this is the nature of the wise among men,
That such a burden comes to the one who is mature." (Jātaka 2.17.60)

Thus, when entreated by the sages for the sake of Sakka and others, He said:
"Sirs, I have given the opportunity; ask any question
That is desired by your mind without limit.
Having personally known this world and the next,
I shall answer those various questions for you." (Jātaka 2.17.61)
142:
In this way, when he was the ascetic Sarabhaṅga, and also in the Sambhava Jātaka, after wandering through the whole of Jambudīpa three times without finding anyone who could bring an end to the questions, a Brahmin named Sucirata asked for the opportunity to pose a question. At that time, the Bodhisatta, who was only seven years old and playing with dust in the street, sat down in the middle of the road in a cross-legged posture and said:

“Indeed, friend, I shall explain the question to you just as one who is skilled would. The King certainly knows this, whether he acts upon it or not.”

## He made an invitation like that of an Omniscient Buddha.

Thus, when the Blessed One made the invitation like that of an Omniscient Buddha, King Ajātasattu was delighted and, wishing to ask the question, said: “Venerable Sir, what about these crafts?” and so on. In that context, the craft itself is called the ‘base of craft’ (sippāyatana). ‘Puthu-sippāyatanāni’ means many crafts. ‘Seyyathidaṃ’ means ‘what are they?’ By terms such as ‘hatthāroha’ (elephant riders), he shows those who live by depending on various crafts. This is the meaning of the question: “Just as the visible fruit of the craft is evident to those who live by these crafts, depending on their respective skills, is it possible to point out a similar visible fruit of recluseship in the present life?” Therefore, he brought up the various crafts and showed those who live by them.

In that passage, by the term ‘hatthāroha’, he shows all elephant riders, including elephant teachers, elephant doctors, and elephant keepers. By ‘assāroha’, all horse riders, including horse teachers, horse doctors, and horse keepers. By ‘rathika’, all charioteers, including chariot teachers, chariot warriors, and chariot guards. ‘Dhanuggaha’ refers to archers who are teachers of the art of the bow. ‘Celaka’ refers to those who go at the very front in battle, holding the victory banner. ‘Calaka’ refers to military strategists who arrange the army’s formation, saying, ‘Let the King’s place be here, let such-and-such a great minister’s place be here.’ ‘Piṇḍadāyaka’ refers to great, fierce warriors. It is said that they enter the enemy army and cut off the enemy’s heads one by one like clusters of palm fruits and carry them away. It means they can leap up and depart after cutting them off. Alternatively, it is also a name for those who serve food to the soldiers in the middle of the battlefield. ‘Uggā rājaputtā’ refers to noble princes who are highly renowned and experienced in battle. ‘Pakkhandino’ refers to those who say, ‘Whose head or weapon...’
143:
“...we shall bring,” and when told, “Bring the head or weapon of such-and-such a person,” they rush into the battlefield and bring that very thing; because they rush in (pakkhandanti), they are called ‘pakkhandino’. ‘Mahānāgā’ refers to heroes who are like great elephants; it is a designation for warriors who do not retreat even when faced with elephants and the like. ‘Surā’ refers to absolute heroes who are able to cross the ocean even with nets or leather coverings. ‘Cammayodhino’ refers to those who fight either by wearing leather armor or by holding a leather shield that protects against arrows. ‘Dāsikaputtā’ refers to warriors who are sons of household slaves and have strong affection [for their masters]. ‘Āဠārikā’ refers to bakers. ‘Kappakā’ refers to barbers. ‘Nhāpakā’ refers to those who bathe others. ‘Sūdā’ refers to cooks. Florists (mālākāra) and others are well-known. ‘Gaṇakā’ refers to those skilled in the art of calculation. ‘Muddikā’ refers to those who live by the art of counting using fingers and joints. “And whatever other crafts” refers to crafts such as blacksmithing, ivory carving, painting, and so on. “Such as these” means crafts that exist in this way. These elephant riders and others, by showing those many bases of craft, receive great wealth from the royal families and live depending on the visible fruit of their craft in this very life. “They make themselves happy” means they bring happiness to themselves. “They make themselves full” means they make themselves endowed with strength and power. Among the terms beginning with ‘uddhaṅgika’, because it brings about results in a higher life, a gift that has its peak above is called ‘uddhaṅgika’. Because it is worthy of heaven, it is called ‘sovaggika’. Because it has a happy result, it is called ‘sukhavipāka’. Because it leads to or produces the ten things known as the most excellent forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, long life, beauty, happiness, retinue, and sovereignty, it is called ‘saggasaṃvattanika’. The meaning is that they establish such a noble gift. In this context of ‘sāmaññaphala’, in the ultimate sense, the Path (magga) is ‘sāmañña’. The Noble Fruit (ariyaphala) is ‘sāmaññaphala’. As the Blessed One said: “Monks, what is recluseship? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View... etc... Right Concentration. This, monks, is called recluseship. And what, monks, are the fruits of recluseship? The fruit of stream-entry... etc... the fruit of arahantship.” This King does not yet know that point. He asks with reference only to the examples of the slave and the farmer that will come later.

Then the Blessed One, without answering the question immediately, thought: “Many royal ministers who are followers of other sects have come here. If I speak by distinguishing the dark side and the bright side, they might disparage me, saying, ‘Our King came here with great effort, but since the time he arrived, the ascetic Gotama has only been making a recluse-uproar and causing recluse-quarrels.’ They will not listen to the Dhamma respectfully. However, if I preach with reference to the King, they will not be able to disparage me and will only follow the King’s wish. Indeed, does not the world follow the wish of the one who is in power? Now, I shall carry the King’s burden.” Having thought thus, wishing to address the King’s situation, he spoke the words beginning with ‘Abhijānāsi no’. In that phrase, the word ‘no’ should be understood as ‘nu’ (a question particle). This ‘no’ should be understood in connection with the word ‘pucchitā’ that follows.
144:
They will criticize, saying that [the monks] are only speaking of the quarrels of recluses, and they will not listen to the Dhamma with respect. But if the King speaks, they will not be able to criticize and will only follow the King's wish. Indeed, the world follows the powerful. Thinking, "Now I shall take up the King's burden," [the Buddha] said, "Great King, do you remember...?" and so forth, for the sake of the King.

In that passage, "Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ" means "Do you remember?" This word "no" should be connected with the subsequent word "pucchitā." The intended meaning is: "Great King, have you ever questioned other recluses and brahmins about this problem? Do you remember having questioned them, or have you forgotten?"

"If it is not a burden to you" means if it is not troublesome for you to speak here in the same way they answered you, and if there is no unsuitable condition, then please speak. Why did he say, "Venerable Sir, it is not a burden to me"? It is difficult to speak in the presence of those who merely pretend to be wise; such people find fault in every word and every syllable. However, those who are truly wise, after listening to a speech, praise what is well-spoken; and in the case of poorly spoken Pali, words, meanings, or syllables that are contradictory, they correct them and make them straight. There is no one truly wise like the Blessed One. Therefore, he said, "Venerable Sir, it is not a burden to me in a place where the Blessed One, or one like the Blessed One, is seated."

## Explanation of Pūraṇa Kassapa's Doctrine

"Ekamidāhaṃ" should be resolved as "Ekaṃ idaṃ ahaṃ." "Having exchanged greetings and words of courtesy" means having concluded the conversation that generates joy and is worthy of being remembered.

In the words "Great King, to one who acts, to one who causes to act," and so forth, "one who acts" refers to one who does evil with his own hands. "One who causes to act" refers to one who causes it to be done by giving an order. "One who mutilates" refers to one who cuts off the hands and so forth of others. "One who tortures" refers to one who oppresses others with a stick. "One who causes sorrow" refers to one who personally causes sorrow to another through such acts as stealing their property, or [causes it] through others...
145:
"To one who causes to act" refers to causing oneself to be weary or causing others to be weary through the deprivation of food, imprisonment, and so on. "One who trembles, one who causes to tremble" means trembling oneself upon seeing another tremble, or making another tremble. "One who kills, one who causes to kill" means killing a living being oneself or ordering another to kill. Thus, in all these terms, the meaning should be understood through the power of doing it oneself and causing others to do it.

"House-breaking" refers to breaking through the joints of a house. "Plundering" refers to destroying a village or country and taking [property]. "Single-house robbery" refers to surrounding and robbing only a single house. "Waiting in ambush" refers to standing on the road to rob whoever comes along. "Even if one acts, no evil is done" means that even if one acts with the thought, "I will do some evil," it is not called doing evil; there is no evil. It only intends to show that beings have the perception, "We are doing evil."

"With a weapon as sharp as a razor-edged wheel" means with a weapon that has an edge like a razor-wheel or a razor's blade. "A heap of meat" refers to a large mass of flesh. "Puñja" is a synonym for that heap of meat. "Because of that cause" means because of the cause of making a single heap of meat.

"The south bank" refers to the people living on the south bank of the Ganges who are rough and cruel; with reference to them, he said "killing" and so forth. The people living on the north bank of the Ganges have faith and devotion, and they cherish the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; with reference to them, he said "giving gifts" and so forth. In that passage, "offering a sacrifice" means performing a great sacrifice. "Taming the faculties" means controlling the senses or observing the Uposatha. "Restraint" means guarding one's virtue (sīla). "Speaking the truth" means uttering truthful words. "Āgama" means arising (pavatti). In this way, in every respect, he denies the performance of both evil and merit.

"Asked about a mango, he answers with a breadfruit" means that when asked, "What is a mango like? What are the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a mango like?" one answers, "A breadfruit is like this; the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a breadfruit are like this." "In the area where his authority extends" means in the region where his power is effective. "Should be oppressed" means to be harassed. "Without delighting" means without praising it as "Excellent, excellent!" "Without protesting" means without forbidding it by saying, "You have spoken the words of a fool." "Without accepting" means without recognizing it as having any essence. "Without taking it to heart" means without keeping it in mind as having essence, thinking, "This is the way of escape, this is the ultimate truth." However, King Ajātasattu did memorize the syllables (the text) of that speech and kept them in his mind.
146:
## Commentary on the Doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla

167-169. In the doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla, the word 'condition' (paccaya) is merely a synonym for 'cause' (hetu). By both these terms, he denies the condition for the defilement of beings, such as bodily misconduct and the like, which is clearly evident, as well as the condition for the purification of beings, such as bodily good conduct and the like. 'Self-agency' (attakāra) refers to the effort (kamma) performed by oneself. He denies that by which beings, through their own performed kamma, attain the state of a deva, a Mara, a Brahma, the knowledge of a disciple's enlightenment (sāvaka-bodhi), the knowledge of a private Buddha's enlightenment (pacceka-bodhi), or omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). By the second term, 'agency of another' (parakāra), he denies the effort of others by which all beings—excluding the Great Being (Mahāsatta)—attain states ranging from human prosperity to Arahatship, depending on the advice and instruction of others. Thus, this fool is said to strike at the Wheel of Authority (jinacakka) of the Buddha. 'There is no human effort' (purisakāra) means he denies that human effort by which beings reach the aforementioned attainments. 'There is no strength' (bala) means he denies that strength of one's own, established in which beings make an effort and reach those attainments. 'There is no energy' (vīriya) and so forth are all merely synonyms for human effort. However, these are taken separately by way of denying statements such as, "This exists because of our energy, this because of human strength, this because of human effort."

'All beings' (sabba-sattā) includes all beings without exception, such as camels, oxen, and donkeys. 'All breathing things' (sabba-pāṇā) refers to beings with one sense-faculty, two sense-faculties, and so on. 'All creatures' (sabba-bhūtā) refers to beings born within an egg-shell or a membrane-sheath. 'All souls' (sabba-jīvā) refers to rice, barley, wheat, and the like. In these, he (Makkhali) has the perception of 'soul' (jīva) because of their nature of growth. He says they are 'without power, without strength, without energy' because they have no power, strength, or energy of their own. In the phrase 'evolved by destiny, coincidence, and nature' (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇata), 'destiny' (niyati) means fixed destiny (kamma). 'Coincidence' (saṅgati) means the wandering into various existences within the six classes of birth (abhijāti). 'Nature' (bhāva) is simply inherent nature (sabhāva). Thus, they are evolved and reach various states through destiny, coincidence, and nature. He shows that whatever is to be, that alone happens; whatever is not to be, that does not happen. He shows that beings experience pleasure and pain only while established in the six classes of birth, and that there is no other ground (bhūmi) for the occurrence of pleasure and pain.

There are 1,400,000 principal modes of birth (yoni-pamukha), another 6,000, and another 600. There are five hundred...
147:
By the statement 'there are five hundred kammas', he shows a futile false view based on mere speculation. The same method applies to the terms 'five kammas', 'three kammas', and so forth. Some teachers, however, say: 'He speaks of five kammas in terms of the five sense-faculties, and three kammas in terms of bodily kamma and so forth.' In the phrase 'kamma and half-kamma', his doctrine is that bodily kamma and verbal kamma are 'kamma', while mental kamma is 'half-kamma'. He speaks of 'sixty-two paths' (dvāsaṭṭhi-paṭipadā). Regarding 'sixty-two intermediate aeons' (dvāsaṭṭhantara-kappa), although there are sixty-four intermediate aeons in one great aeon, he says sixty-two because he does not know the other two.

The six classes of birth (cha-abhijāti) are: the black class, the blue class, the red class, the yellow class, the white class, and the supreme white class. Among them, he says that sheep-slaughterers, bird-slaughterers, hunters, pig-slaughterers, deer-hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, jailers, and any others who follow a cruel livelihood belong to the 'black class'. He says that monks belong to the 'blue class'; it is said that they eat by putting thorns into the four requisites. 'Monks are thorn-dwellers' (kaṇṭaka-vuttika) is his very text. Or else, he means that only certain ascetics are called thorn-dwellers. He says that the Nigaṇṭhas (Jain ascetics) who wear a single cloth belong to the 'red class'. These are said to be brighter than the previous two. He says that white-clothed laypeople and the disciples of the naked ascetics (acelaka) belong to the 'yellow class'. In this way, he makes his own supporters even more eminent than the Nigaṇṭhas. He says that Ājīvaka men and women belong to the 'white class'. They are said to be brighter than the previous four. He says that Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla belong to the 'supreme white class'. They are said to be the brightest of all.

The eight stages of man (purisabhūmi) are: the stage of dullness (manda-bhūmi), the stage of play (khiḍḍā-bhūmi), the stage of testing steps (padavīmaṃsa-bhūmi), the stage of walking straight (ujugata-bhūmi), the stage of learning (sekkha-bhūmi), the stage of asceticism (samaṇa-bhūmi), the stage of victory (jina-bhūmi), and the stage of prostration (panna-bhūmi). Among these, for seven days from the day of birth, because they have just emerged from the narrow place (the womb), beings are dull and bewildered; he calls this the 'stage of dullness'. Those who have come from an unhappy destination (duggati) cry and wail constantly, while those who have come from a happy destination (sugati) smile, remembering that state; this is called the 'stage of play'. Holding the hand or foot of the parents, or a couch or a bench, and placing the feet on the ground is called the 'stage of testing steps'. The time when one is able to walk by foot is called the 'stage of walking straight'. The time of learning arts and crafts...
148:
The period of learning the arts and sciences is called the stage of the trainee (sekkha-bhūmi). The period of leaving the household life and ordaining as a monk is called the stage of the recluse (samaṇa-bhūmi). The period of understanding the arts and sciences after serving a teacher is called the stage of the conqueror (jina-bhūmi). When a monk or a wanderer becomes a conqueror and is no longer fit to perform any further tasks, such a recluse who does not regain [monkhood] is called the stage of the fallen (panna-bhūmi).

'Ekūnapannāsa ājīvakasata' refers to the four thousand nine hundred modes of livelihood of the Ājīvakas. 'Paribbājakasata' refers to the one hundred types of wandering recluses. 'Nāgāvāsasata' refers to the one hundred abodes of the Nāgas. 'Vīse indriyasata' refers to the two thousand faculties. 'Tiṃse nirayasata' refers to the three thousand hells. 'Rajodhātu' (dust-elements) refers to the places where dust falls, such as the backs of the hands and the backs of the feet. 'Satta saññīgabbha' (seven sentient births) refers to camels, oxen, donkeys, goats, deer, and buffaloes. 'Satta asaññīgabbha' (seven non-sentient births) refers to hill rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, panic seed, and kudrūsaka grain. 'Nigaṇṭhigabbha' refers to those born from knots, such as sugarcane, bamboo, and reeds. 'Satta devā' (seven gods) refers to the fact that although there are many gods, Makkhali Gosāla says there are only seven. Although humans are infinite, he says there are seven. Although demons (pisācā) are many, he says there are seven. 'Sarā' refers to the seven great lakes: Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Sīhappapāta, Chaddanta, Mandākinī, and Kuṇāla.

'Pavuṭā' refers to the seven types of knotted trees. 'Papātā' refers to the seven great precipices. 'Papātasatāni' refers to the one hundred small precipices. 'Supinā' refers to the seven great dreams. 'Supinasatāni' refers to the one hundred small dreams. 'Mahākappino' refers to the number of great aeons (mahākappa). Among those great aeons, it is said that if one were to take a single drop of water from a great lake once every hundred years using the tip of a blade of kusa grass, the time it takes for that lake to become dry after repeating this seven times is one great aeon. Only after passing through eighty-four thousand such great aeons do both the fool and the wise make an end of suffering; this is his [Makkhali Gosāla's] view. It means that even the wise cannot be purified in the interval, and the fool cannot go beyond that period.

'By virtue' (sīlena) means by the virtue of the naked ascetics (acelaka-sīla) or any other kind of virtue. 'By vows' (vatena) means by such religious vows. 'By asceticism' (tapena) means by ascetic practices. 'Ripening the unripened [karma]' refers to one who thinks, "I am wise," and tries to become purified in the interval. 'Exhausting the ripened [karma] by experiencing it' refers to one who thinks, "I am a fool," and goes beyond the specified time. There is no such thing as doing this. Both of these...
149:
He shows the meaning that one is not able to do both of these. 'Doṇamita' means as if measured by a doṇa measure. 'Sukha-dukkha' means pleasure and pain. 'Pariyantakata' means having a limit made by the duration of the aforementioned eighty-four thousand great aeons. 'Natthi hāyanavaḍḍhana' means there is no decrease or increase. The meaning is that saṃsāra does not decrease for the wise, nor does it increase for the fool. 'Ukkhaṃsāvakaṃsa' means increase and decrease; this is a designation for decrease and increase.

Now, wishing to establish that matter with a simile, he said, "Seyyathāpi nāma," and so on. In that passage, 'suttaguḷa' refers to a ball of string made by winding it. "Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paleti" means that a ball of string thrown while standing on a mountain or a treetop goes only as far as it is unwound according to the length of the string; when the string is exhausted, it stays right there and goes no further. Likewise, he shows that one does not go beyond the stated time.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambala
170-172. In Ajita's doctrine, "natthi dinnaṃ" (there is no giving) is said with reference to the absence of the fruit of a gift given. A great sacrifice is called 'yiṭṭha'. 'Huta' refers to the honor of an offering. He rejects both of these with reference only to the absence of fruit. 'Sukata-dukkaṭānaṃ' refers to the meaning of good and bad deeds, that is, wholesome and unwholesome actions. Whatever result is called 'phala' (fruit) or 'vipāka' (ripening), he says that it does not exist. "Natthi ayaṃ loko" means that for one staying in the next world, this world does not exist; "natthi paro loko" means that for one staying in this world, the next world does not exist. He shows that all beings are annihilated right in their respective places. "Natthi mātā natthi pitā" is said in terms of the absence of the fruit of right conduct or wrong conduct toward those parents. "Natthi sattā opapātikā" means he says there are no beings who are born spontaneously after passing away.

'Cātumahābhūtika' means composed of the four great elements. "Pathavī pathavikāyaṃ" means the internal earth element [goes to] the external earth element. "Anupeti" means it follows or goes to. "Anupagacchati" is just a synonym for that term. "Anugacchati" is also the meaning. He shows by both terms that it reaches or approaches. The same method applies to the liquid element (āpo) and others. 'Indriyāni' (faculties) means the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, pass into space. "Āsandipañcamā" refers to those who are the fifth along with the bier on which the corpse lies. The four men standing and holding the four legs of the bier...
150: 'Sā' means the meaning. 'Yāvāḷāhanā' means up to the cemetery. 'Padāni' refers to terms of merit and demerit such as "This person was thus virtuous, thus immoral," and so forth; or in this context, 'padāni' is intended to mean the corpse itself. 'Kāpotakāni' means bones having a color like that of a pigeon's wing. 'Bhassantā' means ending in ashes, or it is as the Pali text stands. 'Āhutiyo' means that all various offerings, such as gifts to guests and the like, end only in ashes; it means they do not continue to bear fruit after becoming ashes. 'Dattupaññattaṃ' means that which is prescribed by fools. This means: "This giving is prescribed only by the ignorant fools, not by the wise. Fools give, and the wise receive." Among those three teachers, Pūraṇa Kassapa denies action by saying, "In acting, no evil is done." Ajita denies the result by saying, "With the breakup of the body, one is annihilated." Makkhali denies both by saying, "There is no cause." Among action and its result, one who denies action also effectively denies the result, and one who denies the result also effectively denies action. Thus, all of them, in essence, are deniers of both, holding the doctrines of non-causality (ahetukavāda), non-action (akiriyavāda), and nihilism (natthikavāda). Those who adopt their views and sit in their night-quarters or day-quarters, reciting and investigating them—for them, wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati) remains fixed on that object: "In acting, no evil is done; there is no cause, no condition; at death, one is annihilated." The mind becomes concentrated, and the javanas (impulse moments) run. In the first javana, it is still remediable; likewise in the second and so on. But at the seventh javana, even the Buddhas cannot remedy it, and they become irreversible like the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇṭaka. Among those views, some enter into one view, some into two, and some into all three. Whether entering one, two, or three, one becomes a person of fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). One reaches the state of obstructing the path to heaven and the path to the magga, phala, and nibbāna. Immediately after that present existence, one is not even fit to go to heaven, let alone reach nibbāna. This being is called a "stump in the cycle of rebirth" (vaṭṭakhāṇu) and a "guardian of the earth." Generally, for such a person, there is no emergence from existence.
