Therefore, the wise man who desires prosperity should avoid an unwholesome person from afar, like a snake with fierce poison.
151:
## Commentary on the Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana
173-175. In the doctrine of Pakudha, 'akaṭā' means things that are unmade (by anyone). 'Akaṭavidhā' means things for which there is no creator. It means they are not caused to be made by someone commanding, "Do it this way." 'Animmitā' means things that are not fashioned even by psychic power. 'Animmātā' means things that are not caused to be fashioned by others. Some mention the term 'animmāpetabbā,' but that term is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Commentary. The meanings of the three terms beginning with 'vañjhā' (barren) are just as previously stated. 'Na iñjanti' (they do not shake) means they do not move because they stand firm like a gatepost. 'Na vipariṇamanti' (they do not change) means they do not abandon their original nature. 'Na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti' (they do not harm one another) means they do not oppress each other. 'Nālaṃ' means they are not capable.

In the terms beginning with 'pathavikāyo,' the earth itself is the earth-body, or the collection of earth elements is the earth-body. 'Tattha' (therein) means in those bodies, of which the soul (jīva) is the seventh. 'Sattannaṃ tveva kāyānaṃ' (among the seven bodies) means just as a weapon struck into a heap of beans enters between the beans, so the weapon enters through the gap or space between the seven bodies. In such an act of cutting, saying "I deprive this person of life" is shown to be merely a perception (saññā).

## Commentary on the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta
176-178. In the doctrine of Nāṭaputta, 'cātuyāmasaṃvarasaṃvuto' means restrained by a restraint consisting of four parts. 'Sabbavārivārito' means all water is forbidden, all cold water is rejected. It is said that he has the perception that there are living beings in cold water; therefore, he does not use it. 'Sabbavāriyutto' means he is endowed with the prevention of all evil. 'Sabbavāridhuto' means he has evil shaken off by the prevention of all evil. 'Sabbavāriphuṭo' means he is pervaded by the prevention of all evil. 'Gatatto' means he has a mind that has reached the pinnacle. 'Yatatto' means he has a restrained mind. 'Ṭhitatto' means he has a well-established mind. Although there are some points in this doctrine of Nāṭaputta that are in accordance with the Teaching (Sāsana), because it is an impure doctrine, the entire view is simply wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi).

## Commentary on the Doctrine of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta
179-181. The doctrine of Sañjaya is just according to the method stated in the Amarāvikkhepa (Eel-wriggling) doctrine.
152:
## Commentary on the First Visible Fruit of Recluseship

"So'haṃ, bhante" means "I, venerable sir." The meaning is that, like a man who squeezes sand and does not obtain oil, I did not find any essence in the doctrines of the sectarians (titthiyas), and thus I ask the Blessed One.

"Yathā te khameyya" means as it pleases your mind. "Dāso" (servant) refers to one of the four types of servants: one born in the house, one bought with money, one captured in war, or one who has voluntarily entered servitude. "Kammakāro" (worker) refers only to one who is not lazy and is habitual in performing work. A servant who, upon seeing the master from afar, rises first is called "pubbuṭṭhāyī" (one who rises first). Having risen in this way, he prepares the master's seat, performs duties such as washing the feet, and only then goes to sleep; therefore, he is called "pacchānipātī" (one who lies down last). Alternatively, he is called "pubbuṭṭhāyī" because he rises before the master wakes from sleep. He is called "pacchānipātī" because he performs all duties from dawn until the master falls asleep at night, and only then goes to sleep. He is called "kiṃkārapaṭissāvī" (one who waits for orders) because he goes about constantly listening for what needs to be done, asking, "What shall I do? What shall I do?" He is called "manāpacārī" (one who acts pleasingly) because he performs only those actions that are pleasing to the heart. He is called "piyavādī" (one who speaks pleasantly) because he speaks only endearing words. He is called "mukhullokaka" (one who looks at the face) because he goes about watching the master's joyful and delighted face.

"Devo maññe" means like a deva. "So vatassāhaṃ puññāni kareyyaṃ" means "If only I were a person of such a nature, if only I could perform meritorious deeds, oh, how happy I would be!" Although there is also a reading "so vatassa'ssa," the meaning is the same. By the phrase "yannūnāhaṃ," he shows his intention to go forth (renounce), thinking, "If I were to give gifts, I would not be able to give even a hundredth part of what the king gives in a single day, even if I gave for the rest of my life."

"Kāyena saṃvuto" means being restrained in body, having closed the door through which unwholesome states enter. The same method applies to the other two terms (speech and mind). "Ghāsacchādanaparamatāya" means being content with the highest form of livelihood, which is just enough food and clothing; for the sake of this, he abandons improper search and is satisfied with supreme austerity. "Abhirato paviveke" means delighting in the three types of solitude: "kāya-viveka (physical solitude) for those with secluded bodies, citta-viveka (mental solitude) for those delighting in renunciation with extremely pure minds, and upadhi-viveka (solitude from acquisitions) for those persons who have reached supreme purity, free from acquisitions and conditioned things."
153:
Abandoning the company of the group, he dwells alone physically. Abandoning the company of defilements that distress the mind, he dwells alone by the power of the eight attainments (samāpatti). Entering the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), he dwells focusing on Nirvana. "Yagghe" is a particle used in the sense of exhortation.

"We would also invite him with a seat" means dusting the sitting place and saying, "Please sit here." "We would also invite him by bringing forward [offerings]" means inviting him by bringing requisites forward. In this context, bringing forward (abhihāra) is of two kinds: by word and by body. Saying, "Venerable sir, whenever you wish, I will provide robes and so on; please tell me whatever requisition you need," is called inviting by bringing forward by word. Noticing a deficiency in robes and so on and giving them, saying, "Please take this," is called inviting by bringing forward by body. Referring to both types, it is said, "We would also invite him by bringing forward [offerings]."

In this context, "gilānappaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāra" refers to any medicine suitable for the sick. Its etymology is stated in the Visuddhimagga. "Rakkhāvaraṇagutti" refers to the provision of security, described as protecting and warding off. Such protection is not called righteous (dhammika) if it is arranged by stationing armed men. However, arranging so that wood-cutters, leaf-gatherers, and others do not enter the monastery at improper times, and so that hunters and others do not catch animals or fish within the monastery precincts, is called righteous protection (dhammika-rakkhā). Referring to such an arrangement, it is said, "dhammika."

"If it were so" means "If your servant were to receive salutation and so on from you." "Addhā" is a word expressing certainty. By saying "first" (pathamaṃ), he indicates that there are other benefits as well. For that very reason, the king asked, "Is it possible, venerable sir, that there is another [benefit]?" and so on.

## Commentary on the Second Visible Fruit of Recluseship

186-188. He is called a "kassaka" (farmer) because he is capable of farming. He is called a "gahapatika" (householder) because he is the master of a house, or the head of a single household. He is called a "karakāraka" (taxpayer) because he pays the tax known as tribute (bali). He is called a "rāsivaḍḍhaka" (increaser of wealth) because he increases the heap of grain and the heap of wealth.
154:
"Appaṃ vā" means a small amount, even as little as a measure of rice. "Bhogakkhandhaṃ" means a mass of wealth. "Mahantaṃ vā" means a great amount of wealth. Both are mentioned to show that just as it is difficult to renounce great wealth to become a monk, it is likewise difficult to renounce even a small amount of wealth. In the case of a slave, however, a slave is not even his own master, so how could he be the master of wealth? Since whatever wealth he has belongs only to his masters, the word "bhoga" (wealth) was not used. Only the circle of relatives is called "ñātiparivaṭṭa."

## Description of the More Exalted Fruits of Recluseship
When it was asked, "Is it possible, Bhante, to have another (fruit of recluseship) in this very life?", why was it not said "Even so" (evameva) here? If "Even so" were said, the Blessed One could continue to show the fruits of recluseship with such similes for a whole day and night, or even longer. Although there is no limit to hearing the words of the Blessed One, [the King] thought that the meaning would be the same, and wishing to ask for a further distinction, he did not say "Even so" but said "more pleasing and more exalted." In that context, "abhikkantatara" means more pleasing, more excellent. "Paṇītatara" means more exalted. "Tena hi" is a particle used in the sense of exhortation. Wishing to exhort him to listen, He said, "If that is so, listen." "Suṇohi" means "Listen to the more pleasing and more exalted fruit of recluseship."

In the phrase "Sādhukaṃ manasikarohi," the two words "sādhukaṃ" and "sādhu" have the same meaning. This word "sādhu" is found in the senses of requesting, accepting, rejoicing, goodness, and firming, etc. It is found in the sense of requesting in such passages as, "Bhante, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief." It is found in the sense of accepting in such passages as, "'Very well, Bhante,' that monk, having greatly delighted in and approved of the Blessed One's words..." It is found in the sense of rejoicing in such passages as, "Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!"

"Good is the king who delights in the Dhamma, good is the man who is wise,
Good is non-betrayal of friends, and the non-doing of evil is happiness."

In such passages, it is found in the sense of goodness. In such passages as, "Brahmin, if that is so, listen well (sādhukaṃ), pay attention," the word "sādhuka" is in the sense of firming or exhortation. In this text "Sādhukaṃ manasikarohi," this word "sādhuka" is also in the sense of firming. Therefore, the meaning of that word "sādhuka" should be understood as firming or exhortation. It is also appropriate in the sense of goodness. Wishing to show the appropriateness in those three senses in detail, He said "Daḷhīkammattena hi" (By way of firming), etc. The meaning of that Pāḷi is: By the word "sādhuka" in the sense of firming, the meaning "Listen to this Dhamma, noting it firmly and well" is shown. By the word "sādhuka" in the sense of exhortation, the meaning "Listen to this Dhamma by my exhortation" is shown. By the word "sādhuka" in the sense of goodness, the meaning "Listen to this Dhamma respectfully, listen to this Dhamma well" is shown. "Manasikarohi" means reflect, pay attention. It means to investigate and reflect with an undistracted mind, to keep it in the mind. Alternatively, I (shall show) another way.
155:
In this context (of "Sādhukaṃ manasikarohi"), this word "sādhuka" should be understood in the sense of firming (daḷhīkamma) and exhortation (āṇatti). It is also suitable in the sense of good (sundara). By the sense of firming, it is shown as "Listen to this Dhamma firmly, grasping it well." By the sense of exhortation, it is shown as "Listen by my command." By the sense of goodness, it is shown as "Listen to this beautiful and good Dhamma."

"Pay attention (manasikarohi)" means reflect, keep in the mind. It means to investigate and reflect without a wandering mind, to place it in the mind. Alternatively, in this context, "Listen (suṇohi)" is the prevention of the distraction of the ear faculty (sotindriya). "Pay attention well (sādhukaṃ manasikarohi)" is the prevention of the distraction of the mind faculty (manindriya) by firm exhortation in paying attention. The former term prevents the wrong grasp of the phrasing (byañjana), and the latter term prevents the wrong grasp of the meaning (attha). By the former, He exhorts one to listen to the Dhamma; by the latter, He exhorts one to retain and investigate the Dhamma that has been heard. By the former, He shows "This Dhamma is endowed with phrasing, therefore it should be heard." By the latter, He shows "It is endowed with meaning, therefore it should be well attended to."

Or, the word "sādhuka" should be understood as being connected to both terms (suṇāhi and manasikarohi). Because this Dhamma is deep in subject matter (dhamma) and deep in teaching (desanā), it should be understood as "Listen well." Because it is deep in meaning (attha) and deep in penetration (paṭivedha), it should be understood as "Pay attention well."

"I will speak (bhāsissāmi)" means "Great King, I am able," and thus He will speak in detail the Sāmaññaphala Sutta which has been promised. The word "I will teach (desessāmi)" implies showing in brief, while the word "I will speak (bhāsissāmi)" implies showing in detail. Therefore, the Elder Vaṅgīsa said:

"He teaches in brief, and he speaks in detail,
His voice is like that of a salika bird, giving rise to inspired wit."

When this was said, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, the son of the Videha princess, became enthusiastic and replied to the Blessed One, "Even so, Bhante." This means he accepted and received the word of the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One said this to the king. It means He spoke the entire Sutta beginning with "Here, Great King," which is to be spoken now. In that passage (beginning with "Idha mahārāja"), the word "idha" is a particle indicating place. That word "idha" is sometimes used in reference to the world. As it was taught: "A Tathāgata arises here in the world." Sometimes it is used in reference to the Dispensation (sāsana)...
156: As it was said: "Monks, only in this teaching is there the first recluse (Stream-enterer); only in this teaching is there the second recluse (Once-returner)" (Aṅguttara Nikāya). In some places, it refers to a location. As it was said: "O sirs, I, who was a deva and a virtuous one, staying in this place, have regained life once more; know it thus, dear sirs" (Dīgha Nikāya). In some places, it is merely a filler word (padapūraṇa). As it was said: "Monks, in this teaching, I would have finished my meal and been invited (pavārita)" (Majjhima Nikāya). Here, however, (the word 'idha') should be understood as being said in reference to the world. "Great King," as he had promised to give the discourse, he addresses him again as "Great King." This is the meaning: "Great King, in this world, the Tathāgata arises, the Worthy One... the Buddha, the Blessed One." In that statement, the term "Tathāgata" was explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta. The attributes beginning with "Arahaṃ" were explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. In the phrase "arises in the world," the world is of three kinds: the world of space (okāsa-loka), the world of beings (satta-loka), and the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka). Here, the world of beings is intended. Although he arises in the world of beings, the Tathāgata does not arise in the deva realm, nor in the Brahma realm; he arises only in the human realm. Even in the human realm, he does not arise in another world-system (cakkavāḷa), but only in this world-system. Even in this world-system, he does not arise in all places. "In the eastern direction is the market town named Kajangala, and beyond that is Mahāsāla (the great Sal tree); beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). In the south-eastern direction is the river named Salalavatī; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country. In the southern direction is the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country. In the western direction is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country. In the northern direction is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the border regions, and the inner side is the Middle Country." Thus defined, he arises only in the Middle Country, which is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. Not only the Tathāgata, but also Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Elders, the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, Cakkavatti kings, and other noble brahmins and householders who have attained excellence, arise only in this Middle Country.
157: ...and also the Buddha's father, the Cakkavatti king, and other noble brahmins and householders who have attained excellence, arise only in this Middle Country. In the phrase "Tathāgato uppajjati," the Tathāgata is said to be "arising" (uppajjati) during the period from the time he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā until the Path of Arahatship. At the Fruition of Arahatship, he is said to be "arisen" (uppanna). Alternatively, he is "arising" from the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahatship; or from the Tusita heaven until the Path of Arahatship; or from the time he received the prophecy at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the Path of Arahatship. At the Fruition of Arahatship, he is "arisen." In this sutta, "uppajjati" (arises) is said with reference to his arising before all others. "The Tathāgata has arisen in the world" is the meaning here. "So imaṃ lokaṃ" means that the Blessed One (knows) this world. This phrase points to the words that will follow. "Sadevakaṃ" means the world together with the devas. Likewise, "samārakaṃ" means with Māra; "sabrahmakaṃ" means with Brahmā; "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ" means with recluses and brahmins (here, it is expressed in the feminine gender in consideration of the word 'pajā'). "Pajā" (generation/beings) is so called because they are born again and again; it refers to those beings. "Sadevamanussaṃ" means with devas and humans. Among those words, it should be understood that by the word "sadevaka," the five heavens of the sense-sphere are to be taken. By the word "samāraka," the sixth sense-sphere heaven (Vasavatti) is to be taken. By the word "sabrahmaka," the Brahma realms such as Brahmakāyika are to be taken. By the word "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī," both the recluses and brahmins who are enemies and opponents of the Sāsana, and the recluses and brahmins who have calmed their defilements and abandoned evil, are to be taken. By the word "pajā," the world of beings (satta-loka) is to be taken. By the word "sadevamanussa," the conventional gods (kings) and the remaining humans are to be taken. Thus, in this context, the world of beings together with the world of space is taken by three terms. By two terms, only the world of beings is taken by way of "pajā" (beings). Another method: by the view of "sadevaka," the formless-sphere (arūpāvacara) deva world is taken. By the view of "samāraka," the six sense-sphere deva worlds are taken. By the view of "sabrahmaka," the fine-material (rūpa) Brahma realm is taken. By the view of "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇādi," the human world together with conventional gods by way of the fourfold assembly, or all the remaining world of beings, is taken. Furthermore, here, by the word "sadevaka," it is said that he has realized the entire world by way of the highest distinction. Moreover, for those who thought: "Māra has great power, he is the lord of the six sense-sphere heavens, he is the Vasavatti who brings others under his control; has even this Māra been realized by this Blessed One?", he said "samārakaṃ" to dispel their doubt. For those who thought: "Brahmā has great power, with one finger he spreads light throughout a thousand world-systems..."
158:
With two fingers... and so on... with ten fingers, he pervades the ten thousand world systems with light. He also experiences the incomparable bliss of meditative attainment. To dispel the doubt of those who wonder, "Has the Blessed One also realized that Brahmā?" He said, "the world with its Brahmās (sabrahmaka)." Then, to dispel the doubt of those who thought, "There are many ascetics and brahmins who are enemies of the Dispensation; has the Blessed One realized those ascetics and brahmins too?" He said, "this generation with its ascetics and brahmins (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ)." Having thus shown the state of realization regarding those who are most excellent, and then including the conventional gods, namely kings, and the rest of humanity, wishing to show the state of realization regarding the rest of the world of beings by way of the highest limit, He said, "the world with its devas and humans (sadevamanussaṃ)." This is the sequence of meaning here.

The ancient commentators, however, say: "With its devas" (sadevakaṃ) means the rest of the world together with the devas. "With its Māras" (samārakaṃ) means the rest of the world together with Māra. "With its Brahmās" (sabrahmakaṃ) means the rest of the world together with the Brahmās. Thus, having included all beings belonging to the three realms in three terms through three modes, and wishing to encompass them again with two terms, He said, "this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, the world with its devas and humans." Thus, even with five terms, only the generation of beings in the three realms is encompassed in various ways.

In the phrase "Having personally known and realized, He makes it known (sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti)": "Personally" (sayaṃ) means by himself, without being led by another. "Having known" (abhiññā) means having known through direct knowledge, having known with knowledge superior to other types of knowledge. "Having realized" (sacchikatvā) means having made manifest; by this term, the rejection of inference (anumāna) and so on is made. "He makes it known" (pavedeti) means He awakens, He informs, He clarifies.

"He teaches the Dhamma, good in the beginning... good in the end" means that the Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, even gives up the incomparable bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) to teach the Dhamma. And when He teaches it, whether a little or much, He teaches it only in the manner of being good in the beginning and so on. It means He teaches by making it good, auspicious, and faultless in the beginning, in the middle, and in the end. In that teaching, there is a beginning, middle, and end of the discourse (desanā), and there is a beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation (sāsana). In a discourse, even in a four-line verse, the first line is the beginning, the next two are the middle, and the one at the end is the end. Of a sutta with a single sequence (anusaandhi), the introduction (nidāna) is the beginning, and the words "This is what [the Blessed One] said" is the end.
159:
The space between the two is the middle. Of a sutta with many sequences, the first sequence is the beginning, the sequence at the end is the end, and the one, two, or many sequences in the middle are just the middle. The beginning of the Dispensation consists of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and insight (vipassanā). This has also been said: "What is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified and view that is straight (diṭṭhi)" (SN 5.369). The Noble Path, spoken of as "Monks, there is a middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā) fully awakened to by the Tathāgata," is called the middle. The Noble Fruit (phala) and Nirvana are called the end. "Brahmin, this holy life has this attainment of fruition as its purpose, this as its core, this as its end" (MN 1.324)—in this passage, the Fruit is called the end. "Friend Visākha, the holy life is merged in Nirvana, it has Nirvana as its destination, Nirvana as its end" (MN 1.466)—in this passage, Nirvana is called the end. Here, the beginning, middle, and end of the discourse are intended. For the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, shows virtue in the beginning, the Path in the middle, and Nirvana at the end. Therefore, it is said: "He teaches the Dhamma, good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end." Therefore, another Dhamma-preacher, when preaching the Dhamma:

"Should show virtue in the beginning, should clarify the Path in the middle, and should show Nirvana at the end; this is the proper standing of a preacher."

"With meaning (sātthaṃ) and with phrasing (sabyañjanaṃ)": If one's teaching is based on praising gruel, rice, women, men, and so on, he does not teach a Dhamma that is "with meaning". The Blessed One, however, having abandoned such teaching, teaches the Dhamma based on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness and so on. Therefore, He is said to teach the Dhamma "with meaning". If one's teaching is joined with only a single syllable, or has phrasing entirely devoid of meaning, or has phrasing where every nasal sound (niggahīta) is fully articulated, then his teaching is "without phrasing" (abyañjana), like the language of the Damiḷas, Kirātas, Savaras, and other barbarians (milakkha), because of the lack of completeness in phrasing. The Blessed One, however, (said):

"Lax and tense, long and short, heavy and light, nasalized, connected, distinct, and released—thus the division of phrasing by intelligence is tenfold."
160:
He teaches the Dhamma without corrupting the ten kinds of phrasing (syllables) mentioned, making it only with complete phrasing; therefore, it is said that He teaches the Dhamma 'with phrasing' (savyañjanaṃ). In the term 'entirely complete' (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ), 'kevala' is a word for the whole. 'Paripuṇṇa' is a word for being neither deficient nor excessive. This means He teaches only what is entirely complete; there is not even a single part that is incomplete. Because there is nothing to be added and nothing to be removed, it should be understood as 'entirely complete' (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ). 'Pure' (parisuddhaṃ) means being free from the defilements of corruption. If someone teaches thinking, 'By depending on this teaching of Dhamma, I shall obtain gain or honor,' his teaching is impure. But the Blessed One teaches without regard for worldly gain, with a soft heart through the development of loving-kindness by spreading welfare, and with a mind established in the nature of lifting others up (from suffering). Therefore, it is said that He teaches the 'pure' (parisuddhaṃ) Dhamma.

In the phrase 'He proclaims the holy life' (brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti), the word 'brahmacariya' is found in these meanings: in giving, in service, in the five precepts of virtue, in the immeasurables, in abstinence from sexual intercourse, in contentment with one's own wife, in energy, in the factors of the Uposatha, in the Noble Path, and in the Dispensation (Sāsana).

'O Naga King, what is your practice? What is your holy life (giving)?
By what well-practiced merit is there this attainment of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy?
And is this great mansion yours?
My wife and I, in the human world,
Were both faithful masters of giving.
At that time, my house was like a well or a pond,
And recluses and brahmins were satisfied.
O Wise One, that very act of pleasing recluses and brahmins was my practice;
That very act of pleasing them was my holy life.
Due to that well-practiced merit of giving,
There is this attainment of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy;
And this great mansion is mine.'
In this Punnaka Jātaka, giving is called 'brahmacariya'.

'Why does your palm give whatever is desired? Why does honey flow from your palm?
By what kind of holy life (brahmacariya) is merit fulfilled in your palm?'
161:
'By performing such deeds related to merit, my hand gives whatever is desired; by performing those deeds, my hand causes sweet flavor to flow; by that holy life, merit is fulfilled in my hand' (as found in the Petavatthu).

In this Aṅkura Petavatthu, service (veyyāvacca) is called 'brahmacariya'. 'Monks, in this way, that practice was formerly the holy life known as the Tittira practice,' in this Tittira Jātaka, the five precepts of virtue are called 'brahmacariya'. 'Pañcasikha, that holy life of mine does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation... it leads only to rebirth in the Brahma world,' in this Mahāgovinda Sutta, the four immeasurables are called 'brahmacariya'. 'Others will be those who practice unchastity; we here shall be those who practice the holy life of abstaining from sexual intercourse,' in this Sallekha Sutta, abstinence from sexual intercourse is called 'brahmacariya'.

'We do not practice by transgressing against our wives,
Nor do our wives transgress against us;
We practice the holy life in matters other than those wives,
Therefore, the young ones in our family do not die.'

In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one's own wife (sadārasantosa) is called 'brahmacariya'. 'Sāriputta, I know that I have practiced the holy life endowed with four factors; I have been one who practiced asceticism,' in the Lomahaṃsana Sutta, energy (vīriya) is called 'brahmacariya'.

'By a low holy life, one is reborn in the royalty;
By a middling one, one reaches the state of a deity;
By a superior holy life, one is purified (from defilements).'

Thus, in the Nemi Jātaka, the eightfold Uposatha performed by way of self-discipline is called 'brahmacariya'. 'Pañcasikha, this holy life of mine indeed leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation... it is none other than this Noble Eightfold Path,' in the same Mahāgovinda Sutta, the Noble Path is called 'brahmacariya'. 'This holy life is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, become popular, and well-proclaimed as far as gods and humans,' in the Pāsādika Sutta, the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) comprised of the three trainings is called 'brahmacariya'. In this context as well, it is this Dispensation that is intended as 'brahmacariya'. Therefore, 'He proclaims the holy life' means that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma which is good in the beginning... and pure. By teaching in this way, [the Dhamma] which is comprised of the three trainings...
162:
In this context, the entire Dispensation (Sāsana), which is reckoned by the three trainings, is shown as the 'Holy Life' (Brahmacariya); this is how the meaning should be understood. 'Brahmacariya' means a practice that is noble (brahma) in the sense of being excellent. Alternatively, it is said to mean the practice of those who have become noble, such as the Buddhas and others.

Regarding 'that Dhamma': it refers to the Dhamma endowed with the qualities aforementioned. In the phrase 'A householder (gahapati) or... hears [that Dhamma],' why is the householder mentioned first? It is because they have subdued pride and because they are numerous. Indeed, those who go forth from noble (khattiya) families often act out of pride based on their birth. Those who go forth from brahmin families act out of pride based on the Vedas. Those who go forth from low-caste families are unable to establish themselves because of their low birth. However, the sons of householders (farmers), who till the earth with sweat pouring from their armpits and salt forming on their backs, are free from such pride and arrogance. Having gone forth, without showing pride or arrogance, they learn the entire Word of the Buddha to the best of their ability and, by practicing insight (vipassanā), they are able to establish themselves in the fruit of Arahantship. Furthermore, those who go forth from other families are not many; householders (farmers) are the most numerous. Thus, because of their lack of pride and their great numbers, the householder is mentioned first.

Regarding 'or in some other family': this refers to someone born in any family other than that of a householder. 'Paccājāto' means born. 'He gains faith in the Tathāgata': having heard the pure Dhamma, he gains faith in the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata, thinking, 'The Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One.' 'He reflects thus': he contemplates in this manner. 'Household life is crowded': even if a husband and wife live in a house sixty cubits wide or even a hundred yojanas wide, the household life is still 'crowded' for them because of the nature of their attachments and impediments. 'A path of dust (rajopatho)': the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā states it is the place where the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth arises. Some also say it is the 'path of arrival' (for defilements). The life of a monk is called 'open air' (abbhokāsa) because it is like the open air in the sense of being unattached. Indeed, even if a monk lives in a gabled house, a jeweled palace, or a celestial mansion with doors and windows closed and secured, he does not cling, does not get attached, and is not bound. Therefore, it is said, 'Going forth is the open air.' Alternatively, household life is 'crowded' because there is no opportunity for performing wholesome deeds. It is a 'path of dust' because it is a gathering place for the dust of defilements, like a place where unswept rubbish accumulates. Going forth is 'open air' because there is the presence of opportunity to perform wholesome deeds as one pleases.
163:
In the passage 'This is not easy... to go forth,' this is the summary: This holy life of the three trainings must be practiced with absolute completeness, bringing it to the final consciousness (at death) without breaking it for even a single day. It must be practiced with absolute purity, bringing it to the final consciousness without letting it be stained by the taints of defilements for even a single day. 'Saṅkhalikhita' means it should be practiced as purely as a polished conch shell or a washed conch shell. 'This is not easy for one living in a house... to practice with absolute completeness,' etc. (He thinks:) 'What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes—garments dyed with astringent juice that are suitable for those practicing the holy life—and, having gone forth from the home life, enter the homeless state?' Here, the work of householders such as farming and trade is called 'agāriya' (domestic affairs). Since that work does not exist in the life of a monk, the state of a monk should be known as 'anagāriya' (homelessness). 'Pabbajeyyaṃ' means 'I shall practice.'

192-193. 'Small or...': A mass of wealth less than a thousand is called 'small'; from a thousand upwards, it is 'large.' A circle of relatives is called 'ñātiparivaṭṭa' because of the nature of being bound together. That too is called 'small' if below twenty; from twenty upwards, it is 'large.' 'Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha' means being endowed with the Pātimokkha restraint. 'Endowed with proper conduct and resort' means being endowed with both conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara). 'In the slightest...': in very small matters. 'Faults': in unwholesome states. 'Seeing danger': one who habitually sees danger. 'Having undertaken': having properly taken up. 'He trains in the rules of training': having undertaken each specific training rule among the rules of training, he trains. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is given in the Visuddhimagga.

In the phrase 'Endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action, he is of pure livelihood,' although wholesome bodily and verbal actions are already included by the mention of 'conduct and resort,' this 'virtue of livelihood purity' (ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla) does not arise in the sky or at the tops of trees, but only at the doors of body and speech. Therefore, to show the doors of its arising, it is said, 'Endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action.' Because he is endowed with that, he has a 'pure livelihood.' Alternatively, this is said according to the Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta Sutta (M. Ni. 2.260). In that Sutta, it is asked, 'Householder, what are wholesome virtues?'
164:
“Householder, I say that wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action, and pure livelihood are established in virtue.” Thus it is said. Because one is endowed with that purity of livelihood, one should be known as a person of pure livelihood. One possessed of virtue means one who is endowed with the threefold virtue as taught in the Brahmajāla Sutta. One with guarded doors in the sense faculties means having the doors closed in the six sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth. One endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension means being endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven situations, such as in going forward and returning. One who is contented means one who is contented with the four requisites through the threefold contentment.

## Description of the Minor Section on Virtue (Cūḷasīla-vaṇṇanā)

194-211. Having thus laid down the matrix (mātikā) and wishing to explain it in order, he said: “And how, O Great King, is a bhikkhu possessed of virtue?” and so forth. In that text, “this also is part of his virtue” means that the bhikkhu’s abstaining from taking life is one virtue among the collection of virtues. Alternatively, this locative case is used in the sense of the nominative case. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā also, this very meaning is stated: “this also is the virtue of that ascetic (samaṇa).” The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta. “This also is part of his virtue” means this is his virtue.

He sees no danger from any quarter arising from restraint of virtue. This is because when there is restraint, there is an absence of dangers rooted in non-restraint. Anointed on the head (muddhābhisitta) is like a king who has been consecrated on the head with the royal regalia according to the prescribed ritual. Just as that king, having defeated his enemies, sees no danger from any enemy, so it is here. Internally (ajjhattaṃ) means within one’s own continuity (santāna). Blameless happiness (anavajja-sukha) means experiencing bodily and mental happiness that is blameless, uncensured by the wise, and embraced by states such as freedom from remorse, joy, rapture, and tranquility, which have wholesome virtue as their proximate cause. “Thus, O Great King, a bhikkhu is possessed of virtue.” In this way, having explained in detail, he concluded the talk on virtue by showing that a bhikkhu endowed with the threefold virtue is called one possessed of virtue.
165:
## Discussion on Restraint of the Sense Faculties (Indriya-saṃvara-kathā)

In the detailed explanation of guarded doors in the sense faculties, in the passage ‘with the eye, a form’ (cakkhunā rūpaṃ), the word ‘eye’ (cakkhu) in some places refers to the Buddha-eye (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa), as in the statement: “With the Buddha-eye, he surveyed the world.” In some places, it refers to the all-seeing eye (samanta-cakkhu), which is synonymous with omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), as in: “O Sumedha, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, which is like a mountain peak, you who possess the all-seeing eye...” In some places, it refers to the Dhamma-eye (dhamma-cakkhu); in the passage “the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose,” it refers to the wisdom of the three lower paths. In the passage “the eye arose, knowledge arose,” the knowledge such as the recollection of past lives is called the wisdom-eye (paññā-cakkhu). In places where it occurs as “with the divine eye,” it refers to the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). In the passage “dependent on the eye and forms,” it refers to the sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu). Here, however, this word ‘eye’ refers to eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) by way of the sensitive eye. Therefore, the meaning here is “having seen a form with eye-consciousness.” Whatever needs to be said regarding the remaining terms has all been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Unalloyed happiness (abyāseka-sukha) means that because of being free from the alloy of defilements, one experiences unmixed, pure happiness of the higher mind (adhicitta-sukha).

## Discussion on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension (Sati-sampajañña-kathā)

In the detailed explanation of mindfulness and clear comprehension, in the passage ‘in going forward and returning’ (abhikkante paṭikkante), first, ‘going forward’ refers to moving ahead, and ‘returning’ refers to turning back. Both of these are found in the four postures. In walking, first, one who carries the body forward is said to ‘go forward.’ One who turns back is said to ‘return.’ In standing, even while standing, one who leans the body forward is said to ‘go forward,’ and one who leans backward is said to ‘return.’ In sitting, even while sitting, one who moves toward the front part of the seat is said to ‘go forward,’ and one who moves back toward the rear part is said to ‘return.’ The same method applies to lying down.

‘Acting with clear comprehension’ (sampajāna-kārī) means one who habitually performs all tasks with clear comprehension. Or, it means one who habitually exercises clear comprehension itself. For such a person certainly exercises clear comprehension in going forward and so on. At no time is he devoid of clear comprehension. In that context, there are four types of clear comprehension: clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). Among these, when the thought of going forward arises, instead of just going according to the mind’s whim, one considers, “Is there a purpose for me in going there or not?” and thus grasping the purpose is called clear comprehension of purpose.
166:
In this clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), 'purpose' (attha) means the growth of wholesome qualities through seeing a pagoda (cetiya), seeing the Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing elder monks (theras), or contemplating foulness (asubha), and so on. By seeing a pagoda or the Bodhi tree and taking the Buddha as the object, or by seeing the Saṅgha and taking the Saṅgha as the object, a monk generates joy (pīti). Then, by contemplating that very joy in terms of its rise and fall (impermanence) with insight (vipassanā), he can reach the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). By seeing elder monks and being established in their advice, or by contemplating foulness and attaining the first absorption (jhāna) therein, and then contemplating that very absorption in terms of its rise and fall with insight, he can reach the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, seeing these things like the pagoda is said to be purposeful. Some teachers, however, say that growth in terms of material requisites (āmisa) is also a purpose, because by depending on those requisites, one can practice to support the holy life (brahmacariya).

In going about, reflecting on what is suitable and unsuitable and choosing what is suitable is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña). For example: while seeing a pagoda is purposeful, if a great festival is held for the pagoda and crowds from ten or twelve leagues away gather, where men and women, adorned according to their wealth, move about like painted figures—in such a place, greed may arise in that monk for a pleasant object, anger for an unpleasant object, or delusion from looking without reflection. Or he may commit an offense of bodily contact (kāya-saṃsagga), or there may be danger to his life and the holy life. In such a case, that place is unsuitable (asappāya). If such dangers are absent, it is suitable (sappāya). The same method applies to seeing the Bodhi tree. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. However, if a large pavilion is built inside a village and people gather for an all-night Dhamma talk, and if there are crowds and dangers as mentioned before, then that place is unsuitable. It is suitable only when there is no danger. The same method should be understood for seeing elder monks who have large followings.

Contemplating foulness is also purposeful. To illustrate this purpose, there is this story: It is said that a young monk took a novice (sāmaṇera) and went to find tooth-sticks. The novice stepped off the path and, going ahead, saw a corpse. He attained the first absorption and, using that very absorption as a basis, contemplated conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) with insight. He realized the three lower fruits and remained standing, practicing meditation for the sake of the higher path. The young monk, not seeing the novice, called out, "Novice!" The novice thought, "Since the day I was ordained, I have never spoken even two words with a monk [unnecessarily]. I will attain the higher distinction on another day." He then replied, "What is it, Bhante?" When told, "Come here," he came with just that one word and said, "Bhante, please go along this path and..."
167:
(The novice said:) "...stand for a moment at the place where I stood, facing east, and look." The monk did so and attained the very same distinction that the novice had reached. Thus, a single corpse became beneficial for two people. Even though it is purposeful in this way, for a man, a female corpse is unsuitable, and for a woman, a male corpse is unsuitable; only a corpse of the same sex is suitable. Such reflection on suitability is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña).

A monk who has thus maintained the clear comprehension of purpose and suitability, having grasped an object of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) according to his preference from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, and going to the village for alms while carrying that meditation subject, is said to have clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña). To clarify this, this fourfold set should be understood: Here, a certain monk carries (the meditation subject) on the way there but not on the way back; another carries it on the way back but not on the way there; another carries it neither on the way there nor on the way back; and another carries it both on the way there and on the way back.

Among these four, a certain monk purifies his mind from hindering states through walking and sitting throughout the day. Likewise, he sleeps during the first and middle watches of the night, and spends the final watch in sitting and walking. Early in the morning, he performs the duties at the pagoda courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, waters the Bodhi tree, sets out drinking and washing water, and undertakes all the duties of the Khandhakas, such as duties toward teachers and preceptors. Having performed his bodily grooming, he enters his dwelling, sits cross-legged two or three times to relieve fatigue, and practices meditation. At the time for alms-round, he rises and, taking his bowl and robes while keeping the meditation subject foremost, leaves the dwelling. While reflecting on the meditation subject, he goes to the pagoda courtyard. If his meditation is the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), he enters the pagoda courtyard without letting go of it. If it is another meditation subject, he should leave it at the foot of the stairs as if placing down a bundle held in the hand, and taking up the joy that has the Buddha as its object, he should ascend the pagoda courtyard. If it is a large pagoda, he should circumambulate it three times to the right and pay homage at four places. If it is a small pagoda, he should likewise circumambulate it and pay homage at eight places. After paying homage to the pagoda, when he reaches the Bodhi tree courtyard, he should pay homage to the Bodhi tree with a respectful manner as if in the presence of the Blessed Buddha. Having thus paid homage to the pagoda and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where he left his things, and as if picking up the stored bundle with his hand, he takes back the meditation subject he had left. Keeping the meditation subject foremost, he puts on his robe near the village and enters the village for alms. Then, when people see him and say, "Our venerable one has arrived," they come to meet him, take his bowl, and lead him to the alms-hall or a house...
168: Or, having made the monk sit down and offered gruel, they wash his feet and anoint them with oil until the meal is finished. These people, sitting before him, ask questions or desire to listen to the Dhamma. Even if the people do not ask for a sermon, the teachers of the Commentaries state that a Dhamma talk should indeed be given out of compassion for the people. Truly, a Dhamma talk is never devoid of a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna); therefore, having given a Dhamma talk based on meditation, and having partaken of food based on meditation, and having performed the thanksgiving (anumodanā), he departs from the village followed by the people who are returning. Having sent them back near the village, he sets out on his path. Then, seeing the novices and young monks who had departed earlier and finished their meal outside the village, they come to meet him and take his bowl and robes. It is said that the monks of old did not perform their duties by looking at the face, thinking 'This is our preceptor (upajjhāya) or our teacher (ācariya),' but performed them according to the circumstances at hand. They ask him: 'Venerable sir, how are these people related to you? Are they relatives from the mother's side or the father's side?' When asked, 'What did you see that made you ask?', they reply, 'We ask because we see the great love and respect these people have for you.' 'Friends, these people do for us what even parents find difficult to do. Our bowl and robes are also their gifts. Because of their kindness, we do not know fear in times of danger, nor hunger in times of famine. We have never had such benefactors,' he says, praising their virtues as he goes. This monk is called 'one who carries [the meditation] forth but does not bring it back.' For a certain monk, while performing the aforementioned duties early on, the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) blazes up. That fire element releases the unclung-to matter (anupādinnaka-rūpa) and takes hold of the clung-to matter (upādinnaka-rūpa). Sweat flows from his body. He cannot enter the path of meditation. That monk, taking his bowl and robes early, quickly pays homage to the Cetiya, and at the very time the cattle go out to pasture, enters the village for alms-gruel. Having obtained the gruel, he goes to the refectory and drinks it. Upon swallowing just two or three times, the fire element born of kamma releases the clung-to matter and takes hold of the unclung-to matter. As if bathed with a hundred jars of water, the burning of the fire element is extinguished. Having partaken of the gruel based on meditation, he washes his bowl and mouth, and in the interval before collecting alms-food, he applies his mind to the meditation subject. He wanders for alms in the remaining places, partaking of food based on meditation. From that time on, he returns holding onto the meditation subject that has become continuously clear. This monk is...
169: ...called 'one who brings it back but does not carry it forth.' What is the monk who brings it back but does not carry it forth? Monks of such nature, having drunk gruel and practiced insight (vipassanā), attained Arahatship in the Buddha's Dispensation; they are so numerous that they are beyond counting. In the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka) alone, there is no refectory in various villages where there have not been monks who attained Arahatship after drinking gruel. However, the one who dwells in negligence (pamāda-vihārī), without a mind committed to meditation, breaking all duties, and dwelling with a mind fettered by the five mental barrennesses (cetokhila), enters the village for alms without even the perception that 'there is such a thing as meditation.' He wanders and eats, associating with laypeople in an unsuitable manner, and returns empty-handed. This monk is called 'one who neither carries forth nor brings back.' The one who is called 'one who both carries forth and brings back' should be understood by virtue of the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgata-vatta). Sons of good family, desiring their own welfare, having gone forth in the Dispensation, live together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred, and live by making a pact: 'Friends, you did not go forth because of debt, nor because of fear, nor merely for a livelihood, but you went forth here desiring to be liberated from suffering. Therefore, suppress the defilements (kilesa) that arise while walking, even while walking; likewise, suppress the defilements that arise while standing, sitting, or lying down, in those very postures.' Having made such a pact, as they go to the village for alms, there are stones at distances of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, and one gāvuta. Using those stones as landmarks, they go while applying their minds to the meditation subject. If a defilement arises in any monk while walking, he suppresses it right there while walking. If he is unable to suppress it while walking, he stands still. Then, the monk coming behind him also stands still. That monk reproaches himself, thinking, 'This monk behind you knows the thought (vitakka) that has arisen in you; this is not suitable for you,' and developing insight, he reaches the stage of a Noble One (ariya) right where he stands. If he is unable to suppress it while standing, he sits down. Then, the monk coming behind him also sits down. This is the same method as before. Even if he cannot yet reach the stage of a Noble One, he discards that defilement and goes while applying his mind to the meditation subject. He does not lift a foot with a mind devoid of meditation. If he does lift a foot with a mind devoid of meditation, he turns back and returns to the previous spot. Like the Elder Mahāphussadeva who resided in Ālindaka.
170:
That Elder Mahāphussadeva lived for nineteen years fulfilling only the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgata-vatta) with meditation. People, while plowing, sowing, and threshing in the fields along the way, saw the Elder repeatedly turning back and going, and they remarked, "This Elder keeps turning back and going; is he lost, or has he forgotten something?" The Elder, disregarding those words, practiced the recluse's Dhamma with a mind united with meditation, and within twenty years, he attained Arahantship. On the day he attained Arahantship, a deity residing at the end of his walking path lit a lamp with their fingers and stood there. The Four Great Kings, Sakka the king of gods, and Sahampati Brahma also came to attend upon him. Seeing that radiance, Vanavāsī Mahātissa Thera asked him the next day, "A radiance appeared near the Venerable One during the night; what was that radiance?" The Elder, wishing to deflect the conversation, said, "What is called radiance could be the light of a lamp, or the radiance of a gem," and so on. Later, being repeatedly urged with "Venerable Sir, please do not conceal it," he admitted it, saying "Yes," and informed him. 

It was also like the case of Elder Mahānāga, a resident of Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa. That Elder Mahānāga, while fulfilling the duty of going and returning, first thought, "I will honor the Great Exertion (Mahāpadhāna) of the Blessed One," and for seven years, he undertook only standing and walking. Then, after fulfilling the duty of going and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahantship. That Elder would lift his foot only with a mind united with meditation; if he lifted his foot with a mind disunited from meditation, he would turn back. Going near a village, he would stand in a place where people might doubt, "Is it a cow or a monk?" and after robing himself, he would wash his bowl with water from a vessel carried under his arm and take a mouthful of water (udakagaṇḍūsa). For what reason? He thought, "Let there be no distraction of meditation even by the mere words 'May you live long' to the people who come to offer alms or to pay homage." If he was asked about the day, such as "Venerable Sir, what day is today?" or about the number of monks, or a question, he would swallow the water and answer. If there were no questioners about the day and so on, he would spit it out at the village gate upon leaving and go his way. 

It was also like the fifty monks who entered the Vassa at Kalambatittha Monastery. On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, they made a pact: "We will not speak to one another until we attain Arahantship." When entering the village for alms, they also took a mouthful of water...
171:
...and entered. When asked about the day and so on, they acted in the same manner as previously mentioned. Then, the people, seeing them spitting out water, knew, "Today one monk has come, today two have come." Furthermore, they thought, "Is it only with us that these monks do not speak, or is it also among themselves? If they do not speak even among themselves, they must surely be in a state of dispute. Come, let us go and make them ask for each other's forgiveness." When all the people went to the monastery, they did not see even two monks together in one place among the fifty monks. Then, a wise man among those people said, "Friends, the dwelling place of those who are quarreling cannot be like this. The courtyard of the shrine and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree are well-swept; the brooms are neatly stored; the drinking water and utility water are well-prepared." Hearing this, the people returned from there. Those monks attained Arahantship within the three months of the Vassa and performed the Pure Pavāraṇā (Visuddhi-pavāraṇā) on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā.

In this way, like Elder Mahānāga residing at Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa and the monks who entered the Vassa at Kalambatittha Monastery, one should lift one's foot only with a mind united with meditation. Upon reaching the vicinity of a village, one should take a mouthful of water, observe the streets, and enter a street where there are no drunkards, scoundrels, or such quarrelsome people, nor wild elephants or horses. When wandering for alms there, one should not go with speed as if in a great hurry. Indeed, there is no such thing as a dhutaṅga practice of collecting alms by going quickly. One should go steadily, like a water-cart that has reached uneven ground. Having entered house by house, one should observe whether someone wishes to give or not, wait for a suitable time accordingly, and after receiving alms, return to the village interior, the village outskirts, or the monastery. Sitting in a comfortable and suitable place, one should reflect on meditation, establish the perception of the repulsiveness of food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), and consume the food endowed with eight factors, reflecting on it with the similes of greasing an axle, applying medicinal ointment to a wound, or eating the flesh of one's own son. It is not for fun, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for adornment... After eating, having performed the duty of washing, and having rested for a moment to relieve the fatigue caused by the meal, one should reflect on meditation just as before the meal, so also after the meal, and during the first watch and the last watch of the night. Such a monk is said to "carry (meditation) while going and carry it back while returning."

A monk who fulfills this duty called the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgata-vatta), if he is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), attains Arahantship in the first stage of life. If he does not attain it in the first stage, then in the middle stage. If he does not attain it in the middle stage, he attains it at the time of death. If he does not attain it at the time of death, he attains it as a deity. If he does not attain it as a deity, he becomes a monk in a time when no Buddha has appeared and realizes Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa. If he does not realize Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa, he becomes a person of quick intuition (khippābhiññā) in the presence of the Buddhas, like Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya. He also becomes one of great wisdom like Elder Sāriputta, one of great psychic power like Elder Mahāmoggallāna, a dhutaṅga-observer like Elder Mahākassapa, or one with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) like Elder Anuruddha.
172:
If that monk who fulfills the perfections (pāramī) is endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits, he attains the fruit of Arahatship in the first stage of life. If he does not attain it in the first stage of life, he attains it in the middle stage of life. If he does not attain it in the middle stage of life, he attains it at the time of death. If he does not attain it at the time of death, he attains it after becoming a deva. If he does not attain it after becoming a deva, and if he is born in a time when a Buddha has not appeared, he realizes the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. If he does not realize the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, then in the presence of the Buddhas, he becomes one of swift direct-knowledge (khippābhiññā) like the elder Bāhiya Dārucirīya. Or he becomes one of great wisdom like the elder Sāriputta. Or he becomes one of great psychic power like the elder Mahāmoggallāna. Or he becomes one who speaks on the ascetic practices like the elder Mahākassapa. Or he becomes one with the divine eye like the elder Anuruddha. Or he becomes an expert in the Vinaya like the elder Upāli. Or he becomes a preacher of the Dhamma like the elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta. Or he becomes a forest dweller like the elder Revata. Or he becomes one of great learning like the elder Ānanda. Or he becomes one desirous of training like the elder Rāhula, the son of the Buddha. Thus, in this group of four, for the monk who carries (the mind) in going and carries it back, his clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) reaches its peak.

Non-delusion in such acts as moving forward is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). That clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood thus: In this Dispensation, when a monk is moving forward or moving backward, he is not deluded like the foolish worldlings who are deluded in moving forward and so on, thinking, "The self moves forward, the movement forward is produced by the self," or "I move forward, the movement forward is produced by me." Instead, when the thought "I will move forward" arises, together with that thought, the air element (vāyo-dhātu) born of the mind arises, producing intimation (viññatti). Thus, by the power of the diffusion of the air element, which is an action of the mind, this skeleton, which is conventionally called a body, moves forward. In each step of the skeleton moving forward in this way, at the moment of lifting the foot, the two elements of earth (pathavī) and water (āpo) are inferior and weak. The other two elements (fire and air) are superior and strong. It is the same in carrying forward and carrying across. At the moment of releasing the foot, the two elements of fire (tejo) and air (vāyo) are inferior and weak. The other two elements (earth and water) are superior and strong. It is the same in lowering and pressing the foot to the ground. In that process, the mental and physical phenomena (rūpa-arūpa dhamma) that occur during the lifting of the foot do not reach the stage of carrying forward. Likewise, those occurring during the carrying forward do not reach the stage of carrying across; those occurring during the carrying across do not reach the stage of releasing; those occurring during the releasing do not reach the stage of lowering; and those occurring during the lowering do not reach the stage of pressing the foot down. Having become joint by joint, connection by connection, and section by section in each of those places...
173:
They break up, making a 'pata-pata' sound, like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan. In that process, who is the one person that moves forward, or whose movement forward is it? In the ultimate sense, there is only the going of elements, the standing of elements, the sitting of elements, and the lying down of elements in each respective part, together with materiality.

One mind arises, another mind ceases.
Linked in an uninterrupted succession, it proceeds like the flow of a river.

Thus, non-delusion in such acts as moving forward is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña).

The meaning of the phrase "he is one who acts with clear comprehension in moving forward and moving backward" is finished.

In the phrase "in looking ahead and looking aside," looking straight ahead is called ālokita. Looking toward the intermediate directions is called vilokita. There are also other types of looking, such as looking down, looking up, and looking behind, known as olokita, ullokita, and apalokita; these are not included here. However, these two are taken because they are appropriate for monks, or all those types of looking are included under these terms (ālokita and vilokita).

In those acts of looking ahead and looking aside, when the thought "I will look ahead" arises, the reflection on the benefit of looking, rather than looking according to one's desire, is called clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). This reflection on the benefit should be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda as a personal witness. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, if Nanda has to look toward the eastern direction, Nanda looks toward the eastern direction after having concentrated his whole mind, thinking: 'While I am looking toward the eastern direction in this way, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief will not flow in upon me.' Thus, he is clearly comprehending therein. Monks, if Nanda has to look toward the western direction... (p)... the northern direction... (p)... the southern direction... (p)... upward... (p)... downward... (p)... or toward the intermediate directions, Nanda looks toward the intermediate directions after having concentrated his whole mind, thinking: 'While I am looking toward the intermediate directions in this way, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief will not flow in upon me.' Thus, he is clearly comprehending therein."

Furthermore, in this context, the state of being purposeful and the state of being suitable should be understood by way of seeing a stupa (cetiya) and so on, as mentioned previously. Not abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is itself called clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña).
174:
Therefore, in this context, monks who practice meditation on the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) should look forward and look aside only by the power of their own meditation; or those who practice meditation on the kasinas and so forth should do so by making the meditation subject primary. Internally, there is no so-called 'self' (attā) that looks forward or looks aside. When the thought 'I will look' arises, the wind element (vāyodhātu) born of that mind arises, producing intimation (viññatti) along with that mind. Thus, through the diffusion of the wind element caused by the mental activity, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper eyelid rises up. It is not as if someone is opening them with a mechanical device. Thereafter, eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) arises, performing the function of seeing. Knowing in this way is called 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammoha-sampajañña) here. Furthermore, clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood here by way of full understanding of the root (mūlapariññā), the state of being a guest (āgantukatā), and the temporary nature (tāvakālika-bhāva). First, it will be explained by way of full understanding of the root:

Bhavaṅga, advertence (āvajjana), seeing (cakkhuviññāṇa), and receiving (sampaṭicchana),
Investigating (santīraṇa), determining (votthabbana), and the seventh is impulsion (javana).

Among these mental states, the bhavaṅga occurs performing the function of a factor of the rebirth-existence. Having adverted to that bhavaṅga, the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) occurs performing the function of advertence (āvajjana). Upon its cessation, eye-consciousness arises performing the function of seeing. Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu) arises performing the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana). Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipāka-manoviññāṇadhātu) arises performing the function of investigating (santīraṇa). Upon its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element (kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) arises performing the function of determining (votthabbana). Upon its cessation, javana runs for seven times. Among those javanas, even in the first javana, there is no such thing as looking forward or looking aside with lust, hatred, or delusion, thinking 'This is a woman, this is a man.' This is the same from the second javana up to the seventh javana. However, just as warriors fall down in a battlefield, after those mental states have broken up and ceased, looking forward or looking aside occurs with lust and so forth, thinking 'This is a woman, this is a man.' Thus, in this context, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of full understanding of the root.

When a visible form comes into the range of the eye-door (cakkhudvāra), starting from the vibration of the bhavaṅga, the mental states such as advertence arise and cease by way of performing their respective functions. At the end, the javana mind arises. That javana mind is like a male guest at the eye-door, which is like the house of the previously arisen advertence and so forth. For that male guest who has entered another's house to beg for something...
175:
Just as it is improper for a guest who enters another's house to beg for something to issue commands while the house-owners remain silent, so too, it is improper for the javana mind (which is like a guest) to have lust, hatred, or delusion while the advertence and so forth, which are like the house-owners of the eye-door, are themselves without lust, hatred, or delusion toward the object. Thus, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of the state of being a guest.

Those mental states that arise in the eye-door ending with determining (votthabbana) break up right there along with their associated states; they do not see one another. Therefore, they are transient and temporary. Among them, for example, if all the people in a house have died, it is not proper for the one remaining person, who is also subject to death at that very moment, to take delight in dancing, singing, and so forth. Similarly, when advertence and so forth, along with their associated states, have arisen and ceased right there in the single eye-door, it is not proper for the javana mind, which is also subject to destruction at that very moment, to take delight by way of lust, hatred, or delusion. Thus, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of the temporary nature.

Furthermore, this clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditions (paccaya). In reviewing these aggregates and so forth: the eye and the visible form are the materiality aggregate (rūpakkhandha); seeing (eye-consciousness) is the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha); the feeling associated with that eye-consciousness is the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha); perception is the perception aggregate (saññākkhandha); and mental factors such as contact (phassa) are the formations aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha). Thus, in the concordance of these five aggregates, looking straight ahead and looking askance are manifested. In that looking, who is the individual that looks straight ahead? Who looks askance?

Similarly, the eye is the eye base (cakkhāyatana); the visible form is the visible form base (rūpāyatana); seeing is the mind base (manāyatana); and the associated states such as feeling are the mental object base (dhammāyatana). Thus, in the concordance of these four bases, looking straight ahead and looking askance are manifested. In that looking, who is the individual that looks straight ahead? Who looks askance?

Similarly, the eye is the eye element (cakkhudhātu); the visible form is the visible form element (rūpadhātu); seeing is the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu); and the associated states such as feeling are the mental object element (dhammadhātu). Thus, in the concordance of these four elements, looking straight ahead and looking askance are manifested. In that looking, who is the individual that looks straight ahead? Who looks askance?

Similarly, the eye is the support condition (nissaya-paccaya); the visible form is the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya); advertence is the proximity, contiguity, decisive support, absence, and disappearance conditions (anantara, samanantara, upanissaya, natthi, vigata paccaya); light is the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya); and feeling and so forth are the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). Thus, in the concordance of these conditions, looking straight ahead and looking askance are manifested. In that looking, who is the individual that looks straight ahead? Who looks askance? Thus, in this phrase 'looking forward and looking aside' (ālokite vilokite), clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.

'In bending and stretching' (samiñjite pasārite) means in the bending and stretching of the joints of the limbs...
176:
Due to the concordance [of the eye-base, etc.], looking straight ahead and looking aside become manifest. In that looking, who is the one person that looks straight? Who is the one that looks aside? (There is no one). Thus, in this looking, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditions (paccaya).

'In bending and stretching' (samiñjite pasārite) refers to the bending and stretching of the joints of the limbs. In that bending and stretching, not doing so merely by the will of the mind, but by considering whether there is benefit or not due to the cause of bending and stretching the limbs, and grasping what is beneficial, is called clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). In that regard, for one who remains with limbs bent or stretched for too long, painful feelings arise at every moment, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) declines, and one does not attain distinction. However, for one who bends at the proper time and stretches at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject reaches growth, and one attains distinction. Thus, the consideration of benefit and non-benefit should be understood.

Even when there is benefit, considering what is suitable and unsuitable and grasping what is suitable is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña). In this matter of suitability and unsuitability, this is the method:

It is said that at the courtyard of the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya), young monks were reciting their studies; behind those young monks, young nuns were listening to the Dhamma. Among those young monks, one monk stretched out his hand and, coming into bodily contact [with a nun], returned to lay life for that very reason. Another monk stretched out his foot and stretched it into a fire; his foot was burnt to the bone. Another stretched into an anthill and was bitten by a venomous snake. Another stretched into a robe-tent pole and was bitten by a green pit viper. Therefore, one should not stretch in such unsuitable places but only in suitable places. This is clear comprehension of suitability here.

Clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) should be illustrated by the story of the Great Elder. It is said that while the Great Elder was sitting in his day-quarters talking with his pupils, he suddenly bent his hand, then put it back in its original position and bent it slowly. His pupils asked, "Venerable sir, why did you suddenly bend your hand, then put it back in its original position and bend it slowly?" "Friends, from the time I began to apply my mind to the meditation subject, I have never bent my hand while letting go of the meditation subject. But just now, while talking with you, I bent it while letting go of the meditation subject. Therefore, I put it back in its original position and bent it again [with the meditation subject]."
177:
"Excellent, venerable sir! A monk should indeed be of such a nature," (the pupils said). Thus, here too, not abandoning the meditation subject is to be understood as clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña).

Internally, there is no such thing as a 'self' (atta) that bends or stretches. It is only due to the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind's activity, as previously described, that bending and stretching occur, like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet pulled by strings. Such discerning knowledge here is to be understood as clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña).

In the phrase 'in wearing the outer robe, bowl, and robes' (saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe), 'wearing' (dhāraṇa) refers to the use of the double robe and robes by way of dressing and covering, and the bowl by way of receiving alms-food, etc. In that wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes, for a monk who goes for alms dressed or covered, the gain of material gifts is a benefit, and the purpose stated by the Blessed One such as 'for the sake of warding off cold,' etc., is also called benefit (attha). By way of that benefit, clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.

For a monk of a hot nature or one who is weak, a fine robe is suitable. For a monk who is sensitive to cold, a thick double robe is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is unsuitable, for the repairing of it with patches, etc., causes him anxiety (palibodha). Similarly, a robe that is desirable, such as those made of silk (paṭṭuṇṇa) or fine cloth (dukūla), is also unsuitable. For such a robe can be a danger to the dressing and even a danger to the life of a monk living alone in the forest. In the ultimate sense, however, whatever robe is obtained through wrong livelihood such as making signs (nimittakamma), etc., or if by using it unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish, that robe is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By way of that suitability, it is clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) here. By way of not abandoning the meditation subject alone, clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood.

Internally, there is no such thing as a 'self' that wears the robe. It is only due to the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind's activity, as previously described, that the wearing of the robe occurs. Between that robe and the body, the robe is insentient (acetana), and the body is also insentient. The robe does not know, "The body is covered by me."
