The body also does not know, "I am covered by the robe." Only elements cover a heap of elements, like the covering of a doll (potthakarūpa) with a rag. Therefore, one should not feel joy upon receiving a good robe, nor should one feel displeasure upon receiving a poor one.
178:
To clarify further: regarding the Nāgavammika Cetiya, its trees, and so forth, some people perform acts of respect and veneration with flowers, perfumes, incense, and garments. Others perform acts of disrespect by striking them with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, or weapons. Because of such respect or disrespect, those Nāgavammika trees and so forth do not feel joy or sorrow. In the same way, one should not feel joy upon receiving a fine robe, nor should one feel sorrow upon receiving a poor robe. Clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) in the use of robes should be understood here through the power of such reflection on the process.

In the use of the alms bowl as well, one does not take the bowl impulsively. Rather, thinking, "By taking this bowl and going for alms, I shall receive food," clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood through the power of the benefit to be obtained by the act of taking the bowl.

For a monk with a weak or frail body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. A bowl that has been mended with four or five patches and is difficult to clean is unsuitable for any monk. A bowl that is difficult to wash is also not allowable, as it causes worry for the monk who must wash it. A bowl with the color of a gem is likely to arouse greed; it is unsuitable in the same manner as mentioned regarding robes. A bowl obtained through improper hints (nimitta-kamma) and so forth, or a bowl the use of which causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, is definitely unsuitable. The opposite of this is a suitable bowl. Clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood here through the power of such a suitable bowl. Clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject.

Internally, there is no such thing as a 'self' (atta) that takes the bowl. The act of taking the bowl occurs only through the diffusion of the air element (vāyo-dhātu) born of consciousness, as previously described. In this process, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are also insentient. The bowl does not know, "I am being held by hands." The hands also do not know, "We are holding the bowl." Elements alone are grasping a collection of elements, just as a pair of tongs grasps a red-hot bowl. Clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) in the carrying of the bowl should be understood here through the power of such reflection on the process.

Furthermore, for example, consider destitute people lying in a shelter for the helpless, whose limbs are severed, with pus, blood, and maggots oozing from their wounds, and surrounded by black flies. Compassionate people, seeing them, provide them with old rags to cover their wounds and medicines in potsherds and so forth. Among those rags, some people receive soft ones, while others receive coarse ones. The potsherds for medicine also...
179:
...some are well-shaped, while others are poorly shaped. Those patients do not feel glad or sad about them. This is because their need is merely for the rags to cover the wounds and the potsherds to hold the medicine. In the same way, a monk regards his robe like a rag for a wound, his alms bowl like a potsherd for medicine, and the alms food received in the bowl like the medicine within the potsherd. Such a monk should be understood as one who practices supreme clear comprehension through the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) in the wearing of the outer robe and the carrying of the bowl.

In the passage beginning with 'asitādīsu' (in eating, etc.): 'asita' refers to eating alms food; 'pīta' refers to drinking gruel and so forth; 'khāyita' refers to chewing snacks, cakes, and so forth; 'sāyita' refers to tasting honey, molasses, and so forth. In these acts of eating and so forth, the eightfold purpose described by the method beginning with 'neva davāya' (not for fun) is called 'attha' (purpose). Clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood through the power of that purpose.

Among foods that are coarse, fine, bitter, or sweet, if a certain food is not agreeable (not conducive to comfort) for someone, that food is unsuitable (asappāya) for him. If a certain food is obtained through improper hints (nimitta-kamma) and so forth, or if unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline in one who eats that food, it is definitely unsuitable. The opposite of this is suitable (sappāya). Clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood here through the power of such suitability. Clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood by eating without abandoning the meditation subject.

Inside the body, there is no such thing as a 'self' (atta) who is the eater. The receiving of the bowl and the lowering of the hand into the bowl occur only through the diffusion of the air element (vāyo-dhātu) born of consciousness as described. Only through the diffusion of the air element born of consciousness do the making of the morsel, the raising of the morsel, and the opening of the mouth occur. No one is opening the jawbones with a key or a mechanical device. Only through the diffusion of the air element born of consciousness do the placing of the morsel in the mouth, the action of the upper teeth like a pestle, the action of the lower teeth like a mortar, and the action of the tongue like a hand occur. Thus, in that eating process, the thin saliva at the tip of the tongue and the thick saliva at the root of the tongue moisten the food. While the tongue-hand turns the food in the lower-teeth-mortar, moistened by the saliva-water and crushed by the upper-teeth-pestle, no one is pushing that food inside with a ladle or a spoon; it enters only by the power of the air element. No one provides a bed of straw to hold the food that has entered; it remains there only by the power of the air element. No one makes a stove and lights a fire to cook the food that is present; it is digested only by the fire element (tejo-dhātu). No one with a stick...
180:
There is no one who brings [food] out by means of a stick or a staff; only the air element (vāyodhātu) brings it out. Thus, the air element performs the functions of bringing forward, moving here and there, holding, turning over, crushing, drying, and bringing out. The earth element (pathavīdhātu) performs the functions of holding, turning over, crushing, and drying. The water element (āpodhātu) performs the functions of moistening and preserving the moistened food. The fire element (tejodhātu) digests the food that has entered within. The space element (ākāsadhātu) serves as the pathway (or open space). The consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu) attends to (or experiences) based on proper exertion in various matters. Through reflection on the manner of these occurrences, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood in this [eating, etc.].

Furthermore, clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood here through reflection on the ten aspects of repulsiveness: going, seeking, consuming, location, storage, the unripened state, the ripened state, the fruit, the result, and the smearing. The detailed explanation of this should be taken from the 'Description of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Food' (Āhārepāṭikūlasaññā-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.

'Uccārapassāvakamme' means in the act of defecating and urinating. In that regard, for one who does not defecate or urinate when the proper time has come, sweat is released from the whole body, the eyes roll, the mind is not concentrated, and other diseases arise. But for one who does [defecate or urinate], all those [ills] do not occur. This is the meaning here. Through the power of that benefit, clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.

For one who defecates or urinates in an unsuitable place, there is the occurrence of an offense (āpatti), increase of ill-repute, and danger to life. For one who does so in a suitable place, all those [ills] do not occur. This is the suitability (sappāya) here, and through the power of that suitability, clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood. Through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) alone, clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood.

Internally, there is no so-called 'self' (attā) who performs the act of defecating and urinating; the act of defecating and urinating occurs only through the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind. Just as when a ripened boil bursts, the pus and blood come out without intention; and just as water comes out of an overfilled water-pot without intention; so too, the feces and urine accumulated in the rectum and bladder, being pressed by the force of the air element, come out even without intention. These feces and urine thus coming out...
181:
For that monk, [the act of defecating and urinating] is neither for himself nor for another; it is merely the outflow of impurities from the body. How? Just as for one who pours out old water from a water-vessel, that old water is neither for himself nor for others, it is merely for the sake of the vessel's cleanliness; so too, through the power of reflection on this occurrence, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood here.

Among the terms beginning with 'gata': 'gate' means in walking; 'thite' means in standing; 'nisinne' means in sitting; 'sutte' means in sleeping; 'jāgarite' means in waking; 'bhāsite' means in speaking; 'tuṇhībhāve' means in being silent. In the Sutta passage, "When walking, he knows 'I am walking'; when standing, he knows 'I am standing'; when sitting, he knows 'I am sitting'; when lying down, he knows 'I am lying down'", the long postures are spoken of. In the Sutta passage, "In going forward and returning, in looking ahead and looking away, in bending and stretching", the middle postures are spoken of. But in this [Satipaṭṭhāna] Sutta, "In walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking", the minor or detailed postures are spoken of. Therefore, in those postures as well, the state of acting with clear comprehension (sampajāna-kāritā) should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsiva, however, said: A certain monk, after walking for a long time or after practicing walking meditation, stands at the end and reflects, "The mental and material phenomena (rūpārūpa-dhamma) that occurred during the time of walking have ceased right here." This monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension in walking.

A certain monk, while performing recitation, answering questions, or attending to the meditation subject, stands for a long time and then sits down at the end and reflects, "The mental and material phenomena that occurred during the time of standing have ceased right here." This monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension in standing.

A certain monk, through the power of performing recitation and so forth, sits for a long time and then rises at the end and reflects, "The mental and material phenomena that occurred during the time of sitting have ceased right here." This monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sitting.

A certain monk, while lying down, performing recitation or attending to the meditation subject, falls asleep and then wakes up and rises at the end and reflects, "The mental and material phenomena that occurred during the time of sleeping have ceased right here." This monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sleeping and waking. In truth, the non-occurrence of functional consciousness (kiriyacitta) that produces intimation is called sleep; its occurrence is called waking.
182:
A monk who speaks does so with mindfulness and clear comprehension, reflecting: "This thing called sound arises depending on the lips, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate, and depending on the mental effort corresponding to that sound." Or else, after a long period of chanting, or preaching the Dhamma, or developing a meditation subject, or answering a question, when he is silent afterwards, he reflects: "The mental and physical phenomena that arose during the time of speaking have ceased right here." This is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking (bhāsite sampajānākārī).

A monk who is silent reflects after a long period of attending to the Dhamma or a meditation subject: "The mental and physical phenomena that were occurring during the time of silence have ceased right here." Indeed, when there is the occurrence and movement of derived matter (upādā-rūpa), it is called speaking; when there is no such occurrence, it is called being silent. This is called one who acts with clear comprehension in silence (tuṇhībhāve sampajānākārī).

This meaning, which focuses on the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) as stated by the Elder Mahāsiva, is intended in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. However, in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta, all four types of clear comprehension are applicable. Therefore, in the manner already stated, one should understand the state of acting with clear comprehension through the power of the four types of clear comprehension in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta. In all the terms for "one who acts with clear comprehension" (sampajānākārī), the meaning should be understood by way of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness. This term "one who acts with clear comprehension" is indeed the detailed explanation of the phrase "endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension." In the Vibhaṅga, however, these terms are analyzed thus: "Mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes forward; mindful and clearly comprehending, he returns." Great King, in this way, a monk who performs going forward and so forth by the power of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness is said to be "endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension."

## Discourse on Contentment (Santosa-kathā)

Great King, in the statement "In this Dispensation, a monk is contented," the word "contented" (santuṭṭho) means being endowed with contentment with whatever requisites are obtained. That contentment is of twelve kinds, namely: three kinds of contentment regarding robes—contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santosa), contentment according to one's strength (yathābala-santosa), and contentment according to what is suitable (yathāsāruppa-santosa). Likewise, there are three kinds each regarding alms-food and so forth. The detailed explanation of that contentment is as follows:

In this Dispensation, a monk receives a robe, whether it is of good quality or poor quality. He sustains himself with only that robe; he does not long for another, and even if he receives another, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santosa) regarding robes. However, if he is naturally weak...
183:
...or if he is weak because he is oppressed by illness or old age, he becomes weary when wearing a heavy robe. If that monk exchanges it with a compatible monk and sustains himself with a light robe, he is still considered contented. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābala-santosa) regarding robes. 

Another monk is one who receives excellent requisites. When he receives an extremely expensive bowl or robe, or many bowls and robes, he thinks: "This is suitable for the senior elders of long standing; this is suitable for those of great learning (bahussuta); this is suitable for sick monks; this is suitable for those who receive few gains," and he gives them away. Then, even if he takes their old robes or collects rags from a dust-heap and wears them after making a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi), he is still considered contented. This is his contentment according to what is suitable (yathāsāruppa-santosa) regarding robes.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives alms-food, whether it is coarse or fine. He sustains himself with only that food; he does not long for other food, and even if he receives more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santosa) regarding alms-food. But suppose a monk receives alms-food that is contrary to his natural constitution or contrary to his illness, such that he would be uncomfortable if he consumed it. If he gives that food to a compatible monk and, after eating suitable food from that monk's hand, performs his recluse-dharma, he is still considered contented. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābala-santosa) regarding alms-food. Another monk receives much fine alms-food. Just as with the robes, he gives that food to senior elders, the learned, those with few gains, and the sick. Then, even if he eats their leftovers or eats mixed food collected from his own alms-round, he is still considered contented. This is his contentment according to what is suitable (yathāsāruppa-santosa) regarding alms-food.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives lodging, whether it is pleasing or unpleasing. He does not give rise to joy or sorrow because of that lodging; he is satisfied with whatever he has received, even if it is only a grass mat. This is his contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābha-santosa) regarding lodging. But suppose a monk receives lodging that is contrary to his natural constitution or illness, such that he would be uncomfortable living there. If he gives that lodging to a compatible monk and lives in a suitable lodging belonging to that monk, he is still considered contented. This is his contentment according to strength (yathābala-santosa) regarding lodging.

Another monk of great merit receives many fine lodgings such as caves, pavilions, and gabled houses. Just as with the robes, he gives those lodgings to senior elders, the learned, those with few gains, and the sick, and he himself lives wherever it may be; he is still considered contented.
184:
This contentment with appropriate lodging is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding the lodging of that monk. Furthermore, another monk reflects repeatedly: 'A noble lodging is a place for heedlessness; sloth and torpor (thinamiddha) overcome one who sits there, and when one is oppressed by sleep and wakes up again, sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) manifest.' Having reflected thus, even if he receives such a lodging, he does not accept it. Rejecting it, even if he lives in the open air or at the foot of a tree and so on, he remains content. This also is called contentment with what is appropriate regarding the lodging of that monk.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives medicine, whether coarse or refined. He is content with whatever medicine he receives; he does not long for another, and even if he could obtain it, he does not take it. This contentment with whatever medicine is received is called contentment with what is obtained (yathālābhasantosa) regarding the medicinal requisites of that monk. Another monk, desiring oil, receives molasses (phāṇita). He gives that molasses to a compatible monk and, having taken oil from that monk's hand or having sought other oil, even if he uses it as medicine, he remains content. This contentment with medicine according to one's strength is called contentment according to strength (yathābalasantosa) regarding the medicinal requisites of that monk.

Another monk of great merit receives many refined medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses. Just like a robe, he gives those medicines to elders, long-ordained monks, learned monks, those who receive little, and sick monks; and even if he subsists on whatever medicine they give back to him without preference, he remains content. Another monk is presented with yellow myrobalan steeped in cow's urine (muttaharīṭaka) in one vessel and the four sweet foods (caturmadhura) in another, with the words: 'Venerable sir, please take whichever medicine you wish.' If his illness could be cured by either of those two, yet he thinks, 'Yellow myrobalan steeped in cow's urine has been praised by the Buddhas and others,' and rejecting the four sweet foods, he uses only the yellow myrobalan steeped in cow's urine as medicine, he remains supremely content. This is called contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding the medicinal requisites of that monk.

For a monk endowed with these twelve types of contentment with whatever requisites are obtained, the eight requisites (attha parikkhāra) are suitable. These eight requisites are: three robes, a bowl, an adze for cutting tooth-sticks, a needle, a waistband, and a water filter. It is also said:

'Three robes, a bowl, an adze, a needle, and a waistband,
With a water filter, these eight are for the monk devoted to spiritual practice.'

All those requisites are both for the care of the body (kāyaparihārika) and for the care of the stomach (kucchiparihārika). How? First, the three robes, when worn and draped while wandering, care for and sustain the body; thus they are requisites for the care of the body (kāyaparihārika). When filtering water with the corner of the robe...
185:
...and drinking it, or when taking various large and small fruits to be eaten, they sustain the stomach; thus the robe is a requisite for the care of the stomach (kucchiparihārika).

The bowl also, when used to draw water for bathing or when pouring water to clean the toilet area (kuṭipari bhanda), is a requisite for the care of the body (kāyaparihārika). When used to receive and eat almsfood, it is a requisite for the care of the stomach.

The adze (vāsī) also, when used to cut tooth-sticks or when carving the frames, legs, robe-racks, or poles of couches and chairs, is a requisite for the care of the body. When peeling sugarcane or splitting coconuts and so on, it is a requisite for the care of the stomach.

The needle also, when sewing robes, is a requisite for the care of the body. When used to pierce and eat cakes or fruits, it is a requisite for the care of the stomach.

The waistband, when tied around the waist while wandering, is a requisite for the care of the body. When used to tie and carry sugarcane and so on, it is a requisite for the care of the stomach.

The water filter, when used to filter water for bathing or when cleaning the monastery, is a requisite for the care of the body. When filtering drinking water, or when using that same filter to hold and eat sesame, rice, popped rice (puthuka), and so on, it is a requisite for the care of the stomach. This mentioned amount is only for a monk who carries eight requisites. For a monk who carries nine requisites, a bedspread (paccattharaṇa) or a key (kuñcikā) for when entering the sleeping quarters is suitable. For a monk who carries ten requisites, a sitting cloth (nisīdana) or a piece of leather (cammakhaṇḍa) is suitable. For a monk who carries eleven requisites, a walking stick (kattarayāṭṭhi) or an oil tube (telanāḷikā) is suitable. For a monk who carries twelve requisites, an umbrella (chatta) or sandals (upāhana) are suitable. Among those monks, it should not be said that only the one carrying eight requisites is content, while the others are discontented, highly ambitious, or heavily burdened. For those who carry nine requisites and so on are also of few wishes (appiccha), content (santosa), easy to support (subhara), and lead a light life (sallahukavutti). The Blessed One, however, did not teach this sutta with reference to those carrying nine requisites and so on, but taught it only with reference to the monk carrying eight requisites. For such a monk, having placed the small adze and the needle in the water filter and putting them inside the bowl, hangs the bowl on his shoulder, and keeping the three robes (ticīvara) inseparable from his body, goes happily wherever he wishes. He has nothing that he must return to fetch.
186:
In this way, wishing to show the lightness of living of this bhikkhu, the Blessed One said: "He is content with a robe just to protect the body," and so forth. In that passage, 'kāyaparihārikena' means just enough to protect the body. 'Kucchiparihārikena' means just enough to protect the belly. 'Samādāyeva pakkamati' means that he goes taking only the eight requisites, making them inseparable from his body. He has no attachment or bond such as "my monastery, my precinct, my attendant." Like an arrow released from a bowstring, or like a rutting elephant that has left the herd, he stays alone or sits alone, making use of whatever dwelling, forest grove, foot of a tree, or mountain cleft he desires. In all postures, he is alone without a second.

"He is one who can go to the four quarters and is without resentment,
Being content with whatever he gets,
Enduring perils, undaunted,
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros."

He thus attains the state of wandering alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, as praised here.

Now, wishing to establish that meaning with a simile, He said: "Seyyathāpi" and so forth. In that passage, 'pakkhī sakuṇo' means a winged bird. 'Deti' means he flies up. The summary of the meaning in this simile is as follows: Birds, knowing that "the fruit of the tree in such and such a place is ripe," come from various directions and eat those fruits, piercing and shaking them with their claws, wings, and beaks. They do not think, "This fruit is for today, this fruit is for tomorrow." When the fruit is exhausted, they do not keep guard over the tree, nor do they leave behind a wing, a claw, or a beak there. Instead, being without concern for that tree, they fly away to whatever direction they desire, carrying only the burden of their wings. In the same way, this bhikkhu goes wherever he likes without attachment or concern. Therefore, it is said: "He goes taking [his requisites] along."
187:
## Discussion on the Abandoning of the Hindrances
What does the Venerable show by the words "In this way" and so forth? He shows the fulfillment of the causes for forest-dwelling. For if a bhikkhu does not have these four causes (virtue, sense restraint, mindfulness and clear comprehension, and contentment), his forest-dwelling cannot be successful. He would come to live together with animals or forest hunters. The deities residing in the forest would make terrifying sounds, thinking, "What is the use of such an evil bhikkhu living in the forest?" and would strike his head with their hands to make him flee. An ill reputation would spread: "Such and such a bhikkhu entered the forest and committed such and such an evil deed." But if a bhikkhu has these four causes, his forest-dwelling is successful. For when he reviews his own virtue and sees no stain or blemish, he gives rise to joy (pīti); then, contemplating that joy in terms of its passing away and vanishing, he enters the noble plane (ariyabhūmi). The deities residing in the forest, being delighted, speak his praise. Thus, his reputation for virtue spreads like a drop of oil dropped into water.

In that text, "vivitta" means secluded, quiet, and free from noise. With reference to this meaning, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "Secluded means that even if the lodging is near a village, it is not crowded with householders or monastics. Therefore, it is called secluded." It is called "senāsana" (lodging) because one sleeps (seti) and sits (āsati) there; this is a designation for beds, chairs, and so forth. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Lodging (senāsana) means a bed is a lodging, a chair is a lodging, a bolster, a pillow, a monastery, a lean-to, a long house, a mansion, a cave, a cell, a shed, a shelter, a bamboo grove, the foot of a tree, a pavilion—all these are lodgings; or wherever bhikkhus stay, all that is lodging." (Vibh. 527).

Furthermore—a monastery, a lean-to, a long house, a mansion, and a cave are called "vihāra-senāsana" (dwelling lodging). A bed, a chair, a bolster, and a pillow are called "mañcapīṭha-senāsana" (bed and chair lodging). A rag-spread, a hide-mat, a grass-mat, and a leaf-spread are called "santhata-senāsana" (spread lodging). Wherever bhikkhus stay is called "okāsa-senāsana" (open-space lodging). Thus, there are four kinds of lodgings, and all of them are included under the term "senāsana."

In this context, however, wishing to show the lodging suitable for a bhikkhu who, like a bird, can go to the four quarters without anxiety, He said: "araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ" (a forest, the foot of a tree) and so forth. In that text, "arañña" (forest) means all the area outside the threshold of a gate. This is the definition concerning bhikkhunīs. For this bhikkhu, a suitable forest is a place at least five hundred bow-lengths away. The characteristics of such a forest have already been stated in the Dhutaṅganiddesa of the Visuddhimagga. "Rukkhamūla" means the foot of a secluded tree. "Pabbata" means a rocky mountain. For one who has bathed in the pools of that rocky mountain and sits in the cool shade of a tree, when the quarters become clear, with the cool breeze...
188:
Stepping outside the threshold, all the surrounding area is called the forest. This meaning is given in the context of bhikkhunīs. The statement, "A forest dwelling must be at least five hundred bow-lengths away," refers to a lodging suitable for this monk. The characteristics of such a forest are already explained in the Dhuṭaṅganiddesa of the Visuddhimagga. 'Rukkhamūla' refers to the foot of any secluded tree that provides good shade. 'Pabbata' refers to a rocky mountain. Indeed, in such a place, after attending to water needs at the mountain pools, the mind of a monk becomes concentrated as he sits in the cool shade of a tree, with the various directions clearly visible, being fanned by the cool breeze.

'Kandara' refers to a mountain cleft or glen eroded by water (called 'kaṃ') or split by water. It is also called a small river or a river bend. In that mountain glen, there are sands resembling silver plates; above, there is a forest canopy like a jeweled pavilion; and water flows like a mass of beryl. Having descended into such a glen, drunk the water, cooled the body, cleared the sand, spread the rag-robe, and sat down to practice the Dhamma of a recluse, the mind becomes concentrated. 'Giriguha' refers to a large cavern like a tunnel between two mountains or within a single mountain. The characteristics of a cemetery (susāna) have already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. 'Vanapattha' refers to a place beyond the village boundaries where humans do not frequent. In such a place, they do not plow or sow. Therefore, it was said, "'Vanapattha' is a name for distant dwellings," and so on. 'Abbhokāsa' refers to the open air without a roof. A monk who desires to do so may live there by making a hut out of robes. 'Palālapuñja' refers to a heap of straw. From a large heap of straw, they pull out straw to make shelters like mountain caves or grottoes. They also place straw on top of bushes and thickets, and sitting underneath, they practice the Dhamma of a recluse. This was said in reference to the straw placed on top of such bushes.

'Pacchābhatta' means after the meal. 'Piṇḍapātapāṭikkanto' means having returned from the search for alms-food. 'Pallaṅka' means sitting with the thighs locked in a circle (cross-legged). 'Ābhujitvā' means having folded or locked. 'Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya' means keeping the upper body erect, aligning the eighteen vertebrae of the spine end to end. For a monk sitting in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews are not bent. Because they are not bent, the pains that would arise moment by moment due to the bending of skin, flesh, and sinews do not occur. When those pains do not arise, the mind becomes concentrated, and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) does not fall away but reaches growth, increase, and abundance. 'Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā' means establishing mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject.
189:
Alternatively, it means having placed [mindfulness] near the mouth. Therefore, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "This mindfulness is established, well-established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth; therefore, it is said, 'establishing mindfulness in front'" (Vibh. 537). Alternatively, the word 'pari' has the sense of grasping (pariggaha). The word 'mukha' has the sense of leading out (niyyāna). The word 'sati' has the sense of establishment (upaṭṭhāna). Therefore, it is called 'parimukhaṃ satiṃ'. The meaning here should also be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. The summary of the meaning in that text is: "Having established mindfulness as a grasped means of leading out."

217. In the phrase "covetousness in the world," the world (loka) refers to the five aggregates of clinging because of their nature of being constantly broken and destroyed. Therefore, the meaning here is: having abandoned lust (rāga) for the five aggregates of clinging and having suppressed sensual desire (kāmacchanda). "With a mind free from covetousness" means with a mind from which covetousness has been abandoned through the power of suppression (vikkhambhana); it does not mean a mind like eye-consciousness. "He purifies the mind from covetousness" means he liberates the mind from covetousness. The meaning is that he acts in such a way that covetousness releases the mind, and once released, it does not take hold of it again.

In the phrases such as "having abandoned ill-will and malevolence," the same method applies. It is called 'byāpāda' (ill-will) because through this, the mind discards its original nature, like rotten barley-gruel and the like. It is called 'padosa' (malevolence) because it is corrupted by reaching a state of deformity, or because it corrupts oneself, or because it destroys others. Both of these are synonyms for anger (kodha). 'Thina' (sloth) is the sickness of the mind (unwieldiness of the aggregate of consciousness). 'Middha' (torpor) is the sickness of the mental factors (unwieldiness of the three aggregates beginning with feeling). The combination of thina and middha is called 'thina-middha'. "One with the perception of light" refers to one endowed with a pure perception, free from the hindrances, and capable of remembering during the night the light seen during the day. "Mindful and clearly comprehending" means endowed with both mindfulness and wisdom. These two are mentioned because they are helpful to the perception of light.

The combination of 'uddhacca' (restlessness) and 'kukkucca' (remorse) is called 'uddhacca-kukkucca'. "One who has crossed over doubt" means one who stands having crossed and transcended 'vicikiciccha'. He is called 'akathaṃkathī' (one free from doubt) because thoughts like "How is this? How is that?" do not occur to him. "In wholesome states" means in blameless states. The meaning is that he does not doubt or hesitate, thinking, "Are these states wholesome? How are these states wholesome?" This is the summary here. All that should be said regarding these hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in terms of their etymology, characteristics, and so on, has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

218. In the simile beginning with "Just as, Great King," "having taken a debt" means having taken another's wealth with interest. "He would bring it to an end" means...
190:
It means that one should repay everything to those creditors so that not even a fraction [the size of a kākaṇika] remains as a remainder. "Tato nidānaṃ" means because of the reason of being debt-free. That person, reflecting "I am debt-free," gains great gladness and attains happiness. Therefore, it is said: "He would gain gladness and attain happiness."

Because of the arising of disagreeable feelings, it is called "ābādha" (affliction) because it oppresses the four postures as if cutting them with a saw. One who has that affliction is called "ābādhika." That person suffers due to the pain caused by that affliction. "Adhimattagilāno" means one who is severely ill. "Nacchādeyya" means not finding food delicious because of being overwhelmed by a very severe illness. "Balamattā" means mere strength. It means that there is no strength in his body. "Tato nidānaṃ" means because of the reason of being free from illness. When that person reflects "I am free from illness," both gladness and happiness arise. Therefore, it is said: "He would gain gladness and attain happiness."

There should not be even a fraction [the size of a kākaṇika] of loss of wealth. "Tato nidānaṃ" means because of the reason of being released from bonds. The remaining words should be applied to all sections in the same manner as already stated.

221-222. "Anattādhīno" means not being under one's own control, not being allowed to do anything according to one's own wish. "Parādhīno" means being under the control of others, acting only according to the wish of others. "Na yena kāmaṃ gamo" means that even if that person has the desire to go to a certain direction, he is not allowed to go there. "Dāsabyā" means from the state of slavery. "Bhujisso" means being one's own master. "Tato nidānaṃ" means because of the reason of being a free man. "Kantāraddhānamaggaṃ" means a long journey through a waterless wilderness. "Tato nidānaṃ" means because of the reason of reaching a safe land.

In this context of "Ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīne," the Blessed One shows the unabandoned hindrance of sensual desire as being similar to a debt. He shows the remaining hindrances as being similar to illness and so on. In showing them thus, the similarity is as follows: Suppose a person takes a debt from others and squanders it. When he is told by the creditors, "Give back the debt," or is spoken to harshly, or is bound...
191:
...even when being mistreated, he is unable to prevent anything and must endure everything. That debt alone is the cause of his endurance. In the same way, when a person is infatuated with a certain object through sensual desire, he takes hold of that object with a mind accompanied by craving. Even if he is spoken to harshly, bound, or mistreated by that object (or person), he endures everything. The cause of his endurance is that very sensual desire. It is like the sensual desire of women who are mistreated by their husbands. Thus, sensual desire should be seen as being like a debt.

Just as a person afflicted with bile disease does not experience the taste of honey, sugar, etc., even when they are given, but only vomits saying "It is bitter, it is bitter" due to the bile disease; in the same way, a person with a corrupted mind (ill-will), even when being slightly admonished by teachers and preceptors who desire his welfare, does not accept the advice. Saying things like "You are harassing me too much," he leaves the monkhood. Just as the bile disease prevents that person from experiencing the taste of honey and sugar, because of being afflicted by anger, he does not experience the flavor of the Sasana, such as the bliss of jhāna. Thus, ill-will should be seen as being like an illness.

Just as a person imprisoned in a jail on a festival day does not see the beginning, middle, or end of that festival. When he is released the next day and hears others saying "Yesterday's festival was wonderful, it was delightful; the dancing and singing were wonderful," he cannot give a reply. For what reason? Because he did not experience the festival himself. In the same way, a monk overcome by sloth and torpor does not know the beginning, middle, or end of the Dhamma being preached, even though it is presented in various beautiful ways. When the Dhamma preaching is over and he hears others praising the Dhamma, saying "Hearing the Dhamma was wonderful, the reasons and similes were wonderful," he cannot give a reply. For what reason? Because he did not experience the Dhamma talk due to the power of sloth and torpor. Thus, sloth and torpor should be seen as being like a prison.

Just as a slave, even while enjoying a festival, is told "There is an urgent task to be done, go there quickly; if you do not go, I will cut off your hands and feet, or your ears and nose," he must go quickly. He does not get to experience the beginning, middle, or end of the festival. For what reason? Because of being dependent on another. In the same way, a monk who is unskilled in the Vinaya, even though he has entered the forest for the sake of seclusion...
192:
If, in a certain matter, even regarding allowable meat, the perception of unallowable meat arises, one must give up seclusion (meditation) and go to a Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) to purify one's virtue; one cannot enjoy the bliss of seclusion. Why is that? Because one is overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca). Thus, restlessness and remorse should be seen as being like slavery.

A man on a dangerous journey through a wilderness (kantāraddhānamagga) where there are robbers, seeing the places where people have been plundered and killed, becomes suspicious and apprehensive even at the sound of a stick or a bird, thinking, "The robbers have come." He goes, he stops, he retreats. The distance he has not yet traveled is much greater than the distance he has already covered. That man may or may not reach a safe land with great difficulty and hardship. In the same way, for one in whom doubt arises concerning the eight points, he, doubting in such ways as "Is it the Buddha, or is it not the Buddha?" and so on, is unable to decide and accept with faith. Being unable to accept, he cannot reach the Path (magga) or the Fruit (phala). Just as in a dangerous journey, repeatedly thinking "Are there robbers or not?", being unable to enter into it, and causing the mind to tremble, creates an obstacle to reaching safety; so too, doubt (vicikicchā), by repeatedly thinking "Is it the Buddha, or is it not the Buddha?" and so on, being unable to enter into it, and causing the mind to tremble, creates an obstacle to reaching the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya). Therefore, doubt should be seen as being like a dangerous journey through a wilderness.

Now, in this passage, "Great King, just as freedom from debt (āṇaṇya)," the Blessed One shows the abandoned hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) as being like freedom from debt, and the remaining hindrances as being like freedom from illness and so on. In this regard, the similarity is as follows: A man, having taken a loan and applied himself to his business, becomes wealthy and thinks, "This thing called debt is the root of anxiety." Having repaid the debt along with the interest, he would have the bond cancelled. From then on, no one sends a messenger or a notice to him. Even if he sees the creditors, he stands up from his seat if he wishes, or does not stand up if he does not wish. Why? Because he has no attachment or connection with them. In the same way, a monk, thinking "This sensual desire is the root of anxiety," abandons the hindrance of sensual desire by developing six things. I will explain those six things in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. To that monk...
193:
For a monk whose sensual desire is abandoned, it is just like a man free from debt who has no fear or trembling even when seeing his creditors. In the same way, he no longer has attachment or bondage to the property of others. Even when seeing divine forms, defilements do not arise. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandonment of sensual desire as being like freedom from debt.

Furthermore, just as a man suffering from a bile disease (pittaroga), having calmed that disease through medical treatment, from then on enjoys the taste of honey, sugar, and so on; in the same way, a monk, reflecting "This ill-will (byāpāda) brings great harm," abandons the hindrance of ill-will by developing six things. I will explain the six things for abandoning all hindrances only in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Not only those, but I will also explain there all the things to be developed for the abandonment of sloth and torpor (thina-middha) and so on. That monk who has thus abandoned ill-will, just as a man freed from bile disease enjoys the taste of honey, sugar, and so on with delight, so too, having respectfully accepted the training rules such as the rules of conduct (ācāra-paṇṇatti), he practices them with delight. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandonment of ill-will as being like freedom from illness and being healthy.

Just as a man imprisoned on a festival day, when the next festival day arrives, thinks, "In the past, I was bound due to the fault of negligence; therefore, I did not enjoy the festival. Now I will be diligent," so that his enemies do not get an opportunity, he enjoys the festival diligently and utters an exclamation of joy, "Oh, what a festival! Oh, what a festival!"; in the same way, a monk, reflecting "This sloth and torpor (thina-middha) brings great harm," abandons the hindrance of sloth and torpor by developing six things. That monk who has thus abandoned sloth and torpor, just as a man released from bondage enjoys the beginning, middle, and end of the festival for seven days, so too, enjoying the beginning, middle, and end of the festival of the Dhamma, he reaches Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandonment of sloth and torpor as being like release from the bondage of prison.

Furthermore, just as a slave (dāsa), relying on a certain friend, gives wealth to his masters and makes himself free from slavery (bhujissa), and from then on does whatever he wishes; in the same way, a monk, reflecting "This restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) brings great harm," abandons restlessness and remorse by developing six things. That monk who has thus abandoned restlessness and remorse, just as a man freed from slavery can do whatever he wishes and no one can force him from that state...
194:
Just as one cannot be forcibly restrained, likewise one practices the practice of renunciation (the practice of the first jhāna) with ease. Restlessness and worry (uddhacca-kukkucca), which have been abandoned by that path, can no longer forcibly restrain one from that practice. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of restlessness and worry as being like freedom from slavery.

Just as a strong man, holding wealth (or essentials) in his hand, well-armed and with attendants, might travel through a difficult desert infested with thieves; and thieves, seeing him from afar, would flee; and that man, having safely crossed that desert and reached a secure land, would be joyful and happy; likewise, a monk, reflecting, 'This doubt (vicikicchā) indeed causes great harm,' develops the six things and abandons doubt. That monk, having thus abandoned doubt, just like the strong man who, well-armed and with attendants, is fearless and regards thieves as mere grass, safely emerges and reaches a secure land; likewise, the monk, having crossed the desert of misconduct, reaches the supreme secure land, the deathless Great Nibbāna. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of doubt as being like reaching a secure land.

'Joy (pāmojja) arises' means the appearance of a state of gladness. 'In one who is joyful, rapture (pīti) arises' means rapture arises, shaking the entire body of the joyful monk. 'In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil' means the mental body (nāma-kāya) of the person whose mind is associated with rapture becomes tranquil and free from distress. 'He experiences happiness' means he experiences both bodily and mental happiness. 'The mind becomes concentrated' means the mind of the person who is happy with this happiness of renunciation becomes concentrated through the power of either access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi).

## Pathamajjhāna-kathā

'That monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna,' etc., should be understood as being spoken to show the higher distinction of the jhāna when the mind is already concentrated by access concentration, and to show the different types of that concentration when the mind is concentrated by attainment concentration. 'This very body' means this physical body (karaja-kāya). 'He drenches' means to moisten, to make sticky, to cause the rapture and happiness to occur throughout the entire body. 'He saturates' means he makes it flow all around. 'He fills' means he fills it like air filling a bellows. 'He pervades' means he touches and spreads all around. 'Of the entire body' means of the body of that monk which has all its parts; in any place where the continuity of the clung-to matter (upādinnaka-rūpa) occurs...
195:
In the sequence of the produced physical body (upādinnaka-rūpa) that follows the skin, flesh, and blood, there is not even a tiny spot that is not pervaded by the happiness of the first jhāna. 'Dakkha' means a person who is skilled and proficient in making, mixing, and kneading bath powders. 'Kaṃsathāla' means a vessel made of any kind of metal. A clay vessel, however, is not stable and tends to break for the one who is kneading. Therefore, he does not show that clay vessel. 'Paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ' means sprinkling water again and again. 'Sanneyya' means holding the bronze basin with the left hand, sprinkling the right amount of water with the right hand, and kneading it to form a ball. 'Snehānugatā' means pervaded by the moisture of water. 'Snehaparetā' means all the powder is saturated with the moisture of water. 'Santarabāhirā' means it is pervaded by the moisture of water in both the inner and outer parts of the powder. 'Na ca paggharaṇī' means the water does not leak out in drops; it can be held by the hand or by two or three fingers and can be formed into a lump.

## Discussion on the Second Jhāna
228-229. In the simile for the happiness of the second jhāna, 'ubbhidodaka' refers to a lake with spring-fed water; it is not water that breaks through and rises from below. It means water that springs up only within the lake. 'Āyamukha' means an entry path or a coming path. 'Deva' means a rain cloud. 'Kālena kālaṃ' means at all times, or once every half-month, or once every ten days. 'Dhāra' means rainwater. 'Na anuppaveccheyya' means it should not let enter, it should not rain. 'Sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvā' means the cool stream of water rises, filling the lake and appearing at the top. Water rising from below and breaking through disturbs the existing water. Water entering from the four directions also makes the water turbid and disturbed with old leaves, grass, wood, twigs, and so on. Rainwater also disturbs the water with falling drops and bubbles. Only water that arises spontaneously, as if created by psychic power, is calm, and there is no limit such as "it pervades this spot but not that spot"; therefore, there is no such thing as an unpervaded spot. In that simile, the physical body (karaja-kāya) should be understood as the lake. The happiness of the second jhāna should be understood as the water. The rest should be understood according to the previous method.
196:
## Discussion on the Third Jhāna
230-231. In the simile for the happiness of the third jhāna, it is called 'uppalinī' because it means 'there are blue lotuses (uppala) in this [pond].' The same method applies to the other two terms (paduminī and puṇḍarīkinī). Here, among the white, red, and blue lotuses, any lotus is simply called 'uppala.' A lotus with fewer than a hundred petals is called 'puṇḍarīka,' and one with a hundred petals is called 'paduma.' Alternatively, without regarding the number of petals, a white lotus is called 'paduma' and a red one is called 'puṇḍarīka'; this is the decision here. 'Udakānuggatāni' means they have not emerged from the water. 'Anto nimuggaposīni' means they thrive and grow while remaining submerged under the surface of the water. The rest should be understood according to the previous method.

## Discussion on the Fourth Jhāna
232-233. In the simile for the happiness of the fourth jhāna, in the phrase 'pari-suddhena cetasā pariyodātena' (with a mind purified and bright), it should be understood that it is 'parisuddha' (purified) because it is free from the defilement of impurities, and 'pariyodāta' (bright) because it is endowed with radiance. The phrase 'odātena vatthena' (with a white cloth) is spoken for the purpose of the spreading of the aura (utu-pharaṇa). Indeed, the spreading of the aura does not occur with a dirty cloth; the spreading of the aura is powerful (distinct) only with a clean cloth washed at that moment. In this simile, the physical body (karaja-kāya) should be understood as the cloth, and the happiness of the fourth jhāna as the spreading of the aura. Therefore, just as when a well-bathed man sits wrapped in a clean cloth including his head, the aura from his body spreads through the entire cloth, and there is no part of the cloth not reached by it; in the same way, there is no part of the monk's physical body not reached by the happiness of the fourth jhāna. Thus should the meaning be understood here. The sequential explanation and the method of development of these four jhānas have been stated in the Visuddhimagga, so they are not elaborated here.

By this much, it should not be understood that this person is only a gainer of fine-material jhānas (rūpa-jhāna) and not a gainer of immaterial jhānas (arūpa-jhāna). This is because the attainment of higher knowledge (abhiññā) is not possible without having mastered (vasībhāva) the eight attainments (samāpatti) in fourteen ways. Although only the fine-material jhānas appear in the Pali text, the immaterial jhānas are also included and spoken of.

## Discussion on Insight Knowledge
By the passage 'So evaṃ samāhite citte... āneñjappatte' (With the mind thus concentrated... having reached imperturbability), it refers to the monk who has mastery in the eight attainments in fourteen ways.
197:
It shows (that meaning). The rest here should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. In the passage 'He directs the mind towards knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharati), 'knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassana) refers to Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), Fruition Knowledge (phala-ñāṇa), Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), Reviewing Knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), and Insight Knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). In the passage, 'Friends, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the sake of purification of knowledge and vision?', Path Knowledge is called 'knowledge and vision.' In the passage, 'This is another state beyond human level, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, an attained comfortable abiding,' Fruition Knowledge is called 'knowledge and vision.' In the passage, 'To the Blessed One also, the knowledge and vision arose: Āḷāra Kālāma has been dead for seven days,' Omniscience is called 'knowledge and vision.' In the passage, 'Knowledge and vision arose in me: My liberation is unshakable, this is my last birth,' Reviewing Knowledge is called 'knowledge and vision.' But in this (Sāmaññaphala Sutta), in the phrase 'the mind towards knowledge and vision,' Insight Knowledge is called 'knowledge and vision.'

'Abhinīharati' (he directs) means he makes the mind incline, lean, and tend towards that insight knowledge for the purpose of producing it. The meanings of terms such as 'rūpī' (having form) have already been stated. 'Odanakummāsūpacayo' (nourished by boiled rice and barley bread) means it is built up and grown by boiled rice and barley bread. 'Aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo' means it is of an impermanent nature (anicca) because it does not exist after having been. It is subject to anointing (ucchādana) with perfumes to remove bad odors. It is subject to massaging (parimaddana) by gentle rubbing to remove the aches of the limbs. Or, in childhood, it is subject to massaging by means of pulling and pressing to perfect the shape of various limbs that were poorly formed due to staying in the mother's womb while lying on her thighs. Even when thus cared for, it is subject to breaking and dissolution, meaning it both breaks and scatters; such is its nature. 

Among those terms, the six terms starting with 'rūpī cātumahābhūtiko' (having form, consisting of the four great elements) describe origination (samudaya). Together with the term 'anicca' (impermanent), the last two terms describe passing away (atthaṅgama). 'Dependent on this, bound to this' means it is both dependent on and bound to this body made of the four great elements.

'Subho' means beautiful. 'Jātimā' means of pure origin. 'Suparikammakato' means well-prepared, with stones and pebbles removed. 'Accho' means of clear luster. 'Vippasanno' means very bright. 'Sabbākārasampanno' means endowed with all aspects such as washing and boring. By the terms 'nīla' (blue) etc., the perfection of color is shown. For when a thread of such color is strung, it is distinct. In the phrase 'even so,' the correlation between the simile and the thing illustrated should be understood thus: the physical body (karaja-kāya) should be seen as the gem.
198:
Insight knowledge is like a thread that has been strung. Just as a gem is clear to a man with good eyesight when he reflects on it, holding it in his hand, saying, 'This is a gem,' so too insight knowledge is clear to a monk who has attained insight. To a monk who dwells having directed [his mind], the body composed of the four great elements becomes clear, just as the thread becomes clear when it is strung through that gem. To the monk who dwells having directed [his mind], there is the time when the five groups beginning with contact (phassa), which are the objects of that insight knowledge, or all consciousness and mental factors, or insight knowledge itself, become clear.

This insight knowledge occurs immediately after Path knowledge. Even so, because there is no intervening stage when the section on supernormal powers (abhiññā) is begun, it is shown right here. Furthermore, one who has not practiced contemplation of impermanence and so on might experience fear and terror when hearing a terrifying sound with the divine ear, or when recollecting terrifying aggregates with the recollection of past lives, or when seeing a terrifying form with the divine eye. However, fear does not arise for one who has practiced contemplation of impermanence and so on. Therefore, this insight knowledge is shown right here also for the purpose of fulfilling the cause for dispelling the fear of one who has attained supernormal powers. Alternatively, it should be understood that it is shown here from the beginning because what is called the 'happiness of insight' (vipassanā-sukha) produces the happiness of the Path and Fruition, and is a distinct, visible fruit of recluseship.

## Manomayiddhi-ñāṇa-kathā

236-237. 'Mind-made' (manomaya) means produced by the mind. 'Complete in all limbs and parts' (sabbaṅgapaccaṅgi) means endowed with all major and minor limbs. 'Not lacking any faculties' (ahīnindriya) means having faculties that are not deficient in terms of their form. For if the possessor of supernormal power is fair-skinned, the form created by him is also fair-skinned. If his ears are not pierced, that form also has unpierced ears. Thus, in every aspect, it is just like that possessor of power. The three similes, beginning with 'the reed from the sheath,' are mentioned only to show this similarity. The pith inside the reed is just like the reed itself. The sword is just like the scabbard; they put a curved sword into a curved scabbard and a straight sword into a straight scabbard. 'Karaṇḍa' is also a name for a snake's slough, not for a wicker basket. A snake's slough is just like the snake. In that simile, although it is shown as if a man were pulling a snake out of its slough with his hand, it should be understood as pulling it out with the mind alone. This snake, while remaining in its own kind, depending on the space between logs or trees, pulls its body out from the skin...
199:
...by means of the strength known as the effort of pulling out, as if it were eating its own body, it discards the slough by itself out of disgust for the old skin. It is not possible for another to pull it out from there. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference to pulling it out with the mind. Thus, the body of this monk is like the reed, and the created form is like the pith. This is the comparison of the simile and the thing illustrated here. As for the method of creation, and the discussion of the five supernormal powers such as the various psychic powers (iddhividha) that follow, these have been explained in detail in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, they should be understood according to the method stated in that text. Only the similes are additional here [in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta].

## Iddhividha-ñāṇa-kathā

238-239. In that simile, the monk who has attained the knowledge of various psychic powers should be seen like a skilled potter and others. The knowledge of various psychic powers should be seen like well-prepared clay and so on. The monk's transformation through power should be seen like the making of various types of vessels as desired.

240-241. In the simile of the divine ear element (dibbasota-dhātu), a long desert road where there are thieves is full of fear and danger. A person who is anxious and suspicious on that road cannot distinguish, 'This is the sound of a drum,' or 'This is the sound of a tabor.' Therefore, without using the desert, the Buddha said, 'a man traveling along a long road,' wishing to show a safe road. On a safe road free from danger, a man traveling slowly with his upper cloth on his head can easily distinguish the aforementioned sounds. Just as the various sounds become clear to him simply by hearing them, so too should it be understood that divine and human sounds, both far and near, become clear to the meditator.

242-243. In the simile of the knowledge of discerning others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), 'dahara' means young. 'Yuvā' means endowed with the prime of youth. 'Maṇဍanakajātika' means that although he is young, he is not lazy, nor are his clothes or body dirty; rather, he is of a nature to adorn himself, meaning he is in the habit of bathing two or three times a day, wearing clean clothes, and decorating himself. 'Sakaṇika' means having a defect such as a mole, a pimple, a facial distortion, or a blemish. In that simile, just as a defect on the face becomes clear to one reflecting on his facial features, so it should be understood that the sixteen types of minds of others become clear to a monk who has directed his mind toward the knowledge of discerning others' minds.
200:
244-245. In the simile for the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives (Pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), the actions performed on that day are clear; therefore, only the three villages visited on that day are taken. In that simile, the person who has attained the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives should be understood as the man who went to the three villages. The three realms of existence (bhava) should be understood as the three villages. Just as the actions performed by that man in the three villages on that day are clear to him, so too should it be understood that the actions performed in the three realms of existence are clear to the monk who sits directing his mind toward the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives.

246-247. In the simile for the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu), 'vīthiṃ sañcarante' means wandering to and fro. There is also a reading 'vīthiṃ carante'; the meaning is the same. In that simile, the physical body (rūpa-kāya) of this monk should be understood as the mansion at the crossroads in the middle of the city. This monk who has attained the Divine Eye should be understood as the man with sight standing on the mansion. Those entering the mother's womb by way of rebirth should be understood as those entering a house; those leaving the mother's womb as those leaving a house; beings wandering from one existence to another as those wandering on the main road; and beings arising here and there in the three realms of existence as those sitting in the middle of an open crossroads. Just as those people are clear to the man standing on the upper floor of the mansion, so too should it be understood that beings arising in the three realms of existence are clear to the monk who sits directing his mind toward the Knowledge of the Divine Eye. This is stated merely for the ease of teaching. In reality, there is no object for the Divine Eye in the formless realm (arūpa-bhava).

## Discussion on the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa-kathā)

In the phrase 'so evaṃ samāhite citte' (he, with his mind thus concentrated), the fourth jhāna mind, which is the basis for insight (vipassanā), should be understood. 'Āsavānaṃ khaya-ñāṇāya' means for the purpose of producing the knowledge that takes Nibbāna—the end of the taints (āsava)—as its object. Here, the 'destruction of taints' (āsavakkhaya) refers to the Path (magga), the Fruit (phala), Nibbāna, and dissolution (bhaṅga). In the phrase 'khaye ñāṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇaṃ' (knowledge of destruction, knowledge of non-arising), the Path is called the destruction of taints. In the phrase 'āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hoti' (by the destruction of taints, one becomes a recluse), the Fruit is called the destruction of taints. In the verse: 'For one who observes the faults of others, who is always prone to disparaging, his taints increase; he is far from the destruction of taints (Nibbāna),' Nibbāna is called the destruction of taints. In this phrase 'āsavānaṃ khaya-ñāṇāya', Nibbāna is intended as the destruction of taints; it can also refer to the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga).
201:
In this context, Nibbāna is intended. In the passage 'āsavānaṃ khayo vayo bhedo aniccatā antaradhānaṃ,' the destruction of the taints refers to dissolution (bhaṅga). However, here Nibbāna is intended as the destruction of the taints. The Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) is also appropriate.

'He directs the mind' means he makes the insight-consciousness (vipassanā-citta) lean, slope, and incline toward that Nibbāna. The meaning is that he understands as it really is, through the penetration of individual characteristics, the entire Truth of Suffering, thinking: 'This is suffering; there is only this much suffering, nothing more than this.' He understands as it really is, through the penetration of individual characteristics, the craving that produces that suffering as 'This is the origin of suffering (samudaya).' He understands as it really is, through the penetration of individual characteristics, Nibbāna—the state where both suffering and its origin cease upon reaching it, the non-occurrence of those things—as 'This is the cessation of suffering (nirodha).' And he understands as it really is, through the penetration of individual characteristics, the Noble Path that leads to that Truth of Cessation as 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (magga).'

Having thus shown the Truths in their own nature, he speaks of 'These are the taints,' etc., wishing to show them figuratively by way of the defilements (kilesa). 'For him thus knowing, thus seeing' means for that bhikkhu who thus knows and sees, the Buddha taught the Path that has reached its summit along with insight. 'Kāmāsavā' means from the taint of sensual desire. By the word 'is liberated' (vimuccati), the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa) is shown. By the word 'when liberated' (vimuttasmiṃ), the moment of the Fruit (phala-khaṇa) is shown. By the phrase 'the knowledge arises: it is liberated' (vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti), the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) is shown. By the words 'birth is exhausted' (khīṇā jāti), etc., the object of that reviewing knowledge is shown. For, when an Arahant reviews with that knowledge, he knows 'birth is exhausted,' and so on.

What kind of birth is exhausted for him? And how does he know it? His past birth is not what is exhausted, for it was already exhausted previously. Future birth is not what is exhausted, for there is no effort in the future. Present birth is not what is exhausted, for it is currently existing. Rather, it is the birth consisting of one, four, or five aggregates in the one-constituent, four-constituent, or five-constituent realms of existence that would have arisen because the Path had not been developed; that birth is exhausted by reaching the state of non-arising in the future because the Path has been developed. That Arahant, having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the development of the Path, knows: 'When defilements are absent, even existing kamma does not provide for rebirth in the future.'

'Vusitaṃ' means it has been fully lived and practiced. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' refers to the holy life of the Path. For, the seven types of trainees (sekha) along with the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) are said to be living the holy life. But the Arahant is one who has lived it. Therefore, that Arahant, reviewing his own living of the Path-practice, knows: 'The holy life has been lived.' 'Kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ' means, regarding the four Truths, by the four Paths...
202:
The sixteenfold task has been completed through the power of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriya), and development (bhāvanā). This means that the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path have been abandoned, and the root of suffering has been completely cut off. Noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) and others are still in the process of performing that task, but the Arahant is one who has already done what was to be done. Therefore, when that Arahant reflects on his own duty, he knows: "Done is what was to be done."

"There is no further task for this state of being" means he knows that there is no further task of developing the path to be done by me now for such a state, either for the completion of the sixteenfold task or for the destruction of defilements. Alternatively, "for this state of being" means from this present state of such a kind. He knows: "Now, apart from this present continuity of aggregates, there is no further continuity of aggregates for me. These five aggregates, having been fully understood, remain like trees whose roots have been cut; with the cessation of the final consciousness, they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel and will reach the state of being beyond designation (apaṇṇattika-bhāva)."

"A mountain pool" refers to a pool at the top of a mountain. "Unclouded" means without mud. Shells and cowries are called "shells and cowries." Pebbles and potsherds are called "pebbles and potsherds." A collection of fish is called a "shoal of fish." In the phrase "standing and moving," the pebbles and potsherds only stand still, while the others—shells, cowries, and fish—both move and stand still. Just as when there are cows standing or lying down here and there, one says "these cows are grazing" based on those that are moving, so too, based on the pebbles and potsherds which only stand still, the other two (shells/cowries and fish) are also said to be standing. And based on the movement of the other two, the pebbles and potsherds are also said to be moving. In that simile, just as the time when the shells, cowries, and so on are clearly visible to a man with good sight standing on the bank, so should the time when the Four Noble Truths become clear to a monk be understood, who sits having directed his mind toward the destruction of the taints.

By this much of the discourse, ten knowledges have been shown: insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), mind-made power (manomaya-ñāṇa), various psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa), divine ear (dibba-sota-ñāṇa), knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), the two knowledges produced by the power of the divine eye—knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) and knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa)—the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa), and knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). The classification of the objects of these knowledges should be understood. Among them, insight knowledge has seven kinds of objects by way of the limited (sense sphere), the exalted, the past, the future, the present, the internal, and the external. Mind-made power has as its object only the created visible-form base (rūpāyatana).
203:
Because the mind-made power (manomaya-ñāṇa) takes as its object only the created visible-form base, it has as its object a present external phenomenon of the sense sphere. The knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) has as its object the immeasurable external phenomena and concepts (paññatti). The classification of the objects of the remaining knowledges has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. With the words "nothing further or more excellent," the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship, showing that there is no fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) more excellent than this Arahantship by any other means.

## The Account of Ajātasattu's Declaration as a Lay Follower

King Ajātasattu, expressing his appreciation for each of the fruits of recluseship and having listened respectfully from the beginning, middle, to the end, thought: "For a long time indeed, I have been asking these questions to many recluses and brahmins, but like a man pounding hollow husks, I did not obtain any essence. Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Blessed One! Like lighting a thousand lamps, he has created a great light and answered these questions. For a very long time, I have been deceived, not knowing the power of the virtues of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." Thus thinking, his whole body was suffused with the fivefold joy born from the recollection of the Buddha's virtues. Desiring to make his devotion clear, he declared his status as a lay follower (upāsaka). To show that declaration, the passage beginning with "When this was said, the King..." was begun.

In that passage, "It is excellent, Bhante" (abhikkantaṃ bhante)—this word "abhikkanta" is seen in the senses of exhaustion, goodness, extreme beauty, and great delight (approval). In passages such as "The night is exhausted (abhikkantā), Bhante; the first watch has passed; the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting for a long time," it is seen in the sense of exhaustion. In passages such as "This person pleases me; among these four persons, this one is better (abhikkantatara) and more excellent," it is seen in the sense of goodness.

"Who is this that worships my feet,
Shining with psychic power and glory,
Illuminating all directions
With a most beautiful (abhikkanta) complexion?"

In such passages, it is seen in the sense of extreme beauty. In passages such as "It is excellent (abhikkantaṃ), Master Gotama," it is seen in the sense of great delight. Here too, it is used only in the sense of great delight. Because it is in the sense of great delight, it should be understood to mean "Excellent, excellent, Bhante."

In fear, in anger, and in praise,
In haste, in curiosity, and in wonder,
In joy, in grief, and in devotion,
The wise should repeat the word twice.
204:
By this characteristic, it should be understood that in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta, the word 'Abhikkanta' (Excellent) is spoken twice by virtue of devotion and by virtue of praise. Alternatively, 'Abhikkanta' means extremely desirable, extremely pleasing, heart-expanding, and very good.

Here, with one 'Abhikkanta' word, he praises the teaching, and with the other, he praises his own devotion. The meaning here is: 'Venerable Sir, this Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One is most excellent; my devotion that has arisen based on the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching is also most excellent.' Or, it praises the Blessed One's words themselves by referring to two meanings for each. The Blessed One's words are most excellent because they destroy faults and because they lead to the attainment of virtues. Likewise, it should be understood by connecting them with such qualities as: generating faith, generating wisdom, being full of meaning, being full of phrasing, having clear words, having profound meaning, being pleasant to the ear, being heart-touching, not exalting oneself, not disparaging others, being cool with compassion, being pure with wisdom, being beautiful in appearance, being able to withstand scrutiny, being pleasant when heard, and being beneficial when investigated.

Furthermore, he praises the teaching itself with four similes. Among those similes, 'nikkujjita' means an object placed face down or one that has become face down. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to make it face upwards. 'Paṭicchanna' means an object covered with grass, leaves, etc. 'Vivareyya' means to uncover it. 'Mūḷhassa vā' means to one who is lost in direction. 'Maggaṃ ācikkhata' means to say 'This is the path' while holding the hand. 'Andhakāre' means in the four-fold darkness consisting of the midnight of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a dense forest, and a thick layer of clouds. This is the meaning of the words that are not yet clear.

This is the application with the intended meaning: Just as someone might set upright what was overturned, even so, the Blessed One, who raises me up from the false Dhamma—I who was turned away from the true Dhamma and fallen into the false Dhamma—has revealed the Dhamma in various ways. Just as one might reveal what was hidden, even so, the Blessed One, who reveals the Dispensation (Sāsana) that has been hidden by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa; just as one might point out the way to one who is lost, even so, the Blessed One, who makes clear the path to heaven and Nibbāna to me who was following a wrong path and a false path; just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, even so, the Blessed One, who holds the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which covers the eyes of me who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the jewels such as the Buddha—because the Dhamma has been manifested to me by the Blessed One through these methods, it is said that the Dhamma has been revealed in many ways.

Having thus praised the teaching, and having a mind devoted to the Triple Gem because of this teaching, desiring to show his gesture of devotion, he said 'Esāhaṃ' and so on. There, 'Esāhaṃ' means 'Esā ahaṃ' (This I).
205:
In the phrase 'I go to the Blessed One for refuge,' it means: the Blessed One is my refuge, my resort, the remover of suffering, and the provider of welfare; with this intention, I approach, I resort to, I serve, and I attend upon the Blessed One. Or, it means I know and understand in this way. This is because roots having the meaning of 'going' also have the meaning of 'knowing.' Therefore, in this word 'gaccāmi' (I go), the meanings 'I know' and 'I understand' are also stated.

In the phrase 'and to the Dhamma and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha'—it is called 'Dhamma' because it upholds beings who have attained the Path, who have realized Cessation, and who practice according to the instruction, so that they do not fall into the four lower realms.
