That Dhamma, in essence, is the Noble Path and Nibbāna. It has been so stated: 'Monks, among conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is said to be the foremost,' and so on in detail. Not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Scriptural Dhamma (Pariyatti-dhamma) together with the Noble Fruits (Ariya-phala) is called Dhamma. It was stated in the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna:

'Go for refuge to this Dhamma which is the fading of lust, the absence of craving, the absence of sorrow, the unconditioned, the non-repulsive,
this sweet, well-mastered, and well-analyzed Dhamma.'

In this verse, the Path is spoken of by the term 'rāgaviraāga' (fading of lust). The Fruit is spoken of by the terms 'aneja' (absence of craving) and 'asoka' (absence of sorrow). Nibbāna is spoken of by the term 'dhamma-masaṅkhata' (unconditioned Dhamma). The collections of Dhamma (Dhammakkhandha) analyzed by the Three Piṭakas are spoken of by the terms 'appaṭikūla' (non-repulsive), 'madhura' (sweet), 'paguṇa' (well-mastered), and 'suvibhatta' (well-analyzed). It is called 'Saṅgha' because it is assembled by the combination of [right] views and virtue. That Saṅgha, in essence, is the group of the eight Noble Persons. It was stated in that very same Vimāna:

'Wherein they say what is given yields great fruit, among the four pure pairs of persons,
these eight persons who have seen the Dhamma (the Truths), go for refuge to this Saṅgha.'

The assembly of monks is the 'Bhikkhu Saṅgha.' By this much, the King proclaimed the three takings of refuge.

## Discussion on Taking Refuge

Now, for the sake of proficiency in those takings of refuge, this procedure should be understood: the refuge (saraṇa), the taking of refuge (saraṇagamana), the one who goes for refuge, the divisions of taking refuge, the fruit of taking refuge, the defilement, and the breach. To explain: firstly, by the meaning of 'refuge,' it is called 'saraṇa' because it harms (destroys). The meaning is that it is called 'saraṇa' because, for those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of taking refuge, it kills and destroys fear, trembling, suffering, and the defilements of the miserable states. This is a designation for the Triple Gem itself.
206:
In another way, the Buddha destroys the fear of beings by promoting their welfare and by preventing harm. The Dhamma also destroys the fear of beings by leading them out of the wilderness of existence and by providing relief and peace. The Saṅgha also destroys the fear of beings by causing even those who perform small meritorious deeds to obtain great benefits. Therefore, for these reasons as well, the Triple Gem is called the Refuge (saraṇa).

The arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that occurs through faith and respect for those three gems, dispelling defilements and taking those three gems as the ultimate resort, is called 'Taking Refuge' (saraṇagamana). A being endowed with that arising of consciousness approaches the refuge. The meaning of 'saraṇaṃ gacchati' (goes for refuge) is approaching with the arising of consciousness in the manner aforementioned, thinking, 'These three gems are my refuge; these gems are my ultimate resort.' Thus, these three—the refuge (saraṇa), the taking of refuge (saraṇagamana), and the person who takes refuge—should be understood.

Regarding the classification of taking refuge, there are two types: the supramundane (lokuttara) taking of refuge and the mundane (lokiya) taking of refuge. Among them, the supramundane taking of refuge is accomplished for the Noble Ones (ariyas) who have seen the Four Noble Truths, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), by the absolute eradication of the defilements that stain the taking of refuge, having Nibbāna as its object, and it is fulfilled in the entire Triple Gem by way of function. The mundane taking of refuge is accomplished for worldlings (puthujjanas) by the suppression of the defilements that stain the taking of refuge, having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object. In essence, it is the acquisition of faith in the objects such as the Buddha, and that right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) rooted in faith is called 'straightening of one's views' (diṭṭhijukamma) among the ten bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu). This mundane taking of refuge occurs in four ways: by self-dedication, by taking them as the ultimate resort, by assuming the state of a disciple, and by prostration.

Among those four, self-dedication (attasanniyyātana) is the relinquishing of oneself to the Buddha and so forth, in this way: 'From today onwards, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha.' Taking them as the ultimate resort (tapparāyaṇatā) is the state of having them as one's resort, in this way: 'From today onwards, I am one who has the Buddha as my ultimate resort, the Dhamma as my ultimate resort, and the Saṅgha as my ultimate resort; please remember me as such.' Assuming the state of a disciple (sissabhāvūpagamana) is the reaching of the state of a disciple, in this way: 'From today onwards, I am a disciple of the Buddha, a disciple of the Dhamma, and a disciple of the Saṅgha; please remember me as such.' Prostration (paṇipāta) is the manner of supreme humility towards the Buddha and so forth, in this way: 'From today onwards, I will perform salutation, rising from one's seat, anjali-salutation, and respectful duties only to these three objects—the Buddha and so forth; please remember me as such.' Indeed, for one who performs any one of these four modes, the refuge is truly taken.

Furthermore, self-dedication should be understood in this way: 'I relinquish myself to the Blessed One, I relinquish myself to the Dhamma, to the Saṅgha; I relinquish my life. My self is indeed relinquished; my life is indeed relinquished. I go to the Buddha for refuge until the end of my life. The Blessed One is my refuge, my shelter, my support.' Indeed, I shall only see the Blessed One who is the Teacher; I shall only see the Blessed One...
207:
...as a refuge. In this way too, self-dedication (to the Triple Gem) should be understood. The reaching of the state of a disciple should be understood like the taking of refuge by the Venerable Mahākassapa, who said: 'If only I could see the Teacher, the Blessed One; if only I could see the Teacher, the Blessed One. Indeed, if only I could see the Teacher, the Blessed One; if only I could see the Teacher, the Blessed One. Indeed, if only I could see the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, the Blessed One; if only I could see the Teacher, the Blessed One.'

The state of having the Triple Gem as the ultimate resort should be understood like the taking of refuge by Āḷavaka and others, who said: 
'I shall wander from village to village, from city to city, 
Paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and the excellence of the Dhamma.'

Prostration (paṇipāta) should be seen in the case of the Brahmin Brahmāyu, who rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, fell with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, kissed the feet of the Blessed One with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name: 'I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu, O Teacher Gotama; I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu, O Teacher Gotama.'

That prostration is of four types by way of: kinship, fear, teacher, and one worthy of offerings. Among these four, the taking of refuge is established only by prostration performed with the thought that 'He is worthy of offerings,' and not by the others. For one takes refuge only by way of excellence, and it is broken only by way of excellence. Therefore, if a Sākyan or a Koliyan prostrates thinking, 'The Buddha is our kinsman,' the refuge is not truly taken. Or if one prostrates out of fear, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and is of great power; if I do not prostrate, he might do me harm,' the refuge is not truly taken. Or if one prostrates thinking, 'He is my teacher,' having remembered some craft learned from the Blessed One during his time as a Bodhisatta, or during his time as a Buddha, such as learning this instruction:

'A wise man living at home should divide his wealth into four parts:
He should enjoy one part of the wealth, and employ two parts for his work,
And he should store the fourth part, thinking it will be for emergencies.'

If one prostrates after learning such an instruction, thinking 'He is my teacher,' the refuge is not truly taken. Only when a person prostrates thinking, 'This Blessed One is the supreme one worthy of offerings in the world,' is the refuge truly taken by him.

For a lay follower (upāsaka or upāsikā) who has thus taken refuge, if they prostrate to a relative who has gone forth among other sectarians, thinking 'This person is my relative,' the taking of refuge...
208:
For one who pays homage to a relative who is a monk, thinking 'This is my relative,' the refuge is not broken. How much less so for one who pays homage to a relative who is not a monk? Similarly, for one who pays homage to a king out of fear, the refuge is not broken. This is because the king is honored by the country, and if not paid homage, he might cause harm. Likewise, for one who pays homage even to a non-Buddhist teacher (titthiya) who taught him a craft, thinking 'This is my teacher,' the refuge is not broken. Thus should the distinctions of the refuge be understood.

Among these, for the supramundane refuge, the four fruits (phala) that immediately follow the path are the direct results (vipāka-phala). Nibbāna, which is the end of all suffering of the round of rebirth, is the beneficial result (ānisaṃsa-phala). Thus it has been said:

'He who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths:
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering,
and the noble eightfold path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This indeed is the safe refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.' (Dhammapada 192)

Furthermore, the beneficial result of that supramundane refuge should be understood through the power of not adhering to [wrong views] such as permanence. Thus it has been said: 'It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any formation as permanent... or any formation as pleasant... or any phenomenon as self... or should deprive his mother of life... or his father... or an Arahant... or with a corrupt mind draw the blood of a Tathāgata... or cause a schism in the Saṅgha... or designate another teacher; this is not possible.' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.290). The result of the mundane refuge, however, is the attainment of [favorable] existence and the attainment of wealth. Thus it has been said:

'Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they will not go to the plane of misery.
Having abandoned the human body, they will fill the heavenly hosts.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.37)

Another statement has also been made: Then Sakka, the lord of devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and, having paid homage, stood to one side. To Sakka, the lord of devas, standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said: 'It is good, O Lord of Devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha. Because of going for refuge to the Buddha, O Lord of Devas, some beings here, with the breaking up of the body and after death...'
209:
...after death, they reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world. ... They surpass other devas in ten respects: in divine life-span, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, divine sovereignty, and in divine sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.341). This same method applies to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. Furthermore, the special benefits of going for refuge should also be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. Thus should the fruit of going for refuge be understood.

Among those two types of refuge, the mundane refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so on regarding the Three Objects; it is not of great luster, nor of great pervasion. For the supramundane refuge, there is no defilement. The breaking of the mundane refuge is of two kinds: blameworthy and blameless. Therein, the blameworthy breaking occurs through such acts as dedicating oneself to another teacher, etc.; that [breaking] results in undesirable consequences. The blameless breaking occurs through death; that [breaking] is said to have no result because it is not a ripening [of kamma]. As for the supramundane refuge, there is no breaking at all. This is because even in another life, a noble disciple does not designate another teacher. Thus should the defilement and the breaking of the refuge be understood.

'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka)' means: 'May the Blessed One regard me, know me, in this way: "This person is a lay follower."' For the sake of skill in the procedure regarding a lay follower, this miscellaneous collection should be understood: Who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower? What is his virtue? What is his livelihood? What is his failure? What is his success?

Among those questions, 'Who is a lay follower?' refers to any householder who has gone for refuge. Thus it has been said: 'Mahānāma, when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to that extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1033).

'Why is he called a lay follower?' Because he attends (upāsana) to the Triple Gem. For he is a lay follower (upāsaka) because he attends to the Buddha; likewise to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.

'What is his virtue?' It is the five abstinences (precepts). As the Blessed One said: 'Mahānāma, when a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given... from sexual misconduct... from false speech... from wines, liquors, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence; to that extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1033).
210:
## What is Livelihood (Ājīva)?

What is livelihood? It is making a living righteously and fairly, having abandoned the five types of wrong trade (micchā-vaṇijjā). It was also said thus: "Monks, these five trades should not be undertaken by a lay follower. Which five? Trade in weapons, trade in living beings (humans), trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poison. Monks, these five trades should not be undertaken by a lay follower" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.177).

## What is Failure (Vipatti)?

What is failure? The failure in virtue (sīla) and the failure in livelihood of that lay follower is failure. Furthermore, that failure because of which this lay follower becomes an outcaste lay follower (upāsaka-caṇḍāla), a stain, and a detestable person, should also be known as the failure of that lay follower. In essence, those qualities are the five things such as lack of faith (assaddhiya). It was also said thus: "Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is an outcaste lay follower, a stain of a lay follower, and a detestable lay follower. Which five? He lacks faith (assaddha); he is immoral (dussīla); he is superstitious (kotūhala-maṅgalika), believing in omens [seen or heard] and not in kamma; he seeks for those worthy of gifts outside of this Sasana and performs his first services there" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.175).

## What is Accomplishment (Sampatti)?

What is accomplishment? The accomplishment in virtue and the accomplishment in livelihood of that lay follower is accomplishment. Furthermore, there are the five qualities such as faith (saddhā) which make that lay follower a jewel and so on. It was also said thus: "Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a jewel of a lay follower, a red lotus of a lay follower, and a white lotus of a lay follower. Which five? He has faith; he is virtuous; he is not superstitious; he believes in kamma and not in omens; he does not seek for those worthy of gifts outside of this Sasana and performs his first services here [in this Sasana]" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.175).

In the word "ajjatagge", this word "agga" is seen in the senses of beginning (ādi), tip or end (koṭi), portion (koṭṭhāsa), and supreme (seṭṭha). In such phrases as "Friend gatekeeper, from today onwards (ajjatagge), I close the door to Nigaṇṭha men and Nigaṇṭha women," it is seen in the sense of beginning (ādi). In such phrases as "One should touch that fingertip with that fingertip; the tip of a sugarcane (ucchagga), the tip of a bamboo (veḷagga)," it is seen in the sense of tip or end (koṭi). In such phrases as "Whether it be a sour portion (ambilagga), a sweet portion (madhuragga), or a bitter portion (tittakagga), or to be distributed by monastery portion (vihāragga) or by precinct portion (pariveṇagga)," it is seen in the sense of portion (koṭṭhāsa). In such phrases as "Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless... the Tathāgata is said to be the supreme (agga) among them," it is seen in the sense of supreme (seṭṭha). Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of beginning. Therefore, "ajjatagge" means "starting from today."
211:
Thus should the meaning in this context be understood. "Ajjataṃ" means the state of today. There is also a reading as "ajjadagge"; the letter "da" is a euphonic particle (padasandhikara). The meaning is "starting from today."

"Pāṇupetaṃ" means endowed with life. For as long as my life lasts, may the Blessed One recognize and know me as a lay follower who is endowed with life, who has no other teacher, who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, and who is a provider of what is allowable (kappiya-kāraka). For even if my head were to be cut off with a very sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, "He is not the Buddha," or of the Dhamma, "It is not the Dhamma," or of the Saṅgha, "It is not the Saṅgha."

Having thus gone for refuge by dedicating himself [to the Triple Gem], wishing to reveal the fault he had committed, he said, "Venerable Sir, an offense (accayo) [has overcome me]," and so on. In that speech, "accayo" means a fault or offense. "Maṃ accagamā" means an offense that arose by transgressing and overcoming me. In the phrase "dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ," he is called "dhammika" because he practices the Dhamma. He is called "dhammarāja" because he became king through the Dhamma itself, not through unrighteousness such as killing his father. "Jīvitā voropesiṃ" means depriving of life (killing). "Paṭiggaṇhātu" means "may you forgive." "Āyatiṃ saṃvarāya" means for the sake of restraint in the future; for the sake of not committing such a fault, an offensive wrong, or a slip again.

"Taggha" is a particle in the sense of "certainly." "Yathādhammaṃ patikarosi" means you have acted according to the Dhamma; it means you have asked for forgiveness. We forgive that offense of yours. "This, O Great King, is growth in the Noble One's Discipline (ariyassa vinaya)": this, O Great King, is called growth in the Noble One's Discipline, in the Dispensation of the Buddha, the Blessed One. What kind of growth? It is the seeing of an offense as an offense, making amends according to the Dhamma, and attaining restraint in the future. However, wishing to give the teaching based on the individual (puggala-adhiṭṭhāna), he said: "Whoever sees an offense as an offense, makes amends according to the Dhamma, and attains restraint in the future [he grows]."

When it was thus spoken by the Blessed One, he said, "Venerable Sir, now we [shall go]," where "handa" is a particle in the sense of indicating the intention to speak. That king, having indicated his intention to depart, spoke thus. "Bahu-kiccā" means having many duties. "Bahu-karaṇīyā" is a synonym for that same "bahu-kiccā." "Yassa dāni tvaṃ" means "O Great King, you now know the time for your departure; you alone should know the time for that departure."
212:
"Having done [this], he departed" (katvā pakkāmi) means that having performed the circumambulation three times, and placing his hands—shining with the radiance of his ten fingernails—upon his head in salutation, he backed away facing the Blessed One as long as he remained within sight. At the spot where he was about to lose sight [of the Buddha], he prostrated with the fivefold touch and departed.

"Bhikkhus, this king is uprooted" (khatāyaṃ bhikkhave rājā) means "Bhikkhus, this king is ruined (due to the kamma of killing his father)." "Upahata" means "this king is impaired." The meaning is: Bhikkhus, this king has destroyed himself, impaired himself, and has become one whose foundation is broken. Because he became a parricide in the Dispensation (Sāsana) which was his refuge, he has destroyed himself; thus he is one whose foundation is broken. "Stainless" (virajaṃ) means free from the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth. Because the impurities of passion and so forth have gone, it is called "faultless" (vītamalaṃ). "The Eye of Dhamma" (dhammacakkhu) means the eye of knowledge regarding the Dhammas, or the eye made of Dhamma. In other contexts, this is a designation for the three higher paths, but in this sutta, it refers only to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga).

The meaning is this: If King Ajātasattu had not killed his father, he would have attained the Path of Stream-entry while sitting right here in this seat. However, due to his association with an evil friend, an obstacle arose for his path-knowledge. Nevertheless, because the king approached the Tathāgata and took refuge in the Triple Gem, by the great power of my Dispensation—just as a man who committed murder might be released with a penalty of only a handful of flowers—this king, after being reborn in the Lohakumbhī hell, will sink downwards for thirty thousand years until reaching the bottom, then rise upwards for thirty thousand years until reaching the surface, and will then be released from hell. It is said that the Blessed One spoke these words, though they were not included in the Pali (the canonical text during the councils).

If it is asked whether the king gained any benefit from hearing this sutta, the answer is that he gained a great benefit. From the time he had his father killed, he could not sleep by day or by night. But from the time he approached the Teacher and heard this sweet and essence-filled Dhamma teaching, he was able to sleep. He performed great offerings to the Triple Gem. Among worldlings (puthujjanas) endowed with faith, there was no one equal to this king. In the future, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī and attain Parinibbāna. The Blessed One said this. The bhikkhus, delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

## Thus ends the Commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta
## in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.
213:
## 3. Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta
## Commentary on the Journey

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "Kosalesu" is the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. Herein is the sequential explanation of the words. "Among the Kosalans" (Kosalesu) refers to the princes who were inhabitants of the country named Kosala. A single country that is the dwelling place of those Kosalan princes is also called "Kosala" by way of conventional usage (rūḷhī). In that Kosalan country (the Blessed One was staying). Ancient teachers, however, say: In the past, King Mahāpanāda's son did not even smile upon seeing various dancers and so forth. Hearing this, the King said, "Whoever makes my son laugh, I shall adorn him with all ornaments." Consequently, people abandoned their work, such as plowing, and gathered together. Although they showed various games for more than seven years, they were unable to make Prince Mahāpanāda laugh. Then Sakka, the king of devas, sent a celestial dancer. That dancer showed a divine dance and made him laugh. Then those people departed toward their respective dwellings. When they met beloved friends and relatives on the way and exchanged greetings, they asked, "Friends, is it well (kusalaṃ)? Friends, is it well?" Therefore, based on that word "kusala," that region is called "Kosala."

"Wandering on a journey" (cārikaṃ caramāno) means traveling on a long-distance journey. The Blessed One's wandering is of two kinds: the urgent wandering (turitacārikā) and the non-urgent wandering (aturitacārikā). Among these, seeing a person capable of being enlightened even in a distant place and going quickly for the purpose of enlightening that person is called "urgent wandering." This urgent wandering is to be understood in instances such as going to meet the Venerable Mahākassapa. For the Blessed One, while going to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, traveled a distance of three gāvutas in a moment. For the sake of Āḷavaka, he went thirty yojanas; likewise for Aṅgulimāla. For Pukkusāti, forty-five yojanas. For Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty yojanas. For Dhaniya, seven hundred yojanas. For the novice Tissa of the Forest (Vanavāsī Tissa), the co-resident of the Captain of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), he traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas plus three gāvutas.

One day, the Elder Sāriputta addressed the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, I shall go to the novice Tissa." The Blessed One said, "I too shall go," and calling the Venerable Ānanda, he said, "Ānanda, let it be known that the Blessed One, together with twenty thousand bhikkhus possessing the six higher powers (abhiññā), will go to the novice Vanavāsī Tissa." On the second day from then, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, he flew into the sky and descended at the gate of the alms-village of that novice Vanavāsī Tissa, one hundred and twenty yojanas away, and [adjusting] his robes...
214:
The Blessed One called the Venerable Ānanda and said, "Ānanda, inform the twenty thousand monks who possess the six supernormal powers that the Blessed One will go to the presence of the novice Tissa, who dwells in the forest." Then, on the second day, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, he rose into the air and descended at the gate of the village where the novice went for alms, a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas, and adjusted his robes. People going to their work saw the Blessed One and said, "Our Master has arrived; do not go to work," and having prepared seats and offered gruel, they were preparing the morning meal and asked the junior monks, "Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One going?" The monks replied, "Lay followers, the Blessed One is not going elsewhere; he has come here to see the novice Tissa." Those people were filled with joy, thinking, "The Master has come to see the Elder who is our mentor; indeed, our Elder is no ordinary person."

Then, when the Blessed One had finished his meal, the novice, having wandered for alms in the village, asked, "Lay followers, is there a large community of monks?" Then they informed him, "Venerable sir, the Master has arrived." He approached the Blessed One and invited him with almsfood. The Master took the bowl from the novice's hand and said, "Enough, Tissa, the meal is finished." Then, having asked permission from his preceptor and sitting in his own seat, the novice took his meal. After the meal, the Master spoke words of blessing, departed, and standing at the village gate, asked, "Tissa, which is the path to your dwelling place?" The novice replied, "Venerable sir, it is this path," and as he pointed out the way, the Master said, "Tissa, you go ahead." Although the Blessed One is the guide for the world including the devas, he made that novice the guide, thinking, "I shall get to see the novice," throughout the journey of three gāvutas.

When the novice reached his dwelling place, he performed the duties for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One asked him, "Tissa, where is your walking path (caṅkama)?" and having gone there and sat on the novice's stone seat, he asked, "Tissa, do you live happily in this place?" He replied, "Yes, Venerable sir, to me living in this place, when I hear the sounds of lions, tigers, elephants, deer, peacocks, and so on, the perception of the forest (araññasaññā) arises; through that, I live happily." Then the Blessed One said, "Tissa, assemble the community of monks; I will give you the inheritance of the Buddha," and when the community of monks had assembled, he granted him full ordination (upasampadā) and returned to his own dwelling place. This is called Turitacārikā (the urgent journey).
215:
The journeying for the benefit of the world by wandering for alms and so forth, according to the sequence of villages and market towns at the rate of one or two yojanas daily, is called Aturitacārikā (the non-urgent journey).

While wandering on such a journey, the Blessed One travels in one of these three circles: the Great Circle (Mahāmaṇḍala), the Middle Circle (Majjhimamaṇḍala), and the Inner Circle (Antomaṇḍala). Among them, the Great Circle is nine hundred yojanas, the Middle Circle is six hundred yojanas, and the Inner Circle is three hundred yojanas. When he wishes to wander in the Great Circle, having performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony at the Great Pavāraṇā, he sets out on the first day of the waning moon, surrounded by a large community of monks. The area within a hundred yojanas all around becomes filled with a great roar of excitement. Those who arrive first get the opportunity to invite him. The offerings made in the other two circles flow into the Great Circle. There, the Blessed One, staying for one or two days in various villages and market towns, benefits the multitude by accepting material offerings and, through the gift of Dhamma (Dhamma-dāna), increases their wholesome states conducive to liberation from the cycle of rebirth, completing the journey in nine months.

If, during the rains retreat (vassa), the monks' tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) are still immature, he does not perform the Pavāraṇā on the Great Pavāraṇā day but gives them the benefit of the Pavāraṇā period, performs the Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Kattika, and sets out on the first day of the month of Migasira, surrounded by a large community of monks, entering the Middle Circle. For other reasons as well, if he wishes to wander in the Middle Circle, he sets out only after staying for the full four months of the rains. In the same manner as mentioned before, the offerings made in the other two circles flow into the Middle Circle. The Blessed One, benefiting the world in the same way as before, completes the journey in eight months.

If, even after staying for the four months of the rains, the beings to be tamed (veneyya) have not yet matured their spiritual faculties (indriya), the Blessed One, waiting for the maturation of their faculties, stays there for another month, or two, three, or four months, and then sets out surrounded by a large community of monks. In the same manner as mentioned before, the offerings made in the other two circles flow into the Inner Circle. The Blessed One, benefiting the world in the same way as before, completes the journey in seven, six, five, or four months.

Thus, when wandering in any of these three circles, he does not wander for the sake of robes and so forth. Rather, he thinks, "There are those who are poor, foolish, old, or sick; when will they be able to come and see the Tathāgata? But when I am wandering on a journey, the multitude will get the opportunity to see the Tathāgata." Among them, some [purify] their minds...
216: Some will gain confidence in their hearts; some will make offerings of flowers and such; some will give a mere ladleful of alms-food; some will abandon wrong view and become those of right view. Such acts, beginning with the gaining of confidence, will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. Thus, out of compassion for beings, he wanders on a journey. Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on a journey for four reasons: to ensure the physical well-being of the body through walking; to wait for the occasion for a teaching to arise; to prescribe training rules for the monks; and to enable those beings in various places who are ready and whose faculties are mature to realize the Four Noble Truths. For another four reasons, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on a journey: thinking, 'They will go to the Buddha for refuge,' or 'They will go to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha for refuge,' or 'I shall satisfy the fourfold assembly with the great rain of Dhamma.' For another five reasons, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on a journey: thinking, 'They will abstain from taking life,' or 'They will abstain from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the use of intoxicants such as wine and liquor which are the cause of heedlessness.' For another eight reasons, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on a journey: thinking, 'They will attain the first jhāna,' or 'the second jhāna ... up to ... they will attain the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' For another eight reasons, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on a journey: thinking, 'They will attain the path of stream-entry,' or 'the fruit of stream-entry ... up to ... they will realize the fruit of arahantship.' This wandering through villages and market towns to benefit those to be guided is called atūritacārikā (unhurried wandering). In this context, cārikā refers to this very meaning. That wandering is of two kinds: anibaddhacārikā (unfixed wandering) and nibaddhacārikā (fixed wandering). Among these, wandering through villages, market towns, and cities in succession is called anibaddhacārikā. That wandering which is undertaken for the sake of a single being who is ready to be guided is called nibaddhacārikā. In this context, this is what is intended. At that time, it is said, at the conclusion of the duties of the last watch of the night, the Blessed One spread his net of knowledge over the ten thousand world systems and, while surveying those kinsmen ready to be guided, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti entered within the net of his omniscient knowledge. Then the Blessed One, reflecting, 'This Brahmin appears in my net of knowledge; does he have the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya)?', saw the supporting conditions for the path of stream-entry. He thought: 'When I go to that district, this Brahmin will send his pupil named Ambaṭṭha to investigate my marks. That Ambaṭṭha will engage in debate with me and speak various improper words. Having tamed him, I shall make him free from pride.'
217:
That young man Ambaṭṭha will tell his teacher. Then, having heard those words, the teacher will come and investigate my marks. I will preach the Dhamma to him. At the end of the discourse, he will be established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). My teaching will be fruitful for the great multitude. Thinking thus, he set out for that district accompanied by five hundred monks. Therefore, it was said: "While wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, about five hundred monks..."

"Yena Icchānaṅgalaṃ" means the direction in which one should go to Icchānaṅgala, or the region where Icchānaṅgala is situated. There is also a variant reading "Ijjhānaṅgalaṃ". "Tadavasarī" means arriving by that direction or reaching that region. "Dwelling at Icchānaṅgala" means that the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, depending on Icchānaṅgala, established a stockade of virtue (sīla) in the Icchānaṅgala forest, raised the banner of concentration (samādhi), and practiced the mantra of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), dwelling according to his pleasure.

## Commentary on the Story of Pokkharasāti

"Tena kho pana samayena" means at that time when the Blessed One was dwelling there. He is called a "Brāhmaṇa" because he recites and chants the Vedas (brahmaṃ aṇati). This is the etymological definition for those who are Brahmins by birth. However, Noble Ones (Ariyas) are called Brahmins because they have discarded evil (bāhita-pāpatta). "Pokkharasāti" is his name. Why is he called Pokkharasāti? It is said that his body was like a white lotus (puṇḍarīka), shining like a silver portal erected in the city of the gods. His head, however, was dark like an indanīla gem. His beard appeared like a dark cloud-streak across the moon's orb. His eyes were like blue lotuses. His nose was well-rounded and pure like a silver tube. The palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, and his mouth shone as if treated with red lac. The physical form (attabhāva) of this Brahmin was exceedingly beautiful. He was fit to be made a king in a place without one. Thus he was full of splendor. Because he resembled a lotus (pokkhara), he was known as "Pokkharasāti".

This Brahmin Pokkharasāti had previously been a master of the three Vedas during the time of Kassapa Buddha. Having given offerings to Kassapa Buddha and heard the Dhamma, he was reborn in the deva realm. When he came from the deva realm to the human realm, he felt revulsion for staying in a mother's womb and was born in the heart of a white lotus in a large lake in the Himālaya region. An ascetic living in a hermitage near that lake saw the lotus and thought, "This lotus is much larger than others; when it blooms, I will take it." That lotus did not bloom for seven days. The ascetic [thought], "Why is this lotus..."
218:
This Brahmin Pokkharasāti was, in the time of Kassapa Buddha, a master who had reached the end of the three Vedas. Having given gifts to the Dasabala (Kassapa) Buddha and heard the Dhamma, he was reborn in the deva world. Coming from there to the human world, he felt revulsion for dwelling in a mother's womb and was reborn in the heart of a lotus (paduma) in a great lake in the Himalayan region. An ascetic lived in a leaf-hut not far from that lake. Standing by the lake, the ascetic saw that lotus and thought, "This lotus is much larger than the others; I will take it when it blooms." Even after seven days, it did not bloom. The ascetic thought, "Why has this lotus not bloomed even after seven days? I shall take it now," and he went down into the water and took it. As soon as he cut it from the stem, it bloomed. Then, inside the lotus, he saw a child of pure appearance, smeared with lotus pollen like a silver image painted with gold dust. Thinking, "This child must be one of great merit; I shall raise him," he took him to his hermitage and cared for him, teaching him the three Vedas from the age of seven. The boy reached the end of the three Vedas, became wise and proficient, and became the foremost Brahmin in Jambudīpa. Later, he demonstrated his skills to King Pasenadi of Kosala. The King, being pleased with his skills, granted him the great city of Ukkaṭṭhā as a noble gift (brahmadeyya). Thus, because he had slept in the heart of a lotus, he was known as "Pokkharasāti."

"Ukkaṭṭhaṃ ajjhāvasati" means he dwells in the city named Ukkaṭṭhā. Or, he dwells there having overcome and governed it. Being the lord of that city, he lived there within the established boundaries. It is said that the site of that city was marked out by setting up torches (ukkā), and it was taken while those torches were burning; therefore, it is called "Ukkaṭṭhā." There is also a variant reading "Okkaṭṭhā," which has the same meaning. Here, it should be understood that because of the prefix (upasagga), the accusative case (dutiyā vibhatti) is used in the sense of the locative case (sattamī vibhatti). This also applies to the remaining words not directly associated with that prefix. The characteristics of such usage should be sought in grammatical treatises.

"Sattussadaṃ" means crowded with beings, full of many people, and teeming with humans. It means a city crowded with many animals such as domesticated elephants, horses, peacocks, and deer. This is because the city is abundant in grass for the fodder of elephants and horses, as well as grass for roofing houses, which grows all around the outskirts. Likewise, it is abundant in wood for fuel and wood for house construction. Furthermore, within the city, there are many lotus ponds of various shapes, such as circular and square, and many lakes adorned with diverse aquatic flowers that are always full of water; therefore, it is called "satiṇakaṭṭhodaka" (a city abundant in grass, wood, and water).
219:
Because it is with grain, it is called 'sadhanya'. It means a city with a vast store of various grains such as early and late crops. By these terms, it is shown that the Brahmin lived in that city with royal splendor, having raised the white umbrella, indicating the abundance of his wealth and prosperity.

'Rājabhoggaṃ' means wealth or possession received from a king. If one asks who gave it, it was given by King Pasenadi of Kosala. 'Rājadāya' means wealth that is a royal inheritance or gift. 'Brahmadeyya' means a noble gift, an endowment to be enjoyed with royal status, as if one were a king under a white umbrella. Alternatively, 'rājabhogga' refers to that which is enjoyed as a king, exercising all powers of punishment such as execution and imprisonment, collecting taxes at river crossings, mountains, etc., and raising the white umbrella. In the phrase 'rājadāya given by King Pasenadi of Kosala,' it is called 'rājadāya' because the city was given by the king. The phrase 'given by King Pasenadi of Kosala' is mentioned to identify the donor king. 'Brahmadeyya' means a noble gift. It refers to a gift that, once given, is not to be taken back, being completely relinquished and surrendered. Such is the meaning of the gift.

'Assosi' means he heard or learned; he understood according to the sequence of the sound of words reaching the ear-door. 'Kho' is a particle used either for emphasis (avadhāraṇa) or merely as a formal filler (padapūraṇa). In the sense of emphasis, it means he 'indeed' heard, implying there was no obstacle to his hearing. As a filler, it is merely for the sake of euphony in the phrasing.

Now, to reveal the matter that the Brahmin Pokkharasāti heard, it says: "The ascetic Gotama, indeed, sirs..." and so on. In that context, he is to be known as 'Samaṇa' (ascetic) because he has calmed all evil. For it was said: "Evil and unwholesome states are calmed in him." The Blessed One has calmed evil through the unsurpassed Noble Path. Therefore, this name 'Samaṇa' is a title acquired through his true qualities. 'Khalu' is a particle indicating hearsay or report. 'Bho' is merely a form of address common among those of the Brahmin caste. It was also said: "He is called a 'Bhovādī' if he still has defilements." By the name 'Gotama,' he praises the Blessed One by way of his lineage. Therefore, the phrase 'Samaṇo khalu bho gotamo' should be understood as: 'The ascetic of the Gotama lineage, so I have heard, sirs.'

'Sakyaputta' (Son of the Sakyans) indicates the Blessed One's high lineage. 'Renounced from the Sakyan clan' indicates his renunciation out of faith. It means he renounced out of faith, leaving behind that royal clan which was not yet diminished, and not because of any misfortune or loss.
220:
It means that he renounced that clan and went forth out of faith while that Sakyan royal clan was not yet depleted. The phrases following that have the meanings already mentioned. The phrases starting with "Taṃ kho pana" have already been explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. "Sādhu kho pana" means it is very good; it means it brings welfare and happiness. "Tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ" refers to the Noble Arahants in the world who have gained the title of "Arahant" because they have attained true qualities, just as the Blessed Gotama is of such a nature. "Dassanaṃ hoti" is said with the intention that even just opening one's clear and cool eyes to behold him is excellent.

## Ambaṭṭha Māṇava Kathā

The word "Ajjhāyaka" (reciter) was used in the sense of "Vāseṭṭha, now these people do not meditate (jhāyanti), they do not meditate," inserting the third letter "jha" to call them "Ajjhāyaka." Thus, in the beginning of the aeon, it was a word of reproach for Brahmins who were devoid of meditation (jhāna). But now, one is called "Ajjhāyaka" because they study the Vedas. It is used as a word of praise in the sense of one who repeatedly recites the Vedas. One is called "Mantadhara" because they bear the mantras (Vedas) in mind.

"Tiṇṇam vedānam" refers to the three Vedas: Iru (Ṛg), Yaju (Yajur), and Sāma. One is called "Pāragū" (expert/gone to the far shore) because they have reached the end through the power of recitation on the lips. They are called "Sanighaṇḍukeṭubha" because they are proficient in the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha treatises. "Nighaṇḍu" is the treatise that explains synonyms for trees and so on. "Keṭubha" is the treatise that makes known gestures, appearances, and causes, and is helpful to poets. They are called "Sākkharapabheda" because they are proficient in the distinctions of letters. "Distinctions of letters" (Akkharapabheda) refers to the treatises of Sikkhā (Phonetics) and Nirutti (Etymology). "Itihāsapañcamānaṃ" means those Vedas of which the Itihāsa (History/Legend) treatise—described as ancient stories connected with the expression "Thus it has been"—is the fifth, with the Atharva Veda being the fourth.

One is called "Padaka" (word-knower) or "Veyyākaraṇa" (grammarian) because they study the collection of words (Pada) and the remaining grammar (Vyākaraṇa) themselves, and also teach others. The Vitaṇḍavāda treatise, which speaks words contrary to the Dispensation (Sāsana), is called "Lokāyata." "Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa" is the treatise, consisting of twelve thousand volumes, that explains the marks of Great Men such as the Buddha. In that treatise of marks, there are the "Buddha Mantras" consisting of sixteen thousand verses. By the power of these mantras, those endowed with such marks are called "Buddhas"; those with such marks are "Paccekabuddhas"; those with such marks are the "two Chief Disciples"; those with such marks are the "eighty Great Disciples"...
221:
...the Great Disciples, the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, the chief male attendant, the chief female attendant, and the Cakkavatti King—thus this distinction is known.

"Anavayo" means one who is not deficient but is fully proficient in these Lokāyata and Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa treatises; it means they are not "Avaya" (incomplete). An "Avaya" is one who is unable to maintain those treatises either by meaning or by text. "Anuññātapaṭiññāto" means being authorized by the teacher and acknowledged by oneself. The teacher authorizes the youth with words such as "What I know, you know." It means he is acknowledged by his own words of reply to the teacher, "Yes, teacher." In what field is he authorized and acknowledged? In the noble words of the three Vedas, which are the tradition of his own teacher. This Brahmin thought: "In this world, many people go about taking the name of one who has arisen saying 'I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha.' Therefore, I should not approach him based on mere hearsay. For one who approaches some people, it is a burden to have to turn back, and it can also be disadvantageous. It would be better if I send my pupil to find out for sure whether he is a Buddha or not, and only then approach him." Having thought thus, he called the youth and said, "Dear youth," and so on.

"That Venerable One" refers to the qualities of that Blessed Gotama. "Just as he is truly famous" means just as he exists according to his fame (or being endowed with those qualities). Here too, the accusative case is used because of the meaning of hearing about one who has reached such a state.

The meaning is: "Sir, how shall I know that Blessed Gotama? Tell me the manner in which he can be known." Or, "yathā" is just a particle, and "kathaṃ" is an inquiry into the manner. The meaning is: "In what manner shall I know that Blessed Gotama?" When this was said, the preceptor (upajjhāya), wishing to show the manner of knowing, said: "Dear youth, do you speak as if you were standing on the earth and saying you do not see the earth, or as if you were standing in the light of the moon and sun and saying you do not see the moon and sun?" and then said, "Dear youth, they have come," and so forth.

In that passage, "mantesu" means in the Vedas. It is said that the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, knowing beforehand that "a Tathāgata will arise," inserted the marks into the Vedas and taught the Vedas in the guise of Brahmins, saying "These are the Buddha Mantras." They taught them with the intention that, following those Vedas, great beings would recognize the Tathāgata. Therefore, in the Vedas of old...
222:
In ancient times, the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇā) were present in the Vedic texts. However, after the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, they gradually disappeared. Because of this disappearance, those marks are no longer found in the Vedic texts today. 'Mahāpurisassa' refers to a man who is great due to such qualities as the aspiration for Buddhahood, the firm undertaking of merit, wisdom, and compassion. 'Dve yeva gatiyo' means there are only two possible destinies. This word 'gati' (destiny/resort) expresses the type of existence in passages such as, "Sāriputta, these five are the destinies." It expresses a dwelling place in passages such as, "The forest is the resort (gati) of wild animals." It expresses wisdom in passages such as, "Thus he is of great wisdom (gatimanto)." It expresses the sense of pervasiveness in passages such as, "gone to the destination (gatigata)." However, in this context, it should be understood as expressing the final destiny (niṭṭhā).

In that regard, although the person endowed with certain marks becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) and does not become a Buddha by those same marks, they are called the same marks because of the commonality of their nature. Therefore, it is said, "To one endowed with those marks." 'Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati' means if he lives the household life. In the phrase 'Rājā hoti cakkavatti', he is called 'Rājā' (King) because he pleases the multitude of people with the four wonderful qualities and the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). He is called 'Cakkavatti' (Wheel-turner) because he turns the wheel-treasure, or because he possesses the four wheels of success (sampatticakka) and establishes others in those wheels, or because he turns the wheels of posture (iriyāpathacakka) for the benefit of others. Here, 'Rājā' is a general title, while 'Cakkavatti' is a specific title. He is called 'Dhammika' (Righteous) because he acts according to the Dhamma. It means he conducts himself appropriately in accordance with the kingly virtues. He is called 'Dhammarājā' (Righteous King) because he became a king by obtaining kingship through Dhamma. Alternatively, he is 'Dhammika' because he performs deeds for the benefit of others, and 'Dhammarājā' because he performs deeds for his own benefit. He is called 'Cāturanta' because he is the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans (adorned with the four great islands). He is called 'Vijitāvī' (Conqueror) because he conquers internal enemies such as anger and all external kings. He is called 'Janapadatthāvariyappatta' because he has attained stability in the country (such that no one can shake him). Alternatively, he is called 'Janapadatthāvariyappatta' because he has subjects who dwell without fear, constantly attending to him, firm in their own duties, unshakable, and undaunted.

'Seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable meaning "What are those (treasures)?" In terms like 'Cakkaratana', it is called 'Cakkaratana' (Wheel-treasure) because it turns (cakka) and is a precious, delightful treasure (ratana). The same method should be understood for all other treasure terms. Among these treasures, the Wheel-turning Monarch conquers unconquered regions with the Wheel-treasure. With the Elephant-treasure and Horse-treasure, he travels as he pleases through the conquered regions.
223:
The Wheel-turning Monarch constantly protects the conquered country with the Counselor-treasure (pariṇāyakaratana) and enjoys sensual pleasures with the remaining treasures. For that Wheel-turning Monarch, the possession of the power of effort (usṣāhasatti) is fulfilled by the first treasure (the Wheel-treasure); the possession of the power of counsel (mantasatti) is fulfilled by the last treasure (the Counselor-treasure/Son-treasure); and the possession of the power of majesty (pabhusatti) is fully perfected by the Elephant, Horse, and Householder treasures. Through the Woman-treasure and the Gem-treasure, he receives the benefits of these three powers. The king enjoys the pleasure of sensual desires through the Woman-treasure and the Gem-treasure, and enjoys the pleasure of sovereignty through the remaining treasures. Specifically, for him, the first three treasures are accomplished by the power of kamma born from the root of non-hatred (adosa-kusalamūla); the middle three treasures are accomplished by the power of kamma born from the root of non-greed (alobha-kusalamūla); and the last one is accomplished by the power of kamma born from the root of non-delusion (amoha-kusalamūla). This is the summary here. The detailed explanation should be taken from the Upadesavāra of the Ratana Sutta in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta.

'Parosahassaṃ' means more than a thousand. 'Sūrā' means those who are brave and fearless by nature. 'Vīraṅgarūpā' means those whose bodies are like celestial beings. Some teachers explain it this way at first. The meaning consistent with the word here is: noble heroes are called 'Vīrā'; the cause (aṅga) of heroes is 'Vīraṅga', which means the cause of being a hero is energy (vīriya). They are called 'Vīraṅgarūpā' because they have the nature (rūpa) of energy, meaning it is as if they have bodies made of energy. 'Parasenappamaddanā' means those capable of crushing enemy armies if they stand before them. 'Dhammena' means (governing) by the Dhamma of the five precepts, such as "one should not kill living beings."

In the phrase, "He is the Worthy One (Arahaṃ), the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddho) in the world, one who has removed the veil (vivatṭacchaddo)," 'Vivatṭacchaddo' means: in the world which is a mass of darkness of defilements covered by the seven veils of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, ignorance, and misconduct, he has opened that veil and stands with the light of wisdom that has arisen all around. Among those three terms, the first term (Arahaṃ) states the state of being worthy of special offerings. The second term states the cause for that worthiness, which is because he is the Fully Enlightened One. The third term states the removal of the veil, which is the cause of Buddhahood. Alternatively, 'Vivatṭacchaddo' means being free from the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and free from the veil (chadda). It means having no round of rebirth and no veil. In that case, he is 'Arahaṃ' because of the absence of the round of rebirth, and 'Sammāsambuddho' because of the absence of the veil; thus, it expresses the two causes for the previous two terms. The first term (Arahaṃ) is accomplished by the second intrepidity (vesārajja); the second term (Sammāsambuddho) is accomplished by the first intrepidity; and the third term (Vivatṭacchaddo) is accomplished by the third and fourth intrepidities. It should be understood that the first term achieves the Eye of Dhamma (dhammacakkhu), the second achieves the Eye of a Buddha (buddhacakkhu), and the third achieves the All-seeing Eye (samantacakkhu). By the words, "You are a receiver (master) of the Vedas," he instills bravery in the young man Ambaṭṭha regarding the Vedas.
224:
Ambaṭṭha the youth, through those words of his teacher, became free from confusion regarding the treatises on marks. As if a light had suddenly shone, he clearly saw the Vedic lore (marks) that indicate the appearance of a Buddha and said, "Yes, sir, let it be so." The meaning of those words is: "Sir, I will do as you say." "Vaḷavārathamāruyha" means mounting a chariot drawn by mares. It is said that the Brahmin Pokkharasāti gave the very chariot he himself used for travel and sent the youth Ambaṭṭha. The youths were also disciples of Pokkharasāti. That Brahmin had given them the instruction, "Go together with Ambaṭṭha."

"Yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi" refers to as far as the ground is accessible by vehicle. "Yānā paccorohitvā" means having reached near the gateway where it is unsuitable to go by vehicle, and then alighting from the vehicle.

"Tena kho pana samayena" refers to the time when the youth Ambaṭṭha entered the monastery. That time was midday. Why were they walking in the cloister at that time? It was to dispel sloth and torpor (thina-middha) that arises from consuming fine food. Or, those monks were practitioners of meditation during the day. For such persons, if they walk in the cloister after the meal, bathe to cool the body, and then sit down to practice the recluse's duties (samaṇadhamma), they can achieve one-pointedness of mind.

"Yena te bhikkhū" refers to how the youth Ambaṭṭha, without wandering from one precinct to another asking "Where is the ascetic Gotama?", looked around and thought, "I will enter only after asking." He then saw the monks wearing rag-robes (paṃsukūla) walking in the great cloister like wild bull elephants and went towards them. This is what is meant by "where those monks were." "Dassanāya" means with the desire to see.

"Abhiññātakolañño" means one born of a well-known family. At that time, in Jambudīpa, the Ambaṭṭha family was a very famous family. "Abhiññātassa" refers to one who is well-known for their physical appearance, birth, Vedas, and lineage. "Agaru" means not burdensome. Only for one who cannot make Ambaṭṭha understand would a conversation with him be burdensome. But for the Blessed One, even with hundreds of such youths...
225:
Speaking with that youth might be considered burdensome. However, even if a hundred or a thousand questions were asked, they thought, "There is no hesitation or delay for the Blessed One in answering," and thus they considered, "It is no trouble at all." By the word "Vihāra," they were referring to the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi).

"Ataramāno" means without haste, placing each step gently and fulfilling the duty, without destroying the sand which was well-leveled and resembled a bed of pearls or a spread of Sinduvāra flowers. "Āḷinda" refers to the front porch (veranda). "Ukkāsitvā" means having made the sound of clearing the throat. "Aggaḷa" is the door-panel. "Ākoṭehi" means to knock gently with the tips of the fingernails near the keyhole. It is said that non-humans (ogres) usually knock on the very top part of the door, while those of the long-birth (serpents) knock on the very bottom. To show the etiquette of knocking on a door, it was said that one should not knock like that, but should knock in the middle near the keyhole.

"Vivari bhagavā dvāraṃ" does not mean the Blessed One himself stood up and opened the door. He merely extended his hand, thinking, "Let it be opened." Then, as if saying, "Blessed One, while you were performing acts of merit such as giving dana for many tens of millions of aeons, you did not perform the act of opening a door with your own hands," the door opened by itself. Since that door opened because of the Blessed One's mental intent, it is appropriate to say, "The Blessed One opened the door."

"They exchanged friendly greetings with the Blessed One" means that just as the Blessed One asked about their health and well-being, they too were in harmonious joy with the Blessed One. They became one, like cold water mixing with hot water. "Venerable Gotama, are you healthy? Are you well? Are you and your disciples free from illness, free from affliction, light in limb, strong, and living in comfort?" With such words, they spoke with mutual joy. Such speech is called "Sammodanīya" because it generates joy known as pīti-pāmojja and because it is suitable for rejoicing. It is called "Sāraṇīya" because it is worthy of being remembered for a long time and being practiced continuously due to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, and because it is worthy of being recollected. It is Sammodanīya because of the happiness of hearing it, and Sāraṇīya because of the happiness of recollecting it. Likewise, it is Sammodanīya due to the purity of its phrasing and Sāraṇīya due to the purity of its meaning. Having thus concluded and finished the exchange of many kinds of polite and memorable talk, they sat down at one side.
226:
The youth Ambaṭṭha, without having even a slight degree of mental devotion toward the Buddha's perfection of physical form (rūpasampatti), thought, "I will show disrespect to the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." He loosened the cloth tied around his waist and hung it over his neck. Holding the edge of his robe with one hand, he ascended the walkway (caṅkama). Showing now his arms, now his belly, and now his back, and making now hand gestures and now distortions of his eyebrows (frowning), he spoke these mocking words, which were indicative of his low character: "O Master Gotama, are your four elements in equilibrium? Are you not fatigued by the search for alms-food? Indeed, only the appearance of being free from fatigue is evident in you. Your major and minor limbs are robust; you are pleasant to behold wherever you go. Those many people, thinking 'He is one who has gone forth from a royal family' and 'He is a Buddha,' have great reverence for you and offer you exquisite and nutritious food. Look, sirs, at this dwelling; it is like a decorated hall, like a celestial palace. Look at this couch, look at this pillow. For one living in such a place, how could it be difficult to practice the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma)?"

Therefore, it is said: "The youth Ambaṭṭha, even while walking, exchanged some polite conversation with the Blessed One who was sitting; even while standing, he exchanged some polite conversation with the Blessed One who was sitting."

Then the Blessed One thought: "This youth is striving for the impossible, like one who wishes to reach the highest point of existence (bhavagga) by stretching out his hand, or like one who wishes to go to the Avīci hell by stretching out his foot, or like one who wishes to cross the great ocean, or like one who wishes to climb Mount Sineru. Now, I shall converse with him." Thinking thus, he said this to the youth Ambaṭṭha. The term "ācariyapācariyena" means with teachers and with the teachers of those teachers.

## Explanation of the First Discourse on the Menials (Ibbhavāda)

Regarding the phrase "gacchanto vā" (or while walking): In truth, a brahmin is fit to converse with a teacher brahmin in three postures. However, this youth, being stiff with pride, intended to employ all four postures in his conversation, and thus said, "Just as, Master Gotama, one who is lying down (converses) with one who is lying down."
227:
Then the Blessed One said to the youth Ambaṭṭha: "Ambaṭṭha, conversation between a walking student and a walking teacher, a standing student and a standing teacher, or a sitting student and a sitting teacher is found among all teachers. But you, while lying down, speak with a teacher who is sitting. Is your teacher a herd of cattle, or are you?" The youth Ambaṭṭha became angry and said, "O Master Gotama, those shavelings..." and so on. In that context, it would be appropriate to call shavelings "shavelings" and recluses "recluses." However, this youth, wishing to revile them, said "little shavelings, little recluses."

"Ibbha" means householders. "Kaṇha" means those who are dark or black. In the term "bandhupādāpacca," "Bandhu" refers to Brahmā. Brahmins address that Brahmā as "Grandfather" (Pitāmaha). "Pādāpacca" means the offspring of the feet; the meaning is that they are born from the tops of Brahmā's feet. This was Ambaṭṭha's view: Brahmins came from Brahmā's mouth, Khattiyas from the chest, Vessas from the navel, Suddas from the knees, and recluses (samaṇas) from the tops of the feet. Although the youth Ambaṭṭha spoke this without specifying anyone in particular, he spoke with the intention of referring only to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One thought: "From the moment he arrived, this youth Ambaṭṭha has spoken with me relying only on pride. He does not know his own measure, like one who grabs a venomous snake by the neck, or like one who embraces a great mass of fire, or like one who grabs a rogue elephant by its trunk. Now, I shall make him know." Thinking thus, he said, "Ambaṭṭha, for your purpose..." and so on. In that phrase, "attha" refers to the business or purpose for which he came; the mind of that youth is called "atthika" because it possesses that purpose. Because he has a mind with such a necessary purpose, Ambaṭṭha is called "atthikavā." The meaning is: "Your coming to this place was for that necessary purpose."

"Kho pana" is merely a particle. "Yāyeva kho panatthāya" means for whatever purpose or reason. "Āgaccheyyātha" means you might come at some time, whether to me or to others. The phrase "tam-eva atthaṃ" is stated according to the masculine gender. "Manasi kareyyātha" means you should keep it in mind. What is meant is: "You were sent by your teacher for his own business, not for the purpose of insulting us; therefore, keep only that business in mind."

Thus, having shown Ambaṭṭha the proper conduct of those who come to others, the Blessed One said, "avusitavāyeva kho pana" and so on, in order to subdue his pride. The meaning of that statement is: "Look, sirs, this youth Ambaṭṭha, in his teacher's house..."
228:
The youth Ambaṭṭha, though he has never lived [under a teacher], never been trained, and is of little learning, thinks of himself: "I have lived [under a teacher], I have been trained, I am a person of great learning." What other reason could there be for such harsh speech than his lack of training? Only those who have not grown up in a teacher's house, are untrained, and have little learning speak in this way.

"Kupito" means angry. "Anattamano" means having a displeased mind. Did the Blessed One say this knowing his anger, or without knowing? He said it knowing. Why did He say it knowing? To crush his pride. For the Blessed One knew: "If I speak thus, this Ambaṭṭha will become angry and revile my kinsmen. Then, just as a skilled physician makes one vomit out poison and removes it, I too, by pointing out lineage by lineage and family by family, shall cut down at the root and fell the banner of pride that has risen as if to the highest point of existence (bhavagga)."

"Khumsento" means wanting to find fault. "Vambhento" means wanting to despise and revile. "Pāpita bhavissati" means he will be brought to faults such as ferocity.

"Caṇḍā" refers to those whose speech is joined with anger based on pride. "Pharusā" means harsh ones. "Lahusā" means those with frivolous speech (or those who act recklessly). They are pleased or offended by very little. Like a gourd shell on the water, they float and bob with very little. "Bhassā" means talkative ones. It is said with the meaning that when the Sakyans open their mouths, there is no opportunity for others to speak. "Samānā" is a synonym for the preceding word "santā". "Na sakkaronti" means they do not treat the Brahmins with good conduct. "Na garuṃ karonti" means they do not show respect to the Brahmins. "Na mānenti" means they do not cherish them with the mind. "Na pūjenti" means they do not honor them with flowers, scents, etc. "Na apacāyanti" means they do not show humility or reverence through salutation, etc. "Tayidaṃ" is "taṃ idaṃ". "Yadime sakyā" is "yaṃ ime sakyā". The meaning is that the Sakyans' failure to respect the Brahmins, etc., is improper and unsuitable.

## Commentary on the Second Reproach of being a Menial (Ibbhavāda)

"Aparaddhuṃ" means they have offended. In "ekamidāhaṃ", "idaṃ" is merely a particle, meaning "once I...". "Santhāgāraṃ" is the hall for governing and instructing the country. The Sakyans are royalty who have been consecrated.
229:
Consecrated kings are called abhisitta-rājāno. Unconsecrated princes are called Sakyakumārā. "In high places" refers to various seats suitable for them, such as couches, benches, wicker chairs, stools, and painted rugs. "Laughing loudly in mockery" means laughing heartily because of a desire to mock. "Playing and sporting" means not just laughing, but also snapping fingers, clapping hands, and so on. "I think they are mocking only me, not anyone else"—this is what I thought.

Why did those Sakyans act in this way? It is said that those Sakyans knew Ambaṭṭha's lineage. At that time, this Ambaṭṭha came along like one intoxicated with pride, holding up the corner of his robe that hung down to his feet with one hand, and bending his neck. Then, saying, "Look, sirs, at the way our slave Ambaṭṭha of the Kaṇhāyana lineage comes," they acted in this manner. That Ambaṭṭha also knew his own lineage. Therefore, he thought, "I think they are mocking only me."

"With a seat" means an invitation by way of a seat, such as "This is a seat, sit here"; no one did so.

## Commentary on the Third Reproach of being a Menial

"Laṭukikā" (quail) is a small bird that lives among the clods of earth in a field. "In her own nest" means in her dwelling place. "Chirping at will" means chirping whatever sound she desires; no goose, crane, or peacock comes to that small bird and forbids her, saying, "Why do you chirp?" "To harbor a grudge" means to be attached through anger.

When this was said, the youth Ambaṭṭha thought, "This ascetic Gotama is making his own kinsmen like quails and making us like geese, cranes, and peacocks; now I have become one whose pride is removed," and he pointed out the four higher castes.

## Commentary on the Reproach of being the Son of a Slave Woman

"Nimmādeti" means to crush pride, to make one free of pride. "If I..." means "If I were to do this...". It is said that Ambaṭṭha said these words (loudly three times): "I am a Kaṇhāyana, Master Gotama."
230: He spoke with a loud voice three times. Why did he speak so? Was it because he did not know his own impurity? In truth, he did know. Even though he knew, because this matter was concealed by past births, Ambaṭṭha could not see it. Thinking, 'What can this Great Ascetic say, not seeing the truth?', he spoke out of stubborn pride. 'Wealth of parents' means things belonging to parents. 'Name and clan' means name by designation and clan by lineage. 'One who remembers' refers to one who repeatedly remembers while purifying the lineage. 'Sons of the master' means the sons of the lord. 'Son of a slave woman' means specifically the son of a household slave. Therefore, it shows that the Sakyans laughed, seeing that he did not approach them as a slave should approach his masters. After this, to clarify Ambaṭṭha's status as a slave and the Sakyans' status as masters, and wishing to bring forth the lineage of himself and Ambaṭṭha, he said, 'The Sakyans indeed...' and so on. In those words, 'they placed' means they designated, 'King Okkāka is our first ancestor.' It is said that when that king spoke, light like a torch issued from his mouth; therefore, they knew him as 'Okkāka'. 'Banished' means expelled. Now, wishing to show those sons by name, he said, 'Okkāmukha' and so on. The sequential story there is as follows: In the line of King Mahāsammata, the first king of the world, there was a son named Roja. The son of King Roja was Vararoja; the son of Vararoja was Kalyāṇa; the son of Kalyāṇa was Varakalyāṇa; the son of Varakalyāṇa was Mandhātu; the son of Mandhātu was Varamandhātu; the son of Varamandhātu was Uposatha; the son of Uposatha was Vara; the son of Vara was Upavara; the son of Upavara was Maghadeva. Through the lineage of King Maghadeva, there were eighty-four thousand kings. After those kings, there were three Okkāka lineages. Among those three, the third King Okkāka had five chief queens: Hatthā, Cittā, Jantu, Jālinī, and Visākhā. Each queen had five hundred female attendants. The eldest queen had four sons: Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍu, Hatthinika, and Sinisūra; and five daughters: Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitaseṇā. Thus, that chief queen passed away after giving birth to nine children. Then the king brought another young and beautiful princess and established her in the position of chief queen. That queen gave birth to a son named Jantu. Then, on the fifth day...
231: (Prince Jantu) was adorned and shown to the king. The king, being pleased, granted a boon to the queen. After consulting with her relatives, she requested the kingdom for her son. The king threatened her, saying, 'Wretched woman, perish! Do you wish harm upon my sons?' She repeatedly pleased the king in private and requested, saying, 'Great King, it is not proper to speak a falsehood,' and so forth. Then the king called his sons and said, 'Dear sons, upon seeing your younger brother Prince Jantu, I hastily granted a boon to his mother. That queen wishes to transfer the kingdom to her son. Leaving behind the auspicious elephant, the auspicious horse, and the auspicious chariot, take as many elephants, horses, and chariots as you desire and go. After my passing, return and rule the kingdom.' Thus, he sent them away along with eight ministers. Those princes, weeping and lamenting in various ways, said, 'Father, please forgive our faults,' and after asking forgiveness from the king and the royal harem, the sisters said, 'We too will go with our brothers,' and after asking the king's permission, they took their sisters and departed from the city, surrounded by a fourfold army. Thinking, 'The princes will return and rule after their father's passing; let us go and serve them,' many people followed them. On the first day, the army was one league long; on the second day, two leagues; on the third day, three leagues. The princes consulted, 'This army is very large. If we were to oppress any neighboring king and seize his territory, even he would not be able to subdue us. But what is the use of harming others? This Jambudīpa is vast; let us establish a city in the forest.' Having thus consulted, they headed toward the Himalayas and searched for a site for the city. At that time, our Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy Brahmin family and, known by the name Kapila the Brahmin, he renounced the world to become an ascetic. He lived in a leaf-hut built in a grove of teak trees (Sāka-vana) on the banks of a pond near the Himalayas. It is heard that this ascetic knew the science called Bhummajāla, by which he could see the merits and defects in the sky eighty cubits above and in the ground below. In that place, the grass, bushes, and creepers grew turning clockwise and facing the east. Lions, tigers, and such, while chasing deer and wild boars, or snakes and cats chasing frogs and mice, were unable to continue the chase once they reached that spot. Those animals...
232: Indeed, [those wild beasts] were only deterred and turned back because they were threatened. That ascetic Kapila, knowing that "this is the most excellent spot on earth," created his leaf-roofed hermitage there. Then, those princes, who were searching for a site to establish a city, saw that they had reached his dwelling place. Having inquired and learned the situation, the ascetic felt compassion for the princes and said: "The city established on the site of this hermitage will be the foremost city in Jambudīpa. Among the men born in this city, each one will be able to overcome even a hundred or a thousand men. Build the city in this place; build the king's palace on the site of the hermitage. For by staying in this location, even the son of a Caṇḍāla can excel others with the power of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti)." When they asked, "Venerable sir, is this not your dwelling place?", he replied, "Do not think of it as my dwelling place. Build my hermitage on one side, establish the city, and name it 'Kapilavatthu'." Those princes did accordingly and took up residence there. Then the ministers thought, "These children have reached maturity. If their father were near, he would arrange their marriages. Now, it is our responsibility." They consulted with the princes. The princes said, "We do not see princesses equal to us, nor do we see princes equal to our sisters. If we unite with those of unequal status, the children born will be impure from either the mother's or father's side, and the lineage will be corrupted. Therefore, we prefer to live together with our own sisters." Fearing the corruption of their lineage, they placed the eldest sister in the position of a mother and lived in marriage with the remaining sisters. Later, as they were increasing in number with sons and daughters, the eldest sister developed leprosy. Her limbs became covered with sores like the Koviḷāra flower. The princes thought, "If we continue to sit and eat with this eldest sister, this disease will spread to us." One day, as if going for an outing in the park, they placed her on a carriage, entered the forest, had a pit dug in the ground, placed her in it along with food and provisions, covered it with a wooden plank, spread earth over it, and departed.
233: At that time, a king of Bārāṇasī named Rāma had leprosy and was loathed by his dancers and concubines. Out of the dismay caused by that leprosy, he handed over the kingdom to his eldest son and entered the forest. There, he created a hermitage and, by consuming roots and fruits, he soon became free of the disease and his skin became golden-hued. While wandering here and there, he saw a large hollow tree. He cleared a space of sixteen cubits inside that tree, fitted it with a door and a window, made a ladder, and took up residence in that tree-hollow. King Rāma would place embers in a fire-pan and sleep at night while listening to the sounds of deer, wild boar, and other animals. He would note, "A lion roared in such a place; a tiger roared in such a place." At dawn, he would go to those places, take the leftover meat from the lions and other predators, cook it, and eat it. Then one day, at the time of dawn, while the king sat having lit a fire, a tiger came, drawn by the scent of the princess's body. It scratched the earth in that spot and made a hole in the wooden plank. Through that hole, the princess saw the tiger and cried out in fear. The king heard that sound and, noting "This is a woman's voice," went there early in the morning and asked, "Who is here?" She replied, "Lord, it is a woman." "Of what lineage are you?" he asked. She said, "Lord, I am the daughter of the Great King Okkāka." "Come out," he said. "Lord, I cannot," she replied. "Why?" he asked. "Lord, I have leprosy," she said. The king inquired about the whole situation. To the princess who would not come out due to her royal pride, he made his own royal status known, saying, "I too am a Khattiya." He gave her a ladder, brought her out, and took her to his dwelling. He gave her the same medicines he had used himself and soon made her free of the disease and golden-hued. He then lived in union with her. From that first union, she became pregnant and gave birth to two sons. Again, she bore two, and in this way, she gave birth sixteen times. Thus, there were thirty-two brothers. When those sons reached maturity, the father taught them all the arts and sciences. Then one day, a hunter from King Rāma's city, while searching for gems in the mountains, saw the king and, recognizing him, said, "Great King, I recognize you." Then the king asked the hunter about all the news. At that very moment, those youths arrived. Seeing them, the hunter asked, "Who are these?"
