When the king said, "They are my sons," the hunter inquired about their mother's lineage and thought, "Now I have obtained a gift..."
234: "This is my gift," he said, going to the city and informing the king. The king, thinking "I will bring my father back," went there with a fourfold army, paid homage to his father, and pleaded, "Great King, please accept the kingship." The father replied, "Enough, dear son, I will not go there. Right here, remove this Kola tree for me and build a city." The son did as his father commanded. Because it was built after removing the Kola tree of that city, it was named 'Kolanagara,' and because it was built on the path of tigers, it was named 'Vyagghapatha.' Having given it these two names and paying homage to his father, he returned to his own city. Furthermore, when the princes reached the age of maturity, their mother said, "Dear sons, there are Sakyans living in the city of Kapilavatthu who are your maternal uncles. The daughters of those uncles have such a habit of holding their hair and such a habit of holding their clothes. When those princesses come to the bathing ghat, you go there, and whichever prince likes a particular princess, let him take her." The princes went exactly as their mother said, and while the princesses were drying their hair after bathing, each prince took the princess he desired, announced his name, and returned. When the Sakyan kings heard of this, they remained silent, saying, "Friends, let it be; they are indeed our relatives." This is the origin of the Sakyans and the Koliyans. In this way, the Sakyans and Koliyans practiced intermarriage, and the lineage continued uninterrupted until the time of the Buddha. Among those lineages, to show the Sakyan lineage, the Blessed One said, "Those princes, having been banished from the country, [dwelt] by the side of a lotus pond at the foot of the Himalayas..." and so on. In that Pali text, "sammanti" means they dwell. "The Sakyans are indeed capable" means that even though they were banished from the country and lived in the forest, they were capable, able, and competent to preserve their family lineage without breaking their caste. "Tadagge" means starting from that point, or from then on. "That king was their ancestor" means that King Okkāka was the original person of these Sakyans. It means there was not even a slight mixing of these Sakyans with the lineage of householders. Having thus clarified the Sakyan lineage, now wishing to clarify the Ambaṭṭha lineage, he said, "To the king..." and so on. "Gave birth to a son named Kaṇha" refers to giving birth to a son who was dark-colored, who had teeth already grown even while in the mother's womb, and who had a full-grown beard and tusks. "Cried out" means that while the household members fled in fear, thinking a demon (yakkha) had been born, and stood with the doors closed, he wandered here and there, making a loud sound and saying, "Wash me," and so forth.
235: Those youths spoke the words "May it not be so," and so forth, to the Blessed One to free themselves from reproach. It is heard that they had this thought: "Ambaṭṭha is the senior student of our teacher. If we do not say even a word or two in such a situation, this Ambaṭṭha will ruin us in the presence of our teacher." Thus, they spoke to free themselves from reproach. In their hearts, however, they desired the humbling of his pride. Because this Ambaṭṭha was arrogant, he was also unloved (disliked) by those youths. "Kalyāṇavākkaraṇa" means having sweet and pleasant speech. "In these words" refers to the words of the three Vedas that he had learned. "To reply" means to answer or clarify the question asked. Alternatively, it refers to replying excessively to the words "son of a slave girl." Then the Blessed One thought, "If these youths sit here making such a loud noise, this conversation will not reach an end. Now, having made those youths silent, I will speak only with Ambaṭṭha," and he said these words to the youths. In that Pali text, "mantavho" means "do speak." "Let him converse with me" means "let him talk with me." When this was said, the youths thought: "When Ambaṭṭha was told 'You are the son of a slave girl,' he could not lift his head again. This thing called 'birth' (caste) is indeed difficult to know. If the recluse Gotama says to someone else, 'You are a slave,' who would be able to discuss the Dhamma with that Gotama? Let Ambaṭṭha himself untie the bundle he himself tied." Thus, freeing themselves and wishing to throw the burden onto Ambaṭṭha alone, they said, "Master Gotama, Ambaṭṭha is well-born," and so forth. "Sahadhammika" means with reason, or in accordance with the cause. "Must be answered even if unwilling" means that even if one does not wish to, one must answer; it means one must certainly explain. "You will cover one word with another" means covering or concealing one statement with another statement. For instance, if someone is asked, "What is your lineage?" and he says, "I know the three Vedas," and so on, this person is said to cover one word with another. "Will go away" means that although he knows the question asked, because he does not wish to answer, he will get up from his seat and depart.
236:
The young man Ambaṭṭha remained silent means—The ascetic Gotama wants me to admit my status as the son of a slave woman myself; and if I admit it myself, I will indeed be known as a slave. Thinking, "This ascetic Gotama will remain silent after urging me twice, and then I will turn back and leave," he remained silent.

He is called Vajirapāṇi because he has a thunderbolt (vajira) in his hand. Yakkha here is not just any spirit, but should be understood as Sakka, the king of gods. Āditta means having a color like the color of fire. Sampajjalita means very brilliant. Sajotibhūta means being a mass of flames all around, meaning becoming a single mass of fire. "He stood" means he stood having created a terrifying appearance with a large head, tusks like the buds of a kandala flower, and frightening eyes, nose, and so on.

Why did this Sakka come? He came to make him abandon his wrong view. Alternatively, while the Blessed One was residing with little concern for teaching the Dhamma, thinking, "I alone shall teach the Dhamma, but others might not understand my teaching," Sakka came together with Mahābrahmā and made a pledge: "Venerable Sir, please teach the Dhamma; we shall make those who do not abide by your authority abide by it. May yours be the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka), and ours be the Wheel of Authority (Āṇācakka)." Therefore, he came thinking, "Today I will frighten Ambaṭṭha and make him answer the question."

Only the Blessed One and the young man Ambaṭṭha saw that spirit. If others had seen him, it would not have been a serious matter (it would have been open to criticism). They might have said, "This ascetic Gotama, knowing that Ambaṭṭha did not enter into his own view, summoned a spirit and showed it; only then did Ambaṭṭha speak out of fear." Therefore, only the Blessed One and Ambaṭṭha saw him. As soon as Ambaṭṭha saw him, sweat poured from his entire body. It was as if his insides were turning upside down, and he let out a loud cry. Looking around to see if others also saw, he did not see even a sign of hair-standing-on-end in anyone. Then he thought, "This danger has arisen only for me. If I say it is a spirit, they might say, 'Do you alone have eyes? Do you alone see the spirit? Did you not see the spirit at first, but only see it when your views clashed with the ascetic Gotama?'" Thinking, "Now..."
237:
Thinking, "I have no other refuge here except the ascetic Gotama," the young man Ambaṭṭha then... said this to the Blessed One.

Tāṇaṃ gavesī means seeking one who can prevent danger. Leṇaṃ gavesī means seeking a hiding place. Saraṇaṃ gavesī means seeking one who can remove suffering. Here, he is called tāṇa because he protects from danger. He is called leṇa because he is a place where beings take shelter. He is called saraṇa because he oppresses and destroys danger. Upanisīditvā means having approached and sat on a lower seat. Bravītu means "please speak."

## The Story of the Ambaṭṭha Lineage

273-274. Dakkhiṇajanapada is the well-known district south of the Ganges River known as the Dakkhiṇāpatha region. At that time, there were many brahmin ascetics in the Dakkhiṇāpatha region. That Kaṇha went there and pleased an ascetic by performing great and small duties. Seeing Kaṇha's service, the ascetic said, "My good man, I will give you a mantra; take whichever mantra you desire." Kaṇha said, "Teacher, I have no need for any other mantra. Give me that mantra by whose power weapons cannot fall [on me]." The teacher said, "Very well," and gave him the science called Ambaṭṭha, which makes one unapproachable by bows and arrows. Kaṇha learned that science, tested it right there, and thinking, "Now I will fulfill my desire," took the form of an ascetic and went to King Okkāka. Therefore, it is said, "Having gone to the Dakkhiṇajanapada, learned the Brahma-mantras, and approached King Okkāka."

Here, brahmamante means noble mantras because they are endowed with great power. "Friend, who is this son of my slave woman? Why does he speak thus?" is the meaning. Because that king wanted to kill the ascetic Kaṇha, he could neither shoot the arrow he had set nor put it back down due to the power of the ascetic's mantra; at that very moment, sweat broke out over his whole body, and he stood trembling with fear.

Amaccā means the great ministers. Pārisajjā means the other members of the assembly. Etadavocuṃ means "The entire kingdom of King Daṇḍakī, who offended the ascetic Kisavaccha, was rained upon by weapons..."
238:
...destroyed. King Nāḷikera, having offended five hundred ascetics, and King Ajjuna, having offended the ascetic Aṅgīrasa, were swallowed by the earth and entered hell. Thinking thus and being afraid, they said, "Venerable sir, may this matter be safe," and so on.

"There will be safety for the king"—this statement was made by the sage Kaṇha after remaining silent for a long time and being repeatedly entreated. He said, "Your king has committed a grave unwholesome deed by aiming a feathered arrow at a sage like me," and so on, before speaking further. "Will be destroyed" means it will break and be scattered like a handful of chaff. The sage Kaṇha said this falsely, intending to "frighten the people." His psychic power was only sufficient to stop the arrow in mid-air, not beyond that. The same principle applies to the words spoken hereafter.

"Pallomo" means the hair lying flat. Not even a single hair on that prince would stand on end. It is said he spoke this after making the king promise, "If the king gives me that maiden." Placing the arrow on the prince means when the sage Kaṇha recited the mantra "Let the arrow descend," those arrows landed on the prince's navel. Giving the daughter means having her head washed, freeing her from servitude, and giving her away, placing her in an exalted position. "Young men, do not be afraid"—the Blessed One said this to reassure Ambaṭṭha, revealing that "On one side, Ambaṭṭha is a relative of the Sakyans." Then Ambaṭṭha, feeling as if he had been consecrated with a hundred jars of water, his distress subsided and he was reassured, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama, wishing to please me, makes me a relative on one side; I am indeed of the kshatriya (warrior) caste."

## Commentary on the Excellence of the Kshatriya

Then the Blessed One thought, "This Ambaṭṭha perceives himself as a kshatriya and does not know his non-kshatriya status. Let me make him know." To show the kshatriya lineage, he expanded the discourse further, saying, "What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?" and so on. In that context, "idha" (here) means in this world of humans. "Among Brahmins" means in the midst of Brahmins. "A seat or water" means the best seat or the best water. "Saddhe" refers to food offered dedicated to the deceased. "Thālidāke" refers to rice cooked for auspicious ceremonies and the like. "Yaññe" refers to sacrificial food. "Pāhune" refers to food prepared for guests or food given as a gift. "Api nussā" means whether there would be a prohibition for that prince regarding Brahmin daughters, or whether he could obtain a Brahmin daughter or not. "Anuppapatti" should be understood as not attaining kshatriya status, or impurity.

276. "Treating a woman as a woman" means by searching for faults in a woman. "In some matter" means because of doing something inappropriate or forbidden for Brahmins. "With a bag of ashes" means by scattering ashes over the head from a bag. 277. "Among the multitude" should be understood as among the multitude of beings. "They remember the lineage" means among those who remember their lineage, saying "I am of the Gotama lineage, I am of the Kassapa lineage," the kshatriya is the best in the world. "Permitted" means "I permit it because it is preached by comparing and correlating with my omniscience."

## Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge and Conduct

278. In this verse, upon hearing the phrase "endowed with knowledge and conduct (vijjā-caraṇa-sampanno)," Ambaṭṭha thought, "Knowledge (vijjā) refers to the three Vedas, and conduct (caraṇa) refers to the five precepts. We indeed possess this knowledge and conduct."
239:
The word 'vā' (or) refers to whether there was a prohibition regarding the daughters of Brahmins for that prince, or not; whether he obtained a Brahmin daughter, or not. 'Anuppanno' means one who has not attained the status of a Khattiya, one who is impure.

'Itthiyā vā itthiṃ karitvā' means seeking a woman (a fault) through a woman. 'Kismiñcideva pakaraṇe' means because of committing an improper or forbidden act against Brahmins in some matter of fault. 'Bhassapuṭenāti' means by scattering ashes on the head with a bag of ashes.

'Janetasmiṃ' means among the multitude of people or among beings. 'Ye gotta-paṭisārino' means those who, among that multitude of people, recall their lineage, saying, 'I am of the Gotama lineage, I am of the Kassapa lineage.' Among those who thus recall their lineage, the Khattiya (warrior-noble) is the best in the world. 'Anumata mayā' means these are words approved by me, as they were taught in accordance with my Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

## The First Recitation Section is Finished (Paṭhama-bhāṇavāra-vaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā).

## Discussion on Knowledge and Conduct (Vijjā-caraṇa-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

Upon hearing the term 'vijjā-caraṇa-sampanno' (endowed with knowledge and conduct) in this verse, the young man Ambaṭṭha thought: 'Knowledge (vijjā) means the three Vedas; conduct (caraṇa) means the five precepts. These knowledge and conduct are already possessed by us. If one endowed with knowledge and conduct is supreme, then we alone are the supreme.' Having reached this conclusion, wishing to ask about knowledge and conduct, he said: 'O Gotama, what is that conduct? And what is that knowledge?' Then the Blessed One, wishing to reject that knowledge and conduct associated with the theory of birth (jāti-vāda) etc., which is established in the Brahmin tradition, and wishing to show the unsurpassed knowledge and conduct, spoke the words beginning with 'Na kho Ambaṭṭha'. In that text, 'jāti-vāda' means speaking based on birth. It means words such as 'This is suitable only for a Brahmin, not for a Sudda (low-caste person).' The same method applies to all other terms. 'Jāti-vāda-vinibaddhā' means those who are bound to the theory of birth. The same method applies everywhere else.

Thereafter, Ambaṭṭha thought: 'Although we previously intended to cling to that knowledge and conduct, the Ascetic Gotama has cast us far away from it, like winnowing chaff in a strong wind. He has joined us only to the knowledge and conduct to which we do not cling. It is necessary to know this endowment of knowledge and conduct.' Having thought thus, he asked again about the endowment of knowledge and conduct.
240:
Then the Blessed One, in order to show knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa) starting from the fulfillment [of perfections], said to Ambaṭṭha: "Ambaṭṭha, here a Tathāgata [appears] in the world..." and so forth.

In this context, the Blessed One, wishing to analyze the threefold virtue (sīla) included within conduct (caraṇa), did not conclude with "This is part of his conduct," but rather concluded with "This also is part of his virtue," by way of virtue. Why? Because even Ambaṭṭha possesses a small amount of virtue. Therefore, if it were concluded by way of conduct, he might get stuck right there, thinking, "We too are accomplished in conduct." Wishing to conclude by way of that [conduct] which Ambaṭṭha had never even seen in a dream, [the Blessed One] said: "He enters and dwells in the first jhāna; this also is part of his conduct... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; this also is part of his conduct," and so forth. By this sequence of words, the eight attainments (samāpatti) are also concluded under the term "conduct" (caraṇa). However, the eightfold wisdom starting from insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) is concluded under the term "knowledge" (vijjā).

## Explanation of the Four Causes of Ruin (Apāyamukha)

Apāyamukhāni means causes of ruin. Anabhisambhuṇamāno means being unable to fulfill, or being incapable. In the phrase "khārividhamādāya," khārī refers to ascetic requisites such as fire-sticks, a water-pot, a needle, and a whisk. Vidha means a shoulder-pole. Therefore, it means "taking a shoulder-pole laden with requisites." Those teachers who read it as "khārivividhaṃ" explain that khārī is the name for the shoulder-pole and vividha refers to the various requisites like the water-pot. Pavatta-phala-bhojano means one who habitually eats fruit that has fallen naturally. Paricārako means an attendant by way of performing duties such as preparing what is allowable, receiving the alms-bowl, and washing feet. Although an Arahant novice (sāmaṇera) who is superior in virtue could be an attendant to a worldling (puthujjana) monk in the manner mentioned, this person is not like that; he is inferior both in terms of virtue and in terms of performing services.

Why is becoming an ascetic (tāpasa-pabbajjā) called a cause of ruin for the Dispensation (sāsana)? Because as the Dispensation continues, it will decline through the practice of becoming an ascetic. In this Dispensation, those monks who are unable to fulfill the three trainings (sikkhā) are shunned and avoided by the shameful monks who desire the training, saying, "There is no Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or legal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) together with you." That monk thinks, "Fulfilling the practice in the Dispensation is difficult and painful, like [walking on] a razor's edge. But becoming an ascetic is easy to do and is also esteemed by many people." Having so reflected, he disrobes and becomes an ascetic. Others see him and ask, "Why have you done this?" He says, "The work in your Dispensation is very heavy, but here we can practice according to our own will..."
241:
"...we can practice according to our own will," he says. Another person, thinking, "If that is so, I too will go forth right here," follows his example and becomes an ascetic. In this way, others and still others follow, and gradually ascetics become numerous. When they have arisen, the Dispensation is said to have declined. It will only be a matter of hearing that "Such a Buddha arose in the world, and such was his Dispensation." With reference to this, the Blessed One said that becoming an ascetic is a cause of ruin for the Dispensation.

Kudāla-piṭaka refers to a hoe and a basket for the purpose of taking roots and fruits. "Or near a village" means being unable to achieve the accomplishment of knowledge and conduct, etc., and thinking it difficult to make a living through farming and so on, he builds a fire-hut near a village or near a market town to deceive and impress the common people. He stays there tending the fire by way of making offerings with ghee, oil, curd, honey, molasses, sesame, rice, and various kinds of wood.

"Having made a house with four openings" means having made a four-sided water-station, building a pavilion at its entrance, setting out drinking water there, and inviting all who come and go with the water. Travelers who are weary and satisfied after drinking the water give him a bundle of cooked rice or raw rice and so forth. Taking all that, he makes sour gruel (ambila-yāgu) and so on, and to obtain more material gains, he gives food to some and cooking vessels to others. He takes the material gifts or grain given by them and employs them for interest. Thus, with increasing wealth, he acquires cattle, buffaloes, female slaves, and male slaves, and establishes a large household. It is with reference to this establishment of wealth that it was said, "Having made a house with four openings, he dwells there." "I will honor that person according to my ability and strength"—this is the beginning of his practice. By this means, he practices in this way. By this much, the Blessed One has shown all [types of] becoming an ascetic.

How are they shown? There are eight kinds of ascetics: those living with wife and children (saputta-bhariyā), gleaners (uñchā-cariyā), those who do not cook with fire (anaggi-pakkikā), those who do not cook for themselves (asāma-pākā), those who crush with stones (asma-muṭṭhikā), those who use their teeth as a bark-stripper (danta-vakkalikā), those who eat naturally fallen fruit (pavatta-phala-bhojanā), and those who eat naturally fallen yellow leaves (paṇḍu-palāsikā). Among these eight, those who live establishing a household like the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya are called "those living with wife and children" (saputta-bhariyā).
242:
Those who, thinking, 'Living with a wife and children is unsuitable for an ascetic,' collect, cook, and consume grains such as rice, green gram, black gram, and sesame from places where crops are harvested and threshed, are called Uñchācariyas (gleaners).

Those who, thinking, 'Wandering from one threshing floor to another, taking grain, pounding it, and consuming it is unsuitable,' receive alms-rice in villages and market towns, cook it, and consume it, are called Anaggipakkikas.

Those who, thinking, 'What is the use of an ascetic cooking for himself?' enter a village and accept only cooked alms-food, are called Asāmapākas.

Those who, thinking, 'Searching for alms-food day after day is painful for an ascetic,' pound the bark of trees such as the hog plum with a fist-sized stone and eat it, are called Asmamuṭṭhikas.

Those who, thinking, 'Wandering about pounding bark with a stone is painful,' peel it off with only their teeth and eat it, are called Dantavakkalikas.

Those who, thinking, 'Peeling and eating with the teeth is painful for an ascetic,' consume fruits that have fallen after being struck with clods of earth or sticks, are called Pavattafalabhojanās.

Those who, thinking, 'Consuming fruits by knocking them down with clods or sticks is unseemly for an ascetic,' sustain themselves by eating only naturally fallen flowers, fruits, and withered leaves, are called Paṇḍupalāsikas.

These ascetics are of three types: keen (ukkaṭṭha), moderate (majjhima), and mild (mudu). Among them, those who do not rise from their sitting place but pick up and eat only what has fallen within reach of their hand are the keen. Those who do not go from one tree to another are the moderate. Those who go to the foot of various trees, search, and eat are the mild.

These eight types of asceticism are included within these four groups. How? Among these ascetics, the Saputtabhariyas (those with wives and children) and the Uñchācariyas resort to a house (a house with a water-pot stand). The Anaggipakkikas and the Asāmapākas resort to the fire-hall. The Asmamuṭṭhikas and the Dantavakkalikas resort to eating roots and fruits. The Pavattafalabhojanās and the Paṇḍupalāsikas resort to eating naturally fallen fruits. Therefore, it is said: 'By this much, the Blessed One has described all forms of asceticism.'
243:
281-282. Now, the Blessed One, in order to show that the young man Ambaṭṭha, along with his teacher, had not even reached the practices (of the ascetics) which are the causes of failure in the perfection of knowledge and conduct, said: "Ambaṭṭha, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The meaning of those words is clear. "Being himself unable to fulfill even the causes of failure" means that he himself is unable to fulfill even the causes of failure (apāyamukha) regarding the perfection of knowledge and conduct.

## Commentary on the Practice of Ancient Sages

"Dattikaṃ" means the wealth that is given. Regarding the phrase "does not even allow a face-to-face meeting," why does he not allow it? It is said that the Brahmin Pokkharasāti knows the art called "Āvaṭṭanī," which is the magic of attraction/turning in one's presence. When the King is adorned with very costly ornaments, the Brahmin stands near the King and takes the name of that ornament. Once the King's name (of the ornament) is taken, he is unable to say, "I cannot give it." After giving it, when the King says on a festival day, "Bring the ornaments," and is told, "Great King, they are no longer here; you yourself gave them to the Brahmin," he usually asks, "Why did I give them?" Then the ministers say, "That Brahmin knows the Āvaṭṭanī magic of attraction; by that magic, he attracted you, took them, and left."

Other ministers, being jealous of the King's great friendship with that Brahmin, said, "Great King, there is a leprosy like a conch-shell (leukoderma) on this Brahmin's body. When you see him, you embrace and touch him affectionately. This leprosy is contagious through bodily contact; do not do this." From then on, the King did not allow the Brahmin a face-to-face meeting.

However, because that Brahmin was wise and skilled in the science of statecraft and architecture (khattavijjā), any work done after consulting him would not fail. Therefore, the King stayed inside a curtained enclosure and consulted with the Brahmin who stood outside. Referring to such consultation, it is said, "He consults from behind a curtain." In that context, "tirodussantena" means by means of a curtain. There is also this variant reading. "Dhammikaṃ" refers to blameless (alms-food). "Payātaṃ" means that which is brought forward and offered. "How then could that King..." means if the Brahmin receives the alms-food of such a King, why would that King not meet the Brahmin face-to-face? However, this Brahmin takes unoffered property through magic; therefore, the King does not meet him face-to-face—this is the conclusion that should be reached here. The Blessed One revealed this with the intention: "No one else besides the King and the Brahmin knows this reason. When he knows even such a secret and hidden matter, they will surely conclude that the Ascetic Gotama is truly the Omniscient One."
244:
At this time, both Ambaṭṭha and his teacher were exceedingly proud, relying on their knowledge of the Vedas. For this reason, the Blessed One, wishing to further expand the teaching to subdue their pride rooted in the Vedas, said: "Ambaṭṭha, what do you think? In this world, a king..." and so forth. In that passage, "rathūpatthare" refers to a place prepared and spread out on a chariot for the king to stand. "Uggehi vā" means with prominent and famous ministers. "Rājanyehī" refers to princes who have not yet been anointed. "Kiñcideva mantanaṃ" refers to a public consultation of this nature: "It is proper to build a lake or a canal in such a place; it is proper to establish a village, a market town, or a city in such a place." "Tadeva mantanaṃ" means that very consultation which the king deliberated upon. One should consult through such gestures as raising the head or raising the eyebrows. "Rājabhaṇitaṃ" refers to the speech spoken by the king concerning a particular benefit, which is capable of achieving that objective. It means that the person also speaks only words capable of achieving that objective.

"Pavattāro" means those who cause to proceed (the originators). "Yesaṃ" means those to whom it belongs. "Mantapadaṃ" refers to the Vedas themselves, known as the three Vedas. "Gītaṃ" means that which was chanted through the perfection of sound by the ten ancient Brahmins, beginning with Aṭṭhaka. "Pavuttaṃ" has the meaning of being taught or spoken to others. "Samihitaṃ" has the meaning of being compiled or gathered into a collection. "Tadanugāyanti" means that Brahmins nowadays chant after the Vedas that were previously chanted by those sages. "Tadanubhāsanti" means they speak after them; this is merely a synonym for the previous term. "Bhāsitamanubhāsanti" means they chant after what was spoken and chanted by those sages. "Vācitamanuvācenti" means they cause others to be taught after what was taught by those sages.

"Seyyathidaṃ" means "Who are they?" Aṭṭhaka and the others are their names. It is said that those sages, having looked with the divine eye without harming others, composed the Vedas in accordance with the dispensation of the Blessed Buddha Kassapa. However, later Brahmins corrupted the three Vedas by inserting practices such as killing living beings, making them contrary to the Buddha's words. "Netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati" means that the reason by which you might become a sage does not exist. Here, the Blessed One, knowing that "this Ambaṭṭha, even when questioned, will not give an answer because he realizes his own lack of standing," rejected his status as a sage without even taking an admission from him.

Now, because those ten ancient Brahmins lived in forest regions and at the foot of mountains, free from the impurities of defilements, free from the scent of women, free from ornamentation, practicing the holy life, and eating roots and fruits. When they wished to go anywhere, they went only through the air by psychic power; they had no need for vehicles. In all directions, the development of the Brahma-vihāras, such as loving-kindness, was their only protection. Therefore, they did not need walls, enclosures, or guards. This is the meaning. By this sequence, he had heard of the practice of those sages. Therefore, of this Ambaṭṭha along with his teacher...
245:
Now, those ten ancient Brahmins (sages) lived in forest regions and at the foot of mountains, subsisting on roots and fruits, being free from the foul odor of defilements, free from the scent of women, free from bodily ornamentation, and practicing the holy life. When they wished to go to any place, they went only through the air by psychic power; they had no business with chariots or vehicles. In all directions, the development of the Brahma-vihāras, such as loving-kindness, was their only protection; they had no need for the benefit of walls or guarding by men. This Ambaṭṭha had also heard of their practice before; therefore, to show this Ambaṭṭha and his teacher their distance from the practice of those sages, the Blessed One said: "Ambaṭṭha, what do you think?" and so forth.

In that passage, "vicitakāḷakaṃ" refers to alms-food from which black grains have been picked out and impurities removed. "Veṭhakanatapassāhi" refers to women whose ribs are bent by ornaments such as waistbands and breast-bands. "Kuttavālehi" refers to horses whose hair (tails) has been trimmed and groomed in suitable places for the sake of beauty. Here, only the hair of the mares is trimmed, not the chariots, but because they are yoked with the mares, the chariots are also called "kuttavāla" (having trimmed-tail ornaments). "Ukkiṇṇaparikhāsū" means in cities that have dug-out moats. "Okkhittapalighāsū" means in cities that have lowered crossbars (gate-bars). In the phrase "nagarūpakārikāsū," "upakārikā" refers to the plasterwork done around the lower part of the city wall to prevent others from climbing up. Here, however, cities endowed with such plasterwork are intended by the term "nagarūpakārikā." "Rakkhāpenti" means that even while living in such cities, they have themselves guarded (by protectors). "Kaṅkhā" is the doubt: "Is he the All-Enlightened One or not?" "Vimati" is a synonym for that very doubt; it means a distorted thought, an intellect unable to decide. The Blessed One thought: "For this Ambaṭṭha, the manifestation of the Path is not possible in this existence; the days are merely passing in vain. He came to investigate the marks, but he has forgotten even that task. Now, I shall give him a way to generate mindfulness," and thus He spoke these words.

## Commentary on Showing the Two Marks

Having spoken thus—because no one is able to investigate the marks of the Buddhas while they are sitting or reclining, but only while they are standing or walking—and since it is the custom of the Buddhas, upon knowing that someone has come to investigate the marks, to rise from their seat and determine to walk, the Blessed One rose from His seat and went outside. For that reason, the words "Atha kho Bhagavā" and so forth were spoken.
246:
"Samannesi" means searches; it means investigating and searching while counting one or two. "Yebhuyyena" means for the most part; it means that he saw most of the marks but did not see a few. To show those marks that were not seen, it is said, "excepting two." "Kaṅkhati" means he gives rise to the longing, "Oh, if only I could see!" "Vicikicchati" means that while investigating those marks in various parts of the body, he is weary, being unable to see them. "Nādhimuccati" means being unable to reach a decision because of that doubt. "Na sampasīdati" means that because of being unable to decide, he does not attain clarity of faith in the Blessed One, thinking, "This person is one of perfect marks." Alternatively, "Kaṅkhā" refers to weak doubt, "Vicikicchā" to medium doubt, and "Anadhimuccanatā" to strong doubt. "Asampasāda" refers to the state of turbidity of the mind caused by those three things.

"Kosohita" means concealed by a sheath. "Vatthaguyha" refers to the male organ. The Blessed One's male organ, enclosed in a sheath, is like that of a noble elephant, golden-colored, and resembling a lotus bud. Because it was covered by cloth, he could not see that organ, and because he could not perceive the extensiveness of the tongue within the mouth, he was hesitant and doubtful regarding those two marks.

"Tathārūpaṃ" means that kind of form. What else is there to be said here? This matter was spoken of by the Elder Nāgasena when asked by King Milinda. When the king said, "Venerable Nāgasena, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task," and was asked, "In what way, Great King?", he replied, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One showed the part that causes shame to the general public to the Brahmin Brahmāyu and his pupil Uttara, to the sixteen Brahmin pupils of Bāvarī, and to the Brahmin Sela and his three hundred young pupils." The Elder replied, "Great King, the Blessed One did not show the actual private organ. The Blessed One showed only a shadow. Great King, having created it through psychic power, he showed only a mere shadow-image that appeared to be wearing an undergarment, bound with a waistband, and covered with a robe." When asked, "Venerable sir, if a shadow is seen, is it not the same as being seen?", the Elder replied, "Let that be, Great King. If there were a being who could understand the Four Noble Truths only upon seeing the form of the heart, the Perfectly Enlightened One would even take out and show his heart-flesh." Then King Milinda said, "You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena."

"Ninnāmetvā" means having taken out. "Anumasi" means he stroked it as if it were a needle used for the Kaṭhina robe. By doing so, the softness of the tongue is revealed. By stroking both ear-holes, the length of the tongue is revealed. By stroking the nostrils, the thinness of the tongue is revealed. By covering the forehead, the breadth and extensiveness of the tongue is revealed.
247:
"Paṭimānento" means waiting, looking forward to and longing for his arrival.

"Kathāsallāpo" means conversation and response; it means speaking and counter-speaking.

"Aho vata" is an expression of self-reproach. "Re" is a form of address used in a disparaging or contemptuous manner. "Paṇḍitakā" was said by the Brahmin Pokkharasāti out of disgust even for his own status as a wise man. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. The phrase "Evarūpena kira bho puriso atthacarakena" is spoken with the intention: "Ambaṭṭha, while there is such a Great Man like the Venerable Gotama, endowed with these major and minor marks and practicing for the welfare of beings, you speak such words; a person like you shall go only to hell and nowhere else." "Āsajja āsajja" means by striking or colliding (or harassing). "Amhepi evaṃ upaneyya upaneyya" means that by speaking the words "The Brahmin Pokkharasāti, Ambaṭṭha," and so on, and by pointing out and revealing the hidden facts, and by excessively attributing the status of a slave and so forth, it means "You have caused us to be insulted." "Padasāyeva pavattesi" means kicking him with the foot and making him fall to the ground. Although that Ambaṭṭha had previously traveled in a chariot with his teacher as the charioteer, now, having been removed from that position of charioteer, he was made to go only on foot in front of the chariot.

## The Description of Pokkharasāti Approaching the Buddha

292-296. "Ativikālo" means very late, so much so that there was no time even for pleasant conversation. "Āgamā nu khvidha bho" should be broken down as "Āgamā nu khō idha bho." "Adhivāsetu" means please accept (or consent). "Ajja tanāya" means "for the sake of the merit and the joy and happiness that I will receive today by performing this service for you." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent, not moving his limbs or speech, but maintaining patience within; this is referred to as "Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena." It means he accepted only with his mind for the sake of favoring the Brahmin.

"Paṇီtena" means with excellent food. "Sahatthā" means with his own hand. "Santappesi" means he satisfied him well and fully as much as was desired.
248:
*Sampavāresi* means he served well; he made a sign with his hand to refuse, saying "Enough, enough." *Bhuttāviṃ* means one who has finished eating. *Onītapattapāṇiṃ* means one who has removed his hand from the bowl; it means the hand is withdrawn. There is also a variant reading *onittapattapāṇiṃ*. The meaning of that term is one whose bowl is separated (detached) from the hand; it means one who has washed both hands and bowl, set the bowl aside in one place, and is sitting down. *Ekamantaṃ nisīdi* means that knowing the Blessed One was in such a state, he sat down in a certain place.

*Anupubbiṃ kathaṃ* means a gradual discourse. What is called a gradual discourse (*ānupubbikathā*) is a talk explaining these benefits: virtue (sīla) immediately after giving (dāna), heaven (sagga) immediately after virtue, and the Path (magga) immediately after heaven. For this very reason, it is said, "Talk on giving (dānakatha)," and so on. *Okāraṃ* means the state of being low or wretched. *Sāmukkaṃsikā* means a teaching discovered by oneself, taken up by oneself, seen through self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), and not shared with others. What is that teaching? It is the teaching of the Noble Truths. For this very reason, it is said, "Suffering, the origin, the cessation, and the path." *Dhammacakkhu* (the Dhamma-eye) here refers to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). To show the manner in which that Path of Stream-entry arises, it is said, "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." For that Path arises while penetrating all conditioned things (saṅkhata) in this way by the power of its function, taking Nibbāna as its object.

## Commentary on the Attainment of Lay Follower Status and the Penetration of Dhamma by Pokkharasāti

He is called *diṭṭhadhammo* because the Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by him. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. He is called *tiṇṇavicikiccho* because he has crossed over doubt (through the Path). He is called *vigatakathaṃkatho* because uncertainty (kathaṃkathā) has departed from him. *Vesārajjappatto* means having attained the state of fearlessness (the state of being free from doubt). Where? In the Teacher's Dispensation. He is called *aparappaccayo* because in this Dispensation, there is no need to rely on another for faith, and it does not occur by following the faith of another. The remaining words are clear because they follow the method already mentioned for all terms and because their meanings are obvious.

## Thus, in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī,

## The Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta is finished.
249:
## 4. Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta

This sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and containing the word "Angesu," is the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta. In this sutta, the sequential commentary on terms is as follows: *Angesu* refers to the princes of the country who are so called because they have pleasant physical features (aṅga). A single country which is the dwelling place of those princes is also called "Anga" by conventional usage; thus, it means "in the country of Anga." *Cārikaṃ* here refers to both unhurried wandering (*aturita-cārikā*) and regular wandering (*nibaddha-cārikā*). At that time, it is said that while the Blessed One was surveying the ten-thousandfold world system, the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa appeared within his net of knowledge. Then the Blessed One thought, "This Brahmin has appeared in my net of knowledge. Does he have the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya)?" Upon investigating, he saw as follows: "When I go to that place, the disciples of this Brahmin will praise the Brahmin's virtues in twelve ways and will not allow him to come to me, forbidding him. However, he will break their arguments and praise my virtues in twenty-nine ways, approach me, and ask questions. At the conclusion of the answering of the questions, he will go for refuge." Seeing this, he set out for that country accompanied by five hundred monks. Therefore, it is said, "Wandering in the country of Anga... he arrived at Campā."

*Gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre* means that not far from the city of Campā, there is a lotus pond called Gaggarā because it was dug by the Chief Queen named Gaggarā. On the shore of that pond, there is a large Champaka grove (campakavana) adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue. The Blessed One stayed in that Champaka grove, which was fragrant with the scent of flowers. Referring to that grove, it is said, "On the shore of the Gaggarā lotus pond." In the phrase *māgadhena seniyena bimbisārena*, that king is called *māgadha* because he is the lord of the Magadhans. He is called *seniya* because he is endowed with a great army. *Bimbī* means gold. Therefore, he is called *bimbisāra* because he has a complexion like that of pure gold.

301-302. They are called *saṅghā* because they are many and gathered together. They are called *saṅghī* because they have a crowd (saṅgha) from each of the various directions. They are called *gaṇībhūtā* because previously they were not a group inside the city, but became a group only after coming outside. *Khattaṃ āmantesi* means he called the high official (*khatta*) who was capable of explaining the questions asked. *Āgamentu* means "Please wait for a moment; do not go yet."
250:
## The Virtues of the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa

"Nānāverajjakānaṃ" refers to those who were born in various other kingdoms such as Kāsi and Kosala, or those for whom those kingdoms are their place of residence, or those who have come from those kingdoms. "Kenacideva karaṇīyena" means that in the city of Campā, the Brahmins gathered for two types of business: for the performance of sacrifices or for the recitation of the Vedas. At that time, there was no other sacrifice in that city. However, these Brahmins were gathering in the presence of the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa for the purpose of Vedic recitation. With reference to this gathering for Vedic study, it is said "kenacideva karaṇīyena." When those Brahmins heard that the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa was going [to see the Buddha], they thought: "This Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is an eminent Brahmin; for the most part, other Brahmins have gone for refuge to the ascetic Gotama, but he alone has not yet gone. If he goes there, he will surely be enticed by the enticing magic of the ascetic Gotama and will certainly go to him for refuge. If that happens, there will no longer be a gathering of Brahmins at the door of this Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa's house." They consulted together, saying, "Come, let us create an obstacle to his going," and went to that place. With reference to their going, it is said, "Atha kho te brāhmaṇā," and so on.

In that passage, "imināpaṅgena" means for this reason also. After stating this reason, they thought: "There is no being who does not delight when their own virtues are praised. Now, let us prevent his going by praising his virtues," and they spoke of reasons such as, "The venerable Soṇadaṇḍa is well-born on both sides, from the mother's side and the father's side."

"Ubhato" means from both sides: from the mother's side and from the father's side. The venerable one's mother is a Brahmin woman, his grandmother was a Brahmin woman, and that grandmother's mother was also a Brahmin woman. His father is a Brahmin, his grandfather was a Brahmin, and that grandfather's father was also a Brahmin. In this way, the venerable one is well-born on both sides, from the mother's side and the father's side. "Saṃsuddhagahaṇiko" means that your mother's womb is very pure. In the phrase "samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā," however, "gahaṇī" refers to the digestive fire (tejo-dhātu) produced by kamma.

In the phrase "yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā," the father's father is called the grandfather (pitāmaha). The lineage of the grandfather is called the grandfather-lineage (pitāmahayuga). "Yuga" refers to the span of life. This is merely a conventional term. In terms of meaning, the grandfather himself is the grandfather-lineage. All those who preceded that grandfather are also included by the term "pitāmaha." In this way, up to the seventh...
251:
...generation of men, he is one who has such a pure maternal womb. Or else, they show that he is one who is not rejected and not reproached in terms of birth. "Akkhitto" means one who is not rejected or cast aside in this way: "Remove this person, what is the use of him?" "Anupakuṭṭho" means one who is not reproached, who has never before received abuse or blame. For what reason? Because of the talk concerning birth. It means (not reproached) by such words as "This person is of low birth."

"Aḍḍho" means a lord of wealth. "Mahaddhano" means one endowed with great wealth. [The young men] show that in the house of the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa, there is much wealth like the dust and sand on the earth, whereas the ascetic Gotama has no wealth and subsists by filling his stomach through alms-round. "Mahābhogo" means one who has great enjoyments by way of the five cords of sensual pleasure. In this way, whatever virtue [of Soṇadaṇḍa] they speak of, they speak thinking that they will show only the lack of virtue in the Blessed One by way of the opposite of each virtue.

"Abhirūpo" means one who has an appearance superior to other people. "Dassanīyo" means worthy of being looked at because one cannot be satiated even if looking all day long. He is called "pāsādika" (inspiring confidence) because he generates clarity of mind just by being seen. "Pokkharatā" refers to a state of goodness; the goodness of complexion is called "vaṇṇapokkharatā," meaning one who is joined with such perfection of complexion. The ancient teachers, however, said: "Pokkhara refers to the body, and vaṇṇa refers only to the complexion." According to their view, complexion and body are "vaṇṇapokkhara." The state of that complexion and body is called "vaṇṇapokkharatā." Thus, "because of the state of having an extremely noble complexion and body" means one who is endowed with a noble, pure complexion and with the perfection of the body's form. "Brahmavaṇṇī" means one who has a sublime complexion. It means one who is endowed with a golden complexion, which is especially praised among pure complexions. "Brahmavacchasī" means one who is endowed with a body similar to the body of Mahābrahmā. "Not a narrow opportunity for viewing" means they show that "the place for viewing on the venerable one's body is not small but extensive; all your major and minor limbs are worthy of being looked at, and those limbs are also great."

Because he has virtue, he is called "sīlavā." Because he has virtue that has been developed, he is called "vuddhasīlī." "Vuddhasīlena" means with developed virtue; "samannāgato" means one who is endowed. This phrase "vuddhasīlena samannāgato" is just a synonym for the term "vuddhasīlī." They speak all these words referring only to the five precepts.

In the terms beginning with "kalyāṇavāco," he is called "kalyāṇavāco" because he has speech that is good and has perfect syllables and phrases. Because he has a pleasant voice...
252:
(The Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa) possesses a beautiful voice. 'Vākkaraṇa' refers to the sound of utterance or articulation. It is called 'porī' (urbane/polite speech) because it is full of qualities or because it originates from the city (pura). This speech is called 'porī' because it is similar to the delicate body of a city woman; he is endowed with such urbane speech. 'Vissaṭṭhā' means speech that is distinct, free from defects such as being muffled, repetitive, or hesitant. 'Anelagalā' means speech free from dribbling. If anyone, while speaking, has phlegm or saliva dripping, or if droplets of spit fly out, that person's speech is called 'elagala'. The term here means the opposite of that. 'Atthassa viññāpaniyā' means being endowed with speech capable of making the meaning understood, making the beginning, middle, and end clear.

'Jiṇṇo' means one who is aged due to the decay of old age. 'Vuddho' means one who has reached the limit of the growth of limbs and body parts. 'Mahallako' means one who is advanced in years by birth; it means one who has lived for a long time. 'Addhagato' means one who has gone a long way, implying one who has lived through two or three reigns of kings. 'Vayoanuppatto' means one who has reached the final stage of life; the final stage of life refers to the last third of a hundred-year lifespan.

Alternatively, 'jiṇṇo' means ancient, implying one who has a long-standing family lineage. 'Vuddho' means one who is endowed with the growth of qualities such as virtue and conduct. 'Mahallako' means one who is endowed with great wealth. 'Addhagato' means one who has reached the path (of the Brahmins), a person of virtue who practices without transgressing the boundaries of Brahminical duties and conduct. 'Vayoanuppatto' means one who has reached the final stage of life as well as being advanced in years by birth.

## Discussion on the Qualities of the Buddha

'Evaṃ vutte' means 'when it was thus spoken' by those Brahmins. The Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa thought: 'These Brahmins are speaking of my merits in terms of birth and so on, but it is not proper for me to delight in my own praise. Now, I shall break their argument, make known the greatness of the ascetic Gotama, and cause them to go there.' Thinking thus, he said, 'Sirs, if that is so, then listen also to my words,' and so on. In that speech, those qualities such as 'being well-born on both sides' are qualities similar to his own.
253:
Those young Brahmins also, thinking, 'Who am I, and what are the qualities of the ascetic Gotama such as his perfection of birth?' regarded the Buddha's qualities as far superior to their own. However, he (Soṇadaṇḍa) declared the remaining qualities specifically to demonstrate the greatness of the Blessed One.

Intending to define the meaning as 'We alone are worthy of approaching,' he shows this in this Sutta: 'If one should be approached because of the greatness of one's qualities—just as a mustard seed is small and inferior when compared to Mount Sineru, or the water in a cow's footprint when compared to the great ocean, or a dewdrop when compared to the water in the seven great lakes—even so, our qualities are small and inferior when compared to the qualities of the ascetic Gotama, such as his perfection of birth. Therefore, we alone are worthy of approaching that Venerable Gotama to see him.'

'Having abandoned a great circle of relatives' means he went forth after abandoning one hundred and sixty thousand families—eighty thousand families from the mother's side and eighty thousand from the father's side.

In the phrase 'wealth stored in the ground and wealth stored in the air,' wealth placed in the ground after filling plastered ponds in the royal courtyard or gardens with the seven kinds of jewels is called 'wealth stored in the ground' (bhūmigata). Wealth placed after filling the rafters and upper structures of the palace is called 'wealth stored in the air' (vehāsaṭṭha). This refers to wealth inherited through family lineage. As for the Tathāgata, on the very day of his birth, four great treasure pots named Saṅkha, Ela, Uppala, and Puṇဍarīka emerged from the earth. Among them, the Saṅkha treasure pot was one gāvuta in size, the Ela treasure pot was half a yojana, the Uppala treasure pot was three gāvutas, and the Puṇဍarīka treasure pot was one yojana. Even as wealth is taken from these pots, they remain constantly full. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One went forth after abandoning a vast amount of gold and silver wealth.

'While still young' means while being youthful. 'With very black hair' means having very dark hair, or it means having hair similar in color to collyrium (añjana). 'With good' means with excellent. 'In the first stage of life' means in the first of the three stages of life. 'Against their will' means while they were unwilling; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). 'Those with tears on their faces' are called assumukhā; 'of those with tears on their faces' means while their faces were wet and stained with tears.
254:
The wealth taken from those four golden jars—the 'Gāvutika' measuring one gāvuta, the 'Ela' measuring half a yojana, the 'Uppala' measuring three gāvutas, and the 'Puṇḍarīka' measuring one yojana—remained constantly full as before. It should be understood that the Blessed One renounced great wealth of gold and silver to become a monk. The phrase "Daharo va samāno" means even while being young. "Susukāḷakeso" means having very black hair (like the black of the eyes). "Bhadrena paṭhamena vayasā" means in the excellent first stage of life among the three stages of age. "Akāmakānaṃ" means while his parents were unwilling (and were shedding tears). Because there were tears on the faces of those parents, they are called "Assumukhā" (those with tearful faces). Alternatively, it means while they had faces smeared with tears.

"Rudantānaṃ" means to those who were wailing and weeping. In the term "Akhuddāvakāso," it should be understood that the opportunity to behold the Blessed One is unlimited (it is very vast).

Regarding this (unlimited nature), there is this story: In the city of Rājagaha, a certain Brahmin heard that "it is impossible to take the measurement of the height of the ascetic Gotama." Therefore, when the Blessed One was entering for alms, the Brahmin took a bamboo pole sixty cubits long and stood outside the city gate. When the Blessed One arrived, he held the bamboo pole and stood nearby to look; that bamboo pole reached only to the Blessed One's knees. On the next day, he joined two bamboo poles together and stood nearby again. The Blessed One appeared only up to his waist above the two bamboo poles and asked, "Brahmin, what are you doing?" "I am taking your measurement, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Brahmin, even if you come with bamboo poles joined together to fill the entire universe, you will not be able to take my measurement. This is because I did not fulfill the perfections for four incalculable periods (asaṅkhyeyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa) in such a way that another could take my measurement. Brahmin, the Tathāgata is incomparable and immeasurable," he said, and then spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

"For one who worships such as these (the Buddhas),
Who have attained Nibbāna and are free from fear,
No one is able to calculate the merit of that wholesome deed,
Saying 'it is only this much.'"

At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of Nibbāna (attained Nibbāna).

Another story: Rāhu Asurinda (the Titan King) was said to be four thousand eight hundred yojanas tall. The span between his arms was one thousand two hundred yojanas. The thickness of his body was six hundred yojanas. The width of his palms and soles was three hundred yojanas. The joints of his fingers were fifty yojanas. The space between his eyebrows was fifty yojanas. His mouth was two hundred yojanas wide, three hundred yojanas deep, and three hundred yojanas in circumference. His neck was three hundred yojanas, his forehead three hundred yojanas, and his head nine hundred yojanas. That Rāhu Asurinda thought, "I am this tall; I will not be able to look at the Teacher without stooping down," and so he did not come. One day, having heard the virtues of the Blessed One, he thought, "I will look at him somehow," and came.

Then the Blessed One, knowing his intention, thought, "With which of the four postures shall I show myself?" He considered, "A person who is standing, even if short, appears tall. (Therefore, I shall show myself while reclining)."
255:
The Blessed One thought, "I will show myself to that Rāhu Asurinda only while reclining," and said, "Ānanda, prepare a couch in the Gandhakuṭi precinct." He then reclined there in the lion's posture (sīhasayya). Rāhu arrived and, looking at the reclining Blessed One, had to crane his neck and look up as if looking at the full moon in the middle of the sky. When asked, "Asurinda, what is this?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I did not come because I thought I would not be able to look at you without stooping down." The Blessed One said, "Asurinda, I did not fulfill the perfections with my face turned downwards. I gave gifts and performed other merits only with my face turned upwards." On that day, Rāhu took refuge in the Triple Gem. In this way, the Blessed One is 'Akhuddāvakāso' (having no narrow opportunity) for beholding.

Because he is endowed with the fourfold purification of virtue (catu-pārisuddhi-sīla), he is called 'Sīlavā' (virtuous). Because that virtue is noble, supreme, and pure, it is said 'Ariyasīlī' (noble in virtue). That same virtue is wholesome (kusala) in the sense of being blameless. Therefore, it is said 'Kusalasīlī' (wholesome in virtue). 'Kusalasīlena' is a synonym (pariyāya) for that term.

In each single Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One, eighty-four thousand beings and countless devas and humans drink the nectar of the Path and Fruit. Therefore, he is the 'Teacher of many' (Ācariya). He is also the 'Teacher of the lineage' (Pācariya) of the disciples to be tamed.

In the term "Khīṇakāmarāgo," although all defilements (kilesa) of the Blessed One are indeed destroyed, the Brahmin Sonadaṇḍa spoke of this virtue only to the extent of his own knowledge, without knowing the full extent of that destruction. "Vigatacāpallo" means being free from the restlessness (cāpalla) such as decorating the bowl, robes, and lodgings, or the grooming and beautifying of this foul body.

"Apāpapurekkhāro" means practicing while putting the nine non-evil supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma) foremost. "Brahmanyāya pajāya" means being the leader of the assembly of noble Brahmins such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others. This is because that assembly of noble ones practices while putting the ascetic Gotama foremost. Alternatively, "Apāpapurekkhāro" means not putting evil foremost and not desiring evil. Toward whom? Toward the assembly of Brahmins. It means that even toward the assembly of Brahmins who were opposed to him, he remained unopposed and desired only their welfare and happiness.

"Tiroraṭṭhā" means from another kingdom. "Tirojanapadā" means from another province. Wise khattiyas and others, as well as devas, brahmas, nagas, and gandhabbas, come to ask questions.
256:
Devas, Brahmas, Nāgas, mountain deities, and others also come, thinking, "We shall prepare questions and ask them." Among those who come, some, reflecting that there might be a fault in the questioning or that they might be unable to accept the answer, remain silent without asking. Some do ask. To some, the Blessed One inspires the effort to ask and then answers. Thus, the doubts of all of them vanish upon reaching the Blessed One, just as the waves of the great ocean break upon reaching the shore.

"Ehi svāgatavādī" means one who, upon seeing various beings—devas, humans, monastics, or laypeople—coming to him, says, "Come, you are welcome." "Sakhilo" means one endowed with pleasant speech, such as "speech that is pleasant to the ear," meaning one who has gentle speech. "Sammodako" means one skilled in polite greeting. To the four assemblies who arrive, he is the first to speak words of welcome, as if allaying all the weariness of the journey, saying, "Monks, is it bearable? Is it supportable?" and so on. "Abbhākuṭiko" means he is not like some who, upon reaching an assembly, become stiff-faced or frown; rather, upon seeing the assembly, the Blessed One’s lotus-like face blooms like a lotus touched by the morning sun, or like the splendor of the full moon. "Uttānamukho" means he is not like some who, as if their faces were turned downwards, say nothing to the arriving assembly and are very difficult to talk to; instead, the Ascetic Gotama is easy to talk to. It shows that those who come to the Venerable Gotama do not feel regret, thinking, "Why did we come here?" but rather become joyful upon hearing the Dhamma. "Pubbabhāsī" means he is the first to speak in conversation. Furthermore, that speech is timely, measured, and connected with benefit; he does not speak useless talk.

"Na tasmiṃ gāme vā" means that in the village where the Blessed One resides, powerful deities take up protection. Depending on them, no harm comes to humans. Indeed, only spirits like the dust-demons (paṃsupisācaka) and others harass humans, and they move far away due to the power of those deities. Moreover, due to the power of the Blessed One’s loving-kindness (mettā), non-human beings do not harass humans.

In the terms "saṅghī" and so on, he is called "saṅghī" because he has a Saṅgha that is to be instructed or a Saṅgha he himself has brought into being. He is called "gaṇī" because he has such a group. This term "gaṇī" is a synonym for the previous term. He is called "gaṇācariya" because he is the teacher of the group by way of teaching conduct and training.

"Puthutitthakarānaṃ" means "of those who create many doctrines." "Yathā tathā vā" means "in whatever way," such as by the mere reason of being naked, etc...
257:
...he is the teacher of the group. "Puthutitthakarānaṃ" means "of many sect-makers." "Yathā vā tathā vā" means "by some reason or another," such as the mere state of being naked. "Samudāgacchati" means "approaches from all sides" or "increases."

"Atithi no te honti" means "they are our guests, newcomers, or visitors." "Pariyāpuṇāmi" means "I know." By the term "aparimāṇavaṇṇo," it is shown that even an Omniscient Buddha of such a nature has immeasurable qualities; "how much more so for someone like me" (how could I compare?). Regarding this, it has also been said:

"Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of a Buddha,
and speak nothing else for an entire aeon,
that long and extended great aeon would come to an end,
but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted."

Upon hearing this talk of the Teacher’s qualities, those Brahmins thought: "Just as the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa speaks the praises of the Ascetic Gotama, that Venerable Gotama is indeed possessed of supreme qualities. Our teacher, knowing his qualities in this way, has waited for a very long time; let us now follow the teacher." Thus they followed him. Therefore, it is said, "Those Brahmins," and so on. In that context, "alameva" means "it is indeed suitable." "Api puṭosenā" refers to a bundle of provisions; it means "it is suitable to approach even while carrying a bundle of provisions." There is also a reading "puṭaṃsenā," which means "one who has a bundle of provisions on his shoulder." It means even if one is carrying a bundle of provisions on one's shoulder (it is suitable to approach).

## Soṇadaṇḍaparivitakkavaṇṇanā

306-308. "Tirowanasaṇḍagatassa" means "of one who has gone into the woods" or "entered the interior of the monastery." Regarding "añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā," those people belonged to two factions, and they thought: "If the followers of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) reproach us, asking, 'Why did you salute the Ascetic Gotama?', we shall reply to them, 'Does salutation consist merely of joining the palms?' If the followers of right view (sammādiṭṭhi) reproach us, asking, 'Why did you not salute the Blessed One?', we shall reply to them, 'Does salutation consist only of striking the ground with one's head? Is the act of joining the palms not also salutation?'..."
258:
Suppose we say, "Can paying homage be done merely by joining the palms?" They thought, "If those with right view (sammādiṭṭhi) should question us, 'Why do you not pay homage to the Blessed One?', then is paying homage only by touching the head to the ground, or is joining the palms also paying homage?"

"Announcing name and clan" means saying, "Venerable Gotama, I am the son of such-and-such a person, named Datta, named Mitta, and I have come here," thus making the name known. Saying, "Venerable Gotama, I am of the Vāseṭṭha clan, of the Kaccāna clan, and I have come here," thus making the clan known. It is said that those poor and elderly sons of good family did this, thinking, "We shall become well-known by name and clan in the midst of the assembly." Those who sat in silence were the deceitful and the extremely foolish. Among them, the deceitful thought, "If one speaks even a word or two, one becomes an acquaintance; once there is acquaintance, it is not proper to remain without offering a meal or two," and so they sat in silence to free themselves from the burden of giving. The extremely foolish sat in silence anywhere, like a lump of clay thrown down, simply because of their ignorance.

## Brāhmaṇapaññatti-vaṇṇanā

309-310. "Knowing the thought in the mind with [His own] mind" means the Blessed One, reflecting, "What is this Brahmin thinking as he sits with his head down and his body stiff since the time he arrived? What indeed is he thinking?", knew that Brahmin's mind with His own mind. Therefore, it is said, "Knowing the thought in the mind with [His own] mind." "Is distressed" means falling into distress or affliction.

311. "Looking around at the assembly" means that because of the Blessed One's questioning regarding a problem from his own tradition, he became like a man about to die in water who is pulled out and placed on dry land, becoming one with a very tranquil body and mind. To favor the assembly and to make his own view known, as if saying, "Sirs, consider my words," he looked around at the assembly and addressed the Blessed One with these words. "Among those who hold the sacrificial ladle" means among the Brahmins who hold the ladle for the purpose of performing a sacrifice, he is the first or the second. The ancient commentators say, "Among those who receive the great sacrifice offered with the ladle." Thus, the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa answered the question properly according to his own tradition. However, the Blessed One, in order to specifically show the state of a supreme Brahmin, spoke the words beginning with "But of these..."

"They spoke these words" means if a person endowed with birth, appearance, and the Vedas is not a Brahmin, then who indeed in the world will be a Brahmin? "Destroys" means they spoke these words thinking, "Now we shall reject the doctrine of this Soṇadaṇḍa." "Reviles" means rejection.
259:
Then those Brahmins, thinking, "This Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa is going to reject our doctrine," spoke these words. "Apavadati" means he rejects. "Anupakkhandati" means he enters into. These words were spoken with the intention: "If you, out of devotion, wish to approach the ascetic Gotama as a refuge, then go; but do not destroy the tradition of the Brahmins."

When the Blessed One saw those Brahmins all shouting at once, He thought, "This talk will not reach an end; let me now silence those Brahmins and speak only with Soṇadaṇḍa," and He spoke the words beginning with "If you..."

315-316. "Sahadhammena" means with reason. "Samasamo" means, setting aside partial equality, being equal in all aspects, equal in every way. In saying "I know his parents," how could he not know the parents of his own sister's son? He says this with the intention of illustrating the pinnacle of the lineage. "He might even speak a lie" refers to a lie that destroys one's welfare. "What can appearance do?" means if there are no internal virtues, what can appearance do? The meaning is: will it be able to protect his status as a Brahmin? Furthermore, if it is said, "It accomplishes the status of a Brahmin for one established in natural virtue," then only virtue (sīla) will accomplish it. Since without that virtue, the status of a Brahmin cannot exist, appearance and so forth are merely delusions. Upon hearing this, those Brahmins remained silent, saying, "The teacher speaks the truth; we have reviled him without reason."

## Sīlapaññā-kathā-vaṇṇanā

Then the Blessed One, wishing to investigate, "The Brahmin has answered the question; will he be able to stand by this answer or not?", spoke the words beginning with "But, Brahmins..." "Sīlaparidhota" means purified by virtue. "Where there is virtue, there is wisdom" means wisdom exists only in a person who has virtue; how could there be wisdom in one who is immoral? Or how could there be virtue in a foolish, dull-witted person who is devoid of wisdom? "Sīlapaññāṇaṃ" refers to virtue and wisdom. "Paññāṇaṃ" is wisdom itself. Thus...
260:
The Blessed One, wishing to permit the Brahmin's words, said: "Brahmin, it is so." In that context, "wisdom purified by virtue" means wisdom purified by the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). How does one wash wisdom with virtue? If a worldling's (puthujjana) virtue remains unbroken for sixty or eighty years, that person, even at the time of death, can destroy all defilements, wash wisdom with virtue, and attain the fruit of Arahantship. This is like the Elder of sixty years of seniority who resided in the Kandarasaala monastery.

It is heard that the Elder was lying on his deathbed, groaning due to intense pain. King Tissa the Great, thinking, "I will go to see the Elder," went and stood at the gate of the monastery. Hearing the groaning, he asked, "Whose voice is this?" Upon hearing it was the Elder's groaning, he said, "Even after sixty years in the monkhood, he has not even achieved the ability to contemplate pain. I will not pay homage to him now," and he turned back to go and worship the Great Bodhi Tree. Then, the young novice who was the attendant said to the Elder, "Venerable Sir, why do you make us ashamed? Even the faithful King has become disappointed and left, saying he will not pay homage."

The Elder asked, "Friend, why is that?" The novice replied, "It is because he heard your groaning, Venerable Sir." The Elder said, "In that case, give me an opportunity," and after suppressing the pain and attaining Arahantship, he gave a sign to the young novice: "Friend, go now and have the King pay homage to us." The novice went and said, "Now, please pay homage to the Elder." The King, prostrating like a crocodile, paid homage to the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, I do not pay homage to your Arahantship; I only pay homage to the virtue you have protected while remaining in the stage of a worldling." This is what is meant by washing wisdom with virtue.

For one who does not have the restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara) within, but is a person of quick intuition (ugghāṭitaññū), they wash virtue with wisdom at the end of a four-line verse and reach Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). This is what is meant by washing virtue with wisdom. This is like the case of the Great Minister Santati.

Why did the Buddha ask, "Brahmin, what is that virtue?" The Blessed One thought: "The Brahmins, in their own tradition, designate the five precepts as 'virtue' and the wisdom of learning the three Vedas as 'wisdom.' They do not know the higher distinction. It would be well if I show the Brahmin the superior Path-virtue (magga-sīla), Fruit-virtue (phala-sīla), Path-wisdom (magga-paññā), and Fruit-wisdom (phala-paññā), and conclude the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship." Then, wishing to teach that Dhamma, He asked, "Brahmin, what is that virtue? What is that wisdom?" Then the Brahmin thought, "I have answered the question according to my own tradition of the Vedas. But the ascetic Gotama asks me again. Now, I will satisfy the mind of the ascetic Gotama and..."
261:
...will I be able to answer or not? If I am unable, the shame that arose in me earlier will be destroyed. There is no fault in saying 'I cannot' for one who is unable." Thinking thus, he retreated and placed the burden back upon the Blessed One, saying, "This is the extent of it," and so on. In that context, "ettakaparama" means the statement "virtue and wisdom are of this extent" is our highest limit; we are of this extent, and we do not know the meaning of the teaching beyond this.

Then, the Blessed One, in order to show the Brahmin virtue and wisdom starting from the arising of the Tathāgata, who is the root of virtue and wisdom, said: "Brahmin, here a Tathāgata arises in the world..." and so on. The meaning of those words should be understood in the same manner as explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. However, the distinction here is that the three types of virtue are concluded as virtue alone, with the phrase "this also is part of his virtue." Although the four jhanas, starting from the first jhana, are in essence the accomplishment of wisdom (paññā-sampadā), they are not concluded by the power of wisdom here; instead, they are shown merely as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), and the conclusion as "wisdom" begins from insight-wisdom onwards.

## The Account of Sonadanda's Declaration as a Lay Follower

319-322. The meaning of the word "svātanāya" should be understood in the same manner as explained for the word "ajjatanāya." "For that reason, that assembly might despise me" means: because of the reason of rising from my seat upon seeing you from afar, that assembly might despise me, thinking, "This Brahmin Sonadanda is an elder in the final stage of life, whereas Gotama is just a young youth, not even old enough to be his grandson; yet this Sonadanda rises from his seat and shows respect to Gotama, who is not even as old as his grandson."

"Let the Master Gotama regard this (salutation) as my rising from the seat" means: it is not that I do not rise because of a lack of respect; I do not rise because I fear the loss of my wealth and status. It is proper that you and I both understand this reason. Therefore, he requested, "Let the Master Gotama regard this gesture as my rising from the seat." A schemer (kuhaka) like this person is rare. Although he had no lack of respect for the Blessed One, he spoke thus through the power of scheming (kuhana) because of the fear of losing his wealth. The same method applies to other terms as well. In the words "dhammiyā kathāya" and so on, the Buddha showed the benefits of the present life and the future life through a Dhamma talk suitable for that moment, established him in wholesome states, encouraged him in those wholesome states to have enthusiasm, and having gladdened him with that enthusiasm and other evident qualities, He rained down the rain of the Jewel of Dhamma.
262:
(The Blessed One) rose from His seat and departed. As for that Brahmin, because of his deceitful nature, even though the Blessed One rained down the rain of Dhamma in this way, he was unable to produce any special attainment. All his preceding and succeeding words merely served as a supporting condition for the benefit of Nibbāna and as a dispositional influence (vāsanā) for the future.

## Thus ends the Commentary on the Sonadanda Sutta
## in the Sumangalavilasini, the Commentary on the Digha Nikaya.
263:
## 5. Commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta

This sutta, beginning with "Thus have I heard" (Evaṃ me sutaṃ) and ending with "among the Magadhans" (Magadhesu), is the Kūṭadanta Sutta. Herein is the sequential explanation of the terms. In the word "Magadhesu," the Magadhans are the princes residing in the country. A single country that is the residence of those princes is also called "Magadha" by conventional usage (rūḷhī-sadda). It means "in that country named Magadha." Following this, it is the same method as mentioned in the previous two suttas. The name "Ambalaṭṭhikā" is also the same as mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta. "Kūṭadanta" is the name of that brahmin. "Upakkhaṭa" means prepared or arranged. "Vacchatarasatāni" means one hundred young bulls. "Urabbha" refers to young sheep (rams). These animals are already mentioned in the Pali text. Even if not mentioned in the Pali, it should be understood that seven hundred each of various wild animals and birds are also included. It is said that this Brahmin Kūṭadanta wished to perform a sacrifice with seven hundred of every kind of animal. "Thūṇūpanītāni" means they were brought near the sacrificial post called a yūpa to be tied and kept.

In the word "Tividhaṃ," "vidhā" means arrangement or establishment. It also means standing. "Soḷasaparikkhāraṃ" means having sixteen accessories or requisites.

330-336. "Paṭivasanti" means they reside to experience the power of the sacrifice. The Buddha spoke the words "Bhūtapubbaṃ" (in the past) to show past conduct covered by previous lives, like bringing out a pot of gold buried in the earth and making a heap in front. "Mahāvijita" means that king conquered the great earth ending at the four oceans. Because he had such a vast conquered territory, he came to be called "Mahāvijita" (Great Conqueror). In the words beginning with "Aḍḍho," any person who is endowed with their own wealth is called "aḍḍho" (rich). This King Mahāvijita was not merely rich but was called "Mahaddhana" because he was endowed with immeasurable and vast wealth. He was called "Mahābhoga" because he had extensive and grand enjoyments through the five cords of sensual pleasure. He was called "Pahūtajātarūparajata" because of the abundance of gold and silver, both in heaps and in the form of gold and silver coins (māsaka). It means he was endowed with gold and silver numbering many crores. "Vitti" means joy or satisfaction. The cause of joy is called "vittūpakaraṇa" (means of joy). Because King Mahāvijita had many various ornaments, gold and silver vessels, and other such delightful possessions, he was called "Pahūtavittūpakaraṇa." Because of the abundance of wealth buried in the earth called the seven treasures and all kinds of grain...
264:
