...he was one who had abundant wealth and grain (pahūtadhana-dhanya). Alternatively, this term "pahūtadhana-dhanya" is said in terms of the wealth and grain circulating through daily expenditures and receipts. In the term "Paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro," the treasury is called "kosa." It means having a treasury full of stored wealth and a granary full of grain. Alternatively, the treasury (kosa) is of four types: elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry. The granary (koṭṭhāgāra) is of three types: wealth granary, cloth granary, and grain granary. King Mahāvijita was full of all these; therefore, he is called "Paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro." "Udapādi" means it arose or occurred. It is said that one day this king went out to inspect his treasures. He asked the treasurer, "Dear son, who collected so much wealth?" The treasurer replied, "Your father, grandfather, and others up to seven generations collected it." The king asked again, "After collecting this wealth, where did they go?" The treasurer replied, "Great King, they have all reached the realm of Death." When asked, "Dear son, did they go without taking their wealth?", the treasurer replied, "Great King, what are you saying? This thing called wealth must be left behind; it cannot be taken along." Then the king returned, sat in his royal chamber, and thought, "I have acquired much wealth," and so on. Therefore, it is said, "Such a thought arose in his mind."

Why is it said, "Brāhmaṇaṃ āmantetvā" (having called the chaplain brahmin)? This king thought: "One who gives gifts should do so after consulting a wise person; an act done without consultation leads to regret later." Therefore, he called him. Then the brahmin thought: "This king wants to give a great gift, but there are many thieves in the country. If he gives while they are not suppressed, thieves will plunder the houses of those bringing milk, curd, rice, and other sacrificial materials when the men are away. The country will be in turmoil due to fear of thieves. Then the king's gift will not last long, and his mind will not be concentrated. Let me inform the king of this matter." Thinking thus, wishing to inform him, he said, "To the Great King..." and so on. In those words, "Sakaṇṭako" means being thorny with the "thorns" of thieves (being dangerous). "Panthaduhanā" means those who wait on the path to plunder, destroy, and kill. "Akiccakārī assā" means...
265:
He would be one who does what should not be done, one who acts unrighteously. 'Dassukhīla' refers to the stake of thieves (rebellion). 'Vadhena' means by execution, by death, or by beating and striking (referring to oppression). 'Bandhanena' means by binding, such as putting in stocks and so forth. 'Jāniyā' means by causing loss of wealth, with the meaning of (oppression) by imposing fines such as "Take a fine of a hundred, take a fine of a thousand." 'Garahāya' means by bringing to censure by doing such things as shaving the head to leave five tufts, pouring cow-dung water over someone, or fastening a wooden block around the neck. 'Pabbājanāyā' means (oppression) by banishing from the country. 'Samūhanissāmi' means "I shall uproot/eradicate by proper means and methods." 'Hata-avasesakā' means those who remain after the dead (survivors). 'Ussahanti' means they exert effort. 'Anuppadetu' means "If the seeds and food already given are insufficient, please grant further seeds, food, and all farming implements." 'Pābhataṃ anuppadetu' means "Please grant capital/funds as an investment without requiring a guarantor or recording it in a register."

Capital is called 'pābhata'. Therefore, it was said: "A wise and discerning man, even with small capital, can raise himself up, just as one fans a small fire into a blaze." 'Bhatta-vetanaṃ' means "Please grant daily food and monthly wages, along with positions, villages, and market towns appropriate to their skill and courage in their respective tasks." 'Sakamma-pasutā' means being intent and occupied with their own work, such as farming and trade. 'Rāsiko' means one who will possess great heaps of wealth and grain. 'Khemaṭṭhitā' means established in peace without danger. 'Akaṇṭakā' means being free from the thorns of thieves. 'Mudā modamānā' means rejoicing with one another. Or, according to the text "Mudā modamānā," it means having hearts delighted with one another. 'Aparutagharā' means having houses with doors left wide open without closing them because there are no thieves. 'Etadavoca' means he said this after knowing the prosperity and abundance of the country in every way.

## Explanation of the Four Requisites (Consultations)

Regarding the words "Then, indeed, your majesty," the Brahmin thought: "This king is very eager to give a great gift. However, if he gives without consulting his followers, such as the Khattiyas, they will not be pleased. I will act in such a way that they will be pleased." Therefore, he said "Then, indeed, your majesty," and so on. In that context, 'negamā' means the inhabitants of the market towns.
266:
'Jānapadā' means the inhabitants of the countryside. 'Āmantayatu' means let him call, let him inform. 'Yaṃ mama assa' means "Whatever permission of yours there may be for me." 'Amaccā' means dear friends. 'Pārisajjā' means the rest who carry out orders. 'Yajataṃ bhavaṃ rājā' means "Let your majesty perform the sacrifice." Those ministers and others said this joyfully: "This king, without giving the gift by force saying 'I am the lord,' has consulted us; the king has done very well." If he had not consulted them, they would not even have gone to see the place of sacrifice. 'Yaññakālo mahārāja' means "When there are no gifts to be given, or when one is old, one cannot give such a gift. But you, Great King, are both wealthy and young; therefore, this is the time for your sacrifice." They say this to show this point. 'Anumati-pakkhā' means the groups who give permission according to their own will. 'Parikkhārā bhavanti' means they become the retinue/accessories. In the passage "The chariot has virtue as its accessory, jhāna as its axle, and energy as its wheel," 'parikkhāra' is said to mean ornament/decoration.

## Explanation of the Eight Requisites (Qualities)

'Aṭṭhahaṅgehi' means by the eight factors, such as being well-born on both sides. 'Yasasā' means being with a retinue because of the ability to exercise authority. 'Saddho' means believing that there is a fruit of giving. 'Dāyako' means being brave in giving. It means not stopping at mere faith but being able to renounce/give away. 'Dānapati' means giving as the lord of the gift, not as a slave or a companion. One who eats sweet food himself but gives unsweet food to others gives as a slave to the gift known as 'dāna'. One who gives exactly what he eats himself gives as a companion. But one who subsists on whatever is available but gives sweet/excellent things to others gives as a lord, a chief, or a master. King Mahāvijita was such a giver. In the phrase 'samaṇa-brāhmaṇa-kapaṇaddhika-vaṇibbaka-yācakānaṃ', those who have calmed evil are 'samaṇas', and those who have barred evil are 'brāhmaṇas'. 'Kapaṇā' means the poor and destitute. 'Addhikā' means travelers. 'Vaṇibbakā' are those who wander about praising the virtues of giving, saying: "A desirable, lovely, pleasing, timely, and blameless gift has been given; may the giver's heart be brightened; may your majesty reach the Brahma-world," and so on. 'Yācakā' are those who wander about begging, saying: "Give a handful of alms-food, give a bowlful," and so on. 'Opānabhūto' means being like a well. It means being like a well dug at a four-way crossroads, which is for the common use of everyone.
267:
It means being like a pond dug at a four-way crossroads. In the term 'sutajātassa', only the Dhamma learned in the past is called 'sutajāta'.

Regarding the phrase 'atītānāgatapaccuppanne atthe cintetuṃ': one who thinks, "This prosperity has arisen for me only because I performed meritorious deeds in the past," is said to be capable of considering past benefits. One who thinks, "Only by performing meritorious deeds now will I be able to attain prosperity in the future," is said to be capable of considering future benefits. One who thinks, "Performing these meritorious deeds is the practice of the virtuous; I possess wealth, and I have the intention to give; therefore, I shall perform meritorious deeds now," is to be understood as one capable of considering present benefits. 'Iti imāni' refers to these eight factors mentioned above. People from all four directions come to the almsgiving of one endowed with these eight factors. Thinking, "This person is of low birth; how long will he be able to give? He will now feel remorse and cut off the almsgiving," and so forth, no one wishes to approach him. Therefore, these eight factors are said to be the 'requisites' (of the sacrifice).

## Description of the Four Requisites and Others

'Sujaṃ paggaṇhantānaṃ' refers to those holding the sacrificial ladle at the place where a great sacrifice is received. 'Imehi catūhi' refers to these four factors, beginning with 'sujāta' (being well-born). If these factors are absent, there would be no one to approach, saying, "How long will the almsgiving organized by such a low-born person last?" and so on. They approach only because there is nothing to blame. Therefore, these four are also said to be 'requisites'.

'Tisso vidhā desesi' means he showed the three modes to be maintained (in almsgiving). That chaplain thought, "Those giving gifts tend to waver in one of three instances; now, I shall first make this king unwavering and firm in those instances." Therefore, he showed the three modes to the king. In the phrase 'so bhoto rañño', the genitive case (sāmivibac) is used in the sense of the instrumental. There is also a variant reading 'bhotā raññā'. 'Vippaṭisāro na karaṇīyo' means, "One should not feel remorse caused by the depletion of wealth; rather, the initial volition (pubbacetanā) should be made unwavering; only then will the gift be of great fruit." This is the same method for the other two instances. The volition during giving (muñcacetanā) and the volition after giving (pacchācetanā) should also be made unwavering and firm. For one who does not do so, the gift cannot be of great fruit. Just as the mind of the wealthy man who was reborn in the Mahāroruva hell did not incline toward his vast wealth, the king's mind also does not incline (with remorse) toward his vast wealth.
268:
The volition of recollecting after giving (pacchāsamanussaraṇacetanā) should also be made unwavering. For one who does not do so, the gift is not of great fruit, nor does the mind incline toward abundant wealth, like the wealthy householder who was reborn in the Mahāroruva hell. 'Dasahākārehi' means by ten reasons. That chaplain priest had this thought: "If this king, seeing those without virtue, thinks, 'My gift is surely ruined, for such immoral people are consuming it,' and develops remorse even toward those with virtue, the gift will not be of great fruit." Remorse in donors usually arises because of the recipients. Thinking, "Now, I shall first dispel that king's remorse," he dispelled the remorse that might arise regarding the recipients who were fit to be excluded by ten reasons. 'Tesaññeva tena' means that the undesirable result will occur only to those immoral people because of that evil deed, and not to others. 'Yajataṃ bhavaṃ' means "May your honor sacrifice (give)." 'Sajjataṃ' means "Let it be prepared." 'Antaraṃ' means "within the mind."

By the phrase 'soḷasahi ākārehi cittaṃ sandassesi', in this sutta, the chaplain priest endeavors to make the king rejoice (anumodanā) in the great sacrifice. Therein, 'sandassesi' means he spoke by repeatedly showing, "The donor of this gift obtains such prosperity." 'Samādapesi' means he spoke by inciting him for that purpose. 'Samuttejesi' means he purified the king's mind by dispelling remorse. 'Sampahaṃsesi' means he spoke by praising him, saying, "Great King, you have done a good deed by giving this gift." 'Vattā dhammato natthi' means there is no speaker according to the Dhamma or according to reason.

'Na rukkhā chijjiṃsu ... barihisatthāya' means they set up large pillars called sacrificial posts (yūpa) and write names on them, such as, "Such a king, such a minister, or such a brahmin performs such a great sacrifice." They also mow Dabbha grass and surround the sacrificial hall with it like a forest garland, or spread it on the ground. Those people did not cut trees, nor did they mow Dabbha grass. It is intended to show: how then could they kill cows, goats, and so forth? 'Dāsā' refers to domestic slaves and the like. 'Pessā' refers to those who perform work after first taking money. 'Kammakārā' refers to those who perform work after taking food and wages. 'Daṇḍatajjitā' refers to those who are threatened with sticks, clubs, and so forth, being told, "Work, work!"
269:
In this way, they were intimidated. Those called 'intimidated by fear' (bhayatajjitā) are those who are threatened thus: "If you do the work, it is well. If you do not, we shall cut off [your hands, etc.], or bind you, or kill you." However, these servants and others were not intimidated by punishment, nor were they intimidated by fear, nor did they perform the duties of the sacrifice with tearful faces and weeping. Indeed, they performed them being addressed only with pleasant speech. In that sacrifice, they did not address a slave as "slave", an attendant as "attendant", or a worker as "worker". Instead, addressing them only with pleasant speech according to their given names, and assigning only work suitable for women, men, the strong, and the weak, they said, "Do this, do that." They, too, performed the work only according to their own desire. Therefore, it is said: "Those who wished to, did; those who did not wish to, did not. What they wished to do, they did; what they did not wish to do, they did not."

"The sacrifice was completed only with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curds, honey, and molasses" means: King Mahāvijita had great alms-halls built in five places—at the four gates outside the city and in the middle of the city. Allocating one hundred thousand for each hall, he spent five hundred thousand daily. From sunrise, he himself held a golden ladle and satisfied the multitude with excellent gruel, hard food, rice, curries, drinks, and so on, mixed with ghee, oil, and the like, according to the appropriate time. For those who wished to fill their vessels and take food away, he had it given just as they desired. In the evening, he honored them with clothes, perfumes, garlands, and so forth. Having filled large jars with ghee and other items, he had them placed in hundreds of locations, thinking, "Let whoever wishes to consume whatever they desire, consume it." Referring to this arrangement, it is said: "The sacrifice was completed only with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curds, honey, and molasses."

"Taking much wealth" means taking a great amount of riches. It is said that those people thought: "This king gives a great alms-offering by bringing forth only his own property, without having ghee, oil, and so on brought from the countryside. It is not proper for us to remain silent, saying, 'The king does not have anything brought.' Indeed, wealth in the king's house is not of an inexhaustible nature, and if we do not give, who else will give to the king? Come, let us bring wealth to the king." Thus they gathered wealth from the village sectors, the market-town sectors, and the city sectors, filled carts, and brought them to the king. Referring to this bringing of wealth, it is said: "Taking much wealth," and so on.
270: 'To the east of the sacrificial enclosure' means in the eastern part of the alms hall at the eastern city gate. Just as princes coming from the eastern direction enter the city after drinking rice porridge in the alms hall and eating in the King's alms hall, they established alms in such places. 'To the south of the sacrificial enclosure' means they established alms in the southern part of the alms hall at the southern city gate, in the same manner as already mentioned. The same method applies to the west and the north. 'Oh, the sacrifice! Oh, the perfection of the sacrifice!' Thus the Brahmins, hearing that it had reached completion with ghee and so on, with joyful hearts, spoke in praise: 'Whatever food in the world is sweet and good, only that food does the Ascetic Gotama preach. Let us now praise the sacrifice of that Gotama.' 'He sits in silence' means sitting silently without making a sound, reflecting on the matter to be spoken of later. 'Does the Venerable Gotama know?' This was spoken by the Brahmin inquiring by way of a circumlocution. For otherwise, if he were to ask directly, 'O Gotama, were you King Mahāvijita at that time, or were you the chaplain Brahmin?' it would seem disrespectful. ## Explanation of perpetual alms and ancestral sacrifice. 'O Gotama, is there yet another?' This was spoken by the Brahmin wishing to inquire: 'For all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, it is very burdensome to exert effort and give alms. If all the people of the countryside do not do their own work, they will perish. Is there for us another kind of sacrifice that requires less preparation of structures but has greater and more magnificent fruit than this sacrifice?' 'Niccadāna' refers to perpetual alms-food given constantly. 'Anukulayañña' refers to sacrifices (alms) that should be continued by later generations, even by those who have become poor, with the thought, 'Our fathers, grandfathers, and so on, performed these.' Such alms dedicated to the virtuous are continued in that lineage without interruption, even if they become poor and destitute. Regarding such uninterrupted giving, there is this story as evidence: It is said that in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, five hundred perpetual alms-meals were given. There were five hundred alms-tickets (salākā) made of ivory. Later, that family was gradually overcome by poverty. A young girl in that family was unable to give more than one ticket's worth. That girl later went to the kingdom called Setavāhana, and with the grain she obtained from cleaning the threshing floor, she gave that one ticket's worth of alms. A certain Elder...
271:
(The matter) was reported to the King. The King had the young woman brought and appointed her to the position of Chief Queen. From that time onwards, she continued to provide five hundred food-tickets (salākabhatta).

"Daṇḍappahārā" (blows with sticks) refers to instances where, during the distribution of offerings, people are seen being struck with sticks or grabbed by the neck while instructions such as "Stand in line! Stand in line!" or "Go straight and take it! Take it!" are being shouted. In the phrase "O Brahmin, this is the cause... it is of greater benefit," the reason is that, unlike in a great sacrifice, this offering of food-tickets does not require many workers or extensive equipment; therefore, this offering involves less preparation. In this offering of food-tickets, there is no oppression known as "toil" (samārambha) caused by many people neglecting their work; therefore, it involves less trouble. Because this offering is dedicated and relinquished to the Saṅgha, it is called a "sacrifice" (yañña). Just as it is not easy to measure the volume of water in the great ocean, it is not easy to measure the flow of merit in an offering endowed with the six factors; this offering is of such a nature. Therefore, it should be understood that this offering has greater fruit and greater benefit.

Upon hearing these words, the Brahmin thought: "Even for this regular meal (niccabhatta), the work of one person is lost every day for the one who strives to give it. New effort must be generated repeatedly. Is there perhaps another sacrifice that involves even less preparation and less trouble than this offering of regular meals?" Therefore, he asked, "Venerable Gotama, is there (a sacrifice with less preparation than this)?" Among those offerings, there is no end to the tasks involved in food-tickets; one person must strive and manage it without doing any other work. In the donation of a monastery (vihāradāna), however, there is a completion of the task. Whether one builds a leaf-hut or a great monastery by spending many millions, once the wealth is relinquished and the construction is done, it lasts for seven or eight years, a hundred years, or even a thousand years. One only needs to perform repairs where it is worn out or fallen down. Therefore, this donation of a monastery involves less preparation and less trouble than food-tickets. Regarding this donation of a monastery, nine benefits such as "for the sake of warding off cold" are taught according to the Suttanta method. According to the Khandhaka method, (the following is taught):

It wards off cold and heat, as well as wild beasts,
Reptiles and mosquitoes, and the cold and rain in the winter.
Furthermore, when fierce winds and the sun's heat arise, they are warded off.
(A monastery is given) for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and for the sake of practicing jhāna and insight (vipassanā).
The donation of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised by the Buddha as the supreme gift.
Therefore, a wise person, perceiving his own welfare,
Should have pleasant monasteries built and settle learned persons therein.
Therefore, he should give food, drink, clothing, and lodgings
To the upright with a clear and confident mind.
They teach him the Dhamma that dispels all suffering.
Having understood that Dhamma in this life, he becomes taintless (anāsava) and attains Parinibbāna.

(In this way,) seventeen benefits are taught. Therefore, it should be understood that this donation of a monastery has greater fruit and greater benefit than food-tickets. It is called a "sacrifice" (yañña) only because it is relinquished and offered to the Saṅgha.
272:
Upon hearing about the gift of a monastery, the Brahmin thought: 'The donation of a monastery involving the relinquishment of wealth is indeed difficult. This is because it is hard for a person to give away even a single coin (kākaṇika) of their own to another. Now, I shall ask about a sacrifice that requires even less effort and less preparation than this gift of a monastery.' Having thought thus, he asked: 'Venerable Gotama, is there another sacrifice more fruitful than this?' and so forth.

350-351. To explain in relation to that question: Even after a monastery has been donated once, there are still duties to be performed, such as repeated roofing and repairing broken or dilapidated parts. As for taking refuge, once it is taken—whether in the presence of a single monk, the Saṅgha, or a group—it is taken once and for all. There is no need to perform it repeatedly. Therefore, taking refuge requires less effort and preparation than the gift of a monastery. Furthermore, since taking refuge is a meritorious deed involving the dedication of one's life to the Triple Gem and is capable of bestowing the bliss of the heavenly realms, it should be understood as having greater fruit and greater benefit. The dedication of one's life to the Triple Gem is also called a sacrifice (yañña).

Upon hearing this, the Brahmin thought: 'It is indeed difficult to sacrifice one's own life for another. Could there be a sacrifice that requires even less effort than this taking of refuge?' Then, wishing to ask about that matter, he again asked: 'Venerable Gotama, is there another sacrifice more fruitful than this?' In that question, regarding the words 'abstaining from taking life' and so forth, abstinence (virati) is of three types: abstinence from a present object (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by destruction (setughāta-virati). Among these three, even without having undertaken the precepts, when one reflects on one's own birth, lineage, family, and status, thinking, 'This is not suitable for me,' and thus refrains from taking life and so on, avoiding the object of misconduct that has presented itself—this is called sampatta-virati.

The abstinence of one who undertakes the precepts, thinking, 'From this day forward, as long as life lasts, I shall not kill a living being even for the sake of my life,' or 'I refrain from taking life,' or 'I undertake the precept of abstinence,' is called samādāna-virati.

The abstinence associated with the Path of the Noble Disciples (ariya-sāvaka) is called setughāta-virati. Among these three types of abstinence, the first two occur by taking as their object the life faculty (jīvitindriya) and other things that would be violated through killing and so forth. The last one, setughāta-virati, however, takes only Nibbāna as its object. In this undertaking of precepts, for one who takes the five precepts together, if one is broken, all are broken. For one who takes them individually, whichever precept he violates...
273:
...only that specific precept is broken. In the case of setughāta-virati, there is no such thing as breaking it; for even in a future life, a Noble Disciple does not kill a living being or drink intoxicants even for the sake of his life. If one were to mix intoxicants and milk and pour them into the mouth of that Noble Disciple, only the milk would enter, not the intoxicants. How is this? It is like when cranes (koñca) are presented with water mixed with milk, only the milk enters and not the water. This occurrence should be understood as being accomplished by nature (yoni) and by the natural order of things (dhammatā).

In the taking of refuge, the straightening of one's view (diṭṭhi-ujuka-karaṇa) is indeed difficult. In the undertaking of precepts, however, it is merely a matter of refraining. Therefore, whether one takes these precepts in any manner or takes them well, they involve less effort and fewer tasks. Since there is no gift equal to the five precepts, the greatness of the fruit and the greatness of the benefits in these five precepts should be understood. For it has been said:

"Monks, these five gifts are great gifts (mahādāna), known as foremost, known for a long time, known as traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, and are not doubted, will not be doubted, and are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins. What are the five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the taking of life, refrains from taking life. Monks, a noble disciple who refrains from taking life gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear (abhaya), freedom from enmity (avera), and freedom from oppression (abyāpajjha). Having given freedom from fear, enmity, and oppression to immeasurable beings, he himself shares in immeasurable freedom from fear, enmity, and oppression. Monks, this is the first great gift... not censured by the wise.

Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned taking what is not given... having abandoned sexual misconduct... having abandoned false speech... having abandoned the use of intoxicants, such as wine and liquor, which are the cause of heedlessness... refrains from them. Monks, these five gifts are great gifts... not censured by the wise." (Thus it was taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.39).

This group of five precepts is also called a sacrifice (yañña) because it is undertaken with the thought, "I shall protect them by relinquishing my love for myself and my love for life." In that statement, if...
274:
The taking of refuge is indeed more noble than the five precepts. However, these five precepts are said to be of great fruit by virtue of the morality observed by being established in the taking of refuge alone.

Hearing this, the Brahmin thought: "It is very difficult to observe the five precepts. Is there perhaps something else of a similar nature that involves less effort than these five precepts but is of even greater fruit?" Then, wishing to inquire about that matter, he spoke again: "But is there, Master Gotama...?" and so on. Then the Blessed One, wishing to show the less effort and greater fruit of the sacrifices such as the first jhāna for a monk established in the fulfillment of the threefold morality, began the teaching starting from the appearance of a Buddha, saying: "Here, Brahmin, in this dispensation..." and so on.

Among those jhānas, a monk endowed with the qualities mentioned below does not become weary in producing the first jhāna; being established in the first jhāna and so on, he does not become weary in producing the second jhāna and so on. Therefore, those are sacrifices involving little effort and little exertion. For among these jhānas, the first jhāna gives a lifespan of one incalculable aeon (kappa) in the Brahma world. The second gives eight aeons. The third gives sixty-four aeons. The fourth gives five hundred aeons. If that same fourth jhāna is developed by way of attainments such as the sphere of infinite space, it gives a lifespan of twenty thousand, forty thousand, sixty thousand, and eighty-four thousand aeons. Therefore, it is of even greater fruit and greater benefit. Because the opposing states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) have been abandoned, it should be known as a sacrifice.

Insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) also involves little effort because it does not weary a monk who produces it while established in the qualities ending with the fourth jhāna. Because there is no happiness equal to the happiness of insight, it is of great fruit. It is called a sacrifice because of the abandonment of opposing defilements. The knowledge of mind-made power (manomayiddhi-ñāṇa) also involves little effort because it does not weary one who produces it while established in insight knowledge. It is of great fruit because of the ability to create a form similar to oneself. It is called a sacrifice because of the abandonment of its own opposing defilements. The various psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) and so on also involve little effort because they do not weary one who produces them while established in the mind-made knowledge and so on. They are called sacrifices because of the abandoning of their respective opposing defilements. Among these, the knowledge of psychic powers is of great fruit because of the ability to demonstrate various types of transformations; the divine ear (dibbasota) because of the ability to hear the sounds of devas and humans; the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) because of the ability to know the sixteen types of minds of others; the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) because of the ability to remember any desired past existence; the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) because of the ability to see any desired form; and the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) because of the ability to achieve the exceedingly sublime happiness of the supramundane path. Because there is no other sacrifice more distinguished than Arahantship...
275:
Intending to conclude the discourse with the attainment of Arahatship as the pinnacle, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Ayam pi kho, brāhmaṇa."

## Commentary on the Declaration of Kūṭadanta the Brahmin as a Lay Follower

354-358. "Evaṃ vutte" means when it was thus spoken by the Blessed One. Kūṭadanta the Brahmin, being inspired by the discourse and wishing to go for refuge, spoke the words beginning with "Excellent, Master Gotama!"

"Upavāyatu" means: let a gentle, cool breeze blow, which, upon reaching the body, calms its distress. After saying this, the Brahmin sent a man, saying, "Go, dear man, enter the sacrificial pit and release all those living beings from their bonds." That man replied, "Very well," and after doing so, returned and reported, "Sir, those living beings have been released."

As long as the Brahmin had not yet heard that news, the Blessed One did not preach the Dhamma. Why? Because there was still a state of disturbance and anxiety in the Brahmin's mind. However, upon hearing it, his mental state became exceptionally clear, thinking, "Indeed, many living beings have been released by me." Knowing that the Brahmin's mind was now clear, the Blessed One began the discourse on the Dhamma. With reference to this beginning, it is said: "Atha kho Bhagavā," and so on. Furthermore, the words beginning with "Kallacittaṃ" (a ready mind) were spoken with reference to the state of having the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) suppressed through the power of the progressive talk (ānupubbīkathā). The remaining words are clear in their meaning.

## Thus the Commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta
## in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, is finished.
276:
## 6. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta
## Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Messengers
The Mahāli Sutta begins with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ". The following is the commentary on the words in this Sutta that are not in sequential order: "Vesāliyaṃ" means in the city named Vesālī because it repeatedly reached a state of vastness (visāla). "Mahāvane" means that outside the city, there is a natural forest connected to the Himālaya mountains; because it is large and extensive, it is called "Mahāvana" (Great Forest). In that Mahāvana forest. "Kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ" means that they established a Saṅghārāma (monastery) in that forest grove. In that monastery, they built a palace resembling a celestial mansion (devavimāna) in the form of a hall with a gabled roof (kūṭāgāra) on top of pillars. Based on that gabled hall, the entire monastery became known as the "Kūṭāgārasālā". The Buddha stayed in that monastery depending on Vesālī. Thus it is said: "Vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ."

"Kosalakā" refers to the residents of the Kosala kingdom. "Māgadhakā" refers to the residents of the Magadha kingdom. "Karaṇီyena" means by a business that must certainly be done. A task that can be left undone is called "kicca", but a task that must definitely be performed is called "karaṇīya".

"Paṭisallīno bhagavā" means withdrawing from wandering among various objects, reaching a state of solitude, and experiencing the bliss of jhāna on a single object. "Tatreva" means in that very monastery. "Ekamantaṃ" means moving away from that place and sitting in the shade of various trees.

## Commentary on the Story of Oṭṭhaddha Licchavī
"Oṭṭhaddho" is the name of one who is so called because of his drooping lips. "Mahatiyā licchavīparisāyā" means that having offered a meal to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha in the morning, having undertaken the Uposatha precepts in the presence of the Buddha, and having people carry perfumes, flowers, etc., he assembled a large retinue of Licchavī princes by proclamation. He approached together with that large Licchavī retinue, adorned with blue, yellow, etc., colored clothes, ornaments, and ointments, resembling the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods. It is not the time...
277:
"Mahāli" is the original name of that Oṭṭhaddha. The Elder Nāgita addresses him as "Mahāli" by that original name alone. He sat together with that Licchavī retinue in suitable tree shades, speaking of the virtues of the Triple Gem.

"Sīho samaṇuddeso" refers to the novice named Sīha, who was the nephew of the Venerable Nāgita, had ordained at the age of seven, and was diligent in the Dispensation. Seeing that large assembly sitting and filling the entire monastery, that novice thought: "This assembly is very large. The Buddha will surely preach the Dhamma to this assembly today with great effort. It would be good if I inform my preceptor and have him report to the Buddha that the assembly has gathered." He then approached the Venerable Nāgita. He addressed the Elder Nāgita by his clan name as "Venerable Kassapa". "This group of people" is the meaning.

In the phrase "You yourself report to the Blessed One," it implies that the novice Sīha was intimate with the Buddha. The Venerable Nāgita was corpulent, and due to the heaviness of his body, he was somewhat prone to laziness in rising and sitting. At that time, the novice Sīha used to perform duties for the Buddha from time to time. Therefore, the Venerable Nāgita said: "You too are intimate with the Buddha; go and report it yourself."

"In the shade of the monastery" means in the area covered by the shade of the great gabled house. That Kūṭāgārasālā hall was long from north to south and faced east, so a large shadow fell in front of the monastery. The novice Sīha prepared a seat for the Buddha there.

Then the Buddha, coming out through the doorways and windows, indicated his departure with the six-colored Buddha-rays running and spreading here and there. Like the full moon emerging from behind the clouds, he came out of the Kūṭāgārasālā and sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat. Thus it is said: "Then the Blessed One, having come out of the monastery, sat on the seat prepared in the shade of the monastery."
278:
364-365. In the phrase, "Venerable Sir, the previous days were the earlier days," yesterday is called "purima" (previous), and the days before yesterday are called "purimatara" (earlier). From that day onwards, all days are both previous and earlier. "Yadagge" means from the original day, taking whichever day as the peak (the final limit) and dwelling therein; it means as long as one has dwelt. Now, showing the extent of that duration, he said, "not long, for three years." Alternatively, "yadagge" means from whichever day one began, dwelling for not long, for three years. It means having started from a certain day, one dwelt for only three years. It is said that this Sunakkhatta once served the Blessed One for three years, carrying the Blessed One's bowl and robes, and he speaks thus in reference to that fact. "Piyarūpāni" means things that are dear and pleasant by nature. "Kāmūpasaṃhitāni" means things connected with the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. "Rajanīyāni" means things that arouse lust. In the statement, "But I do not hear divine sounds," why did Sunakkhatta not hear those sounds? It is said that he approached the Blessed One and requested the method of preliminary practice for the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). The Blessed One taught him, and by practicing as instructed, he attained the divine eye. When he saw the forms of the deities and Brahmas, he thought, "In such bodily forms, there must certainly be melodious sounds; how might I hear them?" He then approached the Blessed One again and asked for the method of preliminary practice for the divine ear (dibba-sota). However, in a past life, this Sunakkhatta had struck a virtuous monk on the ear, making him deaf. Therefore, even though he performed the preliminary practice, he was incapable (abhabba) of attaining the divine ear. For this reason, the Blessed One did not teach him the method of preliminary practice. Because of this, he bore a grudge against the Blessed One and thought, "Indeed, the ascetic Gotama thinks, 'I am a Khattiya and he is also a Khattiya; if his knowledge increases, he too will become an All-Knowing Buddha,' and out of envy, he does not tell me." When he eventually returned to the lay life, he said this while telling the matter to Mahāli the Licchavī.

## Commentary on Concentration Developed One-sidedly
366-371. "Ekamsabhāvito" means developed one-sidedly (partially), or developed for the purpose of either seeing divine forms or hearing divine sounds. "Tiriyaṃ" means in the intermediate directions. "Ubhayamsabhāvito" means developed for both parts (both purposes). "Mahāli, this is the cause" means this concentration developed one-sidedly only for the purpose of seeing divine forms is the cause.
279:
Hearing this matter, that Licchavī thought: "Hearing sounds with the divine ear must be the supreme benefit in this Dispensation. For the sake of this supreme benefit, these monks surely practice the holy life (brahmacariya) that is not contrary to the Dispensation of Gotama for fifty or sixty years. It would be good if I were to ask the Dasabala (the Buddha) about this matter."

Having thought thus, wishing to ask about that matter, he addressed the Buddha, starting with, "Venerable Sir, is it for such a benefit?"

In the phrase "samādhibhāvanānaṃ," concentration itself is called the development of concentration (samādhibhāvanā); it refers to concentrations developed in both ways. Furthermore, because those developments of concentration are external to the Dispensation and not internal, the Blessed One, wishing to set aside those developments of concentration and show the benefit for which monks practice the holy life, said, "Mahāli, it is not so," and so on.

## Commentary on the Four Noble Fruits

"Tiṇṇam saṃyojanānaṃ" refers to the three bonds, such as personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) and others. These things bind beings to the chariot of the suffering of the round of rebirths; therefore, they are called fetters (saṃyojana). "Sotāpanno hoti" means he becomes one who has reached the stream of the Noble Path. "Avinipātadhammo" means one whose nature is not to fall into the four woeful states. "Niyato" means fixed by the law of Dhamma (dhamma-niyāma). "Sambodhiparāyaṇo" means one whose future destination is enlightenment, which consists of the three higher paths.

"Tanutta" refers to the state of being thinned out, both because of the weakening of the obsession of defilements and because of their only occasional occurrence. "Orambhāgiyānaṃ" refers to the fetters that belong to the lower realm of existence (the sensual realm). A person bound by these fetters is unable to be reborn in the higher Suddhāvāsa realms. "Opapātiko" is a term that excludes the other types of birth. In that context, "parinibbāyī" means one whose nature is to attain final Nibbāna in that very higher realm. "Anāvattidhammo" means one whose nature is not to return from that Brahma world by way of rebirth. "Cetovimutti" means the purity of mind; it is a designation for the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala-citta) which is liberated from all bonds of defilements. In the phrase "paññāvimutti," the fruition of Arahantship wisdom itself, liberated from all bonds of defilements, should be understood as liberation by wisdom. "Diṭṭheva dhamme" means in this very present existence. "Sayaṃ" means by oneself. "Abhiññā" means having known through direct knowledge. "Sacchikatvā" means having realized it for oneself. Alternatively, "abhiññā sacchikatvā" means having realized it through distinguished direct knowledge. "Upasampajjā" means having reached or attained.

Hearing this, the Licchavī King thought: "This Dhamma is not like a bird that, having flown up, [can be penetrated], nor is it like a monitor lizard that, going on its breast, can be [penetrated]..."
280:
## Exposition of the Noble Eightfold Path

374-375. Upon hearing this meaning, the Licchavī king thought: "This Dhamma cannot be penetrated by flying up like a bird, nor by crawling on the chest like an iguana. Surely, for one who penetrates this Dhamma, there must be a preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapratipadā); I shall first ask about that practice." Then, he asked the Blessed One, starting with: "Venerable Sir, is there [a path of practice]?"

'Eightfold' (aṭṭhaṅgika) means that it is called eightfold because it consists of only eight factors, just like a five-piece musical instrument or an eight-part village. There is no such thing as a 'path' apart from its factors. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "What are these? They are Right View ...pe... Right Concentration."

Among those eight path factors, Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) has the characteristic of seeing rightly. Right Intention (sammāsaṅkappa) has the characteristic of rightly directing [the mind] onto the object. Right Speech (sammāvācā) has the characteristic of rightly embracing [wholesome verbal conduct]. Right Action (sammākammanta) has the characteristic of rightly originating [wholesome bodily conduct]. Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva) has the characteristic of rightly purifying livelihood. Right Effort (sammāvāyāma) has the characteristic of rightly exerting. Right Mindfulness (sammāsati) has the characteristic of rightly establishing [on the object]. Right Concentration (sammāsamādhi) has the characteristic of rightly stabilizing [associated states] on the object.

Each of these path factors has three functions. These functions are: first, Right View abandons wrong view along with its opposing defilements, takes Cessation (Nibbāna) as its object, and sees the associated states without delusion by destroying the ignorance that covers it. Right Intention and the others likewise abandon wrong intention and so forth, and take Cessation as their object. Specifically, here, Right Intention directs the co-nascent (sahajāta) states onto the object. Right Speech rightly embraces. Right Action rightly originates. Right Livelihood rightly purifies. Right Effort rightly exerts. Right Mindfulness rightly establishes. Right Concentration rightly stabilizes.

Furthermore, this so-called Right View has various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). At the path moment (maggakkhaṇa), however, it has only a single moment and a single object. By way of function, it receives four names such as "Knowledge of Suffering," and so on. Right Intention and the others also have various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage, but at the path moment, they have only a single moment and a single object. Among those path factors, Right Intention receives three names by way of function, such as "Intention of Renunciation" (nekkhamma-saṅkappa). The three abstinences (virati) starting with Right Speech can be either abstinences or volitions [in the preliminary stage]. At the path moment, however, they are only abstinences. This pair, Right Effort and Right Mindfulness, also receives four names each by way of function, as Right Strivings and Foundations of Mindfulness. Right Concentration, however, is called only Right Concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the path moment.
281:
In this way, among these eight factors, the Blessed One taught Right View first because it is of great benefit to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna. This Right View is also called the "light of wisdom" and the "weapon of wisdom." Therefore, by means of this Right View, known as insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) in the preliminary stage of the path, the practitioner (yogāvacara) destroys the darkness of ignorance, kills the thieves of defilements, and reaches Nibbāna in safety. For this reason, it is said: "Right View was taught first because it is of great benefit to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna."

Right Intention, however, is of great benefit to that Right View; therefore, it was taught immediately after it. For example, just as a goldsmith, turning a coin over and over in his hand and looking at it with his eyes, knows: "This is genuine, this is counterfeit." In the same way, the practitioner, having thought over [the objects] with initial application (vitakka) in the preliminary stage and looking at them with the wisdom of insight, understands: "These states belong to the sense sphere, these states belong to the fine-material sphere," and so on. Or to give another example, just as a woodworker uses an adze to carve a large log that has been turned over and over by a man holding it at the end, and then applies it to his work; in the same way, the practitioner, using wisdom, defines the states that have been repeatedly directed to the object by initial application (vitakka) as "These are sense-sphere states, these are fine-material sphere states," and so on, and applies them to his work. Therefore, it is said: "Right Intention is of great benefit to that Right View; therefore, it was taught immediately after it." This Right Intention is helpful to Right Speech just as it is to Right View. As it was said: "Visākha, having first thought and pondered, one afterwards breaks into speech." Therefore, Right Speech was taught immediately after Right Intention.

Because people in the world first arrange with speech, saying "We shall do this and that," and then engage in actions, speech is helpful to bodily action; therefore, Right Action was taught immediately after Right Speech. Because the morality of "livelihood as the eighth" (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) is fulfilled only by one who abandons the four types of verbal misconduct and the three types of bodily misconduct and fulfills both types of good conduct, and not by any other, Right Livelihood was taught immediately after those two. A monk with such purified livelihood should not be content with just saying "My livelihood is pure" and live in sleep and heedlessness; rather, to show that "Effort should be initiated in all postures," Right Effort was taught immediately after Right Livelihood. Then, [it is shown that] even for one with initiated effort, in the four [objects] such as the body...
282: Right Mindfulness is taught immediately after [Right Effort] to show that 'mindfulness should be well-established in the objects.' Because mindfulness thus well-established is capable of investigating the states that are conducive or non-conducive to concentration and of steadying the mind on a single object, it should be understood that Right Concentration is taught immediately after Right Mindfulness. 'For the realization of these states' means for the purpose of the direct realization of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.  ## Dve Pabbajitavatthuvaṇṇanā 376-377.  Why was this statement, 'At one time I...', undertaken (spoken)? It is said that this King (Mahāli) held the view that 'form is the self.' Because of that view, his mind did not incline towards the teaching. Then, the Blessed One, in order to make that view clear and to bring forward a reason, undertook this discourse. Here is the summary of the meaning: 'At one time I was staying at Ghositārāma. While I was staying there, those two renunciants asked me thus. Then, I, wishing to show them the arising of a Buddha and to teach the traditional Dhamma, said this: "Friends, a son of a good family endowed with faith, having gone forth in the Dispensation of such a Teacher, having fulfilled the three kinds of virtue, and remaining established after attaining the first jhāna and so forth, might say, 'Is the soul the same as the body?' and so on. Would it be proper for him to say so?" When they replied, "It would be proper," I refuted that view by saying, "Friends, I indeed know this thus, I see this thus, yet I do not say so." Then, showing the higher state of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), I said, "It is not proper for such a person to speak thus." Having heard my words, they were delighted.' When this was said, King Mahāli also became delighted. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed One said this. Mahāli the Licchavi rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.'  ## Thus, in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī,  ## The Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta is finished.

## 7. Description of the Jāliya Sutta

## Description of the Story of the Two Recluses

The Jāliya Sutta, beginning with "Thus have I heard," took place in the city of Kosambī. Herein is the explanation of terms whose meanings are not clear. "In the Ghositārāma" means in the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita.

In the past, there was a country named Allakappa. From that country, a poor man named Kotūhalika, due to the danger of famine, went to the country of Avanti with his wife and son. Being unable to carry the young son, he abandoned him and went on. The mother turned back, picked up the son, and they went on until they reached a cowherd village. At that time, the cowherd had prepared a large amount of milk-rice (pāyasa), and they received and ate that milk-rice. Then, that man, having eaten a large amount of milk-rice and being unable to digest it, died during the night and was reborn in the womb of a female dog in that same house. That dog became dear to the cowherd. The cowherd also served a Paccekabuddha. After finishing his meal, the Paccekabuddha used to give a handful of rice to the dog. The dog developed affection for the Paccekabuddha and would go to the leaf-hut along with the cowherd. When the cowherd was not present, the dog would go by itself at mealtime and bark at the door of the leaf-hut to announce the time. On the way, if it saw fierce wild animals, it would bark and drive them away. When that dog died with a mind of devotion towards the Paccekabuddha, it was reborn in the celestial realm.

In that celestial realm, he was known as the deva Ghosaka. Passing away from the celestial realm, he was reborn in a family home in the city of Kosambī. A childless merchant gave money to the boy's parents and took him as his son. Later, when his own biological son was born, he attempted to have the boy killed seven times. Because of his great merit, the boy escaped death in all seven places. Finally, he gained his life through the cleverness of a merchant's daughter, and later, upon the death of his father, he attained the position of a merchant and became famous as the merchant Ghosita. In the city of Kosambī, there were two other merchants named Kukkuṭa and Pavāriya. Including this merchant Ghosita, there were three merchants.

At that time, five hundred ascetics from the Himalayas would occasionally come to the city of Kosambī to warm themselves. For those five hundred ascetics, the three merchants built monasteries shaped like the front of a cart in their respective gardens and supported them. One day, when those ascetics were coming from the Himalayas, they became thirsty and exhausted on a long and difficult journey and reached a large banyan tree. They sat there, desiring favor from the deity guarding that banyan tree.

That deity, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, stretched out his hand and gave water, drinks, and so forth to those five hundred ascetics, relieving their exhaustion from the journey. The ascetics, marvelling at the deity's power and majesty, asked, "What good deed did you perform to obtain this prosperity?"
284:
He came to be known as Ghosaka the Treasurer. In the city of Kosambī, there were two other treasurers named Kukkuṭa and Pāvāriya; including Ghosaka, there were three treasurers.

At that time, five hundred ascetics from the Himalayas would occasionally visit Kosambī for the sake of bodily sustenance. These three treasurers built leaf-huts in their respective gardens and provided for the needs of those five hundred ascetics. On one occasion, while the ascetics were traveling from the Himalayas, they became thirsty and exhausted in a great forest. Reaching a large banyan tree, they sat down, hoping for assistance from the deity dwelling in that tree. The deity stretched out a hand adorned with all kinds of ornaments and provided them with drinking water, beverages, and so on, thereby relieving their exhaustion. The ascetics, amazed by the deity's power and majesty, asked, "O deity, what good deed did you perform to obtain such prosperity?"

The deity replied, "A Blessed One named the Buddha has arisen in the world; he is currently staying in Sāvatthī, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍika attends to him. On Uposatha days, that treasurer has his employees observe the Uposatha, giving them only their regular food and wages. One day, I arrived at midday for my morning meal and, seeing that not a single worker was working, I asked, 'Why are the people not working today?' They told me the reason. Then I said, 'Half the day has already passed; is it still possible to observe the half-day Uposatha?' After asking the treasurer, they said, 'It is possible.' I observed the half-day Uposatha for that half-day, died on that very day, and obtained this prosperity."

Then those ascetics, filled with joy and exultation at the news that "The Buddha has arisen," wished to go to Sāvatthī immediately from that spot. However, they thought, "The treasurers who support us are very helpful; we shall inform them of this matter first," and so they went to Kosambī. When the treasurers received them with respect and honor, the ascetics said, "We shall depart this very day." When asked, "Venerable sirs, why are you in such a hurry? Did you not previously stay for four or five months before leaving?", they related the news. The treasurers said, "Venerable sirs, if that is so, we shall also go along with you." The ascetics replied, "We shall go ahead; you may come slowly," and they went to Sāvatthī, where they were ordained in the presence of the Blessed One and attained Arahantship.

Those treasurers also went to Sāvatthī with five hundred carts each, gave gifts and performed other merits, and after inviting the Blessed One to visit, they returned and built three monasteries. Among those monasteries, the one built by Kukkuṭa the Treasurer was named Kukkuṭārāma. The one built by Pāvāriya the Treasurer was named Pāvārikambavana. The one built by Ghosita the Treasurer was named Ghositārāma. With reference to the residence in the monastery built by Ghosita the Treasurer, the phrase "at Ghositārāma" is spoken. Mundiya is the name of that wanderer (paribbājaka). Jāliya is also the name of that same person. The preceptor of that Jāliya used to go for alms with a wooden bowl; therefore, Jāliya is called "the pupil of Dārupattika."
285:
The three treasurers, accompanied by five hundred carts each, went to Sāvatthī, performed acts of charity and so on, and after requesting the Blessed One to come to Kosambī, they returned and built three monasteries. Among these, the one built by Kukkuṭa the Treasurer was named Kukkuṭārāma; the one built by Pāvāriya the Treasurer was named Pāvārikambavana; and the one built by Ghosita the Treasurer was named Ghositārāma. With reference to his stay in the monastery built by Ghosita the Treasurer, it is said: "He was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park."

Mundiya is the name of that wanderer. Jāliya is also the name of the other one. However, because Jāliya's preceptor wandered for alms with a bowl made of wood, Jāliya is called the pupil of Dārupattika. "They said this to him" means they spoke with the intention of finding fault and wishing to challenge his doctrine. It is said that these wanderers had this thought: "If the ascetic Gotama says, 'The soul is the same as the body,' then we shall challenge him thus: 'O Gotama, according to your view, a being is destroyed right here in this life; therefore, your doctrine is a doctrine of annihilation (ucchedavāda).' But if he says, 'The soul is one thing and the body is another,' then we shall challenge him thus: 'In your doctrine, the form is destroyed but the being is not; therefore, in your doctrine, the being becomes eternal (sassatavāda).’" Then the Blessed One, thinking, "These people are asking a question to challenge my doctrine; they do not know that in my teaching there is a Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) that does not approach these two extremes. Now, without directly answering their question, I shall teach the Dhamma to make that path clear," spoke the words beginning with, "In that case, friends."

379-380. In that passage, "Is it fitting for him to say this?" means: Is it appropriate for that clansman, who has gone forth out of faith, fulfilled the threefold virtue, and attained the first jhāna, to say this? Upon hearing those words, the wanderers—considering that a worldling (puthujjana) is not free from doubt and might therefore speak in such a way at some time—said, "It is fitting for him to say this." "But I do not say so" means: I know this meaning in this way, yet I do not say so; rather, I established the perception that for one who develops by performing the kasiṇa preliminary work, this is the exalted consciousness (mahaggata-citta) arisen by the power of wisdom.
286:
"It is not fitting for him [to say] this"—these wanderers said this, thinking: "Because an Arahant (khīṇāsava) is free from delusion and has crossed over doubt, it is therefore not fitting for that Arahant to say this." The remaining words in this Sutta have a clear meaning.

## in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī.

## 8. Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta
## Commentary on the Story of Acela Kassapa
This sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "Uruññāyaṃ viharati," is the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. In this Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, the following is the explanation of the words. "Uruññāyaṃ" is the name of that country as well as the name of that city. The Blessed One was staying depending on the city of Uruññā. "Kaṇṇakatthale migadāye" means that not far from that city, there is a pleasant piece of land named Kaṇṇakatthala. Because that land was given for the safety of animals, it is called "Migadāya" (Deer Park). (He was staying) in that deer park named Kaṇṇakatthala. "Acelo" refers to a naked wanderer. "Kassapo" is the name of that naked wanderer. "Tapassiṃ" refers to one who relies on ascetic practices. "Lūkhājīviṃ" means that because of practices such as nakedness and urinating while standing, that naked wanderer has a harsh livelihood; therefore, he is called one of harsh livelihood. "Upakkosati" means he ridicules. "Upavadati" means he criticizes or disparages. "Dhammassa ca anudhammaṃ byākaronti" means they speak reasons that are consistent with the reasons stated by the Venerable Gotama. "Sahadhammiko vādānuvādo" means: based on the reasons stated by others, does any reason, even a slight one, that should be criticized by the wise, arise in your doctrine or its followers? This is the meaning. It means: is there no reason at all to criticize your doctrine in any way? "Anabbhakkhātukāmā" means they do not wish to speak falsely.

Among the four types of persons beginning with "ekaccaṃ tapassiṃ lūkhājīviṃ," a certain person in this world, because he relies on practices such as being a naked monk, becomes an ascetic and, thinking "I will live by a harsh livelihood," torments himself in various ways such as eating grass and cow dung. Due to having little merit, he does not obtain a comfortable livelihood. That person fulfills the three misconducts and is reborn in hell.

Another person, though relying on such practices, is one with merit and receives gains and honors. That person, thinking "Now there is no one equal to me," places himself in a high position and, thinking "I will generate even more gains," fulfills the three misconducts through wrong livelihood and is reborn in hell. The first method is stated with reference to these two persons.

Another person, though relying on ascetic practices and having a harsh livelihood, is one with little merit and does not obtain a comfortable livelihood. That person, thinking "Because I did not perform merit in the past, a comfortable livelihood does not arise for me; oh, now I will perform meritorious deeds," fulfills the three good conducts and is reborn in heaven.

Another person has a harsh livelihood and also has merit, and thus obtains a comfortable livelihood. That person, reflecting "Because I performed merit in the past, a comfortable livelihood arises for me," abandons wrong livelihood, fulfills the three good conducts, and is reborn in heaven. The second method is stated with reference to these two persons.

One may understand the manner of teaching the first and second methods by looking at the Pāḷi text. A certain person is an ascetic who lives with little suffering; he may be a hermit (tāpasa) endowed with external practices or a clothed wanderer. Because of little merit, he does not obtain pleasant requisites.
288:
...(a comfortable livelihood) does not arise; thinking "Oh, now I will perform meritorious deeds," he fulfills the three good conducts and is reborn in heaven.

Another person, though having a harsh livelihood, is one with merit and obtains a comfortable livelihood. That person, reflecting "Because I have merit performed in the past, a comfortable livelihood arises for me," abandons wrong livelihood, fulfills the three good conducts, and is reborn in heaven. The second method is stated with reference to these two persons.

One person is an ascetic (hermit) who lives with little suffering; he may be a hermit endowed with external (non-Buddhist) practices or a clothed wanderer. Because of having little merit, he does not obtain pleasant requisites. That person, through the power of wrong livelihood, fulfills the three misconducts and, while keeping himself comfortable, is reborn in hell.

Another person is one with merit. That person, generating conceit thinking "Now there is no one equal to me," and generating gains and honors through wrong livelihood, falls into sensual obsession through the power of wrong view, thinking "How pleasant is the touch of this young, soft, and hairy female wanderer," and so forth. Thus, fulfilling the three misconducts, he is reborn in hell. The third method is stated with reference to these two persons.

Another person lives with little suffering and is one with little merit. That person, thinking "Because I did not perform merit in the past, I do not obtain a comfortable livelihood," fulfills the three good conducts and is reborn in heaven.

Another person is one with merit. That person, thinking "Because I performed merit in the past, I obtain happiness; now I will also perform meritorious deeds," fulfills the three good conducts and is reborn in heaven. The fourth method is stated with reference to these two persons. Although these four groups are presented in terms of sectarians (titthiyas), they can also be found within the Sasana (the Buddha's Dispensation).

A certain monk has a harsh livelihood by virtue of undertaking the dhutaṅga practices. Because of little merit, even after wandering through the entire village, he does not obtain enough to fill his stomach. That monk, thinking "I will generate requisites," performs wrong livelihood such as practicing medicine, or by claiming to be an Arahant, or by resorting to the three grounds of scheming (kuhana-vatthu), and is thus reborn in hell.
289:
Another monk is likewise one who undertakes ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and is a person of merit (puññavā). Because of that attainment of merit, he becomes conceited and, desiring to make his gains permanent, he fulfills the three types of misconduct (duccarita) through wrong livelihood (anesana) and is reborn in hell (niraya).

Another monk, though having undertaken ascetic practices, is a person of little merit (appapuñña) and cannot easily obtain a livelihood. He reflects: "I did not perform merit in the past, so I obtain nothing. If I now resort to wrong livelihood, I will find happiness difficult to obtain in the future as well." Thus, he fulfills the three types of good conduct (sucarita) and, though unable to reach Arahantship, he is reborn in a heavenly realm (sagga).

Another person is a person of merit. He reflects: "I am happy now because of merit performed in the past; I will perform merit now as well." Thus, abandoning wrong livelihood, he fulfills the three types of good conduct and, though unable to reach Arahantship, he is reborn in a heavenly realm.

"And the coming" (āgatiñca) refers to the place from which these beings have come. "And the destination" (gatiñca) refers to the place where they must go now. "And the passing away" (cutiñca) refers to the passing away from that life. "And the rebirth" (upapattiñca) refers to the rebirth again after passing away from there. "Why would I blame all practices?" means "For what reason would I blame it? For we blame only what is blameworthy and praise only what is praiseworthy. Just as a king's washerman making a bundle does not put washed and unwashed clothes together, we do not treat the blameworthy and the praiseworthy as one." Now, wishing to clarify this meaning, he said, "Kassapa, there are some recluses and brahmins," and so on.

"That which is some of yours" (yaṃ te ekaccaṃ) refers to the five precepts (pañcasīla); no one in the world says these are not good. Again, "that which is some of yours" refers to the five enmities (vera); no one says these are good. Again, "that which is some of yours" refers to the lack of restraint (asaṃvara) in the five sense-doors; they say, "The eye should not be restrained; one should look at pleasant forms with the eye." This same method applies to the ear and other sense-doors. Again, "that which is some of yours" refers to restraint (saṃvara) in the five sense-doors.

Having thus shown the similarity and dissimilarity of his own doctrine with the doctrines of others, he now says "that which is ours" (yaṃ mayaṃ) and so on, wishing to show the similarity and dissimilarity of others' doctrines with his own. There too, the meaning should be understood by way of the five precepts and so forth.
290:
## Explanation of the Discussion on Cross-examination

"Samanuyuñjantu" means "let them cross-examine." Here, asking about a doctrine (laddhi) is called "samanuyuñjati"; asking about the reason (kāraṇa) is called "samanugāhati"; asking about both is called "samanubhāsati." "Teacher with teacher" (satthārā vā satthāraṃ) means comparing teacher with teacher, as in: "Does your teacher practice having abandoned those states entirely, or does the recluse Gotama?" In the second phrase, the method is the same.

Now, wishing to show the connection of that meaning, he said, "Those of yours, sirs" (ye imesaṃ bhavanto) and so on. There, "unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome" (akusalā akusalasaṅkhātā) means states that are both unwholesome and known as "unwholesome," or placed in that category. This method applies to all phrases. Furthermore, here "blameworthy" (သာဝဇ္ဇာ - sāvajjā) means having faults. "Not fit to be noble" (na alamariyā) means they are not fit or capable of being noble (ariya) because of the sense of being faultless.

386-392. "That which the wise, cross-examining" (yaṃ viññū samanuyuñjantā) means there is a ground or a reason such that when the wise question us or others, they would speak in this way. "Or else, sirs, other teachers of groups" (yaṃ vā pana bhonto pare gaṇācariyā) means that other noble teachers of groups practice having abandoned only a small amount. "They would mostly praise us there" (amheva tattha yebhuyyena pasaṃseyyuṃ)—the Blessed One said this both when cross-examining teacher with teacher and when cross-examining Saṅgha with Saṅgha. Why? Because by praising the Saṅgha, the praise of the Teacher himself is accomplished. For those who have confidence, they gain confidence in the Saṅgha because of the Buddha's perfection, and they gain confidence in the Buddha because of the Saṅgha's perfection.

This is so because, having seen the perfection of the Blessed One's physical form or having heard his Dhamma teaching, people are prone to say, "What a gain for the disciples who dwell in the presence of such a teacher!" In this way, they gain confidence in the Saṅgha through the Buddha's perfection. But having seen the conduct and the range of the monks, their approaching and departing, etc., they are prone to say, "If this is the quality of the peacefulness of the disciples who dwell in his presence, how much more must be the quality of the Teacher himself?" In this way, they gain confidence in the Buddha through the Saṅgha's perfection. Thus, the praise of the Teacher is the praise of the Saṅgha, and the praise of the Saṅgha is the praise of the Teacher. Since the praise of the Teacher is accomplished even by the praise of the Saṅgha, the Blessed One said in both ways, "They would mostly praise us there." In the phrases "The recluse Gotama practices having abandoned these states without remainder" and "Or else, sirs, other teachers of groups," the following is the intention:
291:
There are three types of abstinence: sampatta-virati (abstinence from an arisen opportunity), samādāna-virati (abstinence by undertaking a precept), and setughāta-virati (abstinence by destruction of the bridge/root). Among these, others have only sampatta-virati and samādāna-virati; they do not have setughāta-virati at all. Among the five types of abandonment—tadaṅga-pahāna (abandonment by substitution of opposites), vikkhambhana-pahāna (abandonment by suppression), samuccheda-pahāna (abandonment by eradication), paṭipassaddhi-pahāna (abandonment by tranquilization), and nissaraṇa-pahāna (abandonment by escape)—others have only tadaṅga-pahāna and vikkhambhana-pahāna through the power of the eight attainments or through mere insight. They do not have the remaining three types of abandonment at all. Similarly, there are five types of restraint: sīla-saṃvara (restraint by virtue), khanti-saṃvara (restraint by patience), ñāṇa-saṃvara (restraint by knowledge), sati-saṃvara (restraint by mindfulness), and vīriya-saṃvara (restraint by energy). Among these, others have only a measure of the five precepts and patience through endurance (adhivāsana-khanti); they do not have the remaining restraints at all.

There are five recitations of the Uposatha (uposathuddesa). Among these five recitations, others have only the five precepts. They do not have the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) at all. Thus, regarding the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states, within the three abstinences, five abandonments, five restraints, and five recitations, the Blessed One utters the Lion's Roar (sīhanāda), a bold speech: "In the world, only I and my community of disciples are renowned. There is no teacher like me, and no community like my community of disciples."

## Ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga-vaṇṇanā

Having uttered this Lion's Roar, to make known the unerring truth of that roar, he said: "Kassapa, there is a path," and so on. In that text, "path" (magga) refers to the supramundane path. "Practice" (paṭipadā) refers to the practice of the preliminary stage. Terms such as "speaker in season" (kālavādī) have been explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta. Now, wishing to show the path and practice, which are of two kinds, together, he said: "This alone is the Noble," and so on. Hearing this, the naked ascetic (Acelaka) thought: "The ascetic Gotama thinks that only he has the path and practice, and others do not. Now, I will tell him our practice as well." Having thought so, he described the practice of the naked ascetics. Therefore, it is said: "When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One... he lives devoted to the practice of descending into water."

## Tapopakkama-kathā-vaṇṇanā

In that text, tapopakkama means the undertaking of austerities, the procedures of austerity. Sāmañña-saṅkhātā refers to the duties of an ascetic; brahmañña-saṅkhātā refers to the duties of a brahmin (one who has put away evil). Acelaka means one who does not wear clothes, a naked person. Muttācāra means one of loose conduct (shameless). Being free from the conduct of worldly gentlemen in matters such as defecation, he defecates and urinates only while standing. He chews hard food and eats soft food only while standing. Hatthāpalekhana means one who, if a lump of food (or a lump of excrement) is on the hand, licks the hand with the tongue. Alternatively, after defecating, he perceives his hand as a stick and scrapes it with his hand. When told at the time of alms-gathering, "Please come, venerable sir," he does not come; therefore, he is called na-ehibhadantika. Even when told, "Please stop for a moment, venerable sir," although he is told...
292:
...being free from the conduct of worldly gentlemen, he defecates, urinates, chews, and eats only while standing. Hatthāpalekhana refers to licking the hand with the tongue when a lump of food (or excrement) is on it, or after defecating, perceiving the hand as a stick and scraping with it. He is called na-ehibhadantika because he does not come when told, "Venerable sir, come to receive alms." He is called na-tiṭṭhabhadantika because he does not stop even when told, "Venerable sir, then please stop." He does not comply with both these words, thinking, "If I do, I will be following his word." Abhihaṭa refers to alms food brought forward in advance. Uddissakata refers to alms food announced as, "This has been prepared specifically for you." Na-nimantana means he does not delight in or accept alms food invited with, "Please come to such-and-such a family, street, or village." Na-kumbhimukha means he does not accept alms food offered by being taken out of a pot. Na-kaḷopimukha means he does not accept alms food offered from a rice-pot or a basket. Why? Because he thinks, "Because of me, the pots and baskets are being struck by the ladle." Na-eḷakamantara means he does not accept alms food offered by crossing over a threshold. Why? Because he thinks, "This threshold is being crossed because of me." The same logic applies to sticks and pestles.

Dvinnam means he does not accept food if, while two people are eating, one of them gets up to give it. Why? Because he thinks, "It will be an obstacle to that person's mouthful." Regarding na-gabbhiniyā and so on, he does not accept food thinking, "The child in the womb of the pregnant woman will be distressed; there will be an obstacle to the nursing child's milk; there will be an obstacle to the pleasure of the woman who is with a man." Saṅkittīsu refers to meals prepared collectively. It is said that during times of famine, the disciples of the naked ascetics collect rice and so on from various places for the sake of the naked ascetics and cook a meal. The eminent naked ascetic does not accept even that. Na yattha sā means if a dog is present at a place thinking, "I will get a morsel of food," he does not accept the food brought without giving it to that dog. Why? Because he thinks, "It will be an obstacle to this dog's morsel." Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī refers to moving in swarms. If, seeing a naked ascetic, people enter the kitchen thinking, "We will give alms to this venerable one," and as they enter, flies resting on the pots and so on fly up and move in swarms, he does not accept the alms food brought at that time. Why? Because he thinks, "Because of me, an obstacle has arisen to the flies' feeding ground."
293:
"Thusodaka" refers to Sovīraka medicinal liquid made from all kinds of grains. In this Sovīraka liquid, although only drinking intoxicants is an offense, this naked ascetic (acelaka) considers all types of Sovīraka liquid to be an offense. "Ekāgārika" refers to one who returns after receiving alms from only one house. "Ekālopika" refers to one who subsists on only one morsel of food. The same method applies to two houses and so on. "Ekissāpi dattiyā" means (eating) from a single small bowl. A "datti" is a type of small bowl used to place the first portion of alms. "Ekāhika" means eating once every other day. "Addhamāsika" means eating once every half-month. "Pariyāyabhattabhojana" means eating food in turns. This refers to eating food that comes according to a rotation of days, such as a one-day turn, a two-day turn, a seven-day turn, or a half-month turn.

"Sākabhakkho" refers to one who eats green vegetables. "Sāmākabhakkho" refers to one who eats raw sāmāka rice. Among the terms beginning with "Nīvāra," "Nīvāra" refers to a type of rice that grows naturally in the forest. "Daddula" refers to scraps of leather discarded by tanners after scraping the hide. "Haṭa" refers to either resin or water-weeds. "Kaṇa" refers to rice bran (broken rice). "Ācāma" refers to the burnt rice crust sticking to the rice pot. One takes and eats that rice crust from the place where it was discarded. It is also called "clear rice water." Items such as oil-cake (piññāka) are well-known. "Pavattaphalabhojī" refers to one who habitually eats fruit that has fallen naturally.
