"Sāṇa" refers to garments woven from hemp fibers. "Masāṇa" refers to garments woven from mixed fibers. "Chavadussa" refers to garments discarded from a corpse, or garments made by weaving together grasses such as eraka. "Paṃsukūla" refers to rags discarded on the ground. "Tirīṭa" refers to garments made from tree bark. "Ajina" refers to the skin of the ajina antelope. "Ajinakkhipa" refers to a garment made from that same skin split down the middle. "Kusacīra" refers to a garment made by weaving together kusa grass. The same method applies to garments made of bark (vākacīra) and garments made of wooden boards (phalakacīra). "Kesakambala" refers to a blanket made from human hair.

Regarding that hair-blanket, the Blessed One said:
"Monks, for example, of all woven garments made of thread, the hair-blanket is said to be the worst.
Monks, a hair-blanket is cold in the cold,
hot in the heat,
cheap, ill-colored, bad-smelling,
and very rough to the touch."
294:
"Vāḷakambala" refers to a blanket made from horsehair. "Ulūkapakkhika" refers to a garment made by weaving together the feathers of an owl. "Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutta" refers to one who exerts effort by squatting; even when moving, he goes by hopping and jumping while remaining in a squatting position. "Kaṇṭakāpassayika" refers to one who drives iron spikes or natural thorns into the ground, spreads a skin over them, and then stands or practices walking meditation on them. "Sayya" (bed) means that even when sleeping, he does so only on those thorns. "Phalakasayya" means sleeping on a wooden board. "Thaṇဍilasayya" means sleeping on the bare ground in an elevated place called thaṇḍila. "Ekapassayika" refers to one who sleeps only on one side. "Rajojalladhara" refers to one who smears the body with oil and stands in a dusty place; then, dust and dirt stick to his body, and he carries that dust and dirt. "Yathāsanthatika" refers to one who habitually sits in whatever place he receives without disturbing it. "Vekaṭika" refers to one who habitually eats excrement. Excrement is called "vīkaṭa." "Apānaka" refers to one who rejects the drinking of cold water. "Sāyaṃ tatiyamassa" is called "sāyatatiyaka" because it is the third time in the evening. It refers to one who lives exerting the effort of descending into water, thinking, "I will wash away evil three times a day," namely in the morning, at noon, and in the evening.

## Explanation of the Futility of Ascetic Exertion

Then the Blessed One, wishing to show the futility of those ascetic exertions when devoid of the fulfillment of virtue and so on, said: "Kassapa, even if there be a naked ascetic (acelaka)..." and so forth. In that text, "ārakā vā" means only in a distant place. "Avera" refers to one who is free from the enmity of anger. "Abyāpajja" refers to one who is free from the fault of mental distress.

"It is difficult, O Gotama," this statement was made by Kassapa wishing to show: "Previously, we lived considering only this much practice as the state of a recluse (sāmañña) and the state of a brahmin (brahmañña); but you speak of a different state of a recluse and state of a brahmin." "Pakati kho esā" means this statement is just a natural statement. "Kassapa, by this measure" means: "Kassapa, if by this much small sequence of practice, the state of a recluse or the state of a brahmin were called difficult or very difficult, then it would not be appropriate to say that the state of a recluse is difficult." Thus the meaning should be understood along with the connection of the words. In this way, the connection of words should be understood in all instances.
295: The word 'dujjāno' (hard to know) was spoken by the ascetic Kassapa with reference to this: 'Previously, we practiced thinking that one becomes a recluse or a brahmin by this much practice; but you say otherwise.' Then, the Blessed One, refuting his habitual view and making clear the state of being hard to know by nature, spoke again starting with 'Pakatī kho' (By nature...). There too, the meaning should be understood by connecting the words according to the method already mentioned.  ## Sīlasamādhipaññāsampadāvaṇṇanā 400-401.  Why does he ask, 'Venerable Gotama, what is that fulfillment?' It is said that this wise ascetic Kassapa understood the words even as the Blessed One was speaking. Then, realizing the fruitlessness of his own practice, he thought, 'The recluse Gotama has said, "For him, this fulfillment of virtue, fulfillment of mind, and fulfillment of wisdom are not developed, not realized; indeed, he is far from recluseship." Now, let me ask him about those fulfillments.' Thus, he asked because he wished to know about the fulfillment of virtue and so forth. Then, the Blessed One, showing the arising of a Buddha and teaching the traditional Dhamma, spoke starting with 'Here, Kassapa...' to show those fulfillments. The phrase 'Kassapa, by this fulfillment of virtue' was spoken with reference only to the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). For the Dispensation of the Blessed One has the fruit of Arahantship as its culmination. Therefore, he said that there is no other fulfillment of virtue and so forth that is higher or more excellent than the fulfillment of virtue, mind, and wisdom associated with the fruit of Arahantship.  ## Sīhanādakathāvaṇṇanā  Having spoken thus, now wishing to utter the incomparable Great Lion's Roar, he spoke starting with 'Kassapa, there are some recluses and brahmins...' In that context, 'ariya' (noble) means very pure, free from defilements. 'Parama' (supreme) means excellent. While virtue from the five precepts up to the restraint of the Pātimokkha is merely virtue, only the virtue associated with the supramundane path and fruit is called 'supreme virtue' (parama-sīla). 'I am not there' means that in that virtue, or in that supreme virtue, I do not see any person equal to myself, or anyone with virtue equal to my virtue. 'I alone am superior there' means I alone am the most excellent in that virtue. In which virtue? In the most excellent virtue called 'higher virtue' (adhi-sīla). Thus, he uttered this first Lion's Roar.
296:
"Tapojigucchāvāda" (those who teach asceticism and loathing) refers to those who habitually speak of ascetic practice (tapa) that burns away defilements and the loathing of defilements (jigucchā). In that context, it is called "tapa" because it burns (tapati) defilements; this is a name for energy (vīriya) that burns defilements. That same energy is called "jigucchā" because it loathes those defilements. In the phrase "ariyā paramā" (noble and supreme), it is called "ariyā" because it is faultless. The ascetic loathing (tapojigucchā) known as insight energy (vipassanā-vīriya) which arises by power of the eight grounds of initiation (ārambhavatthu) is just ascetic loathing; only that associated with the Path and Fruit is called "paramā" (supreme). In "adhijeguccha" (higher loathing), the state of loathing is "jeguccha"; excellent loathing is "adhijeguccha". Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "Whatever higher loathing there is, I alone am superior therein." Regarding wisdom (paññā), both the wisdom of the ownership of kamma (kammasakatā-paññā) and insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) are called "wisdom"; wisdom associated with the Path and Fruit is called "parama-paññā" (supreme wisdom). In "adhipaññā" (higher wisdom), a gender transformation (liṅgavipallāsa) should be understood; the meaning here is: "Whatever higher wisdom there is, I alone am superior therein." Regarding liberation (vimutti), liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti) and liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti) are called "liberation"; however, liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquilization (paṭipassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti) should be known as "parama-vimutti" (supreme liberation). Here too, the meaning is: "Whatever higher liberation (adhivimutti) there is, I alone am superior therein."

"Suññāgāre" (in an empty house) means sitting alone in a secluded house. "Parisāsu ca" (and in assemblies) means in the eight assemblies. It has also been said: "Sāriputta, the Tathāgata has these four intrepidities (vesārajja). Endowed with these intrepidities, the Tathāgata claims the supreme place and roars the lion's roar in the assemblies." This sutta should be expanded.

"Pañhañca naṃ pucchanti" (and they ask him questions) means wise devas and humans formulate questions and ask him. "Byākaroti" (he answers) means he explains at that very moment. "Cittaṃ ārādheti" (he satisfies the mind) means he truly gladdens the minds of the great multitude by answering the questions. "No ca kho sotabbaṃ maññanti" (but they do not think it should be heard) means it might be said that even though he speaks satisfying the mind, others do not consider the words of that Venerable Gotama worth listening to. "Sotabbañca'ssa maññanti" (and they think it should be heard) means both devas and humans consider his words worth listening to with great effort. "Pasīdanti" (they become confident) means they become very faithful, with ready and soft minds. "Pasannākāraṃ karonti" (they show signs of confidence) means they are not merely confident in their hearts, but they show signs of confidence by offering excellent robes and so on, and by donating great monasteries such as the Veḷuvana monastery. "Tathattāya" (for the sake of being so) means they practice so that the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One becomes a reality, and to fulfill the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapatipatti). "Tathattāya ca paṭipazzanti" means they practice to become as taught; of that Blessed One...
297:
Indeed, having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, some are established in the refuges, some in the five precepts, and others, having left the household life, go forth. The phrase "those who practice also satisfy" means that those who undertake that practice are able to fulfill it; they fulfill it in every aspect. It should be said that by fulfilling the practice, they satisfy the mind of the Venerable Gotama.

Standing in this place, the bold declarations (sīhanāda) should be combined. "I see a certain ascetic reborn in hell" is one kind of the Blessed One's bold declaration. "I see another reborn in heaven" is another. "In the abandoning of unwholesome states, I alone am supreme" is another. "In the undertaking of wholesome states, I alone am supreme" is another. "In the abandoning of unwholesome states, my Community of Disciples (Sāvaka-saṅgha) alone is supreme" is another. "In the undertaking of wholesome states, my Community of Disciples alone is supreme" is another. "In terms of virtue (sīla), there is no one equal to me" is another. "In terms of energy (vīriya), there is no one equal to me" is another. In terms of wisdom (paññā)... [pe]... In terms of liberation (vimutti)... [pe]... "I will speak while sitting in the midst of the assembly, uttering a bold declaration" is another. "I will speak being confident" is another. "They will ask me questions" is another. "I will answer the questions asked" is another. "I will satisfy the minds of others with the answers" is another. "Having heard, they will consider it worth listening to" is another. "Having heard, they will have faith in me" is another. "They will show signs of faith" is another. "They will practice the way I teach exactly as it is taught" is another. "Those who practice will satisfy me" is another. Thus, for each of the ten previously mentioned, there are ten attendants such as "He roars in the assemblies." In this way, by the power of the attendants of the first ten, there are one hundred, and adding the first ten makes one hundred and ten bold declarations. Such a number of bold declarations is difficult to find in any other sutta; therefore, this sutta is called the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.

## Titthiyaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

Thus, the Blessed One, having refuted the accusation that "The ascetic Gotama roars a lion's roar, but he roars it only in empty houses," now wishing to show the lion's roar previously roared in an assembly, spoke the words beginning with "Ekamidāhaṃ." In that text, "tatra maṃ aññataro tapabrahmacārī" means: to Me, staying at Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) mountain in Rājagaha, a certain ascetic wanderer named Nigrodha (approached).
298:
Nigrodha the wanderer asked a question concerning the loathing of evil through energy with the word "adhijeguccha." This refers to when the Blessed One, while staying at the Great Monastery on Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa), heard with His divine ear the conversation between Nigrodha the wanderer and Sandhāna the lay follower, who were sitting in the park of the Queen Udumbarikā. Having come through the air and sat on the seat prepared near them, He answered the question on higher scrupulousness (adhijeguccha) asked by Nigrodha; it is said in reference to that answer. "Paraṃ viya mattāya" means to a supreme degree, with an extremely great measure. In the phrase "Venerable Sir, who...", it means: setting aside the extremely foolish person with wrong views, what other wise person, having heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One, would not be delighted? The ascetic Kassapa spoke the words "I wish to obtain" after thinking: "For a long time indeed, I have wearied myself by being joined to a view that does not lead out of suffering. Like a man who keeps turning around thinking 'I will bathe on a dry riverbank,' or like a man pounding chaff, I have not achieved any benefit. Now, I will join myself to the practice that is beneficial."

Then, the Blessed One, referring to the sectarian probation (titthiyaparivāsa) prescribed in the Mahākhandhaka, which must be undertaken by one who was formerly a sectarian and stands in the stage of a novice, spoke the words beginning with "Kassapa, one who was formerly a sectarian..." in this manner: "Venerable Sir, I am one who was formerly a sectarian of such a name; I desire full ordination (upasampadā) in this Dhamma-Vinaya. Venerable Sir, I request the four-month probation from the Saṅgha."

In that context, the word "going forth" (pabbajjā) is said only for the sake of smooth phrasing; in truth, one can obtain the going forth without undergoing probation. However, one who desires full ordination must undergo probation while fulfilling the eight duties, such as not entering the village at an improper time. "Āraddhacittā" means those whose minds are delighted by the fulfillment of the eight duties; this is the summary meaning. In detail, this sectarian probation should be understood according to the method stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary, in the explanation of the Pabbajjākhandhaka. "Api ca mettha" should be resolved as "api ca me ettha." "Puggalavemattatā viditā" means the difference between individuals is known. It shows: "This person is worthy of probation, this person is not worthy of probation"—this fact is clear to Me. Then Kassapa thought: "How wonderful is the Buddha's Dispensation, where they thus rub and grind, taking only what is fit and discarding what is unfit!" From that, an even more intense zeal for the going forth arose, and he spoke the words beginning with "Venerable Sir, if..."
299:
“They take only what is appropriate and discard what is inappropriate,” he thought. Having thought thus, with a great surge of enthusiasm for the life of a monk, he addressed the Buddha, saying, “Venerable Sir, if...” and so on.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the intense desire of the naked ascetic Kassapa, thinking, “Kassapa does not deserve the probationary period (parivāsa),” addressed a certain monk: “Go, monk, bathe Kassapa, ordain him as a novice (pabbajjā), and bring him here.” That monk did as commanded, ordained Kassapa as a novice, and came to the Blessed One. The Blessed One had Kassapa sit in the midst of the Sangha and gave him the higher ordination (upasampadā). Therefore, it is said: “The naked ascetic Kassapa received the lower ordination and the higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One.”

“Acirūpasampanno” means not long after receiving the higher ordination. “Vūpakaṭṭho” means being secluded and remote from the objects of sensual desire and the defilements of sensual desire, both in body and mind. “Appamatto” means not abandoning mindfulness in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). “Ātāpī” means possessing the energy that burns away defilements, known as bodily and mental energy. “Pahitatto” means having a mind directed toward Nibbāna without regard for body or life, having relinquished the self-identity (attabhāva). “Yassatthāya” means for the sake of which benefit (the fruit of Arahantship). “Kulaputtā” refers to sons of good family who possess good conduct. “Sammadeva” means only through the proper cause and reason. “Tadanuttaraṃ” means that unsurpassed (fruit of Arahantship). “Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ” means the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the noble life of the Path. It is for the sake of this fruit of Arahantship that sons of good family go forth. “Diṭṭheva dhamme” means in this very life. “Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā” means having realized it through one's own wisdom, without depending on others. “Upasampajja vihāsī” means having attained and fulfilled it, he dwelt; while dwelling thus, he understood: “Birth is exhausted...” and so on.

Thus, having shown the ground of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) for that venerable one and concluding the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship, it is said: “Venerable Kassapa became one of the Arahants.” In that statement, “aññataro” means one person. “Arahatāṃ” means among the Arahants; the meaning here is that he became one among the Arahant disciples of the Blessed One. Those words not mentioned in between are already clear as they have been explained in various suttas.

## Thus ends the Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta
## in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary.

## 9. Poṭṭhapāda Sutta
Explanation of the story of Poṭṭhapāda the Wanderer. This sutta, beginning with “Evaṃ me sutaṃ, Sāvatthiyaṃ,” is the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta. In this Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, the following is the explanation of the new terms. “Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati ... ārāme” means he was staying in the monastery built and donated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika in Prince Jeta's grove, depending on the city of Sāvatthī.

This is stated according to the ancient usage, referring to what was originally Prince Jeta's grove. “Poṭṭhapādo paribbājako” refers to a naked wanderer (paribbājaka) named Poṭṭhapāda. It is said that this Poṭṭhapāda was a wealthy Brahmin (brahmaṇa-mahāsāla) with great possessions during his lay life. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he renounced a fortune of forty crores and became a teacher of a sect of heretics. In the Tindukāsāla monastery, which was Queen Mallikā's park, the heretics used to discuss their own doctrines. Therefore, that park is called “Samayappavādaka” (the place where doctrines are discussed). It is said that Brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, as well as ascetics such as Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and Paribbājakas, gathered there to discuss and debate their own doctrines.
300:
## 9. Explanation of the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta
## Explanation of the Story of Poṭṭhapāda the Wanderer
This sutta, beginning with “Evaṃ me sutaṃ,” is the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta. Herein is the explanation of the terms not previously mentioned. “Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati ဇေတဝနေ အနာထပိဏ္ဍိကဿ အာရာမေ” means he was staying in the monastery built by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika in the grove of Prince Jeta, depending on the city of Sāvatthī.

“Poṭṭhapādo paribbājako” refers to a naked wanderer named Poṭṭhapāda. It is said that in his lay life, he was a wealthy Brahmin of great status who possessed a fortune of forty crores. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he renounced all his wealth, went forth, and became a teacher of a sect of heretics.

Because it was the place where Brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, and ascetics such as Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and Paribbājakas gathered to speak, discuss, and clarify their own doctrines (samaya), that park is called “Samayappavādaka.” It is also called “Tindukācīra” because it was surrounded by a row of Tinduka (ebony) trees. Although there was originally only one hall (sālā) there, many halls were later built depending on a wanderer of great merit. However, it is called “Ekasalaka” (Single Hall) based on the name acquired from that first single hall. That park was the garden of Queen Mallikā, the consort of King Pasenadi of Kosala; because it was endowed with flowers and fruits, it was known as “Mallikā’s Park.” In that Mallikā’s Park, which was the place for discussing doctrines, surrounded by Tinduka trees, and having the single hall, (Poṭṭhapāda dwelt).

“Paṭivasati” means dwelling there because it was a comfortable place to live. Then one day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, spreading his Omniscient Knowledge and surveying the world, saw the wanderer who had entered into the net of his knowledge. Reflecting, “This Poṭṭhapāda appears in my net of knowledge; what will happen?” he saw: “Today I will go there. Then Poṭṭhapāda will ask me about the attainment of cessation (nirodha) and the emergence from cessation. I will explain both to him, consistent with the knowledge of all Buddhas. Then, after a few days, he will bring Citta, the son of the elephant trainer, and come to me. I will preach the Dhamma to them. At the end of the teaching, Poṭṭhapāda will take refuge in me, and Citta, the son of the elephant trainer, will go forth in my presence and attain the fruit of Arahantship.”

Having seen this, he attended to his person early in the morning, put on his well-dyed double robe, tied his belt which was like a flash of lightning, and placed his rag-robe (paṃsukūla)—which was the color of a dark cloud, like a great dark cloud surrounding Mount Yugandhara—over one shoulder. Carrying his stone bowl, which was the color of a young bee, on his left shoulder, he departed from the monastery like a lion king coming out from the foot of the Himalayas, intending to enter Sāvatthī for alms. The Blessed One then spoke the words beginning with, “Then the Blessed One...”
301:
“They will come to me; I will teach them the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, Poṭṭhapāda will take refuge in me, and Citta, the elephant trainer's son, will ordain in my presence and attain Arahantship,” (the Buddha foresaw). After seeing this, in the early morning, he attended to his body (washing his face, etc.), put on his well-dyed double robe, tied his waistband which was like a streak of lightning, and draped his rag-robe (paṃsukūla), which had the color of a dark cloud like a great rain cloud surrounding Mount Yugandhara, over one shoulder. Carrying his new stone bowl on his left shoulder, thinking, “I will enter Sāvatthī for alms,” he departed from the monastery like a lion coming out from the foot of the Himalayas. Regarding this matter, it was said, “Atha kho Bhagavā” and so forth.

“Etadahosi” means that upon reaching the city gate, he looked at the sun as he pleased and, seeing it was still very early, this thought occurred to him. The word “Yannūnāhaṃ” is like a particle expressing doubt, yet Buddhas have no doubt. Thoughts such as “I will do this, I will not do that; I will teach the Dhamma to this person, I will not teach to that person” are natural to all Buddhas. Therefore, it was said “Yannūnāhaṃ,” meaning “What if I...”

“Unnādiniyā” refers to making a loud noise. The sound of that assembly was “high” because it rose upwards and “great” because it spread through the directions. Those wanderers (paribbājakas), upon waking early, had no duties such as the shrine duty (cetiya-vatta), Bodhi-tree duty, teacher or preceptor duty, or wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). Thus, rising early and sitting in the morning sun, they would start conversations about each other's hands and feet, saying “This person's hand is beautiful, this person's foot is beautiful,” or about the appearance of women, men, boys, and girls, or other matters concerning the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and existence. They gradually spoke various kinds of “animal talk” (tiracchānakathā), such as talk about kings. Therefore, it was said: “Unnādiniyā uccāsaddamahasaddāya anekavihitaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentiyā.”

Then Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer looked at those wanderers and thought: “These wanderers are very disrespectful to one another. Since the appearance of the ascetic Gotama, we have become like fireflies at sunrise; our gains and honor have also declined. If the ascetic Gotama, or a disciple of Gotama, or a lay follower were to come here, it would be very shameful. The fault of the assembly falls only upon the leader.” While looking here and there, he saw the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said: “Addasa Bhagavန္တံ.”
302:
“If (the Blessed One or his disciples) were to come, it would be very shameful; the fault of the assembly falls only upon the leader.” While looking here and there, he saw the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said: “Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer saw... and they became silent.”

In that passage, “Saṇṭhapesi” means to train or to conceal a fault. It means to make them well-settled. For example, just as a person about to enter an assembly adjusts their lower robe, adjusts their upper robe, and wipes away dust to hide any flaws, similarly, to hide the faults of his assembly, he trained them by saying, “Sirs, be quiet,” and made them well-settled. “Appasaddakāmo” means desiring silence. It refers to sitting alone or standing alone, not living in the company of a group. “Upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyya” means thinking that he should come to this place.

Why did this Poṭṭhapāda desire the Blessed One's arrival? Because he desired his own welfare. It is said that when the Buddha or his disciples come to the wanderers, they boast to their supporters: “Today the ascetic Gotama came to us, the Venerable Sāriputta came; they do not go to just anyone, look at our excellence!” Thus they uplift themselves and place themselves in a high position. They also try to win over the Blessed One's supporters. When they see the Blessed One's supporters, they say: “Your teacher, the Venerable Gotama, and his disciples come to us; we are in harmony with one another. But you do not even want to look at us with your eyes, you do not perform duties; what wrong have we done to you?” Then some people think: “Even the Buddhas go to them, what more is there for us?” From that day on, when they see the wanderers, they treat them with respect. “Tuṇhီ ahesuṃ” means they sat around Poṭṭhapāda without making a sound.

“Svāgataṃ bhante” means “Welcome, Bhante; the Blessed One's arrival is a good arrival.” It shows that “When the Blessed One comes, there is joy for us; when he leaves, there is sorrow.” Why did he say, “Bhante, it has been a long time since you came”? Had the Blessed One ever been there before? No, he had not. However, it is said according to the custom of people's pleasant speech, such as “Where are you going? Where have you come from? Did you lose your way? You have come after a long time.” After saying this, Poṭṭhapāda did not remain stubborn or proud but rose from his seat and went to welcome the Blessed One. Why did he go to welcome him? Because it is rare to find someone who, seeing the Blessed One arrive, does not invite him to a seat or show respect...
303:
Such words are pleasant greetings; therefore, he spoke thus (saying, "Cirassaṃ kho bhante" — "It has been a long time, venerable sir"). After saying this, he did not remain seated stiffly with pride but rose from his seat and went to meet the Blessed One. It is rare for one to see the Blessed One approaching and not invite Him to a seat or show respect. Why? Because of being born into a high caste. This wanderer also dusted off his own seat and invited the Blessed One, saying, "May the Blessed One sit, venerable sir; this seat is prepared."

"What was the conversation that was interrupted?" means, "From the beginning of your sitting until my arrival, what kind of talk were you engaged in? Which talk did not reach its conclusion because of my arrival? Speak, and I shall preach until it reaches its conclusion." Thus, He made the invitation of the All-Knowing One (Sabbaññupavāraṇā). Then the wanderer, wishing to show that "This talk is useless, without essence, and connected only to the round of suffering; it is not worthy to be spoken in the presence of the Blessed One," said, "Let it be, venerable sir," and so on.

## Explanation of the Talk on the Cessation of Higher Perception

"Let it be, venerable sir" means that if the Blessed One wishes to hear it, it will not be difficult to hear that talk later; however, for us, there is no benefit in this talk. He wished to show that, having the opportunity of the Blessed One's arrival, we shall ask about another suitable matter. Then, wishing to ask about that matter, he said, "Venerable sir, those who were in the past," and so on. In that context, "Kotūhalasālā" (The Hall of Curiosity) does not refer to a specific hall named Kotūhalasālā. Rather, it is called Kotūhalasālā because it is a place where ascetics and Brahmins of various sects engage in various kinds of talk, and it is a place where curiosity (kotūhala) arises among the many people who wonder, "What is this person saying? What is that person saying?"

In the term "Abhisaññānirodha," "Abhi" is merely a prefix. "Saññānirodha" means the cessation of the mind, the momentary cessation; this is the meaning of the talk that arose. This is the reason for the arising of that talk: When the Blessed One preaches a Jātaka or prescribes a training rule (sikkhāpada), the fame of the Blessed One spreads throughout the entire Jambudīpa. When the ascetics of other sects hear that sound, they think, "The ascetic Gotama preaches about past practices; why should we not be able to speak such things?" Wishing to emulate the Blessed One, they speak of a doctrine connected to another life. Thinking, "The ascetic Gotama prescribes training rules; why should we not be able to prescribe them?" they prescribe some training rule for their own disciples. At that time...
304:
The Blessed One, seated in the midst of the eight assemblies, preached the talk on cessation (Nirodhakathā — the talk concerning the cessation of perception). When the ascetics of other sects heard this, they gathered and discussed, saying, "The ascetic Gotama preaches a doctrine called cessation; we too shall preach that cessation." Referring to their discussion, it was said, "A talk arose concerning the cessation of higher perception."

"Some of them" (Tatrekacce) refers to some among those people. Among them, the first person was one who had gone forth in a sect outside the Dispensation. Seeing the fault in the activity of the mind, he thought, "The state of being without mind is peaceful," and developed an attainment. After passing away from this human world, he resided in the realm of non-percipient beings (Asaññasatta) for five hundred aeons and was reborn again in this human world. Not seeing the cause for the arising and cessation of perception, he said, "It is without cause, without condition."

The second person, refuting the first, based his view on the state of being without perception of the ascetic Migasiṅga and said, "Perception both approaches and departs." It is said that the ascetic Migasiṅga was one who practiced self-mortification, followed a severe practice, and possessed extremely calm faculties. Due to the power of that ascetic's virtue, the abode of Sakka became hot. Sakka, the king of gods, thought, "Does this ascetic desire my position?" and sent a celestial nymph named Alambusā, saying, "Go and break the ascetic's practice." She went there. On the first day, as soon as the ascetic saw her, he fled and entered his leaf-hut. On the second day, however, overcome by the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), he took her by the hand. Touched by that divine touch, he lost consciousness and regained perception only after three years had passed. That holder of wrong view, thinking, "He emerged from the attainment of cessation after three years," spoke thus.

The third person, refuting him, referred to the practice of the Atharva Veda (Āthabbaṇa) and said, "They both pull perception in and pull it away." It is said that those skilled in the Atharva Veda use that lore to make beings appear as if their heads were cut off, their hands were cut off, or as if they were dead. When that holder of wrong view saw the being return to its normal state, he thought, "This person has emerged from cessation," and spoke thus.

The fourth person, refuting him, referred to the drunken sleep of the Yakkhadāsīs and said, "Indeed, sirs, there are deities," and so on. It is said that the Yakkhadāsīs perform offerings to the deities all night long, dancing and singing. At dawn, they drink a bowl of liquor and fall into a deep sleep, waking up only when it is daytime. Seeing them wake up, the holder of wrong view thought, "While they were asleep, they entered the attainment of cessation, and when they woke up, they emerged from cessation," and spoke thus.
305:
(The goddesses) drink, turn this way and that, sleep, and then rise during the day. Seeing them rise, that person of wrong view, thinking, 'They enter the attainment of cessation while sleeping and emerge from cessation when waking,' spoke thus.

But this wanderer Poṭṭhapāda was of a wise nature. Therefore, upon hearing those words, dissatisfaction arose in his mind. 'The talk of these people is like the talk of fools. They are designating four types of cessation. In reality, cessation should be only one, not many. That single cessation should also be of one kind. That cessation cannot be known by anyone other than the All-Knowing Buddha. If the Blessed One were here, he would make it clear today, as if lighting a thousand lamps, saying "This is cessation, this is not cessation,"' thus he recollected only the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala). Therefore, he spoke the words beginning with 'Tassa mayhaṃ bhante.' In that passage, 'Aho nūna' are two particles used in the sense of recollection. Because of that recollection, this thought occurred to Poṭṭhapāda as he recollected the Blessed One: 'How good it would be if the Blessed One (were here), how good it would be if the Sugata (were here).' 'Yo imesaṃ' means: 'How good it would be if that Blessed One, who is very skillful, subtle, and expert in these dhammas of cessation, would teach; how good it would be if the Sugata would teach.' This is the meaning here. 'Pakataññū' means one who knows the natural state (pakati-sabhāva) due to having practiced and mastered it. The wanderer spoke the words 'Kathaṃ nu kho' wishing to entreat: 'Venerable Sir, we do not know; you know, please teach us.' Then the Blessed One, wishing to teach, spoke the words beginning with 'Tatra Poṭṭhapāda.'

## Commentary on the Explanation of the Arising and Cessation of Perception Without a Cause

In that passage, 'Tatra' means among those recluses and brahmins. 'Āditova tesaṃ aparaddhaṃ' means they have been mistaken from the very beginning; it shows they have slipped even in the middle of the house. In the phrase 'Sahetū sappaccayā,' both 'hetu' and 'paccaya' are names for 'cause.' It means 'with cause.' Wishing to show that cause, he spoke the words beginning with 'Sikkhā ekā.' In that passage, 'Sikkhā ekā saññā uppajjanti' means that some perceptions arise because of the training (sikkhā) that is to be practiced.

When the Blessed One said 'Kā ca sikkhā,' he spoke by way of a question with the desire to elaborate, 'What is that training?' After asking thus...
306:
There are three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Therefore, wishing to show those trainings, and to demonstrate the arising and cessation of perception along with its cause, the Blessed One, setting forth the sequential Dhamma starting from the appearance of a Buddha, spoke the words beginning with 'Idha Poṭṭhapāda, tathāgato loke.' In that text, only the two trainings—higher virtue and higher mind—appear in their own form. As for the third, the training in higher wisdom, it should be understood as being included by way of right view and right intention in this passage: 'Poṭṭhapāda, I have taught this Dhamma which is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā) as a certainty.' 'Kāmasaññā' refers to both the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure and the sensual conduct that has not yet arisen in the first jhāna. Among these two, the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is utterly eradicated by the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). However, the sensual conduct that has not yet arisen is applicable in this context. Therefore, for one possessed of the first jhāna, it is called 'former sensual perception' because it is similar to the sensual perception that arose previously. That sensual perception ceases; it means that the unarisen sensual perception simply does not arise.

At the time of the first jhāna, the subtle perception called rapture and pleasure born of seclusion is manifest and truly exists. Alternatively, because it is subtle due to the abandoning of gross factors such as sensual desire, and it is 'true' (sacca) because it is manifest, it is called 'subtle true perception' (sukhuma-sacca-saññā). Because it is a subtle true perception associated with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, it is called 'subtle true perception of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.' Because that person has that perception, he is called 'one having the subtle true perception of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion' (vivekaja-pītisukha-sukhuma-sacca-saññī). This is how the meaning should be understood here. This method applies everywhere. In the context of 'thus also training' (evampi sikkhā), because one who enters, resolves upon, and emerges from the first jhāna is training, that first jhāna is called 'training' (sikkhā) because it is to be trained in. Through that first jhāna, which is called training, one such subtle true perception of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion arises. It means that one such sensual perception ceases. When the Blessed One said, 'This is a training,' He meant that this first jhāna is one such training. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all places.

Because the contemplation of the eighth attainment by its individual factors (aṅgato) belongs only to the Buddhas; among the disciples, it is not found even in those like Sāriputta. For disciples, there is only contemplation by groups (kalāpato). And this, by way of factors as 'perception, perception'...
307:
The investigation [sammāsana] has been extracted. Therefore, after showing the perception that has the Sphere of Nothingness as its culmination, in order to show that very perception as the "summit of perception," He said: "Poṭṭhapāda... at whatever time... he touches the summit of perception."

In that passage, "Yato kho Poṭṭhapāda bhikkhu" means: Poṭṭhapāda, whatever monk. "In this Dispensation, he is one possessing his own perception" means: in this Dispensation, he possesses perception through his own first jhāna perception. That monk, from that first jhāna to that second jhāna, from there to that third jhāna, thus possessing his own perception through various jhāna perceptions, gradually touches the summit of perception. "Summit of perception" [saññagga] refers to the Sphere of Nothingness [ākiñcaññāyatana]. Why? Because it is the peak of mundane attainments that perform a function. For, established in the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness, they enter the Sphere of Neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of cessation. Thus, because it is the peak of mundane attainments that perform a function, it is called the "summit of perception"; "touches" means he reaches it.

Now, to show the higher cessation of perception [abhisaññānirodha], He said: "To him standing at the summit of perception..." etc. In both terms "ceteyyaṃ" [should intend] and "abhisaṅkhareyyaṃ" [should process], one who enters jhāna is said to "intend" [ceteti], meaning he contemplates repeatedly. One who develops desire for the sake of a higher attainment is said to "process" [abhisaṅkharoti]. "May these perceptions of mine cease" means: may these perceptions of the Sphere of Nothingness cease. "And other gross perceptions arise" means: other gross life-continuum [bhavaṅga] perceptions arise. "He neither intends nor processes"—here, although he might intend, it is as if he does not intend; although he might strive, it is as if he does not strive. For this monk, after emerging from the Sphere of Nothingness and entering the Sphere of Neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no advertence or attention like "I will remain for one or two thought-moments." There is only advertence for the sake of the higher attainment of cessation. This meaning should be understood through the illustration of telling about the son's house.

It is said that if one goes through the middle of the father's house, the son's house is at the back. Taking excellent food from that son's house and coming to the refectory, a senior elder asked a novice: "Where was this pleasant almsfood brought from?" The novice mentioned only the house where he received the food, saying "From such-and-such a person's house." Even though he went through the middle of the father's house...
308:
...just as there was no attention to it in his coming and going. In that analogy, the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness should be seen as the refectory. The attainment of the Sphere of Neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the father's house. The attainment of cessation as the son's house. Just as standing in the refectory, without attending to the father's house, one speaks of the son's house; so too, emerging from the Sphere of Nothingness and entering the Sphere of Neither-perception-nor-non-perception, without attending to the father's house [the Sphere of Neither-perception-nor-non-perception] with the thought "I will remain for one or two thought-moments," there is attention only for the sake of the higher attainment of cessation. Thus, even though this person makes an effort, he does not enter [other objects]; even though he strives for the sake of the higher attainment, he no longer processes [anything else].

"And those perceptions" means those jhāna perceptions cease. "And others" means other gross life-continuum perceptions do not arise. "He touches cessation" means the monk practicing in this way touches, experiences, and attains the cessation of perception and feeling [saññāvedayitanirodha].

In the term "anupubbābhisaññānirodhasampajānasamāpatti," "abhi" is just a prefix. The word "sampajāna" is spoken separated by the word "nirodha." The meaning here is: the attainment of the cessation of perception with clear comprehension occurring in sequence. In such a construction, "sampajānasaññānirodhasamāpatti" has the specific meaning: the attainment of the cessation of perception occurring at the end of wisdom, or the attainment of the cessation of perception of a wise monk.

Now, standing at this point, the discourse on the attainment of cessation should be told. Since that attainment of cessation has been described in all its aspects in the chapter on the benefits of the development of wisdom in the Visuddhimagga, it should be taken from what was said there.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken the discourse on cessation to Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer, in order to make him acknowledge that such a discourse does not exist elsewhere, said: "What do you think?" etc. The wanderer, acknowledging, "Venerable Sir, setting aside Your words today, I have never heard such a discourse before," said, "Not so, Venerable Sir," and then, wishing to show that he had respectfully grasped the Blessed One's words, said, "Thus, Venerable Sir, I..." etc. Then the Blessed One, wishing to approve, saying "It has been well grasped by you," said, "So it is, Poṭṭhapāda."

Then the wanderer thought: "The Blessed One said the Sphere of Nothingness is the summit of perception. Is only this Sphere of Nothingness the summit of perception, or is there a summit of perception in the remaining attainments as well?" Wishing to ask about that matter, he said: "Is it only one?" etc. The Blessed One answered Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer. In the passage beginning with "Is it only one?", "puthူpi" means many. "Whatever... he touches" means by whatever kasiṇa among the earth kasiṇa etc., or by whatever jhāna among the first jhāna etc. If a person, entering the attainment with the earth kasiṇa as the object through the earth kasiṇa as the cause, reaches the cessation of the preceding perception, that perception is one summit of perception. If he enters it twice, thrice, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times, and reaches the cessation of the preceding perception, there are a hundred thousand summits of perception. The same method applies to the remaining kasiṇas and jhānas. If he enters once through the first jhāna as the cause and reaches the cessation of the preceding perception, it is one summit of perception. Twice, thrice, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times...
309:
The Blessed One also answered Poṭṭhapada the wanderer. In that statement, 'puthū' has the meaning of 'many'. 'Poṭṭhapada, in whatever way one touches cessation' means by whichever kasiṇa among the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, or by whichever jhāna among the first jhāna and so forth. This is the intended meaning: if a person, by means of the earth-kasiṇa, enters the earth-kasiṇa attainment once and touches the cessation of the preceding perception, there is one saññagga (peak of perception). If they enter it twice, three times, a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times and touch the cessation of the preceding perception, there are a hundred thousand saññaggas. This same method applies to the remaining kasiṇas. Regarding the jhānas as well, if one touches the cessation of the preceding perception once by means of the first jhāna, there is one saññagga. If they touch the cessation of the preceding perception twice, three times, a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times, there are a hundred thousand saññaggas. This same method applies to the remaining jhāna attainments. Thus, whether by the power of entering once or by grouping all together by the characteristic of perceiving, there is one saññagga. However, by the power of repeated attainments, there are many.

'Venerable Sir, does perception (arise first)?' is a question asked regarding a monk who enters the attainment of cessation: 'Does perception arise first?' To that, the Blessed One answered Poṭṭhapada, 'Poṭṭhapada, perception indeed (arises first).' In that context, 'perception' (saññā) refers to jhāna-perception, and 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) refers to insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). Another method: 'perception' is insight-perception, and 'knowledge' is path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Another method: 'perception' is path-perception, and 'knowledge' is fruition-knowledge (phala-ñāṇa). However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said:

'What are these monks saying? Poṭṭhapada previously asked the Blessed One about the attainment of cessation. Now, wishing to ask about emerging from the attainment of cessation, he says, "Blessed One, for one emerging from the attainment of cessation, does the fruition-perception of Arahantship arise first, or does reviewing-knowledge arise first?" Then, because fruition-perception arises first and reviewing-knowledge arises later, the Blessed One said, "Poṭṭhapada, perception indeed (arises first)." In that statement, the arising of perception is the arising of the fruition-perception of Arahantship, and afterwards, the arising of reviewing-knowledge occurs as "This is the fruition of Arahantship." "Because of this cause, (knowledge arises) to me" means that because of the cause of fruition-concentration-perception, reviewing-knowledge has arisen to me.'

## Commentary on the Perception of Self
Now, the wanderer is like a village pig which, even if bathed with scented water, anointed with perfumes, adorned with garlands, and placed upon a splendid bed...
310:
...does not find happiness, but quickly goes to a place of excrement and finds happiness there. In the same way, although the Blessed One bathed, anointed, and adorned him with the teaching endowed with the three subtle and delicate characteristics, and placed him upon the splendid bed of the discourse on cessation, he did not find happiness in that teaching. Instead, clinging to his own view which is like a pit of excrement, and wishing to ask about that view, he asked, 'Venerable Sir, is perception a man's self?' and so forth. Then, the Blessed One, knowing Poṭṭhapada's intention and wishing to answer, said, 'What kind of self do you posit?' and so forth. Then, although Poṭṭhapada held the view that 'the self is a formless self,' he thought, 'The Blessed One is very skillful in teaching; let him not destroy my view from the very beginning.' Thus, concealing his own view, he said, 'Venerable Sir, there is a gross self,' and so forth. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the fault in that view, said, 'Your gross self...' and so forth. In that text, 'evaṃ santaṃ' means 'this being so.' Here, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. Or, the meaning here is 'according to your wish as you return to a self of such a nature.' Because the four mental aggregates arise together and cease together, whatever perception arises, that very perception ceases. However, starting from the sequential occurrence, it is said, 'Other perceptions arise, and other perceptions cease.'

418-420. Now, wishing to show another view, he said, 'Venerable Sir, I posit a mind-made self,' and so forth. When the fault in that view was also shown—just as a madman, as long as his mindfulness is not established, takes up one thing and discards another, but when his mindfulness is established, speaks only what should be spoken—likewise, after taking up one thing and discarding another, he now spoke his true view, saying, 'Venerable Sir, there is a formless self,' and so forth. In that view also, because Poṭṭhapada accepted the arising and ceasing of perception but regarded the self as eternal, the Blessed One, wishing to show the fault in that same way, said, 'Even this being so...' and so forth. Then, the wanderer, being overwhelmed by wrong view, did not understand the distinction even though the Blessed One taught it, and asked, 'Venerable Sir, is it possible for me to know this?' and so forth. Then, the Blessed One, seeing that Poṭṭhapada, though perceiving the arising and ceasing of perception, still regarded the mind-made self as eternal, said, 'It is difficult to know,' and so forth.

The summary of that statement is: Your view is different, your inclination is different, your preference is different. Your vision occurs in a different way. You can only accept and prefer something else.
311: You have an application in something other than this Dispensation; you are intensely devoted to a practice other than this Dispensation; you have a teacher in something other than this Dispensation; you have the status of a teacher in a different sectarian establishment. For you, who have such a different view, a different inclination, a different preference, a different application, and a different teacher, this matter is difficult to understand. Then the wanderer thought, "Whether the self of a person is perception itself, or whether perception is something else, I will ask him about the eternity and so forth of that self." And again he asked, "How is it, Bhante?" and so forth. In that statement, "world" refers to the self. Poṭṭhapāda... this wrong view is not connected with the welfare of this world or the next world; it is not connected with one's own welfare or the welfare of others. It is not connected with the nine supramundane states. It is not even the beginning of the holy life of the Dispensation consisting of the three trainings, not even the training in higher virtue. It does not lead to disenchantment with the round of rebirths. It does not lead to dispassion for the round. It does not lead to cessation of the round. It does not lead to peace from the round. It does not lead to direct knowledge of the round. It does not lead to enlightenment regarding the round. It does not lead to the realization of the great deathless Nibbāna. In the words "This is suffering" and so forth, it means: excluding craving, the five aggregates existing in the three planes are called "suffering"; craving, which together with its causes brings about that suffering, is called the "origin of suffering"; the non-occurrence of both is called the "cessation of suffering"; and the Noble Eightfold Path is the "practice leading to the cessation of suffering." This is what I have declared. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One thought, "For this wanderer, there is no arising of the Path or realization of the Fruition, and it is time for my alms-round," and he remained silent. The wanderer, perceiving that sign, as if informing the Blessed One of the time for his departure, said, "So it is, Bhante," and so forth. "Vācāsannitodakena" means by the prod of words. "Sañjhabbharimakaṃsu" means they constantly oppressed or struck from above. "Bhūtaṃ" means existing by nature. "Tacchā" and "tathaṃ" are synonyms for that "bhūtaṃ". "Dhammaṭṭhitatā" means...
312:
The state of standing in the nine supramundane dhammas (is called dhammaṭṭhitatā). Dhammaniyāmatā refers to the fixed nature of the nine supramundane dhammas. For the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a discourse that is exempt from the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, that practice is of such a nature.

## Commentary on the Story of Citta Hatthisāriputta and Poṭṭhapāda

Regarding Citta Hatthisāriputta: that Citta was the son of an elephant trainer in Sāvatthī. Having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he learned the Three Piṭakas and became skilled in subtle and profound meanings. However, due to the power of unwholesome kamma performed in a previous life, he became restless and disrobed seven times.

It is said that during the dispensation of the Fully Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, there were two monks who were friends. These monks lived in harmony and recited the scriptures together. Among them, one monk became dissatisfied with the dispensation and, having developed a desire to return to the lay life, informed the other monk. That friend monk, showing the disadvantages of the lay life and the benefits of the monkhood, admonished him. Having heard that advice, he became satisfied in the dispensation again.

On another day, when such dissatisfaction arose again, he said to his friend monk, "Friend, such a thought has arisen in me; I shall give this bowl and robes to you." That monk, out of greed for the bowl and robes, showed the benefits of the lay life and spoke of the disadvantages of the monkhood to that dissatisfied monk. Then, upon hearing those words, that monk became disenchanted with the lay life and remained satisfied only in the monkhood.

Thus, because Citta had previously spoken words about the benefits of the lay life to a virtuous monk, he has now disrobed six times and only on the seventh time remained as a monk. This Citta used to interrupt while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were discussing the Abhidhamma. Then, the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika rebuked him. Citta, unable to abide by the great disciple's admonition, disrobed and became a layman again.

This Citta had been a friend of the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda during his lay life. Therefore, two or three days after disrobing, he went to Poṭṭhapāda. When Poṭṭhapāda saw him, he said, "Friend, what have you done? Why have you withdrawn from the dispensation of such a Teacher? Come, it is now proper for you to go forth," and taking him, he went to the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, "Citta Hatthisāriputta and Poṭṭhapāda the wanderer."

"Blind" (andhā) refers to those who are blind because they lack the eye of wisdom; because of that very absence, they are called "eyeless." "You alone among them are one with eyes" means being one with eyes through the eye of wisdom, which is the mere ability to know what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken. "Definitive" (ekaṃsikā) refers to (dhammas) that have a single portion.
313:
They are called blind (andhā) because they lack the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu). Due to the absence of that very eye of wisdom, they are called eyeless. "You alone among them are the one with vision" means being one with vision through the eye of wisdom, which is the mere ability to distinguish between what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken. Ekāṃsika means having a single portion (definite). Paññatta means those things that are established. Anekāṃsika means not having a single portion; it means not being stated by a single portion as either "eternal" or "non-eternal."

## Ekāṃsikadhamma-vaṇṇanā
424-425. Why did the Blessed One begin this discourse with the words, "Poṭṭhapāda, there are..."? It was to show that the conclusions established by outside sectarians (titthiyas) do not lead to liberation (aniyyānika). All sectarians, just as the Blessed One designates the deathless Nibbāna, designate their own conclusions in their own systems based on the end of the world (the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), and so forth. But that designation does not lead to liberation. The Blessed One spoke thus to show that, as designated, it does not lead out, it does not go [to liberation], but rather, being rejected by the wise, it sinks away. In that context, when asked, "Do you know and see a world of exclusive happiness? Do you live knowing and seeing thus: 'In the eastern direction there is a world of exclusive happiness,' or in the western direction, etc.? Have you ever seen the physical forms of the humans in that world?", they replied, "We have not seen them." Appāṭihīrakata means being devoid of the nature that brings about welfare; it means not leading to liberation (aniyyānika).

426-427. Janapadakalyāṇī (The Belle of the Country) refers to a woman who is incomparable to other women in the district in terms of complexion, figure, grace, deportment, and attire.

## Tayō-attapaṭilābha-vaṇṇanā
Thus, after showing that the conclusions of others do not lead to liberation, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with, "Poṭṭhapāda, there are these three acquisitions of self," to show that His own conclusion leads to liberation. In that passage, attapaṭilābha means the acquisition of an individual form (attabhāva). Here, the Blessed One showed the three planes of existence through the three acquisitions of self. By the gross acquisition of self (oḷārika-attapaṭilābha), He showed the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) starting from the Avīci hell up to the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven. By the mind-made acquisition of self (manomaya-attapaṭilābha), He showed the fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava) starting from the plane of the first jhāna up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world. By the formless acquisition of self (arūpa-attapaṭilābha), He showed the immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava) starting from the Brahma world of the sphere of infinite space up to the Brahma world of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
314:
Defiling states (saṃkilesika-dhamma) refer to the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness (akusala-cittuppāda). Cleansing states (vodāniya-dhamma) refer to tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Fulfillment and abundance of wisdom means the fulfillment and abundance of the wisdom of the Path (magga-paññā) and the wisdom of the Fruition (phala-paññā). Gladness (pāmojja) is tender rapture. Rapture (pīti) is strong joy.

In the statement we made, "Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, he attains and dwells in it," for a monk dwelling thus, there will be that gladness, rapture, tranquility of the mental body (nāma-kāya-passaddhi), well-established mindfulness, supreme knowledge, and a happy dwelling. Among all ways of dwelling, this dwelling alone is fit to be called "peaceful, supremely sweet, and happy." Among those jhānas, in the first jhāna, all six factors starting with gladness are obtained. In the second jhāna, gladness, which is described as weak rapture, ceases, and the remaining five factors are obtained. In the third jhāna, rapture ceases, and the remaining four factors are obtained. The same applies to the fourth jhāna. Among these four jhānas, in the Sampasādana Sutta, only the jhāna as a basis for insight (pādaka-jjhāna) is taught. In the Pāsādika Sutta, insight is taught along with the four Paths. In the Dasuttara Sutta, the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) associated with the fourth jhāna is taught. In this Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, however, gladness is treated as a synonym for rapture, and it should be understood that the attainment of fruition associated with the second jhāna is taught.

432-437. In the phrase "ayaṃ vā so," the word "vā" has the sense of clarification. One should answer by clarifying and explaining thus: "This is that acquisition of self." The meaning is that we do not speak as others do, who, when asked, "Do you perceive a self of exclusive happiness?", say, "No."

Sappāṭihīrakata means bringing about welfare (niyyānika). Mogho hoti means it is empty; the meaning is that the acquisition of self does not exist at that time. Sacco hoti means it is real; the meaning is that only that acquisition of self is true and manifest at that time. Here, because of his lack of omniscience, although Citta spoke of the three acquisitions of self, he was unable to point out that "acquisition of self is a mere designation (paññatti)" and held it only as an acquisition of self. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show that in this context there are only phenomena such as form (rūpa), and that "acquisition of self" is a mere name—that such expressions occur because those various phenomena like form exist—took Citta's own words and spoke the passage beginning with "At whatever time, Citta..." to make him understand by way of name-designation.

Having spoken and questioned in this way to remove doubt and to discipline him, He spoke again starting with, "Citta, if they were to ask you thus..." In that text, [the words] "that which was for me in the past..."
315:
In the statement, "The acquisition of self, at that time my acquisition of self was alone true; the future acquisition of self was void, the present acquisition of self was void," this meaning is first shown: Because those past states do not exist now and have only reached the designation of "having been," therefore, that past acquisition of self of mine was true only at that time. Because the future and present states did not exist then, at that time, he acknowledges the acquisition of self as a mere name in reality, saying, "The future acquisition of self is void, the present acquisition of self is void." The same method applies to the future and present as well.

439-443. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to compare His own explanation with that of Citta, spoke the words beginning with "Even so, Citta," and again, wishing to establish that meaning through a simile, spoke the words beginning with "Citta, just as from a cow comes milk." The summary of the meaning in that simile is as follows: Just as milk comes from a cow, and from milk and so on come curds and so on; at the time when there is milk, it does not reach the designation, expression, name, or usage of "curds" or any of the others like fresh butter. Why? Because of the absence of those states depending on which the usage "curds" and so on occur. Rather, at that time, it only reaches the designation of "milk." Why? Because of the presence of those states depending on which the designation, expression, name, and usage of "milk" occur. This method is the same in all cases.

"Citta, these are" means that these names such as "acquisition of a gross self," "acquisition of a mind-made self," and "acquisition of a formless self" are merely worldly designations, merely worldly labels, merely worldly agreements. Likewise, these words are merely worldly expressions, merely paths of speech, merely usages, and merely designations of names. Thus, the Blessed One, having previously taught the three kinds of acquisition of self, now states that all this is merely usage. Why? Because from the ultimate standpoint, there is no such thing as a "being," and this world is empty and void of a self.

The teachings (kathā) of the Buddhas are of two kinds: conventional teaching (sammutikathā) and ultimate teaching (paramatthakathā). Among them, terms such as "being, person, deity, Brahmā" are called "conventional teaching." Terms such as "impermanence, suffering, non-self, aggregates, elements, sense-bases, foundations of mindfulness, right efforts" are called "ultimate teaching." Between these two, if a person is able to understand, penetrate, escape from the round of suffering, and seize the victory of the fruit of Arahantship when spoken to in terms of "being," "person," "deity," or "Brahmā" through conventional teaching, the Blessed One teaches him from the beginning using terms like "being," "person," "deity," or "Brahmā"...
316:
(If a person) is able to penetrate, to escape from the round of suffering, and to seize the victory of the fruit of Arahantship, the Blessed One teaches him from the very beginning as "a being," "a person," "a deity," or "a Brahmā." If a person is able to understand, penetrate, escape from the round of suffering, and seize the victory of the fruit of Arahantship upon hearing any one of the teachings such as "impermanence" or "suffering" through the ultimate teaching, He teaches him only one of those teachings such as "impermanence" or "suffering."

Likewise, to a being who will understand the Four Noble Truths through conventional teaching, He does not first teach the ultimate teaching. Having made him understand through conventional teaching, He later teaches the ultimate teaching. To a being who will understand the Four Noble Truths through ultimate teaching, He does not first teach the conventional teaching. Having made him understand through ultimate teaching, He later teaches the conventional teaching. By nature, however, the teaching of the Blessed One who teaches the ultimate teaching from the very beginning would be harsh in manner; therefore, the Buddhas first teach the conventional teaching and later teach the ultimate teaching. Even when teaching the conventional teaching, they teach only the truth, only the reality, only the non-falsehood. Even when teaching the ultimate teaching, they teach only the truth, only the reality, only the non-falsehood.

The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers,
Declared two truths:
Convention and the Ultimate;
A third is not found.

The speech of symbols is true,
Based on worldly convention.
The speech of the ultimate is true,
The actual characteristic of phenomena.

"By which the Tathāgata speaks without grasping" means that by those worldly designations and worldly expressions, the Tathāgata speaks without grasping because of the absence of the graspings of craving, conceit, and wrong view. Thus, having turned the discourse, He concluded it with the pinnacle of Arahantship. The remaining words have a clear meaning in all places.

## Thus ends the explanation of the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī.
317:
## 10. Commentary on the Subha Sutta
## Commentary on the Story of Subha Māṇavaka

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ... pe... Sāvatthiyaṃ"—this is the Subha Sutta. In this Subha Sutta, the following is the explanation of the obscure terms. "Shortly after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna" (aciraparinibbute bhagavati) means a time about one month after the Parinibbāna. As stated in the explanation of the introduction (nidāna), this was said in reference to the day when [Venerable Ānanda] arrived in Sāvatthī carrying the Buddha's bowl and robes, and was staying at the monastery after having taken a purgative mixed with milk.

"Todeyyaputta" means the son of the Brahmin named Todeyya. It is said that there was a village named Tudi not far from Sāvatthī; because he was the head of that village, he came to be known as "Todeyya." That Brahmin possessed great wealth amounting to forty-five crores, yet he was extremely stingy. Thinking, "There is no such thing as the non-depletion of wealth for one who gives (i.e., wealth can be exhausted)," he gave nothing to anyone. He even instructed his son:

"Seeing the depletion of collyrium,
The accumulation of anthills,
And the gathering of honey,
A wise man should manage his household."

Having thus taught only the practice of non-giving (adāna), when his body broke up, he was reborn as a dog in that very house. Subha the young man was extremely fond of that dog. He fed it only the same rice he ate himself and would lift it up to sleep on a magnificent bed.

Then one day, while the young man was out of the house, the Blessed One entered that house for alms. Seeing the Blessed One, the dog went near him and barked. Then the Blessed One said to it, "Todeyya, in the past you also insulted me by saying 'Hey, you!' and were reborn as a dog; now you bark again and will go to the Avīci hell." Hearing these words, the dog felt remorse and went to sleep in the pile of ashes between the tripod legs of the stove. The people were unable to lift the dog and make it sleep on the bed.

When Subha the young man returned, he asked, "Who removed this dog from the bed?" The people replied, "No one did," and told him the whole story. Hearing this, the young man became angry, thinking, "My father was reborn in the Brahma realm, but the ascetic Gotama claims my father has become a dog; this ascetic says whatever comes to his mouth." Wishing to accuse the Blessed One of lying, he went to the monastery and inquired about the matter. The Blessed One spoke to the young man just as before, and to ensure there was no doubt, He asked, "Young man, is there any wealth that your father did not tell you about?"

He replied, "Venerable Gotama, there is a golden necklace worth a hundred thousand, golden sandals worth a hundred thousand, a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, and a hundred thousand coins."

"Go then," the Blessed One said, "feed that dog milk-porridge with very little water, place it on the bed, and when it is slightly asleep, ask it. It will tell you everything. Then you will know, 'This is indeed my father.'" Subha the young man did exactly as the Blessed One instructed, and the dog revealed all the wealth. At that time, knowing "This dog is my father," he gained faith in the Blessed One, went to Him, and asked fourteen questions. At the conclusion of the answers, he took refuge in the Blessed One...
318:
Subha the young man, wishing to accuse the Blessed One of lying, went to the monastery and inquired about the matter. The Blessed One spoke to the young man in that very same way, and to ensure there was no doubt, He said, "Young man, is there any wealth that your father did not tell you about?" He replied, "Venerable Gotama, there is a golden flower (necklace) worth a hundred thousand, golden sandals worth a hundred thousand, a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, and a hundred thousand coins." "Go then, feed that dog milk-porridge with little water, place it on the bed, and when it is slightly asleep, ask it; it will tell you everything. Then you will know, 'This is indeed my father.'" The young man did so. The dog told him everything. Then, knowing "This is indeed my father," he gained faith in the Blessed One, went to Him, and asked fourteen questions. At the conclusion of the answers, he reached the state of taking refuge in the Blessed One. In reference to this, it is said, "Subha the young man, the son of Todeyya." "Lives in Sāvatthī" means he came from his own revenue-village and resided there.

445-446. "He addressed a certain young man" means that after the Teacher's Parinibbāna, hearing that "Venerable Ānanda has arrived carrying the Blessed One's bowl and robes, and the great multitude is approaching to see him," [Subha] thought, "It is not possible to converse comfortably or listen to a Dhamma talk in the midst of a great crowd by going to the monastery. Only when he comes to the house will I see him and converse comfortably. Moreover, I have a doubt; I will ask Venerable Ānanda about that doubt." Thus he addressed a certain young man.

In the words beginning with "appābādha," "ābādha" (illness) refers to painful feelings that arise in one part of the body and afflict the four postures as if they were bound with iron plates; the question asks about the absence of such feelings. "Appātaṅka" (free from disease) refers to a disease that makes life difficult; the question also asks about the absence of such disease. For a sick person, rising is heavy and there is no strength in the body; therefore, the question asks about being free from illness and having strength. "Phāsuvihāra" (comfortable living) refers to living happily in the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying. Then, wishing to show the manner in which the young man should inquire, [the text] says "Subha," and so on.

"Depending on the time and occasion" (kālañca samayañca upādāya) means grasping and considering the time and occasion with wisdom. It means: "If tomorrow is the time for us to go, and if there is sufficient strength in the body, and if because of the journey, other..."
319:
If there was no exhaustion from traveling, considering the coincidence of the cause of going and the time, it means "we shall come tomorrow."

The monk named Cetaka is so called because he was born in the Cetī country. Pleasant and memorable talk means: "Venerable Ānanda, what kind of illness did the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) have? What kind of alms-food did the Blessed One partake of? Indeed, did sorrow arise in you because of the Teacher's Parinibbāna? The Teacher did not attain Parinibbāna for you alone; it is a great loss for the whole world including the devas. Who now can escape from death? Even the supreme person in the world with its devas has attained Parinibbāna. Seeing whom will the King of Death now be ashamed?" After exchanging such pleasant and memorable talk related to death in this manner, he offered the Elder food suitable for the medicine he had taken yesterday, and when the meal was finished, he sat to one side.

An attendant who stays near means one who is an attendant and stays nearby, not a fault-finder. Nor is he one with the intention of testing. "One who practices nearby" is just a synonym for the previous term. Why did the youth Subha ask? It is said that he had this thought: "The Venerable Gotama established this world in certain dhammas; have those dhammas disappeared after the passing of the Venerable Gotama, or do they still exist? If they exist, Ānanda will know; let me ask him." Therefore, he asked.

Then the Elder Ānanda, wishing to show the three Pitakas by grouping them into three aggregates (khandhas), said, "These three aggregates," and so on. The youth, unable to grasp what was said in brief, thought, "I will ask in detail," and asked again, "What are those three?" and so on.

## Sīlakkhandhavaṇṇanā

450-453. Then, when the Elder showed "the Noble Aggregate of Virtue" (ariya sīlakkhandha), he asked one by one, "Venerable Ānanda, what is that Noble Aggregate of Virtue?" The Elder, showing the arising of the Buddha and preaching the Dhamma, answered everything in sequence, just as the Blessed One had taught. In that context—
320:
"There is still something further to be done in this teaching"—in this statement, in the teaching of the Blessed One, virtue alone is not the essence; this virtue is merely the foundation. He showed that there is indeed something else to be done above this virtue. "Outside of this teaching" means outside of the Buddha's teaching (referring to recluses and brahmins of other sects).

## Samādhikkhandhavaṇṇanā

"Young man, how is a monk one who has the doors of his senses guarded?"—even though the Venerable Ānanda was thus asked about the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha) with the question "Venerable Ānanda, what is that Noble Aggregate of Concentration?", he began by pointing out the dhammas that are beneficial to both virtue and concentration, such as sense-restraint (indriyasaṃvara), which come immediately after virtue, saying "one possessed of virtue, one who has the doors of his senses guarded, one possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, one who is content." Having explained these, he began with the desire to show the aggregate of concentration. In this Subha Sutta, only the fine-material jhānas (rūpajjhāna) appear, not the immaterial jhānas (arūpajjhāna). However, the immaterial jhānas should be brought in and explained. This is because there is no immaterial attainment (arūpasamāpatti) that is not included within the fourth jhāna.

471-480. "There is still something further to be done in this teaching"—in this statement, in the teaching of the Blessed One, there is no such thing as reaching the end merely by one-pointedness of mind; he shows that there is indeed something else to be done above this concentration. "There is nothing further to be done in this teaching"—in this statement, in the teaching of the Blessed One, there is nothing more to be done beyond this Fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala); he shows that the teaching of the Blessed One has the Fruit of Arahatship as its conclusion. All the remaining words have clear meanings.

## Thus ends the Commentary on the Subha Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī.
321:
## 11. Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta
## Commentary on the Story of Kevaṭṭa, the Householder's Son
The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "Nāḷandāyaṃ" is the Kevaṭṭa Sutta. In this sutta, the explanation of terms not previously mentioned is as follows: "Pāvārikambavane" means in the mango grove of the wealthy merchant Pāvārika. "Kevaṭṭo" is the name of that householder's son. It is said that this householder's son named Kevaṭṭa was a great wealthy householder (gahapati-mahāsāla) possessing forty crores of wealth, and he was extremely faithful and devoted to the Triple Gem. Due to his excessive faith, he thought: "If a monk were to fly into the sky and perform various miracles (pāṭihāriya) once every fortnight, or once a month, or once a year, all the people would become greatly devoted. It would be good if I were to request the Blessed One to allow a monk to perform such miracles." Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One and spoke in this manner.

In that request, "iddhā" means that this city of Nāḷandā is prosperous. "Phītā" means it has reached a state of flourishing and abundance due to the many kinds of goods and wealth. "Ākiṇṇamanussā" means it is crowded with people moving about as if rubbing shoulder to shoulder. "Samādisatu" means 'please command' or 'please appoint to a position.'
