"Uttari-manussadhamma" refers to states beyond human nature, or states superior to the human Dhamma consisting of the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha). "Bhiyyosomattāya" means they will become excessively devoted, just as a lamp that is already bright by nature shines even more intensely when it receives the essence of oil. The reason the Blessed One said "Na kho ahaṃ" (I do not...) is that He had already prescribed a training rule (sikkhāpada) in the story of the Rajagaha merchant; therefore, He spoke beginning with "Na kho ahaṃ."

"Na dhaṃsemi" means 'I do not destroy by ruining virtues.' It means He does not cause one to fall from a high position to a low one by causing a breach of morality (sīla). Rather, it shows that he (Kevaṭṭa) was saying, "I speak because I desire the growth of the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana)." Regarding "Tatiyampi kho," there is no one who dares to speak in opposition to the words of the Buddhas up to three times. However, because this householder's son was very intimate with the Blessed One, he increased that intimacy, became a favorite, and thinking "I am one who desires [the Buddha's] welfare," he spoke for the third time.

## Commentary on the Miracle of Psychic Power
483-484. Then the Blessed One thought: "This lay follower continues to entreat Me repeatedly even though I refuse him. Now, I shall show this lay follower the danger (ādīnava) of performing miracles."
322:
Having thought thus, He spoke the words beginning with "Tīṇi kho." In that text, "amāhaṃ bhikkhu" should be resolved as "amum ahaṃ bhikkhuṃ" (I [to] this monk). "Gandhārī" refers to an art made by a seer (rishi) named Gandhara, or an art that originated in the Gandhara kingdom. It is said that many seers lived in that Gandhara kingdom, and the meaning is that it was an art created by one of those seers. "Aṭṭīyāmi" means 'I feel as if I am being oppressed.' "Harāyāmi" means 'I am ashamed.' "Jigucchāmi" means 'I feel disgust, as if seeing excrement.'

## Commentary on the Miracle of Mind-reading
"Parasattānaṃ" means 'of other beings.' The second term is merely a synonym (vevacana) of the first. "Ādisati" means 'he tells' or 'he declares.' "Cetasikaṃ" refers to the feelings of joy (somanassa) and grief (domanassa). "Evampi te mano" means 'thus is your mind,' whether it is associated with joy, grief, or thoughts of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka), and so on. The second term is also a synonym. "Itipi te cittaṃ" means 'thus is your thought,' in the sense that your mind arises thinking of such and such a meaning. The art named "Maṇikā" refers to an art in the world known as "Cintāmaṇi." It is shown that one can know the minds of others through that art.

## Commentary on the Miracle of Instruction
"Evaṃ vitakketha" means 'think thus,' by bringing forth thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) and the like. "Mā evaṃ vitakkayittha" means 'do not think thus,' by bringing forth thoughts of sensual desire and the like. "Evaṃ manasi karotha" means 'attend thus,' to the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) or to any one of the perceptions such as suffering (dukkha-saññā). "Mā evaṃ" means 'do not attend' in the way of permanence (nicca) and so on. "Idaṃ" means 'abandon this' lust (rāga) for the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Idaṃ upasampajja" means 'attain this' supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) consisting of the four paths and four fruits, and having reached and accomplished it, dwell therein. In this way, the Blessed One showed the various psychic transformations as the "miracle of psychic power" (iddhipāṭihāriya). He showed the speaking after knowing another's mind as the "miracle of mind-reading" (ādesanāpāṭihāriya). He showed the constant preaching of the Dhamma by the disciples and the Buddhas as the "miracle of instruction" (anusāsanīpāṭihāriya).

Among those miracles, performing the miracle of instruction by means of the miracle of psychic power was the habit of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Performing the miracle of instruction by means of the miracle of mind-reading was the habit of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. When Devadatta split the Sangha and took five hundred monks to Gayāsīsa, preaching the Dhamma to them in the manner of a Buddha, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta—one of the two chief disciples sent by the Blessed One—preached the Dhamma after knowing the mental inclinations of those five hundred monks. Upon hearing the Dhamma of Venerable Sāriputta, the five hundred monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Then, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna preached the Dhamma while displaying various psychic powers. Upon hearing that Dhamma, all those monks were established in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala).

Then the two chief disciples, who were Great Nagas (noble beings), took the five hundred monks and, flying through the sky, returned to the Veḷuvana Monastery. The miracle of instruction is the constant preaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas. Among these three miracles, the miracle of psychic power and the miracle of mind-reading are subject to reproach and are blameworthy. Long...
323:
(Venerable Sāriputta) preached; having heard the Elder's Dhamma teaching, five hundred monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Then, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having repeatedly displayed various psychic transformations, preached the Dhamma to them; having heard that teaching, all those monks were established in the fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala). Then, both Chief Disciples, taking the five hundred monks, rose into the air and returned to the Veluvana Monastery. The miracle of instruction (Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya) is the constant Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas. Among these miracles, the miracle of psychic power (Iddhi-pāṭihāriya) and the miracle of mind-reading (Ādesanā-pāṭihāriya) are associated with oppression and are faulty; they do not endure for a long time, and because they do not endure, they do not lead to liberation (from Saṃsāra). However, the miracle of instruction is without danger and without fault; it endures for a long time, and because it endures, it leads to liberation. Therefore, the Blessed One censures the miracle of psychic power and the miracle of mind-reading, and praises only the miracle of instruction.

## Commentary on the Story of the One Seeking the Cessation of Elements (Bhūtanirodhesakavatthuvaṇṇanā)
Why did the Blessed One begin with the words "Bhūtapubbaṃ" (In the past)? He did so to show the non-liberating nature of the miracle of psychic power and the miracle of mind-reading, and to show the liberating nature of the miracle of instruction alone. Furthermore, in the time of all Buddhas, there is always a certain monk who searches for the place where the great elements (mahābhūta) cease. That monk, while searching for the cessation of the great elements, wanders as far as the Brahma world, and not finding anyone capable of answering the question, he returns and asks the Buddha alone, thereby becoming free from doubt. Therefore, to manifest the greatness of the Buddhas, and because this matter was hidden, the Blessed One, wishing to reveal and preach this hidden cause, said "Bhūtapubbaṃ," and so on.

In that passage, "Kattha nu kho" (Where indeed?) means: In what place, based on what, and for one who has attained what state, do these great elements cease without remainder (by way of non-arising)? As for this discussion on the great elements, it has been stated in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, it should be understood from that text alone.

"Devayāniyo maggo" (The path leading to the gods) means there is no separate physical road called the path to the celestial realm; rather, this is a designation for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (Iddhividha-ñāṇa). By means of that knowledge, this monk, making his body follow his will, can go to the celestial realm even as far as the Brahma world. Therefore, that knowledge is called "the path leading to the gods." "Yena Cātumahārājikā" (Where the Four Great Kings are) means that without asking the Blessed One who was nearby, being urged by the nature of things (dhammatā), and thinking that the deities possess great power, he approached them. "We too do not know, monk" means in the range of the Buddhas...
324:
The deities, having been asked the question, did not know; therefore, they spoke thus (stating their ignorance). Then that monk pressured and harassed those deities, saying, "You are unable to answer this question of mine; answer it quickly!" and asked them repeatedly. Those deities thought, "This monk is harassing us; come, let us release ourselves from his hands," and said, "Monk, there are the Four Great Kings," and so on. In that text, 'Abhikkantatarā' means those who possess particularly transcendent power and wisdom. 'Paṇītatarā' means those who are particularly noble in terms of appearance, retinue, and sovereignty. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

491-493. The following point is a special distinction. It is said that Sakka, the king of gods, thought: "This question is only within the range of the Buddhas; no one other than a Buddha is able to answer it. This monk, like one who abandons a fire to blow on a firefly, or like one who abandons a great drum to beat his own belly, wanders about asking deities, having abandoned the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the Supreme Person in the world. I shall send him to the presence of the Teacher." Then again, Sakka thought: "Even if he goes very far, he will only become free from doubt in the presence of the Teacher. Such a person indeed exists; let him wander a bit and be exhausted first, then he will know later." Therefore, he said to that monk, "I too..." and so on. Brahmayāniya (the vehicle to the Brahma world) is just like Devayāniya (the vehicle to the celestial realm). Whether called 'Devayāniyamagga', 'Brahmayāniyamagga', 'Dhammasetū' (the bridge of Dhamma), 'Ekacittakkhaṇika-appanā' (one-moment absorption), 'Sanniṭṭhānika-cetanā' (decisive volition), 'Mahaggata-citta' (exalted mind), or 'Abhiññā-ñāṇa' (supernormal knowledge)—all these are names for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (Iddhividha-ñāṇa) alone.

'Pubbanimittaṃ' means the sign that appears prior to the arrival. Just as the rising of the dawn before the sun rises is a sign that the sun is about to appear. Therefore, they showed, "Even now the Brahma is about to arrive; thus we know." 'Pāturahosi' means it became manifest. Then that Brahma, having been questioned by that monk and knowing that it was not within his own range, thought: "If I say 'I do not know,' these deities will despise me. If I say something as if I know, this monk, being dissatisfied with my explanation, will find fault with me. Moreover, no one will believe my words if I say 'Monk, I am Brahma,' and so on. It would be better if I were to deflect the question and send this monk to the presence of the Teacher." Having thought thus, he said, "Monk, I am Brahma," and so on.
325:
495-496. In the phrase "stepping aside to one side," why did he do this? It was because of deceitfulness. "Seeking outside" means that just as a person desiring oil might squeeze sand, he reaches the point of searching outside as far as the Brahma-world. "Sakuna" refers to a crow or a hawk. Why did the Blessed One say, "Bhikkhu, this question should not be asked in this way"? Because this question should be asked only in part, but this monk, including even the elements born of temperature (utuja-rūpa), asked it without remainder; therefore, the Buddha prohibited it. It is the custom of the Buddhas to show the fault in the question to a person confused about asking, teach the method of questioning, and then answer the question. Why? Because it is difficult to make someone understand if they ask without knowing how to ask. Desiring to teach the question, He said, "Where do the elements of water..." and so on.

There, "na gādhati" means not standing. The meaning is: "Depending on what do these four great elements have no footing?" He asks with reference only to clung-to matter (upādinnaka-rūpa). By the two terms "long and short" (dīghañca rassañca), He spoke of derived matter (upādā-rūpa) by way of shape. By "small and large" (aṇuṃ thūlaṃ), He spoke only of the color/appearance within derived matter. By "beautiful and ugly" (subhāsubhaṃ), He also spoke of derived matter. Is there actually beauty or ugliness in derived matter? No. He spoke only with reference to desirable and undesirable objects. "Name and form" (nāmañca rūpañca) refers to mentality and materiality, which is divided into "long" and so on. "Uparujjhati" means to cease. The meaning is: "Depending on what does this name and form cease without remainder?"

Having shown the way to ask, "Thus should the question be asked," He now wishes to show the answer, and saying, "There is an explanation for that," He said "Viññāṇa" and so on.

There, it is called "Viññāṇa" because it is to be known (vijānitabba). This is a name for Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is called "anidassana" (invisible) because it cannot be seen by eye-consciousness. It is called "ananta" (infinite) because it has no limit in terms of arising, falling away, or change while persisting. The word "pabha" is a name for a ford (landing place). It is called "papa" because beings descend there; the letter "pa" is changed to "ba". "Sabbatopabhaṃ" means Nibbāna which has fords on all sides. Just as in the great ocean, wherever one wishes to descend, that very place is called a ford, and there is no place that is not a ford; likewise, among the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), by whichever entrance one wishes to enter Nibbāna, that very meditation subject is called a ford. There is no such thing as a non-ford in Nibbāna. Therefore, He said "sabbatopabhaṃ". "Ettha āpo ca" means...
326:
In this Nibbāna, with Nibbāna as the object, all these clung-to phenomena (upādinnaka-dhamma) mentioned by way of "water" and so on, cease; they come to a state of non-occurrence.

Now, wishing to show the cause for the cessation of those clung-to phenomena, He said, "With the cessation of consciousness, all this ceases here in this Nibbāna." In that text, "consciousness" (viññāṇa) refers to both the final consciousness (carimaka-viññāṇa) and the kamma-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa). For, with the cessation of the final consciousness, all this ceases here in this Nibbāna. It reaches a state that cannot be designated, like the flame of a lamp when the wick is exhausted. Also, with the cessation of the kamma-formative consciousness by way of non-arising, it ceases by way of non-occurrence. As it is said: "With the cessation of the kamma-formative consciousness through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, the name and form that would have arisen in the beginningless saṃsāra, excluding seven lives, cease here in this Nibbāna." All this should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Cūḷaniddesa. The rest of the words are clear in all places.

## Thus the Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta
## in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī is finished.
327:
## 12. Lohiccasutta-vaṇṇanā
## Commentary on the Story of Lohicca the Brahmin

"Thus have I heard... among the Kosalans"—this is the Lohicca Sutta. Herein is the explanation of the obscure terms. "Sālavatikā" is the name of that village. It is said that it was surrounded on all sides by rows of Sal trees, as if by a fence. Therefore, it is called Sālavatikā. "Lohicca" is the name of that Brahmin.

502-503. "Pāpakaṃ" (evil) refers to a low view because it is devoid of compassion for others; it does not refer to either annihilationism or eternalism. "Uppannaṃ hoti" means it has arisen. It was not merely born in his mind; that Brahmin used to speak in this way even in the midst of an assembly by the power of that view. "Kiñhi paro parassa" means: one person is exhorted by another; what benefit can that person who is exhorted provide to the exhorter? He says that one should live by respecting and honoring only the wholesome state (kusala dhamma) that one has attained oneself.

504-507. In the passage "He addressed Rosika the barber," he addressed the barber who received the name "Rosikā" by way of the feminine gender. It is said that when that barber heard of the Blessed One's arrival, he thought: "Going to the monastery to see Him is a burden; I will invite Him to my house and see Him, and I will offer alms-food for visiting monks as much as I am able." Therefore, he had the barber called in this way.

"Piṭṭhito piṭṭhito" (closely behind) means following behind and behind for the sake of ease of conversation. "Vivacetu" means to release; he says, "May He dispel that wrong view." It is said that this lay follower (upāsaka) was a dear friend of Lohicca the Brahmin. Therefore, out of a desire for the Brahmin's welfare, he spoke thus. In the passage "Appeva nāma siyā," with the first statement, the Blessed One roars; with the second statement, He roars again. The intention here is: "Rosika, for this very purpose—to dispel the wrong views of others—I fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) by performing various difficult deeds for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons. For this very purpose, I penetrated the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). It is not a burden for me to break the wrong view of Lohicca." Wishing to show this meaning, the Blessed One roared with the first statement. "Rosika, of the mere Lohicca...
328:
“Rosika, let Lohicca come to me, or sit, or engage in conversation. Even if a hundred thousand brahmins like Lohicca had doubts, I am capable of dispelling their wrong views. What burden would it be for me to dispel the view of Lohicca alone?” It should be understood that the Blessed One proclaimed this for the second time, wishing to show this meaning.

## Commentary on the Questioning of Lohicca the Brahmin

“Samudayasañjāti” means the arising of the mass of wealth, the production of riches. “Tato uṭṭhitaṃ dhanaññanyaṃ” refers to the wealth and grain arising therefrom. “Ye taṃ upajīvanti” refers to those people such as relatives, attendants, slaves, and workers who live depending on you. “Antarāyakaro” means one who creates an obstacle to gain. In the word “hitānukampī”, “hita” means welfare (prosperity). One is called “anukampī” because of being compassionate; it means one who desires welfare. The meaning is whether one desires welfare or not. “Nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā” means that if that wrong view is perfected and becomes a fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi), one is certainly reborn in hell; if not, one is reborn in the animal realm.

510-512. Now, because beings are aware of obstacles to their own gain but not so of obstacles to others' gain, the Blessed One spoke the second reason beginning with “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi” (What do you think?), wishing to make the brahmin understand well. “Ye cime” should be resolved as “ye ca ime”. Those clansmen who, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata, are not yet able to enter the noble plane (ariya-bhūmi), obtain “dibbā gabbhā” (divine wombs/conceptions). “Dibbā gabbhā” is a designation for the six deva worlds. “Paripācenti” means they mature, bring to fruition, and bring to completion [their practice] by fulfilling the practice leading to the deva world, such as giving gifts, observing virtue, making offerings with perfumes and garlands, and developing meditation. “Dibbānaṃ bhavānaṃ abhinibbattiya” means for the purpose of the arising of the divine mansions of the devas. Alternatively, “dibbā gabbhā” refers to special merits such as giving. “Dibbā bhavā” refers to the resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandhā) in the deva world. The meaning is that they perform those merits for the arising of those resultant aggregates. “Tesaṃ antarāyakaro” means one who creates an obstacle to their attainment of the path, the attainment of the fruit, and the special divine existences.
329:
## Commentary on the Three Teachers Worthy of Reproach

By this much, the Blessed One, through this indefinite method of similes, having broken the pride of the brahmin which had risen as high as the peak of existence (bhavagga), now spoke the words beginning with “Lohicca, there are these three [teachers in my dispensation]” in order to show the three teachers worthy of reproach. In that text, “codanā” refers to the act of reproaching by one who criticizes the three teachers. “Na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapenti” means they do not apply their minds for the sake of understanding. “Vokkammā” means they practice by deviating from that teacher’s instruction, not following it continuously. “Osakkantiyā vā ussakkeyya” means it is like one who would approach a woman who is withdrawing (unwilling), or like one who desires union with a woman who does not desire it. “Parammuhkiṃ vā āliṅgeyya” means it is like going from behind and embracing someone who stands turning away, not even wishing to look. “Evaṃsampadamidaṃ” means although these disciples practice by deviating from the instruction, this teacher still teaches them out of greed, thinking “these are my disciples”; therefore, I call this greedy nature something like this (like embracing one who turns away). Thus, your greedy nature of such a kind deserves that reproach because it is like approaching one who withdraws unwillingly or embracing one who turns away. “Kiñhi paro parassa karissati” means: in whatever Dhamma you instruct others, first make yourself perfect and upright in that Dhamma. It is worthy of the reproach: “What can another do for another?”

“Niddāyitabbāṃ” means that grass which resembles crops should be weeded out to make the field pure.

In the third reproach, “kiñhi paro parassa” means that from the time the instruction is not accepted, should another be instructed? What will he do for the other who is the instructor? Is it not that one should then become indifferent (appossukka), and dwell honoring and worshipping only the Dhamma that one has personally realized? This is the meaning of how it deserves reproach.
330:
## Commentary on the Teacher Not Deserving Reproof

"Na codanāraho" means that because this teacher first establishes himself in proper practice and then teaches the Dhamma to his disciples. The disciples also listen to that teacher and practice according to the instruction; because of such practice, they attain great distinction. Therefore, he does not deserve reproof.

"Narakapapātaṃ papatanto" means "I am one who is falling into the abyss of hell due to the wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) I have held." "Uddharitvā thale patiṭṭhāpito" means that by destroying that wrong view and by the hand of the Dhamma teaching, he is lifted out of falling into the lower realms (apāya) and placed upon the dry land of the path to the heavenly realms. The remaining words in this sutta are clear.

## In the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,
## the Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta is finished.
331:
## 13. Commentary on the Tevijja Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ..." etc., "in the Kosala country"—this is the Tevijja Sutta. In this Tevijja Sutta, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: "Manasākaṭa" is the name of that village. "To the north of Manasākaṭa" means in the northern direction, not far from the village of Manasākaṭa. "In the Mango Grove" means in a grove of young mango trees. That area of ground is said to be delightful. Below, sand similar to silver plates is scattered. Above, there is a mango grove with thick branches and leaves like a jeweled canopy. It means [the Buddha] dwells in that mango grove, which possesses the bliss of seclusion suitable for Buddhas.

"Famous" refers to those who are well-known in various places due to their accomplishments in lineage, conduct, and so on. "Caṅkī" and others are the names of those Brahmins. Among them, the Brahmin Caṅkī lives in Opāsāda. The Brahmin Tārukkha lives in the district of Icchānaṅgala. The Brahmin Pokkharasāti lives in the city of Ukkaṭṭha. The Brahmin Jāṇusoṇီ lives in the city of Sāvatthī. The Brahmin Todeyya lives in the village of Tudi. "And others" means many other people also come from their respective residences and live in that mango grove for the purpose of reciting and chanting the Vedas. Because of the pleasantness of the village of Manasākaṭa, those Brahmins had houses built on the riverbank and fenced them in, preventing many others from entering, and they go and stay there from time to time.

520-521. "Of Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja" refers to the words of Vāseṭṭha, a student of Pokkharasāti, and Bhāradvāja, a student of Tārukkha. These two, being of noble birth, reached the end of the three Vedas. "Walking for exercise" (jaṅghavihāra) means walking on foot to dispel the fatigue caused by sitting for a very long time. Having recited [the Vedas] all day, they rose in the evening, had their attendants bring the necessary materials for bathing—perfumes, flowers, oil, and washed clothes—and desiring to bathe, they went to the riverbank and walked back and forth on the sand plain, which was as white as silver plates. When one walked, the other followed; then when the other walked, the first one followed. Therefore, it is said, "walking back and forth, wandering about." "On the path and the non-path" means on what is the path and what is not the path. It means they started a conversation concerning the path and non-path, such as, "By fulfilling what practice and by which path can one go happily to the Brahma world?" "Añjasāyana" is a synonym for a straight path.
332:
"Añjasāyana" is the name of a straight path. Alternatively, by this path, one arrives or comes straight to the Brahma world. Because it has the power to lead there, that path is called "Añjasāyana". "Niyyāniko niyyāti" means the one who goes out, goes out; the one who goes, goes.

"Takkara's companionship with Brahma" means for the one who performs or practices that path, it leads to being with Brahma, to appearing in the same Brahma realm. "Yvāyaṃ" is "yo ayaṃ" (this which). "Akkhāto" means preached or shown. With the words "by the Brahmin Pokkharasāti," Vāseṭṭha refers to his own teacher. Thus, Vāseṭṭha wanders about praising and upholding only his teacher's doctrine. Bhāradvāja also does the same for his own [teacher's doctrine]. Therefore, it is said, "Vāseṭṭha was not able," and so on.

Then Vāseṭṭha thought, "The words of both of us do not lead to the goal. In this world, there is no one like the Venerable Gotama who is skilled in the path. The Venerable Gotama is also staying nearby. He will cut off our doubt like a merchant sitting with a pair of scales." Having thought thus, he informed Bhāradvāja of the matter, and both went and reported their conversation to the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, "Then Vāseṭṭha... this which was preached by the Brahmin Tārukkha."

"Here, O Gotama" means in this matter of path and non-path. In "dispute and contention" (viggaho vivādo), etc., the initial dispute is called "viggaha". The subsequent dispute is called "vivāda". Both these views are called "nānāvāda" (various doctrines) because they are the doctrines of different teachers.

"Then in what [is your dispute]?" means "You also stand upholding only your teacher's doctrine, saying 'This alone is the path.' Bhāradvāja also stands upholding only his teacher's doctrine. There is no doubt in one about the other's [position]. This being so, in what does your dispute lie?"—this is the question.

"On the path and non-path, O Gotama" means "O Gotama, we dispute on the path and the non-path, on the straight path and the non-straight path." It is said that this Brahmin does not say "it is not a path" even to the path of another Brahmin. However, just as his teacher's path is a straight path, he does not acknowledge the paths of others as straight paths. Therefore, desiring to show that matter, [the Buddha] said, "Although, O Gotama," and so on. "Sabbāni tāni" is said with a change of gender, meaning "all those paths." "Many" (bahūni) means there are eight paths or ten paths. "Various paths" (nānāmaggāni) means many different kinds of paths, such as elephant paths, cart-merchants' paths, etc., which come from rivers, lakes, fields, etc., within the village and enter the village.

## Opening of the Questioning of the Youth Vāseṭṭha

525. With these words, "Vāseṭṭha, you say they lead out," the Blessed One spoke three times to make Vāseṭṭha give his assent. Why did He make him assent by speaking three times? Because when kings are oppressed even after giving their assent, they tend to deny it. Therefore, thinking that if this Vāseṭṭha assents three times, he will not be able to deny it, He made him assent by speaking three times.

527-29. "Tevijjā" refers to those Brahmins. The letter "va" is merely an euphonic insertion (āgamasandhi). "Andhaveṇī" means a line of blind men (andhapaveṇī).
333:
"Bahūni" means eight or ten paths. "Nānāmaggāni" refers to various kinds of paths, such as elephant paths and cart paths, which come from places near a village like rivers, lakes, and fields, and enter the village.

## Explanation of the Inquiry to the Youth Vāseṭṭha

525-526. "Vāseṭṭha, do you say (these paths) lead to liberation?" Thus the Blessed One made him admit it by speaking three times. Why? Because sectarians (titthiyas), after admitting something, tend to deny it when they are later refuted. Thinking that if Vāseṭṭha admits it three times, he will not be able to deny it, the Buddha made him admit it three times.

527-529. "Te tevijjā" refers to those Brahmins who bear the three Vedas. The letter "va" is merely a euphonic junction (āgamasandhi). "Andhaveṇī" means a line of blind men. One blind man holds the end of a staff held by a sighted man; another blind man holds that blind man, and another holds him; thus, a line of fifty or sixty blind men connected in succession is called "andhaveṇī" (a line of blind men). "Paramparasaṃsattā" means those who are connected to one another and are devoid of a sighted person holding the staff.

It is heard that a rogue, seeing a group of blind men, encouraged them saying, "In such-and-such a village, food and snacks are easy to get." When the blind men said, "Master, if so, please lead us there; we will give you such-and-such property," the rogue took the bribe, turned off the path midway, went around a large thicket, made the one behind hold the armpit of the one in front with his hand, said "I have some work to do, you go on ahead," and fled. Although those blind men traveled the whole day, they did not find the path and lamented, "Where is our sighted leader? Where is the path?" Not finding the path, they died right there. Referring to those deceased blind men, it is said "paramparasaṃsattā" (connected in succession).

"Purimopi" means not even one among the first ten Brahmins (saw Brahma). "Majjhimopi" means not even one among the middle teachers and teachers' teachers (saw Brahma). "Pacchimopi" means not even one among the present-day Brahmins versed in the three Vedas (saw Brahma). "Hassakaññeva" means it is just laughable. "Nāmakaññeva" means it is just inferior (vain). That inferior thing is empty because it has no meaning; because it is empty, it is vain.

Now, let the matter of the Brahma-world, which has never been seen by the three-Veda Brahmins, stand for a while. To show that they are not even able to point out the path to union with the Moon and the Sun, which they do see, the Buddha said, "What do you think of this?" and so on.
334:
In that passage, "from where the Moon and Sun rise" means the time when they rise. "And where they set" means the time when they vanish and set. It means they see them both at the time of rising and at the time of setting. "They pray" means they pray thus: "May the Lord Moon rise; may the Lord Sun rise." "They praise" means they praise by saying, "The Moon is gentle, the Moon is circular, the Moon is radiant," and so on. "With joined palms" means with hands raised in the gesture of reverence (añjali). "Worshipping" means saying "Namo, Namo" (Homage, Homage).

531-532. In the phrase "which (the Moon and Sun) they see," "yaṃ" is merely a particle. In the phrase "what can be said," it means what can be said in this matter which is not seen face-to-face. It should be understood that in this context, the three-Veda Brahmins have never seen Brahma face-to-face.

## The Simile of the River Aciravatī

"Full to the brim" (Samatittikā) means completely filled. "Crow-drinkable" (Kākapeyyā) means the river is called crow-drinkable because a crow standing anywhere on the bank is able to drink from it. "Wishing to cross to the other shore" means wishing to go to the opposite bank after crossing the river. "Should call out" means should summon. "O other shore, come to this shore" means "O other shore, come to this shore; then take me and go quickly; I have urgent business to attend to."

"Those qualities that make one a Brahmin" refers to the five precepts and the ten wholesome courses of action; these should be understood as the qualities that make one a Brahmin, while their opposites make one a non-Brahmin. "They call upon Indra" means they call upon or summon Sakka. Having thus shown the pointlessness of the Brahmins' calling, the Blessed One, shining like the sun in the midst of the ocean, surrounded by five hundred monks, sitting on the bank of the Aciravatī river, brought forth another river simile and said, "Just as if," and so on.

"Sense pleasures" (Kāmaguṇā): they are called 'kāma' in the sense of being desired, and 'guṇa' in the sense of being bonds. In the passage, "Monks, I allow a double-layered outer robe (saṅghāṭi) made of new cloth," the word 'guṇa' has the meaning of a layer. In the passage, "Times pass, nights fly by, the stages of life (vayoguna) leave in succession," the word 'guṇa' has the meaning of a mass (group). "A gift with a hundredfold (sataguṇā) benefit..."
335:
In the phrase "Pāṭikaṅkhitabbā," the word *guṇa* signifies the sense of benefit (*ānisaṃsaṭṭha*). In the phrases "Antaṃ antaguṇaṃ" and "Kayirā mālāguṇe bahū," the word *guṇa* signifies the sense of a bond (*bandhanaṭṭha*). In the context of these sensual pleasures (*kāmaguṇa*), only this sense of a bond is intended. Therefore, it is said, "They are called *guṇas* because of the sense of binding." "Cakkhuviññeyyā" refers to those things that are to be seen by eye-consciousness. In this manner, the meaning should also be understood for "sotaviññeyyā" (ear-consciousness) and so forth. "Iṭṭhā" refers to objects that are desirable, whether they are sought after or not. "Kantā" means lovely. "Manāpā" means mind-expanding (pleasing). "Piyarūpā" means of a dear nature. "Kāmūpasañhitā" means connected with the sensuality that arises by making them an object. "Rajanīyā" means lust-inducing, or objects that are the cause for the arising of passion (*rāga*).

"Gadhitā" means being overwhelmed by greed. "Mucchitā" means being overwhelmed by intense craving that has reached the state of infatuation. "Ajjhopannā" means being excessively immersed and submerged, having reached the final conclusion that "this alone is the essence." "Anādīnavadassāvino" means not seeing the danger. "Anissaraṇapaññā" means the absence of the wisdom that discerns, "this is the escape here," and the absence of usage with reflection.

Among the terms beginning with "Āvaraṇā," they are called "āvaraṇa" (obstructions) because they cover up wholesome states. They are called "nīvaraṇa" (hindrances) because they prevent wholesome states. They are called "onāhana" (shrouds) because they bind (cause forgetfulness of) wholesome states. They are called "pariyonāhana" (envelopments) because they completely envelop wholesome states. The detailed explanation of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth should be taken from the Visuddhimagga.

549-550. The terms "āvutā, nivutā, onaddhā, pariyonaddhā" are spoken by way of "āvaraṇa" and so forth. "Sapariggaho" asks whether one is with the possession of a woman. In the phrases "Apariggaho bho Gotama" and so forth, "apariggaha" means being without the possession of a woman due to the absence of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). "Avera" means being without a mind of enmity toward anyone due to the absence of ill-will (*byāpāda*). "Abyāpajjo" means being without the affliction called "sickness of mind" due to the absence of sloth and torpor (*thīna-middha*). "Suparisuddhamānaso" means having a very pure mind, being unstained by defilements such as restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*) due to their absence. Because of the absence of doubt (*vicikicchā*), one brings the mind under one's control. Unlike the Brahmins who follow the whims of the mind, one does not follow the mind's whims but is a "vasavattī"—one who masters the mind.
336:
“Idha kho pana” means on this journey to the Brahma world. “Āsīditvā” means approaching what is not the path as if it were the “path.” “Saṃsīdanti” means sinking, just as those who step into mud with the perception that it is level ground sink down. “Saṃsīdityā visāraṃ ပါပုဏန္တိ” means sinking in this way and reaching the destruction of limbs, just as one sinks into mud and meets with ruin. “Sukkhataraṃ maññe taranti” is like being deceived by a mirage and, with the perception that it is a “river drinkable by crows,” making an effort with hands and feet to cross the dry mirage. Therefore, just as hands and feet reach destruction, so too do they reach destruction in the four woeful states (*apāya*). Even in this present life, they obtain neither happiness nor joy. Therefore, “tasmā idaṃ tevijjānaṃ brာဟ္မဏာနံ” means this teaching of the three Vedas, which points out the path for companionship with Brahma, is the word of instruction for the three-Veda Brahmins. “Tevijjāiriṇaṃ” means the forest of the three Vedas. “Iriṇa” refers to a great forest where there is no village. “Tevijjāvivanaṃ” means a waterless forest covered with trees whose flowers and fruits are not fit for use. It refers to a forest where, having strayed from the path, one is unable even to turn back; with reference to such a forest, it is said, “It is also called *tevijjāvivanaṃ*.” “Tevijjābyasanaṃ” means this three-Veda system of the Brahmins is like the five kinds of ruin. Just as there is no happiness for one who has reached the ruin of kin, health, wealth, view, or virtue, so too, the Buddha shows that there is no happiness by relying on the teacher’s word which is the three-Veda system of the Brahmins.

“Jātasaṃvaḍḍho” means one who was both born and raised (in a place). If a person was only born there but raised elsewhere, the village roads in the vicinity would not be entirely clear to him; therefore, it is said, “jātasaṃvaḍḍho.” Even for one who was born and raised there, if he has been away for a long time, the paths would not be entirely clear to him. Therefore, it is said, “tāvadeva avasaṭaṃ,” which means one who has just recently departed. “Dandhāyitattaṃ” means slowness due to doubt, such as “Is this the path, or is this not the path?” “Vitthāyitattaṃ” means the rigidity of the body, just as the body of someone who is suddenly asked about a subtle matter becomes stiff. By the words “na tveva,” the Buddha shows the unimpeded nature of Omniscient Knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). For that man, there might be an impediment to his knowledge through the deceptions of Māra and so forth.
337:
There would be an obstruction of knowledge. Because of that obstruction, that person might become slow or his mind might be agitated. However, Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) is unobstructed; it is shown that no one can cause any danger to that Omniscience. "May the Venerable Gotama lift [me] up" means may the Venerable Gotama lift [me] up from the path to the lower realms. "Brāhmaṇapajaṃ" refers to a young Brahmin; the meaning is: "May the Venerable Gotama lift me, who am a son of a Brahmin, from the path to the lower realms and establish me on the path leading to the Brahma world."

## Commentary on the Teaching of the Path to the Brahma World

The passage beginning with "Vāseṭṭha... a powerful conch-blower" is new in this Sutta. In that passage, "balavā" means one endowed with strength. "Saṅkhadhamo" means a conch-blower. "Appakasirena" means without difficulty or hardship. Indeed, a weak conch-blower, even when blowing the conch, is unable to make the sound known to the four directions; his conch sound does not pervade everywhere. But the sound of a powerful one is far-reaching; therefore, He said "balavā" and so on. In this phrase "mettāya cetovimuttiyā" (deliverance of mind through loving-kindness), when "mettā" is mentioned, both access concentration (upacāra) and absorption (appanā) are appropriate; however, when "cetovimutti" is mentioned, only absorption is appropriate.

"Limited action" (pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ) refers to sense-sphere action (kāmāvacara-kamma). "Immeasurable action" (appamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ) refers to fine-material and immaterial sphere action (rūpāvacara and arūpāvacara kamma). That immeasurable action is called "immeasurable" because it is performed by transcending limits and by developing it through pervading specific and non-specific directions. "That [sense-sphere action] does not remain there, it does not stay there" means that sense-sphere action does not linger or stay behind in the presence of that fine-material or immaterial sphere action. What is meant is this: that sense-sphere action is unable to get stuck or stay in the midst of that fine-material or immaterial sphere action, nor can it overwhelm and exhaust the fine-material or immaterial sphere action to take its own place and establish itself. Rather, it is the fine-material or immaterial sphere action itself that, like a great flood overwhelming a small amount of water...
338:
...overwhelms and exhausts it, taking its own place and remaining there. It blocks the result of that sense-sphere action and itself leads one to companionship with the Brahmas. "One who dwells thus" refers to a monk who dwells thus with the jhānas of loving-kindness and so forth. "We go to the Venerable Gotama [for refuge]"—this is the second time these two [Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja] have gone for refuge. They had already gone for refuge previously after hearing the Vāseṭṭha Sutta in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa; now, after hearing this Tevijja Sutta, they go for refuge for the second time. After a few days, they ordained and attained higher ordination (upasampadā) and Arahantship during the Aggañña Sutta. The rest of the words are clear in meaning in all places.

## Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya,
## The Commentary on the Tevijja Sutta is finished.
## The explanation of the meaning of the Sīlakkhandhavagga,
## adorned with thirteen suttas, is also finished.
## The Commentary on the Sīlakkhandhavagga is finished.
